Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"
    }
  ],
  "observacao_geral": "<1-2 frases>"
}

Bucket: medianas
Total de reviews analisadas neste bucket: 40

[7] nota=3.0 estrelas:
É um bom filme. mas sinceramente achei um pouco superestimado.a ideia é excelente e é impressionante como conseguem sustentar praticamente o filme inteiro em uma única sala, dependendo quase que unicamente dos diálogos e das discussões entre os personagens. A tensão funciona e a forma como os argumentos são construídos é satisfatória. Mas talvez eu tenha assistido com expectativas que não foram atendidas. Dado a reputação que o filme carrega, frequentemente aparecendo em rankings de melhores filmes de todos os tempos, eu esperava uma experiência mais marcante e impactante talvez. Reconheço completamente sua relevância para a história do cinema em si pois acredito que o contexto histórico e o fato do filme inteiro se passar dentro de uma única locação e sendo sustentado por 12 homens conversando era uma demonstração impressionante de inovação na escrita e direção. Ainda assim, é fácil entender por que virou um clássico. Só não entrou pra mim nesse nível de “obra-prima intocável” que tanta gente coloca.

[8] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Sırf kült ya da klasik diye yüksek puan veremicem çünkü o kadar sinir olarak izledim ki… Klasik adamlar. Sırf birkaç tanesi bir çocuğun hayatını önemsiyor diye yeterince erkek olmamakla suçlanıyorlar. Ayrıca filmi açtığım anda filmin sonunda çocuğun suçsuz olacağını anlamak zor değildi. Sonunu bilerek de izlemek keyif vermedi açıkçası. Bir de önlerindeki mantıklı bile olmayan, hiç bir bilimsel bilgiye dayanmayan, birkaç sanığın verdiği ifadelerle düpedüz karar veriyorlar sırf konuşma uzamasın diye. Ve sıkılmaktansa bi çocuğu idam etmek daha makul geliyor onlara. Konunun anlattıklarımdan çok daha derin olduğunun farkındayım ama izlerken zevk almadım gerçekten. Sadece son sahnesini beğendim. Tüm o “erkek olmak” kalıplarını bırakıp “not guilty” demesi güzeldi.

[9] nota=3.0 estrelas:
The writing was great. I found this film humorous despite gravity of the plot. This style of English is one of my favorites and I liked the attire of everyone except Juror #1 and #6. I believe this film would be as enjoyable by just hearing the audio. I also loved the collective shunning of the racist guy. Lastly, never seeing the boy again and not hearing the final verdict added a cool mist of mystery

For such an old movie it was actually way better than i thought itd be! not a masterpiece of cinematography or the sound tracks or anything, acting wasnt world-class either BUT the message it was meant to convey especially for that time is amazing and the way its being presented to us viewers makes a lot of sense and leaves you thinking about it! Good movie to have seen atleast once :)

An hour and a half of 12 men yelling and arguing about the fate of some 18 yo who supposedly murdered his father, and I LOVED it. Although the movie was kinda boring at first, I ended up wanting more of it; the unique traits of each of the 12 made their interactions very interesting and so was seeing them change their verdict after being subjected to different arguments. Nice watch.

Watched this for ap english last year, there was a lack of understanding in the classroom. Very unfortunate. Anyways it's a good movie, i understand why people might view it as boring, I was very entertained though. For a product of its time it's good, and has lots of layers.

Although this movie was not the most interesting to me, I appreciated the filming techniques and styles. I liked how in some scenes, the camera would zoom in on a specific area or character, or pan to a specific view. I think this added to the tension felt in the room, reinforcing the feeling of being in that cramped area. I also appreciated how each characters’ own story somehow connected back to the case they were working on. This added a large amount of emotion to the film.

Yeteri kadar court/ mahkeme filmi izlediyseniz buna coşmazsınız ama, benim gibi ‘etkileyici final bağımlısı’ysanız bile olay örgüsü için izlenmeli. ikna oldukları şeyleri kendilerini ikna etmeyesiceye kadar kurcalıyorlar. ‘Delil yetersizliği’ni kanıtlama filmi diyebiliriz :)

It has the elements of an all time movie but unfortunately it’s just frankly not that entertaining compared to more modern movies. I can usually lock in for a 3 hour movie but I struggled to do so for this one even tho it’s an hour and a half

Very well acted with some great moments. It was a bit overbearing for my taste though. 95 minutes of constant talking all set in one room with nothing to break it up. And I know I probably have too short an attention span and it's probably too clever for me. But I didn't feel satisfied at the end and I certainly couldn't sit through it again. Well at least I've seen it now. I appreciate it's greatness, but it doesn't work all that well for me personally.

Definitely an interesting movie with a simple but compelling plot. The ending was predictable, but I think that is because I have seen several tv shows make spoofs with this as the basis. Also very interesting to note how ahead of its time this film was. Produced in 1957, this film touched heavily on topics of many of the hot topics of today.

From the start there is tension surrounding the characters… The moment they walk in the room the sudden heat they feel can showcase how intense the deliberation would become… The different positions of the camera help portray the emotions the characters feel which in my opinion helps strengthen the story as a whole.

iki kere izledim. filmi ilk izleme tarihi 2014. muhtemelen sınıfta su şişesini afiyetle yerken sıkılarak izlemiştim. ikincisi sanırım 2019. neden oybirliği arandığını açıklasınlar. 2/3 yap oh miss. ayrıca makul şüphe evrensel bir kavramdır. yeteri kadar mütalaa ve kovuşturma yapılırsa hakikat mutlaka değilse bile mutlakanın çok yakını bir ihtimal ortaya çıkacaktır. bu anglo sakson jury sistemini beğenmiyorum ama belki daha iyidir emin değilim.

Kind of a hard movie to rate. Very good film for the time but not extremely entertaining like movies today. I also don’t think I’ve ever seen a movie with one setting for the entire film. Overall good watch.

I've never been a Lumet guy and this one doesn't sway me. About the only thing that interested me was the conclusion, in which the jurors aren't at all in alignment, even if they've all voted to acquit. (Jack Warden's character, presumably, is still smarting from being shamed for changing his vote purely out of impatience.) And for all the big acting being showcased throughout, I was only really moved by E. G. Marshall turning the volume down all the way during his big closeups.

Only three stars because this did not contain dinosaurs. Just think about it, what if one of the jurors had been a velociraptor? That would have been a crazy twist.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

This movie was made 30 years before DNA and I think it’s a stronger movie for the reason that there is no DNA to think about. I genuinely believe this to be a pillar of not only filmmaking but story telling. The script, is perfect as well as the screenplay. The film tskes place in one room for the majority of its duration, so how do you keep it interesting? You craft the perfect script. Perhaps the most important aspect to really carry the script is the acting. The acting must be independent, each character must be written as though they are the first to be so. 12 Angry Men is built around identity. Each man comes from a unique walk of like with unique experiences and unique opinions. The point of 12 Angry Men is the men coming together. The crux of the story is development, every character changes in some way. The men, despite their unique outlooks, upbringings, and actions must come to a civic and unanimous decision to determine the life of a young man. In order to convey said developments there must be a identity to each character thst is their own entire, and they must be played perfectly for those characterizations. Juror 1, the "leader". He directs the room, but he does not lead it. He is no dictator or supreme leader of thr room, but he has the clipboard, he must declare a vote, he must deliver the decisions. He is not the toughest man in the room, he, more or less, just guides the men. He has his own opinion and he states it clearly. But juror 1 is not stern nor is he Stark. Juror 2, the newbie. Juror 2 has never been on a jury. He doesn't exactly know the directions of debate, but he knows the inner workings of the court. He knows how the court plays and he knows the evidence rather well. He doesn't know how to use his voice clearly over the elders at first, usually being pushed around and silenced. His opinion isn't the clearest either. He says the boy is guilty "just because he is" he's nearly unsure of his own stance, meek in his closed answer. But over time he starts to find his voice. He establishes his knowledge and his eventual confidence. He's inexperienced, coy, and easily pushed around. But he eventually finds himself to reslly prove and get his opinion out. Juror 3, the antithesis. Juror 3 is even labeled by 8 a sadist, which isnt false at all, but his character is deeper than that. He's experienced, older while still having mobility, confidence, and a voice to shout with. He has his definite opinion upon the evidence and he stands by it. He has a solid opinion, he has a genuine belief and he sticks right by it. At his core, he blames the child more than anything. Being a stern father of a son he hasn't seen in two years, he blames the defendant. He knows of his living condition yet he blames the society, he blames the child himself for the possibility of the murder. His pent up rage of his own life pours out in the room, in his opinion. He knows his interpretation of the facts and he knows his opinions, but he is not understanding. He sees his words as the definite truth, he screams and antagonizes and he belittles. He does not work in the view of justice, he works in the view of punishment and of competition, of winning some kind of game of being the 'right one'. Above all else, the man is shadowed by his own life, especially his life with his son, who he in a way blames for their divide. On the same side of the coin, his ultimate anger at the end after he is now the lone juror unleashes and is what ultimately makes him see the error of his ways. He bursts out in an angry monologue. How could anyone, let alone everyone, oppose his definite fact. He takes the photo of his son from his wallet and after seeing what has been the anchor of his rage, rips it to pieces. As soon as he does, he realizes this error, maybe he really is the problem, maybe the boy isn't to blame, maybe it isn't a fact, but it is possible. Juror 4, the statue. Similarly to juror 3, he nearly sees his opinion as fact, but where they differ is approach. Juror 4 knows the evidence well, he knows well upon his own interpretation and opinion, but he is calculated, he is thoughtful in the court system. He does not see this as a game or a competition. He hopes to find whatever Justice he truthfully believes, he is opinionated but he is tolerant in a way. He nearly never sweats and he nearly never moves. As all the men do, he gets angrier as the heat increases and as the temperature rises, but he is clear and concise in his approach. He wants an end, but a right one. He knows his truth but, perhaps begrudgingly, he listens to the other side of the story, and through hearing that he coukd possibly be wrong, he sees the error and realizes that he could possibly be wrong. Juror 5, the experienced. Juror 5 grew up in the same conditions as the defendant. He knows the conditions of the slums, what it can do to a person and how they can operate. Because of his experience, he is particularly sensitive to the prejudices of the other men. He has his beginning opinion but he is nearly embarrassed and certainly unsure of it from the beginning, choosing to pass when asked why he initially votes guilty. He sees the prejudice of the room and he applies his own personal experience with the defendants upbringing and sees that there may be a chance that the boy did not do it. Juror 6, the working man

Por vezes, alguns dos considerados "cânones" do cinema são ainda mais fascinantes do que sua fama tende a sugerir. Assisti 12 Angry Men (1957) com uma noção abstrata prévia, mas realmente não estava esperando que o filme fosse ser tão intrigante e instigante. Não atoa é um filme tão aclamado, é uma obra tão meticulosa em cada um de seus aspectos — sobretudo sua blocagem e encenação — que chega a ser gratificante um filme que se preocupa tanto em trabalhar o cinema numa premissa tão teatral. Ele exemplifica bem, inclusive, a relação que estas duas artes tem. Desde a criação do cinematógrafo, o cinema extraiu muito de sua base no teatro como também em outras artes. Conceitos como mise-en-scène, por exemplo, são emprestados. Mas justamente dessa raiz que a sétima arte se ramificou. No teatro, o olhar vem de amplas perspectivas. Organizar atores, cenários e objetos é um trabalho cuidadoso que oferece um guia em comum a cada pessoa em cada acento. No cinema, essa organização é voltada a um único olhar: o olhar da câmera. Ela permite um close-up em qualquer detalhe que tanto a pessoa da primeira fileira como a última irão observar com perfeita nitidez. Mas também, quando o diretor confia no uso da profundidade de campo em seu filme, ele ganha uma liberdade e oferece um direito ao espectador para olhar o que lhe chama mais atenção no plano — seja no primeiro quanto no segundo plano — .  Num filme de ambiente pequeno e fechado como este, o uso desta ferramenta pode não parecer em primeiro momento, mas é tão relevante quanto o close-up. Quando se há uma visão dos jurados na mesa, o espectador tende a prestar mais atenção naquele que mais lhe gera interesse ou intriga. Conferir por conta própria um pequeno detalhe na interpretação de cada ator na mesa (independente dele ser ou não o principal foco naquele instante). Quando um dos jurados começa a ser abertamente racista e cada um sutilmente se retira da mesa/desvia o olhar/vira as costas, o plano aberto junto a profundidade do campo montam diante de nossos olhos quase que uma pintura. Quando um dos jurados tira a faca do bolso e crava na mesa, a forma como o choque de todos gera desorganização ainda é organizada pela maneira como cada um está presente na imagem de acordo com sua própria expressividade. São inúmeras cenas marcantes. O filme se declara humanista, independente dos fatos. Neste sentido ele é metalinguístico: Independente da verdade, as perspectivas subjetivas são inevitavelmente manipuladas. Votar pela inocência do réu é algo que fere egos, pisa em tabus e preconceitos, indaga convicções, nenhum deles nem o espectador estava na cena do crime. Eles encenam, simulam, deduzem, o cinema é a verdade simulada do mesmo modo. E a indagação que a obra faz segue sendo fundamental sobretudo numa geração tão insensível e  apática quanto a nossa. Cinco minutos é tempo para decidir por uma vida sem pensar em sua realidade, seu contexto, sem se por no lugar? Mais do que a verdade, é isto o que importa para o filme, e para a arte, a única verdade é a de quem reflete a obra.

The acting must be independent, each character must be written as though they are the first to be so. 12 Angry Men is built around identity. Each man comes from a unique walk of like with unique experiences and unique opinions. The point of 12 Angry Men is the men coming together. The crux of the story is development, every character changes in some way. The men, despite their unique outlooks, upbringings, and actions must come to a civic and unanimous decision to determine the life of a young man. In order to convey said developments there must be a identity to each character thst is their own entire, and they must be played perfectly for those characterizations. Juror 1, the "leader". He directs the room, but he does not lead it. He is no dictator or supreme leader of thr room, but he has the clipboard, he must declare a vote, he must deliver the decisions. He is not the toughest man in the room, he, more or less, just guides the men. He has his own opinion and he states it clearly. But juror 1 is not stern nor is he Stark. Juror 2, the newbie. Juror 2 has never been on a jury. He doesn't exactly know the directions of debate, but he knows the inner workings of the court. He knows how the court plays and he knows the evidence rather well. He doesn't know how to use his voice clearly over the elders at first, usually being pushed around and silenced. His opinion isn't the clearest either. He says the boy is guilty "just because he is" he's nearly unsure of his own stance, meek in his closed answer. But over time he starts to find his voice. He establishes his knowledge and his eventual confidence. He's inexperienced, coy, and easily pushed around. But he eventually finds himself to reslly prove and get his opinion out. Juror 3, the antithesis. Juror 3 is even labeled by 8 a sadist, which isnt false at all, but his character is deeper than that. He's experienced, older while still having mobility, confidence, and a voice to shout with. He has his definite opinion upon the evidence and he stands by it. He has a solid opinion, he has a genuine belief and he sticks right by it. At his core, he blames the child more than anything. Being a stern father of a son he hasn't seen in two years, he blames the defendant. He knows of his living condition yet he blames the society, he blames the child himself for the possibility of the murder. His pent up rage of his own life pours out in the room, in his opinion. He knows his interpretation of the facts and he knows his opinions, but he is not understanding. He sees his words as the definite truth, he screams and antagonizes and he belittles. He does not work in the view of justice, he works in the view of punishment and of competition, of winning some kind of game of being the 'right one'. Above all else, the man is shadowed by his own life, especially his life with his son, who he in a way blames for their divide. On the same side of the coin, his ultimate anger at the end after he is now the lone juror unleashes and is what ultimately makes him see the error of his ways. He bursts out in an angry monologue. How could anyone, let alone everyone, oppose his definite fact. He takes the photo of his son from his wallet and after seeing what has been the anchor of his rage, rips it to pieces. As soon as he does, he realizes this error, maybe he really is the problem, maybe the boy isn't to blame, maybe it isn't a fact, but it is possible. Juror 4, the statue. Similarly to juror 3, he nearly sees his opinion as fact, but where they differ is approach. Juror 4 knows the evidence well, he knows well upon his own interpretation and opinion, but he is calculated, he is thoughtful in the court system. He does not see this as a game or a competition. He hopes to find whatever Justice he truthfully believes, he is opinionated but he is tolerant in a way. He nearly never sweats and he nearly never moves. As all the men do, he gets angrier as the heat increases and as the temperature rises, but he is clear and concise in his approach. He wants an end, but a right one. He knows his truth but, perhaps begrudgingly, he listens to the other side of the story, and through hearing that he coukd possibly be wrong, he sees the error and realizes that he could possibly be wrong. Juror 5, the experienced. Juror 5 grew up in the same conditions as the defendant. He knows the conditions of the slums, what it can do to a person and how they can operate. Because of his experience, he is particularly sensitive to the prejudices of the other men. He has his beginning opinion but he is nearly embarrassed and certainly unsure of it from the beginning, choosing to pass when asked why he initially votes guilty. He sees the prejudice of the room and he applies his own personal experience with the defendants upbringing and sees that there may be a chance that the boy did not do it. Juror 6, the working man

Por vezes, alguns dos considerados "cânones" do cinema são ainda mais fascinantes do que sua fama tende a sugerir. Assisti 12 Angry Men (1957) com uma noção abstrata prévia, mas realmente não estava esperando que o filme fosse ser tão intrigante e instigante. Não atoa é um filme tão aclamado, é uma obra tão meticulosa em cada um de seus aspectos — sobretudo sua blocagem e encenação — que chega a ser gratificante um filme que se preocupa tanto em trabalhar o cinema numa premissa tão teatral. Ele exemplifica bem, inclusive, a relação que estas duas artes tem. Desde a criação do cinematógrafo, o cinema extraiu muito de sua base no teatro como também em outras artes. Conceitos como mise-en-scène, por exemplo, são emprestados. Mas justamente dessa raiz que a sétima arte se ramificou. No teatro, o olhar vem de amplas perspectivas. Organizar atores, cenários e objetos é um trabalho cuidadoso que oferece um guia em comum a cada pessoa em cada acento. No cinema, essa organização é voltada a um único olhar: o olhar da câmera. Ela permite um close-up em qualquer detalhe que tanto a pessoa da primeira fileira como a última irão observar com perfeita nitidez. Mas também, quando o diretor confia no uso da profundidade de campo em seu filme, ele ganha uma liberdade e oferece um direito ao espectador para olhar o que lhe chama mais atenção no plano — seja no primeiro quanto no segundo plano — .  Num filme de ambiente pequeno e fechado como este, o uso desta ferramenta pode não parecer em primeiro momento, mas é tão relevante quanto o close-up. Quando se há uma visão dos jurados na mesa, o espectador tende a prestar mais atenção naquele que mais lhe gera interesse ou intriga. Conferir por conta própria um pequeno detalhe na interpretação de cada ator na mesa (independente dele ser ou não o principal foco naquele instante). Quando um dos jurados começa a ser abertamente racista e cada um sutilmente se retira da mesa/desvia o olhar/vira as costas, o plano aberto junto a profundidade do campo montam diante de nossos olhos quase que uma pintura. Quando um dos jurados tira a faca do bolso e crava na mesa, a forma como o choque de todos gera desorganização ainda é organizada pela maneira como cada um está presente na imagem de acordo com sua própria expressividade. São inúmeras cenas marcantes. O filme se declara humanista, independente dos fatos. Neste sentido ele é metalinguístico: Independente da verdade, as perspectivas subjetivas são inevitavelmente manipuladas. Votar pela inocência do réu é algo que fere egos, pisa em tabus e preconceitos, indaga convicções, nenhum deles nem o espectador estava na cena do crime. Eles encenam, simulam, deduzem, o cinema é a verdade simulada do mesmo modo. E a indagação que a obra faz segue sendo fundamental sobretudo numa geração tão insensível e  apática quanto a nossa. Cinco minutos é tempo para decidir por uma vida sem pensar em sua realidade, seu contexto, sem se por no lugar? Mais do que a verdade, é isto o que importa para o filme, e para a arte, a única verdade é a de quem reflete a obra.

Première fois depuis les Hunger Games que je vois un film juste après avoir lu le livre donc je vais me faire plaisir. Les images, les décors et les grandes scènes d’action sont vraiment très bonnes. Le plan d'ouverture, puis de fin, est peut-être l’une des plus belles manières d’exposer la futilité de la guerre dans un seul dialogue, juste un simple plan fixe sur une forêt. Néanmoins, le film prend le parti de suivre les négociations de l’armistice en parallèle de l’histoire des protagonistes. Or, dans le livre, c’est justement l’absence totale de point de vue autre que celui de Paul qui rend le récit si tragique. À chaque instant, la guerre pourrait s’arrêter dans 2 minutes ou dans 10 ans, ça ne fait aucune différence pour les soldats engagés. Pire, le film introduit à la moitié cet espèce de compte à rebours avant l’armistice pour rajouter de la tension, décision qui dessert totalement son propos. Autre parti pris décevant, l’incarnation d’un grand méchant par le général allemand. “Regardez comme c’est dommage, tout les gens aux autres postes de commandement étaient bien intentionnés, c’est juste un seul méchant monsieur qui cause la mort de tout ces jeunes”. Encore une fois, dans le livre, personne n’est nommé comme responsable de la souffrance des soldats. Toute l’horreur repose là-dedans : des gamins de 20 ans, pris dans un engrenage bien au-delà de leur échelle, et aussi inutile qu’implacable. Une réalité beaucoup plus nuancée et dure que le sosie de Dr Eggman qu’on retrouve. En bref, un film qui incarne visuellement très bien les horreurs de la guerre, mais qui omet totalement les éléments narratifs les plus essentiels du matériel de base. Un film de guerre qui fait coquille vide ?? Chokbar (non)

O cineasta François Truffaut possui uma frase popular: “não existe filme antiguerra”. Em sua tese ele conceitua e discorre sobre a linguagem sensual e entretida do cinema, isso leva a conclusão que não importa o quanto você faça um filme sobre guerra, mostrando inúmeros lados horríveis deste acontecimento horrível, o cinema sempre vai romantizar isso, não por que os criadores quiserem muito das vezes, mas por que é assim que a sétima arte se depõe em nossos olhos e signos. Dito isso, a obra de Edward Berger anda em um liminar tão amedrontador, com um visual tão profundo e melancólico, criticaram as esferas de mais privilégios as bases mais sofridas de uma guerra que por um momento parece que a súmula de Truffaut se equivoca aqui, mas tudo isso para demonstrar que às vezes a maior busca por um sentimento antiguerra traz o amor a guerra. O diretor resolve adicionar a essa obra de trilhagem tão interessante e obscura, com retoques de profundidade de símbolos inclusos como é o exemplo da raposa e das florestas, para no fim adaptar de certa forma uma espécie de jornada do herói. O começo do filme é didático em mostrar um dos melhores acertos do filme, a guerra aqui é trabalhada como produto, como venda. Os soldados morrendo, as costureiras refazendo uniformes, as substituições… tudo aqui mostra um tom legível de repetição e precificação da vida de cidadãos, atitudes essas que realmente acontecem em tempos de guerra. E quando o filme volta para essa leitura é quando ele mais acerta na minha opinião. Todavia, o filme ainda não se desprende totalmente de uma leitura protagonista, jornada e inclusive tem ate mentor. Esse ponto não necessariamente é ruim, tendo em vista que muitas vezes são esses laços que passam a mensagem de humanidade em um cenário de morte, porém é perceptível que na maioria dos filmes grandes de guerra, aqui não diferente, neste posso de sujeira, sangue e morte há um quê de realismo, sempre tem, “o meu filme de guerra tem mais tons de real e de verdade” e quando se tenta sair na contramão da citação que falei no começo deste texto é quando se dá conta do tom persuasivo e nada antiguerra de um filme. O protagonista aqui possui laços, possui dor e temos medo de perder os amigos dele, e isso é um romance de guerra no final das contas! é ruim? É bom? É o cinema persuadindo nós mais uma vez. __dantas

The only thing that made me DNF it is that I just couldn't get into it. I tried. I genuinely tried sticking through it, and I just couldn't. Here's the thing for me. I just wasn't able to develop any kind of connection to the characters. Paul, to me, just felt like another young man and another character. I can't remember for the life of me who the other four people are, whether they're his friends, his higher ups, or whatever. And because I couldn't develop that connection with any of them, it became really hard for me to root for them. I know that sounds horrible, but I just found myself not being able to get into it. I couldn't sit there for more than ten minutes without eventually looking around my room or getting distracted, and that's sort of a deal breaker for me when I'm watching a movie. I think a lot of people are probably going to be disappointed with my take on this. I'm sure some people would tell me that I don't know what I'm talking about or that I just don't understand the movie, but I genuinely tried to give it a chance. I mean, I made it about three fourths of the way through the movie before finally giving up. I just couldn't find myself rooting for Paul or really any of the other characters. Obviously, when they're in battle, I'm rooting for Paul and his buddies to survive and make it through, but there wasn't that deeper emotional connection where I genuinely felt attached to them. I think one of the reasons this movie still gets three stars from me is because it does an incredible job of showing the horrifying reality of trench warfare during World War I. And if I'm being so honest, I was really interested in seeing more of that side of the war. I'm not going to say I wanted to see trench foot, but trench foot was a massive part of the horrible conditions soldiers experienced during World War I, and I was interested in seeing more of those details. I'm glad I got to see the flamethrowers, the tanks, the actual trenches, and just how brutal and terrifying that kind of warfare was. Those parts were genuinely interesting to me. But even with all of that, I just couldn't get into the actual movie. I don't know what it is. Sometimes a movie just doesn't connect with you, and this one didn't connect with me. So I'll give All Quiet on the Western Front three stars out of five, and that's really only because I couldn't get into it. This movie isn't bad whatsoever. The visuals aren't bad. The acting isn't bad. The storyline isn't bad. The screenplay, the cinematography, the coloring, all of it is incredibly well done. Bleak as hell, but pretty damn effective. I really liked how completely this strips war of any grandeur and reduces it to mud, panic, exhaustion, and young men being fed into this enormous machine for objectives that become increasingly abstract and meaningless. It’s huge in scale without ever confusing scale for heroism, and I think that distinction is where the movie is strongest. The brutality lands because it rarely feels ornamental; it’s constantly reinforcing the idea that war functions through attrition, reducing individual lives to bodies, numbers, and territory gained or lost. I never connected with the characters quite enough for it to completely devastate me, but the human cost still registers, especially in the quieter moments where all the military rhetoric falls away and you’re just left with frightened people trying to survive. Really well made, appropriately miserable, and impressively committed to its anti-war perspective. It didn’t hit me on some profound emotional level, but I admired a lot of what it was doing, particularly how effectively it makes the entire machinery of war feel both enormous and completely fucking senseless.

O cineasta François Truffaut possui uma frase popular: “não existe filme antiguerra”. Em sua tese ele conceitua e discorre sobre a linguagem sensual e entretida do cinema, isso leva a conclusão que não importa o quanto você faça um filme sobre guerra, mostrando inúmeros lados horríveis deste acontecimento horrível, o cinema sempre vai romantizar isso, não por que os criadores quiserem muito das vezes, mas por que é assim que a sétima arte se depõe em nossos olhos e signos. Dito isso, a obra de Edward Berger anda em um liminar tão amedrontador, com um visual tão profundo e melancólico, criticaram as esferas de mais privilégios as bases mais sofridas de uma guerra que por um momento parece que a súmula de Truffaut se equivoca aqui, mas tudo isso para demonstrar que às vezes a maior busca por um sentimento antiguerra traz o amor a guerra. O diretor resolve adicionar a essa obra de trilhagem tão interessante e obscura, com retoques de profundidade de símbolos inclusos como é o exemplo da raposa e das florestas, para no fim adaptar de certa forma uma espécie de jornada do herói. O começo do filme é didático em mostrar um dos melhores acertos do filme, a guerra aqui é trabalhada como produto, como venda. Os soldados morrendo, as costureiras refazendo uniformes, as substituições… tudo aqui mostra um tom legível de repetição e precificação da vida de cidadãos, atitudes essas que realmente acontecem em tempos de guerra. E quando o filme volta para essa leitura é quando ele mais acerta na minha opinião. Todavia, o filme ainda não se desprende totalmente de uma leitura protagonista, jornada e inclusive tem ate mentor. Esse ponto não necessariamente é ruim, tendo em vista que muitas vezes são esses laços que passam a mensagem de humanidade em um cenário de morte, porém é perceptível que na maioria dos filmes grandes de guerra, aqui não diferente, neste posso de sujeira, sangue e morte há um quê de realismo, sempre tem, “o meu filme de guerra tem mais tons de real e de verdade” e quando se tenta sair na contramão da citação que falei no começo deste texto é quando se dá conta do tom persuasivo e nada antiguerra de um filme. O protagonista aqui possui laços, possui dor e temos medo de perder os amigos dele, e isso é um romance de guerra no final das contas! é ruim? É bom? É o cinema persuadindo nós mais uma vez. __dantas

This movie won four Oscars, and I can't complain about the visuals, the acting, the screenplay, or really anything about how the movie was made. The only thing that made me DNF it is that I just couldn't get into it. I tried. I genuinely tried sticking through it, and I just couldn't. Here's the thing for me. I just wasn't able to develop any kind of connection to the characters. Paul, to me, just felt like another young man and another character. I can't remember for the life of me who the other four people are, whether they're his friends, his higher ups, or whatever. And because I couldn't develop that connection with any of them, it became really hard for me to root for them. I know that sounds horrible, but I just found myself not being able to get into it. I couldn't sit there for more than ten minutes without eventually looking around my room or getting distracted, and that's sort of a deal breaker for me when I'm watching a movie. I think a lot of people are probably going to be disappointed with my take on this. I'm sure some people would tell me that I don't know what I'm talking about or that I just don't understand the movie, but I genuinely tried to give it a chance. I mean, I made it about three fourths of the way through the movie before finally giving up. I just couldn't find myself rooting for Paul or really any of the other characters. Obviously, when they're in battle, I'm rooting for Paul and his buddies to survive and make it through, but there wasn't that deeper emotional connection where I genuinely felt attached to them. I think one of the reasons this movie still gets three stars from me is because it does an incredible job of showing the horrifying reality of trench warfare during World War I. And if I'm being so honest, I was really interested in seeing more of that side of the war. I'm not going to say I wanted to see trench foot, but trench foot was a massive part of the horrible conditions soldiers experienced during World War I, and I was interested in seeing more of those details. I'm glad I got to see the flamethrowers, the tanks, the actual trenches, and just how brutal and terrifying that kind of warfare was. Those parts were genuinely interesting to me. But even with all of that, I just couldn't get into the actual movie. I don't know what it is. Sometimes a movie just doesn't connect with you, and this one didn't connect with me. So I'll give All Quiet on the Western Front three stars out of five, and that's really only because I couldn't get into it. This movie isn't bad whatsoever. The visuals aren't bad. The acting isn't bad. The storyline isn't bad. The screenplay, the cinematography, the coloring, all of it is incredibly well done. I can completely understand why other people love this movie and why it won the awards that it did. It just wasn't for me. That's it.

Bleak as hell, but pretty damn effective. I really liked how completely this strips war of any grandeur and reduces it to mud, panic, exhaustion, and young men being fed into this enormous machine for objectives that become increasingly abstract and meaningless. It’s huge in scale without ever confusing scale for heroism, and I think that distinction is where the movie is strongest. The brutality lands because it rarely feels ornamental; it’s constantly reinforcing the idea that war functions through attrition, reducing individual lives to bodies, numbers, and territory gained or lost. I never connected with the characters quite enough for it to completely devastate me, but the human cost still registers, especially in the quieter moments where all the military rhetoric falls away and you’re just left with frightened people trying to survive. Really well made, appropriately miserable, and impressively committed to its anti-war perspective. It didn’t hit me on some profound emotional level, but I admired a lot of what it was doing, particularly how effectively it makes the entire machinery of war feel both enormous and completely fucking senseless.

Forging your parent's signature for a field trip is good.  Forging your parent's signature to join an ongoing war is bad. The 2022 adaptation of Erich Maria Remarque's seminal anti-war novel isn't what I'd call a remake of Lewis Milestone's Best Picture-winning film from 1930 (or the Delbert Mann version which was made for television in 1979) but rather another interpretation of the story.  It's the same sentiment I have regarding the new Sense and Sensibility coming out.  Rather than remaking the Ang Lee one, it appears to just be the next go-around of filming Jane Austen's book. Director Edward Berger goes all in on the "war is hell" imagery here.  His tasteful eye, combined with the astonishingly great cinematography by James Friend, allows All Quiet on the Western Front a certain visceral heft that may not have been possible given the constraints of its earlier predecessors.  Nothing in the film is particularly new if you've seen its contemporaries but it still manages to achieve its purpose emotionally, thematically and cinematically. Just to get my negative out of the way, I don't get why Volker Bertelmann snagged the Oscar here.  Those three notes sound too much like dubstep for my taste.  Anachronistic scores can work but it took me out.  That said, Bertelmann's other compositions in the film are quite effective but maybe I'm bitter that Justin Hurwitz's Babylon score, easily one of the decade's most memorable film soundtracks, lost to this.  Then again, considering the same branch didn't even nominate Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for Challengers, I can't say I'm surprised. Felix Kammerer gives a remarkable debut performance.  His face screams someone whose pure innocence will be decimated by the brutality of war, not unlike the young boy from Come and See.  Albrecht Schuch is great too as Kat.  He was a highlight from that Berlin Alexanderplatz in 2020.  Daniel Brühl is easily the most recognizable actor here, lending credibility as Matthias Erzberger, a German politician instrumental in the armistice that ended the war. I was mesmerized by Berger's command of the camera.  He puts you down and dirty in those trenches.  It's a harmonious mixture of some phenomenal production design by Christian M. Goldbeck, seamless integration of visual effects and some awesome makeup that cakes our actors in mud to resemble the horrifically obscuring conditions that it takes to engage in this level of combat.  There's a reason Paul goes from smiling and chipper at the start to absolutely stone-faced by the end. The assembly line nature of the youth as they enter their regiments is frightening.  A batch of young soldiers dies only to be replaced by younger soldiers whose eyes can't fathom the terrifying things they're about to inflict and be inflicted upon.  The scene of Paul engaging in a one-on-one with the French soldier is devastating because it's a fight or flight scenario while also an acknowledgement of how war encourages the loss of our humanity little by little until we can't even comprehend the actions we commit. Paul is one of many millions of people who were indoctrinated into thinking that what they were doing was a good thing and that the future tales of heroics will far exceed anything on the battlefield.  Meanwhile, the people with the power to the end the war only did so when it mathematically didn't make sense to continue and even still there were those who pridefully refused to concede, thus dragging on the war.  You just become numb to it all, senseless to the feeling that you're a pawn, an eventual casualty in a long list of obituaries. If the Germans pulled a Reynolds Woodcock and simply sewed the names into the fabric it'd make the whole recycling uniforms thing easier.

All Quiet on the Western Front is one of a small group of Netflix original movies that is both impressive to look at and actually worth watching. Sure it isn’t a particularly unique story, instead essentially playing as a remake of a remake, but if you’re looking for a brutal and striking depiction of war then you’ll be hard pressed to find better. What fascinates me about war is that despite every distinct conflict being inherently awful, each of them are terrible in their own unique way. You’ve obviously got the raw numbers with WW2, the insanity and trauma of Vietnam and the boredom of the Gulf war, but I honestly don’t think anything can ever top WW1. It’s kinda the perfect culmination of everything awful people associate about war. It happened at a time when people still thought fighting and dying for your country was honourable, so you had poor recruits thinking they were going on an adventure and generals who thought any problem could just be solved by throwing bodies at them. You’ve also got undoubtedly some of the worst conditions in any modern conflict with the trenches and their mud, disease and rats, on top of the insanity element thanks to spending years fighting for a few extra metres and watching your friends get blown to pieces. Truly as far as picking a bad experience to live through, I think you’d be hard pressed to find anything worse than ‘The Great War’ and All Quiet on the Western Front really excellently captures that vibe. What this movies really excels at is getting across how every soldier as an individual was treated like absolute dirt. They were given hammy down clothes from the last lot who had been slaughtered and then sent to die in the mud just so some stuck up boffins could pat themselves on the back and eat a fancy pastry. Their lives were viewed as completely without value besides dying for their country, despite each of them being people in their own right with families and hopes. The fact that this story is told from a distinctly German perspective further helps manifest that idea, since ultimately every young man in every country during the war got the same speech about how righteous they were and how they will bring glory to their fatherland. They couldn’t all be right and realistically none of them were. It’s easy to solidify yourself in the ‘us vs them’ mindset when looking at historical conflicts, hence why stories like this one are so important. That scene in the mortar crater really gets the point across. Everyone was told to hate and kill each other, but looking in the eyes of another innocent young lad and taking his life away remains genuinely one of the most horrific things you could be forced to do. Scenes like that are used effectively throughout All Quiet on the Western Front and really draw into question the inhumanity that was rife during WW1. The other aspect of All Quiet which is undoubtedly great is how terrific it looks. Maybe it’s because I’m used to the green screen/volume vibe of most straight to Netflix movies, but this movie really blew me away from the visuals. The cinematography is gorgeous with its use of colours and its framing of the central events, sometimes heightening the tension like with that tank sequence and sometimes contrasting the chaos with more quiet, tender moments. I wasn’t expecting this movie to be as Terrence Malick as it is, but it’s quite a nice homage to movies like The Thin Red Line whilst further helping demonstrate the shear chaos unleashed by the war. On that note, the gore in this movie is also excellent. It doesn’t pull any punches, with bodies just lying everywhere, often missing parts, all whilst being framed with such a blasé and unfazed perspective. It’s an essential aspect of capturing the vibe of this conflict, given that soldiers at the time had to live around decaying corpses rife with disease all whilst never knowing if they or their mates would be next. All Quiet honestly gets pretty dark at times and I really appreciate it. It’s absolutely not afraid to delve into the traumatic and damaged mindset of the German soldiers, making the movie overall all the more effective. All that glazing being said, I had heard claims that this was an easy contender for ‘the best war movie ever made’ and I just don’t know if I’d agree. It’s very good don’t get me wrong, but it feels like it’s missing something that the best of the genre absolutely aren’t. I can’t help but get the feeling that the ending of this movie and the emotional stakes would have been much more impactful if the first half an hour wasn’t so rushed. I haven’t seen the original in completion, but I understand that a big part is dedicated to introducing the characters and seeing them be all excited and giddy before they go off to war. In this version, it kinda feels like the filmmakers were anxious to get them straight into conflict and as a result only left maybe three scenes of the characters before they become damaged (maybe the Netflix influence creeped in there). Whilst I do think that their descent into nihilism is portrayed effectively, I would have liked to get to know the characters a bit more before they became broken. Some war movies can get away with having bland characters because they frame their stories as something that could have just happened to anyone, but All Quiet definitely feels like it’s trying to zoom in and tell a personal story and I’m not sure it’s done as well as people say. I couldn’t really name any of the characters other than Paul, and even then I can’t say I related to him personally, outside of his situation which everyone else around him was also in. I feel like if I really liked him and his mates as guys, then that ending scene would have been brutal, but as is I was almost indifferent. Their fates were quite predictable and at the end of the day they were all probably better off than if they were forced to continue their suffering. Something like Saving Private Ryan for example always leaves me shattered since I love those characters so much, but the same doesn’t really apply to All Quiet. Maybe another little thing, and this is more of a personal problem than an objective complaint, but the scope of the story just didn’t particularly strike me. All Quiet kinda feels like it’s running the gamut of WW1 things, and whilst they’re all done very well individually, the way they are all connected together to produce the final narrative felt a little lacking. It’s just Paul running from battle to battle trying to survive without any particular goal in mind. It’s a tough complaint for sure, but in such an overplayed genre where every major conflict has been covered by a dozen famous movies (in this case also the exact same story multiple times)  I think All Quiet feels a little bit lacking in what it has to offer. Even if the ideas are very strong, they have absolutely been covered elsewhere and have been occasionally done just as well, which in my eyes makes this movie feel a tad more generic than it probably should. A very good watch all and all. It’s probably one of the few foreign language films that you could convince your dad to watch and there is absolutely a reason for it. Even if it isn’t the most original or character driven story, it would be pretty hard to execute this narrative much better. Maybe that means we won’t get a fourth go at it, but with how creatively bankrupt executives are nowadays I honestly wouldn’t be surprised. Watch this space.

In my line of work, we often omit the usage of the word “remains” — if nothing has changed, it should be left unsaid. But “remains” can mean a lot of things. What hasn’t changed, the splintering of bodies, what is left behind. The main audial motif of the movie is titled “remains”, and the audience is almost berated with it, like the relentless barrage of artillery fire, again and again and again and again. Its scenes feel almost post-apocalyptic in its delivery of the past. What was once memory is now history. History tends to mysteriously vanish, a case of the universal forgetting. The lessons learnt are what remains. But nothing remains at all except remains. Even that is buried on unmarked soil. And to think that, after humanity has gone through so much in a little over a century, it has learnt nothing. Perhaps nothing has really changed, and that is the most upsetting of all.

Forging your parent's signature for a field trip is good.  Forging your parent's signature to join an ongoing war is bad. The 2022 adaptation of Erich Maria Remarque's seminal anti-war novel isn't what I'd call a remake of Lewis Milestone's Best Picture-winning film from 1930 (or the Delbert Mann version which was made for television in 1979) but rather another interpretation of the story.  It's the same sentiment I have regarding the new Sense and Sensibility coming out.  Rather than remaking the Ang Lee one, it appears to just be the next go-around of filming Jane Austen's book. Director Edward Berger goes all in on the "war is hell" imagery here.  His tasteful eye, combined with the astonishingly great cinematography by James Friend, allows All Quiet on the Western Front a certain visceral heft that may not have been possible given the constraints of its earlier predecessors.  Nothing in the film is particularly new if you've seen its contemporaries but it still manages to achieve its purpose emotionally, thematically and cinematically. Just to get my negative out of the way, I don't get why Volker Bertelmann snagged the Oscar here.  Those three notes sound too much like dubstep for my taste.  Anachronistic scores can work but it took me out.  That said, Bertelmann's other compositions in the film are quite effective but maybe I'm bitter that Justin Hurwitz's Babylon score, easily one of the decade's most memorable film soundtracks, lost to this.  Then again, considering the same branch didn't even nominate Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross for Challengers, I can't say I'm surprised. Felix Kammerer gives a remarkable debut performance.  His face screams someone whose pure innocence will be decimated by the brutality of war, not unlike the young boy from Come and See.  Albrecht Schuch is great too as Kat.  He was a highlight from that Berlin Alexanderplatz in 2020.  Daniel Brühl is easily the most recognizable actor here, lending credibility as Matthias Erzberger, a German politician instrumental in the armistice that ended the war. I was mesmerized by Berger's command of the camera.  He puts you down and dirty in those trenches.  It's a harmonious mixture of some phenomenal production design by Christian M. Goldbeck, seamless integration of visual effects and some awesome makeup that cakes our actors in mud to resemble the horrifically obscuring conditions that it takes to engage in this level of combat.  There's a reason Paul goes from smiling and chipper at the start to absolutely stone-faced by the end. The assembly line nature of the youth as they enter their regiments is frightening.  A batch of young soldiers dies only to be replaced by younger soldiers whose eyes can't fathom the terrifying things they're about to inflict and be inflicted upon.  The scene of Paul engaging in a one-on-one with the French soldier is devastating because it's a fight or flight scenario while also an acknowledgement of how war encourages the loss of our humanity little by little until we can't even comprehend the actions we commit. Paul is one of many millions of people who were indoctrinated into thinking that what they were doing was a good thing and that the future tales of heroics will far exceed anything on the battlefield.  Meanwhile, the people with the power to the end the war only did so when it mathematically didn't make sense to continue and even still there were those who pridefully refused to concede, thus dragging on the war.  You just become numb to it all, senseless to the feeling that you're a pawn, an eventual casualty in a long list of obituaries. If the Germans pulled a Reynolds Woodcock and simply sewed the names into the fabric it'd make the whole recycling uniforms thing easier.

If x, y, or z had been done differently it would have been glorious.” Plus if you’re on the winning side, it’s easy to lose the anti-war messaging for the catharsis of seeing the Bad Guys lose miserably. As a movie though, I appreciated this more than the original. The tone and pacing were more consistent. My chest felt heavy even through the talky armistice scenes and moments of respite for our young soldiers. Ed Berger’s remake also benefits greatly from modern filmmaking techniques, from VFX to sound design. The scene near the end with the tanks and flamethrowers was one of the most intense, distressing, and downright terrifying things I’ve ever seen on film.

All Quiet on the Western Front is one of a small group of Netflix original movies that is both impressive to look at and actually worth watching. Sure it isn’t a particularly unique story, instead essentially playing as a remake of a remake, but if you’re looking for a brutal and striking depiction of war then you’ll be hard pressed to find better. What fascinates me about war is that despite every distinct conflict being inherently awful, each of them are terrible in their own unique way. You’ve obviously got the raw numbers with WW2, the insanity and trauma of Vietnam and the boredom of the Gulf war, but I honestly don’t think anything can ever top WW1. It’s kinda the perfect culmination of everything awful people associate about war. It happened at a time when people still thought fighting and dying for your country was honourable, so you had poor recruits thinking they were going on an adventure and generals who thought any problem could just be solved by throwing bodies at them. You’ve also got undoubtedly some of the worst conditions in any modern conflict with the trenches and their mud, disease and rats, on top of the insanity element thanks to spending years fighting for a few extra metres and watching your friends get blown to pieces. Truly as far as picking a bad experience to live through, I think you’d be hard pressed to find anything worse than ‘The Great War’ and All Quiet on the Western Front really excellently captures that vibe. What this movies really excels at is getting across how every soldier as an individual was treated like absolute dirt. They were given hammy down clothes from the last lot who had been slaughtered and then sent to die in the mud just so some stuck up boffins could pat themselves on the back and eat a fancy pastry. Their lives were viewed as completely without value besides dying for their country, despite each of them being people in their own right with families and hopes. The fact that this story is told from a distinctly German perspective further helps manifest that idea, since ultimately every young man in every country during the war got the same speech about how righteous they were and how they will bring glory to their fatherland. They couldn’t all be right and realistically none of them were. It’s easy to solidify yourself in the ‘us vs them’ mindset when looking at historical conflicts, hence why stories like this one are so important. That scene in the mortar crater really gets the point across. Everyone was told to hate and kill each other, but looking in the eyes of another innocent young lad and taking his life away remains genuinely one of the most horrific things you could be forced to do. Scenes like that are used effectively throughout All Quiet on the Western Front and really draw into question the inhumanity that was rife during WW1. The other aspect of All Quiet which is undoubtedly great is how terrific it looks. Maybe it’s because I’m used to the green screen/volume vibe of most straight to Netflix movies, but this movie really blew me away from the visuals. The cinematography is gorgeous with its use of colours and its framing of the central events, sometimes heightening the tension like with that tank sequence and sometimes contrasting the chaos with more quiet, tender moments. I wasn’t expecting this movie to be as Terrence Malick as it is, but it’s quite a nice homage to movies like The Thin Red Line whilst further helping demonstrate the shear chaos unleashed by the war. On that note, the gore in this movie is also excellent. It doesn’t pull any punches, with bodies just lying everywhere, often missing parts, all whilst being framed with such a blasé and unfazed perspective. It’s an essential aspect of capturing the vibe of this conflict, given that soldiers at the time had to live around decaying corpses rife with disease all whilst never knowing if they or their mates would be next. All Quiet honestly gets pretty dark at times and I really appreciate it. It’s absolutely not afraid to delve into the traumatic and damaged mindset of the German soldiers, making the movie overall all the more effective. All that glazing being said, I had heard claims that this was an easy contender for ‘the best war movie ever made’ and I just don’t know if I’d agree. It’s very good don’t get me wrong, but it feels like it’s missing something that the best of the genre absolutely aren’t. I can’t help but get the feeling that the ending of this movie and the emotional stakes would have been much more impactful if the first half an hour wasn’t so rushed. I haven’t seen the original in completion, but I understand that a big part is dedicated to introducing the characters and seeing them be all excited and giddy before they go off to war. In this version, it kinda feels like the filmmakers were anxious to get them straight into conflict and as a result only left maybe three scenes of the characters before they become damaged (maybe the Netflix influence creeped in there). Whilst I do think that their descent into nihilism is portrayed effectively, I would have liked to get to know the characters a bit more before they became broken. Some war movies can get away with having bland characters because they frame their stories as something that could have just happened to anyone, but All Quiet definitely feels like it’s trying to zoom in and tell a personal story and I’m not sure it’s done as well as people say. I couldn’t really name any of the characters other than Paul, and even then I can’t say I related to him personally, outside of his situation which everyone else around him was also in. I feel like if I really liked him and his mates as guys, then that ending scene would have been brutal, but as is I was almost indifferent. Their fates were quite predictable and at the end of the day they were all probably better off than if they were forced to continue their suffering. Something like Saving Private Ryan for example always leaves me shattered since I love those characters so much, but the same doesn’t really apply to All Quiet. Maybe another little thing, and this is more of a personal problem than an objective complaint, but the scope of the story just didn’t particularly strike me. All Quiet kinda feels like it’s running the gamut of WW1 things, and whilst they’re all done very well individually, the way they are all connected together to produce the final narrative felt a little lacking. It’s just Paul running from battle to battle trying to survive without any particular goal in mind. It’s a tough complaint for sure, but in such an overplayed genre where every major conflict has been covered by a dozen famous movies (in this case also the exact same story multiple times)  I think All Quiet feels a little bit lacking in what it has to offer. Even if the ideas are very strong, they have absolutely been covered elsewhere and have been occasionally done just as well, which in my eyes makes this movie feel a tad more generic than it probably should. A very good watch all and all. It’s probably one of the few foreign language films that you could convince your dad to watch and there is absolutely a reason for it. Even if it isn’t the most original or character driven story, it would be pretty hard to execute this narrative much better. Maybe that means we won’t get a fourth go at it, but with how creatively bankrupt executives are nowadays I honestly wouldn’t be surprised. Watch this space.

In my line of work, we often omit the usage of the word “remains” — if nothing has changed, it should be left unsaid. But “remains” can mean a lot of things. What hasn’t changed, the splintering of bodies, what is left behind. The main audial motif of the movie is titled “remains”, and the audience is almost berated with it, like the relentless barrage of artillery fire, again and again and again and again. Its scenes feel almost post-apocalyptic in its delivery of the past. What was once memory is now history. History tends to mysteriously vanish, a case of the universal forgetting. The lessons learnt are what remains. But nothing remains at all except remains. Even that is buried on unmarked soil. And to think that, after humanity has gone through so much in a little over a century, it has learnt nothing. Perhaps nothing has really changed, and that is the most upsetting of all.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [

      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,

Arrival: Villeneuve's (failed) Space Odyssey Look, I'm not going to come out and say that this is a bad film, because it clearly isn't, but I would hesitate to say that it's a good film as well. Day by day, my feelings that we as a species should have retired the sci-fi drama genre after Solaris (1972) grow. To be perfectly frank, I felt nothing from this film, one that definitely earned the description of, "a mile wide, and an inch deep." It attempts to tackle so many things at once that it eventually lacks any true identity and fails to separate itself from similar pictures of the 2010's. Even starting the film, I was immediately hit with a rushed, melodramatic sequence of our protagonist and her daughter all throughout her life, which ended before I could even form a thought. Why even include it? Does it serve any purpose besides telling me, "You are going to watch a drama. This will be sad. Feel sad for this person." I will give credit where it's due. The cinematography is obviously gorgeous and is by far my favorite aspect of the film. The sound design and score are both ominous and melancholy. However, I don't love the production value as a whole, because the incredibly dull color palette is a bore to look at. The set design of the military base was also quite bland. The alien itself was without a doubt beautifully surreal, and the scenes of Banks/Donelly attempting to communicate with them are easily my favorites in the film. Even the concepts alone are quite fascinating and even well-executed at times, but I can't help but get the feeling that I've seen this film before. There are so many aspects that are completely run-of-the-mill, such as Banks' "tragic backstory," which we learn later in the film is actually after the main events. Yes, I thought the "recalling the future" concept was quite cool, but it ultimately accomplishes nothing but feel emotionally manipulative yet cold at the same time. Seriously though, how many characters are there in the sci-fi genre that are nearly identical to Banks? A lonely, alienated melancholic genius that gets brought in to "solve the mystery," while everyone else distrusts her and treat her with hostility. She really fits right in with the crowd. I just can't stand the execution of so much of this film. The exposition was actually quite intriguing, but I got to the second act of the film and was fighting the urge to fall asleep. Was it trying to bore me on purpose? I enjoyed the third act much more than the second, as that's when the stakes really raise and we get a bit of well-done suspense. It sucks, because that's when I really felt how much potential this film had! The ending montage didn't do it for me though. Every science fiction film nowadays does this to make it seem "emotional," but it ends up just feeling extremely forced. Without a doubt my least favorite from Villeneuve at the moment, but you never know... perhaps a rewatch could boost it all the way to the top, and I realize how it's secretly a masterpiece. But then again, perhaps not. Not a bad film, but not an especially good one either.

Arrival: Villeneuve's (failed) Space Odyssey Look, I'm not going to come out and say that this is a bad film, because it clearly isn't, but I would hesitate to say that it's a good film as well. Day by day, my feelings that we as a species should have retired the sci-fi drama genre after Solaris (1972) grow. To be perfectly frank, I felt nothing from this film, one that definitely earned the description of, "a mile wide, and an inch deep." It attempts to tackle so many things at once that it eventually lacks any true identity and fails to separate itself from similar pictures of the 2010's. Even starting the film, I was immediately hit with a rushed, melodramatic sequence of our protagonist and her daughter all throughout her life, which ended before I could even form a thought. Why even include it? Does it serve any purpose besides telling me, "You are going to watch a drama. This will be sad. Feel sad for this person." I will give credit where it's due. The cinematography is obviously gorgeous and is by far my favorite aspect of the film. The sound design and score are both ominous and melancholy. However, I don't love the production value as a whole, because the incredibly dull color palette is a bore to look at. The set design of the military base was also quite bland. The alien itself was without a doubt beautifully surreal, and the scenes of Banks/Donelly attempting to communicate with them are easily my favorites in the film. Even the concepts alone are quite fascinating and even well-executed at times, but I can't help but get the feeling that I've seen this film before. There are so many aspects that are completely run-of-the-mill, such as Banks' "tragic backstory," which we learn later in the film is actually after the main events. Yes, I thought the "recalling the future" concept was quite cool, but it ultimately accomplishes nothing but feel emotionally manipulative yet cold at the same time. Seriously though, how many characters are there in the sci-fi genre that are nearly identical to Banks? A lonely, alienated melancholic genius that gets brought in to "solve the mystery," while everyone else distrusts her and treat her with hostility. She really fits right in with the crowd. I just can't stand the execution of so much of this film. The exposition was actually quite intriguing, but I got to the second act of the film and was fighting the urge to fall asleep. Was it trying to bore me on purpose? I enjoyed the third act much more than the second, as that's when the stakes really raise and we get a bit of well-done suspense. It sucks, because that's when I really felt how much potential this film had! The ending montage didn't do it for me though. Every science fiction film nowadays does this to make it seem "emotional," but it ends up just feeling extremely forced. Without a doubt my least favorite from Villeneuve at the moment, but you never know... perhaps a rewatch could boost it all the way to the top, and I realize how it's secretly a masterpiece. But then again, perhaps not. Not a bad film, but not an especially good one either.

Είναι μια ταινία που εστιάζει καθαρά στο πώς στο διάολο καταφέρνεις να επικοινωνήσεις με κάτι που δεν έχει καμία λογική σχέση με την ανθρώπινη φύση. Οπτικά και ηχητικά η ατμόσφαιρα σε πλακώνει. Αυτά τα τεράστια, μονόλιθα σκάφη που απλά αιωρούνται σιωπηλά και ο απόκοσμος ήχος στο background χτίζουν μια συνεχή ένταση, χωρίς να γίνεται τίποτα υπερβολικό στην οθόνη. Εκεί που πραγματικά με κέρδισε, όμως, είναι στο πώς χειρίζεται το θέμα του χρόνου. Παίζει με την ιδέα του ότι η γλώσσα που μαθαίνεις αλλάζει τον τρόπο που αντιλαμβάνεσαι την ίδια την πραγματικότητα, και τελικά το χρησιμοποιεί για να σου ρίξει ένα πολύ βαρύ ψυχολογικό χτύπημα. Αντί για κάποιο φθηνό plot twist με εξωγήινους, η ταινία καταλήγει να σε βάζει να σκεφτείς κάτι πολύ πιο ανθρώπινο: αν θα επέλεγες να ζήσεις μια ιστορία από την αρχή, ξέροντας ακριβώς πώς και πόσο άσχημα πρόκειται να τελειώσει. Ναι, ο ρυθμός του είναι αρκετά αργός και θέλει λίγη υπομονή, αλλά ο τρόπος που κουμπώνουν όλα τα κομμάτια στο φινάλε σε αποζημιώνει στο εκατό τοις εκατό.

[9] nota=1.0 estrelas:
As the end marker for a long running generation of marvel movies, Endgame unfortunately drops the ball in all ways that matter. A lame attempt at reconciling irreversible character and wider plot choices, this film not only disrupts long established character growth and progression, but it also abruptly cuts off any opportunity for what many would call a “happy ending.” Multiple beloved characters are given the “tortured male existence trope,” wherein their wider personality and moral identity are swept to the wayside in order to justify a new generation of characters to swoop in following their exit. For example, by both butchering Peggy Carter and Steve Rogers emotional maturation and individuality in order to manufacture a “romantic reunification” following Steve’s travel back in time, Marvel has essentially removed both Peggy’s autonomy outside of being “Captain Americas love interest,” as well as Steve’s long established faithfulness to Bucky Barnes and his dedication to serving the weak. In no world would Steve rogers abandon a freshly reintroduced to society Bucky, nor a disrupted world reeling with the sudden re-appearance of 50% of the world’s population. In his decision to abandon his shield and interrupt Peggy’s progression towards an accomplished life as a shield founder and agent, as well as her pursuit of future love and motherhood as expressed in the original timeline, Steve is making an exceptionally selfish decision—which as any Marvel fan is aware—is the antithesis of his character. This is just one of the irreconcilable changes made to a central character that insults years of character establishment and development, which is then followed by yet again a female character being fridged for the greater plot. First starting with Gamora in Infinity war and now Natasha in Endgame, it is clear to see that the writers find no use for these strong female characters in these last plot stages other than as a motivation for male suffering and lament. Gamora, both present and past iterations of herself (as featured in this film), have much more worth as a character representing long building abusive deprogramming and female strength and endurance in the face of tragedy, than as a “sad she’s different than my girlfriend” trope—as presented by Peter Quills reaction to her appearance. Prior to this, viewers are slapped in the face with the sacrifice of Natasha for the soul stone, where her death is framed as a noble sacrifice in order to allow Clint Barton to return to his family once the snap is reversed. While faithful to Natasha’s character, one can only reconcile so much with the fact that it had to be only female character of the original Avengers to lose her life first. This is especially exasperated by the emphasized female power scene in the final battle, where every female hero on scene band together to fight, almost as an attempt by the writers to apologize for killing off the woman who pioneered female superhero-dom in modern media not 40 minutes earlier. All in all, these are just some of the many faults within this movie—which in its essence is a blatant attempt to slap a crooked bandaid on Marvels obvious (and clumsy) transition to a newer generation of actors and characters. As entertaining as a battle packed, time travel action movie can be, Avengers Endgame is a lazy attempt at hopefully pushing viewers towards future projects as they kill off their favorite characters one by one. We can only hope that these new superhero’s will be given the opportunity to grow into characters of their own and establish a storyline outside of the shadow of their predecessors.
