"There was an idea, Stark knows this, called the Avengers Initiative. The idea was to bring together a group of remarkable people, see if they could become something more. See if they could work together when we needed them to fight the battles we never could." Sam Jackson's Nick Fury hit us with that way back in 2012's The Avengers. At the time, that movie seemed to be the fulfillment of the promise of a shared universe. It was groundbreaking in its own right and was proof that this could actually work. What resulted was a seismic shift in how studios approached making money. All of a sudden, setting up things to come became more important than the film itself and Marvel was no less guilty in said predisposition. It seemed like Kevin Feige's all-pervading control over every aspect of every film would, ultimately, lead to the death of the MCU. Somehow, it didn't. Audiences (me included) flocked in droves to watch the same movie (albeit with different characters and plot) over and over again. We sat through some real abysmal shit too. The "Marvel Formula", however, did not change much. My main issue was always how the film you were watching was always indebted to the next film in the pipeline to fulfill its promises. It seemed like a cycle that would never stop (and probably won't) but then, I watched Endgame. After the "space trash" (to quote David Ehrlich) that we all know as Avengers: Infinity War, Endgame really knocks it out of the park. For once, something had real consequences in the MCU. The sense of loss and grief is palpable. Don't get me wrong, this also a hodgepodge of random character moments structured around a plot that, if you think about it long enough, makes absolutely no sense but what happens to be Endgame's biggest weakness is also its biggest strength. This mish-mash works because its a mish-mash of much fewer characters. They have, and I can't stress this enough, time. The editing, while much tighter than Infinity War's, holds shots much longer than one would expect from a summer blockbuster studio tentpole and this is why, for once, I cried (more than once) in a Marvel film. Imagine the scene where Peter Parker turns into vacuum cleaner food in Tony's hands. Now imagine if an entire 3 hour film was like that. There is one cut that's absolutely ridiculous and doesn't work at all but it'll probably go unnoticed by the majority (pretty much everyone) of the people that watch this film. As you've probably read in other reviews, “fan service” is a huge part of the film. While that isn’t untrue, I prefer to think of these moments as homages and also, the fulfillment of character arcs and sub-arcs. Despite being 3 hours long, there’s very little to the film that I would call unnecessary. It’s almost as if Feige’s plan was to feed us a staple diet of horseshit (no disrespect to the artists that made those films but they were always tied down by the involvement of Feige and, sometimes, the military) for 11 years so that, when they finally did make a great film, we’d know it. And they have. Additionally, both Alan Silvestri’s score and Trent Opaloch’s cinematography happen to be, at least in my opinion, the best in the MCU. Here, Silvestri, unlike in Infinity War, creates a soundscape that builds upon previously established character themes satisfyingly while introducing new, moodier and much more effective pieces into the mix. He no longer has the burden of scoring for Thanos in almost every scene owing to the fact that this film is more The Avengers than The Avengers. A stride was also made towards embracing Joss Whedon’s influence and that pays off in heaps. The lighting gets a little experimental at times and you can see Opaloch’s Disrict 9 come through a little which is honestly great. The CGI is, well, Marvel CGI; rushed, everywhere, and, at this point, it seems like most major studios have stopped caring about the fact that CGI isn’t supposed to look computer generated in almost every case. Despite all its shortcomings, I laughed, I cried, and, on more occasions than I would like to admit, I got goosebumps. This was the endgame all along and it was worth it. As the end marker for a long running generation of marvel movies, Endgame unfortunately drops the ball in all ways that matter. A lame attempt at reconciling irreversible character and wider plot choices, this film not only disrupts long established character growth and progression, but it also abruptly cuts off any opportunity for what many would call a “happy ending.” Multiple beloved characters are given the “tortured male existence trope,” wherein their wider personality and moral identity are swept to the wayside in order to justify a new generation of characters to swoop in following their exit. For example, by both butchering Peggy Carter and Steve Rogers emotional maturation and individuality in order to manufacture a “romantic reunification” following Steve’s travel back in time, Marvel has essentially removed both Peggy’s autonomy outside of being “Captain Americas love interest,” as well as Steve’s long established faithfulness to Bucky Barnes and his dedication to serving the weak. In no world would Steve rogers abandon a freshly reintroduced to society Bucky, nor a disrupted world reeling with the sudden re-appearance of 50% of the world’s population. In his decision to abandon his shield and interrupt Peggy’s progression towards an accomplished life as a shield founder and agent, as well as her pursuit of future love and motherhood as expressed in the original timeline, Steve is making an exceptionally selfish decision—which as any Marvel fan is aware—is the antithesis of his character. This is just one of the irreconcilable changes made to a central character that insults years of character establishment and development, which is then followed by yet again a female character being fridged for the greater plot. First starting with Gamora in Infinity war and now Natasha in Endgame, it is clear to see that the writers find no use for these strong female characters in these last plot stages other than as a motivation for male suffering and lament. Gamora, both present and past iterations of herself (as featured in this film), have much more worth as a character representing long building abusive deprogramming and female strength and endurance in the face of tragedy, than as a “sad she’s different than my girlfriend” trope—as presented by Peter Quills reaction to her appearance. Prior to this, viewers are slapped in the face with the sacrifice of Natasha for the soul stone, where her death is framed as a noble sacrifice in order to allow Clint Barton to return to his family once the snap is reversed. While faithful to Natasha’s character, one can only reconcile so much with the fact that it had to be only female character of the original Avengers to lose her life first. This is especially exasperated by the emphasized female power scene in the final battle, where every female hero on scene band together to fight, almost as an attempt by the writers to apologize for killing off the woman who pioneered female superhero-dom in modern media not 40 minutes earlier. All in all, these are just some of the many faults within this movie—which in its essence is a blatant attempt to slap a crooked bandaid on Marvels obvious (and clumsy) transition to a newer generation of actors and characters. As entertaining as a battle packed, time travel action movie can be, Avengers Endgame is a lazy attempt at hopefully pushing viewers towards future projects as they kill off their favorite characters one by one. We can only hope that these new superhero’s will be given the opportunity to grow into characters of their own and establish a storyline outside of the shadow of their predecessors.

See if they could work together when we needed them to fight the battles we never could." Sam Jackson's Nick Fury hit us with that way back in 2012's The Avengers. At the time, that movie seemed to be the fulfillment of the promise of a shared universe. It was groundbreaking in its own right and was proof that this could actually work. What resulted was a seismic shift in how studios approached making money. All of a sudden, setting up things to come became more important than the film itself and Marvel was no less guilty in said predisposition. It seemed like Kevin Feige's all-pervading control over every aspect of every film would, ultimately, lead to the death of the MCU. Somehow, it didn't. Audiences (me included) flocked in droves to watch the same movie (albeit with different characters and plot) over and over again. We sat through some real abysmal shit too. The "Marvel Formula", however, did not change much. My main issue was always how the film you were watching was always indebted to the next film in the pipeline to fulfill its promises. It seemed like a cycle that would never stop (and probably won't) but then, I watched Endgame. After the "space trash" (to quote David Ehrlich) that we all know as Avengers: Infinity War, Endgame really knocks it out of the park. For once, something had real consequences in the MCU. The sense of loss and grief is palpable. Don't get me wrong, this also a hodgepodge of random character moments structured around a plot that, if you think about it long enough, makes absolutely no sense but what happens to be Endgame's biggest weakness is also its biggest strength. This mish-mash works because its a mish-mash of much fewer characters. They have, and I can't stress this enough, time. The editing, while much tighter than Infinity War's, holds shots much longer than one would expect from a summer blockbuster studio tentpole and this is why, for once, I cried (more than once) in a Marvel film. Imagine the scene where Peter Parker turns into vacuum cleaner food in Tony's hands. Now imagine if an entire 3 hour film was like that. There is one cut that's absolutely ridiculous and doesn't work at all but it'll probably go unnoticed by the majority (pretty much everyone) of the people that watch this film. As you've probably read in other reviews, “fan service” is a huge part of the film. While that isn’t untrue, I prefer to think of these moments as homages and also, the fulfillment of character arcs and sub-arcs. Despite being 3 hours long, there’s very little to the film that I would call unnecessary. It’s almost as if Feige’s plan was to feed us a staple diet of horseshit (no disrespect to the artists that made those films but they were always tied down by the involvement of Feige and, sometimes, the military) for 11 years so that, when they finally did make a great film, we’d know it. And they have. Additionally, both Alan Silvestri’s score and Trent Opaloch’s cinematography happen to be, at least in my opinion, the best in the MCU. Here, Silvestri, unlike in Infinity War, creates a soundscape that builds upon previously established character themes satisfyingly while introducing new, moodier and much more effective pieces into the mix. He no longer has the burden of scoring for Thanos in almost every scene owing to the fact that this film is more The Avengers than The Avengers. A stride was also made towards embracing Joss Whedon’s influence and that pays off in heaps. The lighting gets a little experimental at times and you can see Opaloch’s Disrict 9 come through a little which is honestly great. The CGI is, well, Marvel CGI; rushed, everywhere, and, at this point, it seems like most major studios have stopped caring about the fact that CGI isn’t supposed to look computer generated in almost every case. Despite all its shortcomings, I laughed, I cried, and, on more occasions than I would like to admit, I got goosebumps. This was the endgame all along and it was worth it. Edit: didn't touch my original review because it's nice, if misguided, but this film is truly just imperialist propoganda

If Infinity War was, as @kernetcetera so eloquently described, ‘television’, then Endgame is the TV finale, the send-off show, the goodbye episode that wraps it all up with a nice little bow and gives the fans an opportunity to pay their respects to characters that had been a part of their lives for so many seasons. On that note, it’s certainly not the type of film that was made for someone like me, and I was a fool for thinking it may otherwise have been. I have highlighted my preference for the more singularly focussed storylines in the MCU within previous reviews, with IW being somewhat of an exception. Infinity War surprised me with its acute balance of multiple character threads and plot lines with the fast-paced and action-packed spectacle of superhero powers punching up against the Mad Titan, Thanos. It felt lean and muscly, where the added padding and lethargic pace of Endgame serves as a complete, and for me, unwelcome juxtaposition to what had preceded it. This, admittedly, is down to personal preference. I had wretchedly hoped for an escalation of the Infinity War saga, and was instead handed exactly what franchise fans had asked for all along. Endgame is fan-service through and through, and I have no doubt that day one MCU faithfuls will be absolutely delighted with what’s served up. Where I see po-faced and heavy-handed self-importance, Marvel’s fanbase will instead see earnest and earned tributes to the characters they love and themselves as supporters. And you know what? We’re both right. We’re just coming at it from different directions. If you’re like me, someone who is far more interested in self-contained stories that can stand on their own two feet and are concerned about only what is delivered within a film’s runtime, not what’s outside of it... you’ll probably walk away feeling a little ripped off. If, however, you have completely invested yourself in the 10 years worth of movies that the Marvel Cinematic Universe consists of, you’re unlikely to be disappointed. Enjoy it.

I think Barbie is one of those movies I wish every little girl could watch before the world gets the chance to tell her who she is supposed to be. Because underneath all the pink and glitter, it is a story about becoming a woman. About growing up and slowly realizing that there is no version of yourself that will ever be enough for everyone. Be beautiful, but not vain. Be smart, but not intimidating. Be strong, but still soft. Have ambition, but don't make anyone feel small. Be independent, but still be desirable. How exhausting it is to be a woman and constantly feel like you're failing at a set of rules that were never meant to be followed. And then Barbie asks you to let all of that go. To exist without having to be perfect. To be messy, uncertain, angry, joyful, ordinary. To grow older without believing you've become less valuable. To understand that your worth was never supposed to depend on how well you fit into someone else's idea of a woman. Maybe that's why this movie means so much to me. I wish little girls could see it before they learn to shrink themselves. Before they learn to apologize for taking up space. Before they learn that being loved sometimes means becoming smaller. I want them to grow up knowing that they don't have to be the prettiest, the smartest, the kindest, or the most accomplished person in the room. They just have to know that their life belongs to them. And maybe that's what Barbie really changed for me: Being a woman isn't about becoming the perfect version of yourself. It's about finally realizing you were never meant to be a version of anyone else.

I think Barbie is one of those movies I wish every little girl could watch before the world gets the chance to tell her who she is supposed to be. Because underneath all the pink and glitter, it is a story about becoming a woman. About growing up and slowly realizing that there is no version of yourself that will ever be enough for everyone. Be beautiful, but not vain. Be smart, but not intimidating. Be strong, but still soft. Have ambition, but don't make anyone feel small. Be independent, but still be desirable. How exhausting it is to be a woman and constantly feel like you're failing at a set of rules that were never meant to be followed. And then Barbie asks you to let all of that go. To exist without having to be perfect. To be messy, uncertain, angry, joyful, ordinary. To grow older without believing you've become less valuable. To understand that your worth was never supposed to depend on how well you fit into someone else's idea of a woman. Maybe that's why this movie means so much to me. I wish little girls could see it before they learn to shrink themselves. Before they learn to apologize for taking up space. Before they learn that being loved sometimes means becoming smaller. I want them to grow up knowing that they don't have to be the prettiest, the smartest, the kindest, or the most accomplished person in the room. They just have to know that their life belongs to them. And maybe that's what Barbie really changed for me: Being a woman isn't about becoming the perfect version of yourself. It's about finally realizing you were never meant to be a version of anyone else.

The memes will lose the fact that this Taylor Russell's movie though. And while it doesn't all work. Every part that does belongs to her. Allow me to explain... Russell stars as Maren and Bones and All is her story. She is shy at school. Her father (André Holland) locks her up at night. We soon learn why. In the world of this film, based on a 2016 novel by Camille DeAngelis, being an “eater” of human flesh is a hereditary condition. It comes with a keen sense of smell which allows the eater to find others like them but for the most veteran eater, an eater can also use their sense of smell to locate homes where someone inside does not have much longer in this world. Because Maren knows nothing of her mother, she thinks maybe this necessary hunger afflicted her, too. And she traverses all over the Great Plains and Great Lakes to find her. First, she meets Sully (Mark Rylance) an older, polite eater whose sense of smell gives him the vibes of a stalker. Despite Sully’s kismet feeling, it’s those stalker vibes (he keeps his victim’s hair to braid into a rope) that puts her back on the road where she eventually meets and falls for Lee (Chalamet). The flesh of the story is the growing fondness and love between the two young eaters. Lee takes Maren on the road to find her mother and she learns more about his former life, too. Back in Kentucky, Lee has a younger sister (Francesca Scorsese) who begs for him to come home. The lovers’ road trip follows a world-building section that is full of tension and well-executed mood. The world-building is the bones of the story. The bones are eerie, and the flesh is twee. It’s a mix that doesn’t always work but the chemistry between Russell and Chalamet is so strong that each cameo (including Michael Stuhlbarg’s) feels extraneous and disruptive. (Of all the cameos in Bones & All, Suspiria’s Jessica Harper fares best as Maren’s grandmother who cannot bring herself to openly talk about her daughter.) Russell portrays Maren as guarded but warm, with a good read on others. And Chalamet has punk swagger that goes beyond his pink hair and torn jeans. Like many young punks, he’s lashing out at a self-centered world until he’s understood and forgiven. In the end, Bones and All starts to run out of gas because—while people are killed and eaten— the film never becomes a lovers-on-the-lam movie so the tension, which was so pronounced at the start, dissipates. The love story is pleasant and will surely be memed with care and admiration (so too will a cornfield rendezvous where Chalamet takes his fresh prey). But it weirdly removes a sense of urgency that they could get caught. The two sides of the story also carry different looks. The opening is full of shadows and darkness, punctuated gorgeously by streetlights and bedroom lights—the places where Maren is escaping and plunging into the unknown. Once it becomes a love story, the look of Bones and All becomes more hopeful with blue skies and open roads. There is a message about needing to accept yourself in order to love someone else, which is tried and true. But, even though there is bloodshed on the screen and gnashing teeth in the sound design, the light overtakes the darkness too much. Perhaps this is due to almost every character we meet being an eater and so the societal structure that they’ve all run away from doesn’t ever make a threatful appearance. Vampire movies, which often incorporate a love story, are usually driven by the threat of discovery. The absence of that in Bones and All, despite leaving evidence all over the Great Plains, makes it a beautiful-looking movie that becomes too devoted to repeating the same note. There is no “all,” just bones.

The opening is full of shadows and darkness, punctuated gorgeously by streetlights and bedroom lights—the places where Maren is escaping and plunging into the unknown. Once it becomes a love story, the look of Bones and All becomes more hopeful with blue skies and open roads. There is a message about needing to accept yourself in order to love someone else, which is tried and true. But, even though there is bloodshed on the screen and gnashing teeth in the sound design, the light overtakes the darkness too much. Perhaps this is due to almost every character we meet being an eater and so the societal structure that they’ve all run away from doesn’t ever make a threatful appearance. Vampire movies, which often incorporate a love story, are usually driven by the threat of discovery. The absence of that in Bones and All, despite leaving evidence all over the Great Plains, makes it a beautiful-looking movie that becomes too devoted to repeating the same note. There is no “all,” just bones.

It carries echoes of John Lasseter's actual masterpiece, Toy Story 2 , yet stumbles through some weaker jokes and cheeky references, most of which I still have an affection for, but contrasted against 3 all-timer voice performances, this movie walks a tight line between generation-defining spectacle and reminders that this is still at its core an animated kid's movie from the 2000's. Hearing Paul Newman is the most obvious standout, bringing his classic charm to kids like me for the first time to drive home a simple yet timeless moral. Owen Wilson is a perfect other half to the main mentor/student dynamic, yet I can't shake the underlying discontent his character spends the first two acts reckoning with, especially with the context of his suicide attempt the following year. His career history of comedic roles aren't a crutch for this role, and instead the occasional vulnerability he shows makes this a surprisingly interesting undertaking for an otherwise straightforward narrative. Michael Keaton still consistently amazes me as the unforgettable asshole Chick Hicks, a role that proved to me how even Keaton's most random or commercial work has a special place in my heart existing long before I ever saw Birdman . As I get older I'll inevitably continue to love the dialogue of nostalgia and accepting change this movie presents even though the words themselves will never change, sometimes thats just what I want from cinema and this movie provides a window into my childhood like no other. Owen Wilson is a perfect other half to the main mentor/student dynamic, yet I can't shake the underlying discontent his character spends the first two acts reckoning with, especially with the context of his suicide attempt the following year. His career history of comedic roles aren't a crutch for this role, and instead the occasional vulnerability he shows makes this a surprisingly interesting undertaking for an otherwise straightforward narrative. Michael Keaton still consistently amazes me as the unforgettable asshole Chick Hicks, a role that proved to me how even Keaton's most random or commercial work has a special place in my heart existing long before I ever saw Birdman . As I get older I'll inevitably continue to love the dialogue of nostalgia and accepting change this movie presents even though the words themselves will never change, sometimes thats just what I want from cinema and this movie provides a window into my childhood like no other. Also why did Sally poop on McQueen when they were going for a drive that is just so strange.

Spielberg agafa la biografia de Frank Abagnale , un precoç estafador estatunidenc que causaria impacte a la societat nord-americana amb la seva habilitat per l'engany. Una cosa és tenir un bon material de fons i l'altra saber portar-lo a la pantalla gran d'una forma completament brillant. Em congratula veure que Spielberg ho aconsegueix i, aparentment, sense cap mena de dificultat. Com a espectador no necessites reflexionar en excés o estar atentíssim per no perdre't el mínim detall. És una pel·lícula que es gaudeix sola: té un ritme lleuger, molt viu i extremadament agradable. La crònica no és monòtona i presenta uns girs i ocurrències que traspassen el predictible. M'agrada pensar que tota història està precedida d'un missatge de fons, d'una intenció clara independentment de l'entreteniment. Aquí se'm complica més identificar-ho, no perquè no hi sigui, sinó perquè crec que se li dona menys importància. La inevitabilitat del protagonista per deixar de mentir és un tret que pot abordar certes reflexions, però per mi no arriba a una profunditat digna de menció. Frank Abagnale (un genial Leonardo DiCaprio ) fa de la mentida patològica el seu modus operandi, un comportament persistent i compulsiu que forma part de la seva identitat. Una característica visiblement present també en el seu pare (interpretat per un grandiós Christopher Walken ) que ens deixaria una metàfora molt il·lustrativa que després heretaria el seu fill: "Two little mice fell in a bucket of cream. The first mouse quickly gave up and drowned. The second mouse, he wouldn't quit. He struggled so hard that eventually he churned that cream into butter and crawled out." Frank Abagnale Sr. viu constantment en un món envoltat de fantasia, s'obliga ell mateix a viure en un ordre construït per les seves autocomplaences i vol sempre anar per un camí que no li correspon i no es pot permetre. Quan la realitat se li fa evident l'única cosa que sembla aprendre és traslladar les responsabilitats als seus perseguidors. La metàfora li serveix per arrossegar al seu fill amb el niu de l'adoctrinament. Projecta el seu ego i deixa de fer-li de pare per fer-li d'animador quan les seves decisions són notòriament reprovables. Aquest suport fa que Frank Abagnale Jr. sigui una versió "millorada" del que és el seu pare. Ell ja no menteix per benefici, menteix perquè li proporciona plaer i fa que la resta de mortals l'admirin. Utilitza constantment als qui l'envolten com a mers instruments a punt per ser manipulats. Tot això l'acaba convertint en un home exteriorment idíl·lic, però interiorment desert. Un narcisisme que, poc a poc i amb l'ajuda d'un agent de l'FBI (Tom Hanks), aconsegueix gestionar. Sí, és un relat de superació personal. No obstant l'anterior, la conclusió, amb tot el que comporta, és el postre en aquest menú de Spielberg .

First time watch. Charming, enjoyable. Mostly false. Probably won't rank among my favorite Spielberg films, but as always, the display of technique is impressive. Effortlessly crafted cinematography and blocking. Sharp editing. Top-notch performances across the board. A script that could easily work as a masterclass in setup and payoff which all builds to a highly satisfying ending. A better film, still, than most directors can pull together on a good day. I'll admit however, searching for details about the real Frank Abignale has soured my enjoyment somewhat. The film does only say it was "inspired" by true events. However, it's still a common misconception that the film is or was at least based on a true story, when many of Frank's claims have been disputed as far back as the late 70s. Meanwhile, his real exploits include allegedly impersonating a doctor to sexually assault Pan Am flight attendants. The film not only supports his lies, but glorifies and exonerates him to an almost comical degree. The real Frank even gets a cutesy cameo. Unlike another, similarly false movie based on "true" events, "21", this film doesn't even give Frank an alias to allow any reasonable separation. It concludes with a wall of wrap-up text to update the audience on his career and assure us that Frank and Tom Hanks' fictional FBI agent remained good friends. Somewhat suspiciously, when it comes to his check fraud, the film goes to great lengths to explain the mechanics of how the scheme works. When it comes to his lengthy impersonations, the film largely glosses over these. As if impersonating a head pediatrician for a year is too ludicrous to even portray. We never see him in an operating room, a cockpit, or a courtroom for more than a minute each. Much of it seems to rely of a lot of adult women being easily manipulated or too horny for this 17 year old to see through him. I don't know if the book cares to elaborate further, but I have my suspicions. Still, it's a highly entertaining, if not slightly frustrating film to engage with.

First time watch. Charming, enjoyable. Mostly false. Probably won't rank among my favorite Spielberg films, but as always, the display of technique is impressive. Effortlessly crafted cinematography and blocking. Sharp editing. Top-notch performances across the board. A script that could easily work as a masterclass in setup and payoff which all builds to a highly satisfying ending. A better film, still, than most directors can pull together on a good day. I'll admit however, searching for details about the real Frank Abignale has soured my enjoyment somewhat. The film does only say it was "inspired" by true events. However, it's still a common misconception that the film is or was at least based on a true story, when many of Frank's claims have been disputed as far back as the late 70s. Meanwhile, his real exploits include allegedly impersonating a doctor to sexually assault Pan Am flight attendants. The film not only supports his lies, but glorifies and exonerates him to an almost comical degree. The real Frank even gets a cutesy cameo. Unlike another, similarly false movie based on "true" events, "21", this film doesn't even give Frank an alias to allow any reasonable separation. It concludes with a wall of wrap-up text to update the audience on his career and assure us that Frank and Tom Hanks' fictional FBI agent remained good friends. Somewhat suspiciously, when it comes to his check fraud, the film goes to great lengths to explain the mechanics of how the scheme works. When it comes to his lengthy impersonations, the film largely glosses over these. As if impersonating a head pediatrician for a year is too ludicrous to even portray. We never see him in an operating room, a cockpit, or a courtroom for more than a minute each. Much of it seems to rely of a lot of adult women being easily manipulated or too horny for this 17 year old to see through him. I don't know if the book cares to elaborate further, but I have my suspicions. Still, it's a highly entertaining, if not slightly frustrating film to engage with.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

My review of Cats (or A Stoner's Journey Into The Heart of Darkness) DISCLAIMER : This review is in no way an endorsement of the movie, please view at your own risk. (Mild Spoilers Ahead) So I finally find did something I had been considering for some time now. I got high and watched Cats and it nearly broke me. To preface, the choice to watch this movie on that very nigjt wasn't exactly random. If you follow me you might know that, immediately before this, I had watched a weird little gem of French cinema called Car Cemetery, a surreal punk rock "musical" mixing grimy, torturous and explicit sexual acts with messianic parable all while taking place in a post-apocalyptic junkyard. In my review of the movie I joked that it was "queerer than Cats." Not having seen Cats before and having an appreciation for strange and queer cinema, naturally I decided to put my money where my mouth is and challenge my assumptions on the matter. From the opening and throughout the first 10-15 minutes of the film I was engaged in an uncontrollable fit of hysterical laughter that seemed unstoppable despite my will to breathe. So early into the film, yet, had I already gone mad? How could this have been made with any intention other than to create a lovecraftian nightmare of fur and surreal landscapes. I believe the terror really set it about the time the Rebel Wilson Cat was concluding her number and began making unmistakeably suggestive petting motions. It was then I began to realized that all of these characters were trapped in an existential race towards death. The performers vying for the coveted "Jellical Choice" for their own reasons wanted to die. They were competing to prove which cat has suffered the most in whichever iteration of their 9 lives this was. Fear then turned to despair and however weird it was staring at Jennifer Hudson's face mapped onto a cartoonish cat body was not enough to distract me from the pain of existence that floated on every vocalization of "Memory." And then, just as it always does, the pain and suffering led to apathy. Maybe I too in some small way wanted to die, to move on from this nightmarish jest. Or maybe my hightened state of consciousness was just wearing off and I was getting bored. By the time the feline personification of Jennifer Hudson started floating off into the sunrise destined for reincarnation, I began foolishly searching for a deeper meaning to the whisical chaos of the film. Do cats experience God like humans are known to do? Does time exist as an infinite line or does it loop-de-loop over and over again until our astral bodies fade from existence. But alas the revelation in the form of Dame Judy Dench(s face on a cats body) staring into the camera and singing about addressing your cat with respect. A message which to me hearkens back to the theme of universal suffering, itself a strangely fitting echo of the words of the Great Buddha and the 4 Noble Truths, simplified to express an even more basic truth. We are all here in this reality together, and as we suffer and fight to mold our existence into something a little less distressing, we should always remember to treat all creatures with the respect they deserve. I shockingly rated this film 3 stars, because despite the unintentionally laughable moments, the uncomfortable character design, and all the many WTF moments, I still found myself in appreciation, if for nothing else, than the sheer insanity that resulted in this film. ...Oh yea, and the fact that it's queer as Fuuuuuck!

My review of Cats (or A Stoner's Journey Into The Heart of Darkness) DISCLAIMER : This review is in no way an endorsement of the movie, please view at your own risk. (Mild Spoilers Ahead) So I finally find did something I had been considering for some time now. I got high and watched Cats and it nearly broke me. To preface, the choice to watch this movie on that very nigjt wasn't exactly random. If you follow me you might know that, immediately before this, I had watched a weird little gem of French cinema called Car Cemetery, a surreal punk rock "musical" mixing grimy, torturous and explicit sexual acts with messianic parable all while taking place in a post-apocalyptic junkyard. In my review of the movie I joked that it was "queerer than Cats." Not having seen Cats before and having an appreciation for strange and queer cinema, naturally I decided to put my money where my mouth is and challenge my assumptions on the matter. From the opening and throughout the first 10-15 minutes of the film I was engaged in an uncontrollable fit of hysterical laughter that seemed unstoppable despite my will to breathe. So early into the film, yet, had I already gone mad? How could this have been made with any intention other than to create a lovecraftian nightmare of fur and surreal landscapes. I believe the terror really set it about the time the Rebel Wilson Cat was concluding her number and began making unmistakeably suggestive petting motions. It was then I began to realized that all of these characters were trapped in an existential race towards death. The performers vying for the coveted "Jellical Choice" for their own reasons wanted to die. They were competing to prove which cat has suffered the most in whichever iteration of their 9 lives this was. Fear then turned to despair and however weird it was staring at Jennifer Hudson's face mapped onto a cartoonish cat body was not enough to distract me from the pain of existence that floated on every vocalization of "Memory." And then, just as it always does, the pain and suffering led to apathy. Maybe I too in some small way wanted to die, to move on from this nightmarish jest. Or maybe my hightened state of consciousness was just wearing off and I was getting bored. By the time the feline personification of Jennifer Hudson started floating off into the sunrise destined for reincarnation, I began foolishly searching for a deeper meaning to the whisical chaos of the film. Do cats experience God like humans are known to do? Does time exist as an infinite line or does it loop-de-loop over and over again until our astral bodies fade from existence. But alas the revelation in the form of Dame Judy Dench(s face on a cats body) staring into the camera and singing about addressing your cat with respect. A message which to me hearkens back to the theme of universal suffering, itself a strangely fitting echo of the words of the Great Buddha and the 4 Noble Truths, simplified to express an even more basic truth. We are all here in this reality together, and as we suffer and fight to mold our existence into something a little less distressing, we should always remember to treat all creatures with the respect they deserve. I shockingly rated this film 3 stars, because despite the unintentionally laughable moments, the uncomfortable character design, and all the many WTF moments, I still found myself in appreciation, if for nothing else, than the sheer insanity that resulted in this film. ...Oh yea, and the fact that it's queer as Fuuuuuck!

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

From the terrifying first trailer to the scathing reviews, I knew at some point in my life I was going to watch Cats. It was too much of an anomaly, too high-budget a disaster for me to ignore, I didn’t want to watch it, I HAD to see just how bad it was. And fuck me was this an absolutely terrifying fever dream filled with an uncomfortable amount of drugs, sex and music without having any drugs or sex and too much music. I’m genuinely scarred for having seen it all the way through. Let’s start with the plot. There isn’t any. And I’m not just saying that to be funny, this entire film is 90 minutes of introductions, 10 minutes of actual story and the other 10 minutes is weird panting and gyrating. Here I’ll give you a rundown of what happens; we open with our lead Victoria being abandoned by her owners, she’s introduced to the Jellicle Cats with their Jellicle Ball – and sidenote, they never explain what a Jellicle is and why it’s important to be one despite them saying Jellicle about 587 fucking times in the first five minutes – who take her to see the cats hoping to become the Jellicle choice and live a new life in the fucking sky or something. I swear to Christ, the little plot I can recognise as a story makes me think this is about a fucking suicide cult. From there Victoria meets Rebel Wilson’s hairy cooch, Jason Derulo’s CGI bulge, James Corden’s fat arse, a couple thieving twins who I couldn’t tell if they were related or not because of the fuck me eyes they were flashing at each other, Judi Dench’s old face and Ian McKellen making Meow noises before we actually get to the Jellicle Ball in which the contestants are STILL being introduced since the bad guy – Idris Elba and his unnervingly smooth fur body – has been stealing all the contestants with magic – oh by the way there’s fucking MAGIC in this film, they kinda dropped that on you without warning – so anyone who’s still taking part in the Ball we’ve never fucking seen before, making their musical numbers an exercise in futility because I don’t know them and I don’t want to fucking know them. Those two paragraphs cover around 80% of the story, all this film has is cats introducing themselves through song for an hour and a fucking half and then getting lucky if they have anything to say afterwards. It’s not a plot, it’s a fucking 2 hour montage of people we’ve never seen before and it doesn’t stop, new characters are still being introduced with their own numbers with over half the film already done. The only time it actually works is with Mr Mistoffelees who, despite a fairly low amount of screen-time, has been shown to be a cowardly magician and needs confidence to do Big Magic, that works but it comes so late into the game that it couldn’t save the rest of this train wreck. And before anyone dares defend this film, I know it’s based on a musical and I know it’s a different medium, but Hamilton managed to tell an entire historical story with only singing, this is just cats singing about themselves without a story to give them a reason to sing about themselves. The cast is absolutely stacked with big names who are given nothing to work with, and the ones that have something are the weakest actors in the film, I feel kinda bad for Francesca Hayward who plays Victoria because she’s suppose to be our lead, our surrogate into this bizarre, fucked up world of the Jellicle Cats and she’s given nothing, out of all the speaking parts she has probably the fewest amount of lines, every face she makes has this big wondrous smile about EVERYTHING, no matter how benign, and sure she dances well but in a film where everyone is dancing that doesn’t stand out. This is Hayward’s big theatrical break and she’s the most forgettable element in the film, which ironically might save her career. Out of everyone Victoria meets during the many MANY introductions she has to suffer through, not one of them make it worthwhile to sit through their number. Jason Derolo  - who I just hate in general anyway – sings about how Rum Tum Tugger  is a fussy little cunt then screams for milk, Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer were the thieving twins who looked like they wanted to do a furry version of a Bratty Sis video, and I didn’t know they were twins until writing this review so that just knocks the film even lower for me. There was also a tap dancing train conductor who serves no fucking purpose, Ray WInstone hissing and wondering where the fuck his career has gone and Taylor Swift who even in a film filled with unnecessary sexual energy, gave off too much sexual energy. Seriously man, I got Lola Bunny flashbacks during her number. Worst of the lot was Rebel Wilson and James Corden as Jennyanyfots and Bustopher Jones respectively, I already dislike these two before going into the film and having them both talk the most out of almost any other character was a kick in the fucking dick. Wilson’s introduction was this disturbing piece where she did the most unsexy sexy poses while the camera focussed on her naked hairy body before bringing in singing mice and marching cockroaches with human faces which Jenny proceeds to eat several of when she’s not singing. Corden meanwhile sings for five minutes about being a fat fuck and eating a lot, that’s the entirety of his character, he’s fucking fat, and the fact that both of them are just allowed to skit and makes shitty jokes is simultaneously distracting from the actual plot while adding nothing to the plot either. Both of them were just playing themselves in fur suits and like I said I think both are fucking overdone anyway so I didn’t give a shit about them either way. The only people I see coming out of here unscathed are Ian McKellen and Judi Dench who both have strong enough careers to look past this blip, although Dench’s monologue at the end where she looks at the camera goes on WAY too long about how a cat is not a dog (the fuck?) and every pause makes you think that it’s finally over but no, she keeps fucking going. Jennifer Hudson as Grizabella should also be ok, despite being important to the film she only has three scenes but among those three is her version of the famous ‘Memories’ number which is unironically good, hell I’d say too good for this turd of a film. I’m also hoping that Idris Elba comes out of this unaffected, his villain Macavity is suitably villainous and his motivations generically evil enough – he wants to be the Jellicle Choice because Fuck You I guess – that Elba can work something out with the material but between nobody being able to recognise the most wanted cat in town and his own horrifying nude cat-body, I doubt he’s getting away from this thing clean. Director Tom Hooper has done a few things of note over the last few years, namely his last three films were all Oscar winners and he brought Les Mes to the big screen so I can see why he’s be chosen for this. But holy hell does he fuck this up, this has to go down as one of the biggest fuck-ups of direction of the 21st Century because while Hooper doesn’t do anything technically wrong, nothing he does is done right. Let’s get the big one out of the way; the cats look fucking weird, I knew the cats looked weird, I saw the trailer, I saw the memes, but nothing prepared me for the seeing them in full CGI horror, the first time I saw a Cat-Man clamber down a brick wall, looking like a human being contorting their body into some kind of fucking Cronenberg nightmare with a tail I realised that this was so much worse than I thought it was going to be. It’s the deepest level of the uncanny valley I’ve seen since The Rock in The Mummy Returns and that was 18 fucking years before this, nobody looks human but they don’t look like a cat either, they’re a disgusting hybrid of the two, these vaguely human looking faces pasted onto what looks like skin-tight cat-suits made with actual cat flesh, it NEVER sits right with you. What makes it even more uncomfortable is that there seems to be no rhyme of reason to the clothing, a few cats wear clothing but most of them are nude and some of them even take off their clothes making them nude and I’m left wondering if this is just a nudist colony with lax rules or if everyone is suppose to be naked and we’re just suppose to accept it. I know I shouldn’t be this focussed on naked cat people but I can’t help it, this movie has forces naked cat people into my fucking brain and given me no fucking logic about why they’re naked, hell I haven’t even touched upon the Rebel Wilson scene where she unzips her naked fur-body, as  in literally takes off her skin, to reveal a dance outfit underneath. It’s the tightness as well, I don’t know why they went out of their way to make the cats sexy but it just feels wrong, all the naked cat actors have all their curves pronounced so that every breast, every bulge, every butt covered in fur is on full display but without any form of genitals. Elba gets the worst of it because his fur colour is identical to his skin colour leaving him looking like a fucking Ken Doll with ears but not one person looks good like this. And that’s not even talking about how horny this film is, I heard the stories, I read the reviews that talked about how sexual the film was but it’s not until you’re seeing this cat people twist their bodies together, panting in unison and nuzzle into each other that you have to take a step back and realise that humans doing cat actions is trying way too hard to be sexy whilst not trying to be sexy. The Jellicle Ball is the most horrific example, it’s the hissing, the panting, the Judi Dench hairy leg spread, I honestly couldn’t tell you if the film was trying to be this sexual and went way too far or if it wasn’t trying at all and just came off that way by accident. I haven’t even touched upon the fucking music because I don’t know how to, the visual disaster overpowers the audio so much that I can’t tell if anyone actual sung during this film or not. Ok, over exaggeration, a few songs worked but only a few, the aforementioned Memories hit well and I was fine with the Mr Mistoffelees number but outside of them I really can’t remember any of the songs being any good. The opening introduction to the Jellicle Cats was upbeat I guess, I was too distracted by the CONSTANT use of Jellicle, Jennyanydots was too distracting with the human cockroaches and under-skin dress change for me to even remember what the song was. Tugger and Bustopher were both boring, end of discussion, McKellen’s small number as Gus felt like a lot of build-up for a limp-dick crescendo and Swift’s piece of Macavity trying to big him up almost worked as a villain song if I wasn’t distracted by the complete lack of Idris Elba penis. Before this film the only knowledge I had of Cats was hearing Memories here and there and the rape story from Team America, having now seen this film I know even less about Cats and I don’t want to know anything more about Cats. This is one of the strangest, most confusing, unsettling and fucked up pieces of cinema I’ve ever seen that wasn’t an intentional horror movie, I’ve never seen anything like Cats so 10/10 for uniqueness but just because nobody’s done it before doesn’t mean it’s a good idea and Cats the Movie was not a good idea. There’s no story, all we have is oversexed sexless Cat People introducing themselves for 2 hours before nothing happens and the film ends, nobody looks good, only a couple sound good, the CGI is a mess, the sexiness uncomfortable, the songs forgettable and the whole experience traumatising. I’d say you have to see it just to get the full picture yourself but honestly you’re safer avoiding this. 2/10

I watched this film three times in theatres. It was my sophomore year of high school and one of the first films I saw when the theatres reopened. Snowbanks piled outside of the theatre, making those tall industrial lampposts seem small by comparison. I begged my friends to join me to watch this film—, which I had been raving about. Not because I thought it was technically apt, not by any stretch would I make such an argument now or then. No, because I found it hypnotic. We ascended the crusted snowbanks and into the theatre. The final viewing there was only six people in the theatre. My two friends and I, and three grown men in the very back row. For the first twenty minutes or so they meowed at us, and naturally we meowed back. By the end of the film I was overcome by what I can only describe as a psychedelic euphoria. My friends and I, as well as the men danced in front of the theatre screen together—, meowing along to the music. We never spoke a word to those men, I don’t think we ever clearly saw their faces, only backlit silhouettes only further eroded by the joy of human connection. This is a moment that will flash before my eyes on my death bed. This is the high I will forever chase and nothing will ever compare. This is why I love Cats.

For the first twenty minutes or so they meowed at us, and naturally we meowed back. By the end of the film I was overcome by what I can only describe as a psychedelic euphoria. My friends and I, as well as the men danced in front of the theatre screen together—, meowing along to the music. We never spoke a word to those men, I don’t think we ever clearly saw their faces, only backlit silhouettes only further eroded by the joy of human connection. messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

I really do love this movie more than I should. I know a lot of people find the visuals and some of the performances pretty detestable, and I understand that, but I think a lot of them are genuinely very good. The only truly awful performance is from Rebel Wilson, who manages to be intrusive in scenes dedicated to her. This is one of only two James Corden performances I defend, because I think he does a good job outside of the barge, where absolutely no one is doing their best work. It’s also fun to see the places where the visual style of the cats does work (mainly Old Deuteronomy and Gus) vs where it decidedly looks like a joke (think Macavity or Victoria). They seemingly removed a lot of the sexiness moving from the stage musical to Cats 2019, Id have to assume to appeal to as wide an audience as possible. Cats (1998) has a lot of the characters specifically play into things that are pretty widely considered hot, especially with someone like The Rum Tum Tugger being an amalgamation of Elvis and Bowie. There’s also this insane scene in the stage musical where they full body feel up Victoria for some reason. All of that has been removed and replaced with some light pawing and head nudges from some of the characters. The hottest thing in the movie is like, Taylor Swift cat doing cunty little dances or whatever.  Not to say this is either bad or good, just sort of interesting. I find this is inevitable when moving from sheer visual spectacle to like, trying to bring a coherent plot from cats. One thing I wasn’t too keen on watching these back to back was taking the songs from being sung about the cat by the rest of the Jellicles to being sung by the cat about themselves. It really goes from feeling like an introduction to these characters from a friendly face to being a railroading not dissimilar to a theme park. It also removes these ensembles that really are the heart and soul of Cats. Cats (1998) has so many moving bodies in every song and scene that the visual identity is never compromised. There’s never blank space if that makes sense. Cats 2019 eschews this in favor of taking on the styling of a 2010’s movie musical with all the various scenes. I’m just not certain it works. For as much as people whinge about the visual inconsistencies, be it size or fur or whatever I find it’s never really bothered me. The size being inconsistent is fine to me. I feel like people largely wouldn’t notice if it wasn’t pointed out to them. The biggest issue with the character design to me is their hands. They clearly don’t know how to give a Cat human hands and as such don’t even bother to try. It ends up being sort of distracting in a lot of scenes. Otherwise, which a few exceptions mentioned above, I actually found it to be unobtrusive after your brain has a second to adjust. Feels not dissimilar to the Navi from avatar to me. I love this movie dearly. Cats has always been THE peak musical to me. It’s got a little bit of everything and as such ends up feeling like this big silly romp. I love Skimbleshanks in this. I think his number in 2019 is maybe my favorite song across both variations (special mention to Growltiger’s Last Stand which I think also stands above) and I’m glad that the viewing populace tends to feel the same way. When I first started preaching about Cats 2019, nobody shared my sentiment that the film was good. Nowadays, it’s built a cult following especially amongst the online transgender crowd. It feels nice to find my people that way in much the same way Victoria does here.

Rebel Wilson and James Corden do improvisational comedy with all the ardor and skill of drama club kids whose families have just been taken hostage at gunpoint. Yet, everything else in this film has the feeling of watching a two hour cutaway gag from prime seasons of The Simpsons; it takes very little imagination to picture Troy McClure starring in this. When I saw this in theaters for the first time, I kept leaning over to my best friend and whispering, with unbridled exhilaration, "They made this into a movie!" Tom Hooper is not a talented director, which makes him perfect for this movie as a workmanlike, or even well made, version of this material would be forgetable to all but a handful of the most debased musical theater perverts. In Hooper's other pictures, he has a baseline level of competence more-or-less sufficient to overcome his penchant for deeply strange choices. Choices like like throwing dutch angles into his period prestige films-- or having the section of the John Adams miniseries where the title characeter goes to France mostly revolve around an elderly woman in clown make up jack off Benjamin Franklin in a tub (to be fair she could've also been milking his prostate; we don't get to see what's going on under the water). Here, however, the adulation Hooper received from his previous movies fried his brain; his hubris is archetypal. Every creative choice he makes big or small, is not merely off-- or sub-optimal-- they are objectively wrong. And that’s what makes Cats so special. There are many bad films, but they usually do some things right-- or alternatively they display a childlike lack of technical ability that reads as charming. Cats, inextricably, lands in neither category. It’s shaped like a movie. It has the bones, sinew, structure, and grammar of a movie in the way something like Birdemic or The Room never would. But despite its (mostly) quite talented cast, it's a series of wildly incorrect miscalculations that immediately begin to compound on one another and do not stop until the credits roll. I have never seen another movie like it and I watch it every chance I get. #Skimblegang

Give me The Room, Jaws 3-D, or Queen of the Damned, and I’m a happy man. Before the movie started, an Alamo employee stepped to the front of the theater. “Good news,” she announced. “Tomorrow Universal is sending us the fixed version. So tonight…you’re getting the butthole cut.” We all went nuts...and then could not stop cracking up. Like my sides hurt the next day and worth the Tylenol. All that being said...I’ve found myself feeling a little bad for director Tom Hooper. Yes, Cats is bizarre. Yes, it’s become a punchline. But this is also the filmmaker who gave us The King’s Speech and Les Misérables. One strange swing shouldn’t earn a lifetime sentence in director jail. The same goes for filmmakers like Martin Brest (BEVERLY HILLS COP, MIDNIGHT RUN) and John McTiernan (DIE HARD, THE HUNT FOR RED OCTOBER). Sometimes talented artists make masterpieces. Sometimes they make beautiful messes. Sometimes they make movies that become legendary for reasons nobody intended. And maybe that’s okay. What I remember most from that night isn’t the movie itself. It’s a packed theater in Los Angeles, filled with people from every background imaginable, sharing food, drinks, and uncontrollable laughter. For a couple of hours, nobody was arguing about politics, doom-scrolling, or yelling at each other online. We were just laughing. I really do love this movie more than I should. I know a lot of people find the visuals and some of the performances pretty detestable, and I understand that, but I think a lot of them are genuinely very good. It’s also fun to see the places where the visual style of the cats does work (mainly Old Deuteronomy and Gus) vs where it decidedly looks like a joke (think Macavity or Victoria). They seemingly removed a lot of the sexiness moving from the stage musical to Cats 2019, Id have to assume to appeal to as wide an audience as possible. Cats (1998) has a lot of the characters specifically play into things that are pretty widely considered hot, especially with someone like The Rum Tum Tugger being an amalgamation of Elvis and Bowie. There’s also this insane scene in the stage musical where they full body feel up Victoria for some reason. All of that has been removed and replaced with some light pawing and head nudges from some of the characters. The hottest thing in the movie is like, Taylor Swift cat doing cunty little dances or whatever.  Not to say this is either bad or good, just sort of interesting. I find this is inevitable when moving from sheer visual spectacle to like, trying to bring a coherent plot from cats. One thing I wasn’t too keen on watching these back to back was taking the songs from being sung about the cat by the rest of the Jellicles to being sung by the cat about themselves. It really goes from feeling like an introduction to these characters from a friendly face to being a railroading not dissimilar to a theme park. It also removes these ensembles that really are the heart and soul of Cats. Cats (1998) has so many moving bodies in every song and scene that the visual identity is never compromised. There’s never blank space if that makes sense. Cats 2019 eschews this in favor of taking on the styling of a 2010’s movie musical with all the various scenes. I’m just not certain it works. For as much as people whinge about the visual inconsistencies, be it size or fur or whatever I find it’s never really bothered me. The size being inconsistent is fine to me. I feel like people largely wouldn’t notice if it wasn’t pointed out to them. The biggest issue with the character design to me is their hands. Otherwise, which a few exceptions mentioned above, I actually found it to be unobtrusive after your brain has a second to adjust. Feels not dissimilar to the Navi from avatar to me. I love this movie dearly. Cats has always been THE peak musical to me. It’s got a little bit of everything and as such ends up feeling like this big silly romp. I love Skimbleshanks in this. messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"
    }
  ],
  "observacao_geral": "<1-2 frases>"
}

Really cool movie. I really liked it and it gave me a unique kind of feeling I don’t really get with most other movies. It’s rough, down right appalling and hard to watch at some points but for all the right reasons. I liked the fact that, while displaying some genuinely shocking things that most people would’ve never experienced or been exposed to, it didn’t glamorise them, focus too much on them or use them simply as shock value. It treated them as completely typical time and time again which I think is how most people growing up in that area (and the inspiration for the movie) saw these things. After a while, you started seeing things the same way. The cinematography was also really cool and effective. Particularly liked the club scene. Why not 5 stars? I mean I just didn’t ‘wow’ me as much as some of the 5 star movies I have. The thing is, I won’t see gang films or films about poverty the same after this, because I think it’s the most accurate portrayal of those themes ever (that also happens to be entertaining). Anyways I digress

This movie reminded me a bit of The Infierno, where the cycle of violence never truly ends—it just gets passed on to the next generation. In City of God, though, the city was literally lawless, so the violence didn't have to wait for one generation to die before continuing. The ambition and brutality were simply passed from one group of kids in the favela to the next. Li'l Zé is one of the most despicable, disgusting, and pathetic characters I've ever seen in a movie. The fact that the film reveals at the end that it's based on a true story hit me hard. People like that are out there. Even though he's a victim of the environment he grew up in, I don't feel any sympathy for him—not even when he was a child. He seemed to have the personality of a psychopath from the very beginning. It's incredible that Bené genuinely enjoyed the company of someone as pathetic as Zé. Not even his death made me feel any better because that rain of bullets wasn't nearly enough punishment for all the pain and terror he caused. Talking about the movie itself, I understand why it's considered a masterpiece. It certainly was for me too. I'm not new to this kind of non-chronological storytelling, but saving the opening scene until the last 15 minutes of the movie felt incredible. I thought it was going to be a Casino situation, where the opening scene doesn't come back until about an hour and a half into the film.

Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10

The ensemble cast is flawless with each character leaving an impact and the vibes are HIGH the entire time. Brutal gang violence never seemed so fun! The story sucks you in with characters you love and root for and characters you want to get turned into swiss cheese, stuff that makes you laugh and stuff that makes you wanna look away, but it’s also just lowkey a vibe. It feels like this could be a great movie to hangout to, and because so much is going on at once it could be amazing on a rewatch. This movie literally has it all I can’t recommend it enough. The ambition and brutality were simply passed from one group of kids in the favela to the next. Li'l Zé is one of the most despicable, disgusting, and pathetic characters I've ever seen in a movie. The fact that the film reveals at the end that it's based on a true story hit me hard. People like that are out there. Even though he's a victim of the environment he grew up in, I don't feel any sympathy for him—not even when he was a child. He seemed to have the personality of a psychopath from the very beginning. It's incredible that Bené genuinely enjoyed the company of someone as pathetic as Zé. Not even his death made me feel any better because that rain of bullets wasn't nearly enough punishment for all the pain and terror he caused. Talking about the movie itself, I understand why it's considered a masterpiece. It certainly was for me too. I'm not new to this kind of non-chronological storytelling, but saving the opening scene until the last 15 minutes of the movie felt incredible. I thought it was going to be a Casino situation, where the opening scene doesn't come back until about an hour and a half into the film.

Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10

[2] nota=1.0 estrelas:
Stephen King’s literary works have birthed some of the most iconic horror masterpieces in cinema history. However, the 1983 film adaptation of Cujo represents a staggering failure in narrative execution, stands as a masterclass in bad screenplaying, and serves as an ultimate waste of audience time. What promises to be a tense, claustrophobic thriller quickly devolves into an exercise in narrative stupidity, structural overkill, and profound boredom. The primary catalyst for the film's failure is the sheer stupidity woven into the fabric of the screenplay. For a horror film to maintain tension, the characters must make choices that feel organic, even if desperate. In Cujo, the characters are driven entirely by contrived ignorance designed solely to force the plot forward. The screenplay relies on a series of absurdly convenient oversights: a breaking car that happens to fail at the worst possible location, characters who refuse to communicate basic information to one another, and a complete lack of survival instincts. Because the script fails to establish intelligent stakes, the audience is left rooting against the human protagonists rather than fearing the antagonist. This structural ineptitude leads directly into the film's most egregious flaw: the central conflict gets boring after exactly five minutes. The novelty of a rabid St. Bernard trapping a mother and child inside a sweltering Ford Pinto wears off almost immediately. Once the physical parameters of the siege are established, the film completely runs out of ideas. The audience is subjected to endless, repetitive cycles of the dog barking at the window, the characters screaming, and the dog retreating, only to repeat the sequence moments later. Stripped of psychological depth or escalating tension, the film ceases to be scary and becomes aggressively monotonous. Compounding this boredom is the screenplay's reliance on overkill. Lacking the nuance required to sustain a feature-length film in a single location, the filmmakers substitute genuine terror with relentless, loud overstimulation. The editing becomes frantic, the score shrieks at every minor movement, and the dog is subjected to an absurd amount of cosmetic gore that feels cartoonish rather than frightening. By dialing every sensory element up to eleven without any narrative progression, the film numbs the audience. The overkill exposes the fundamental emptiness of the script; it is a short story stretched violently beyond its breaking point. Cujo is a monumental waste of time. It takes a terrifying, subtext-rich novel about family fractures and domestic terror and flattens it into a dull, repetitive creature feature. The screenplay lacks the wit to engage the mind, the pacing to hold the attention, or the restraint to build actual dread. Instead of delivering a tight, memorable thriller, Cujo leaves its audience trapped in a stagnant vehicle of poor filmmaking, praying for the credits to roll.

This was not great. A hard thing when adapting books to the screen is capturing all that rich internal narrative. Even with human characters, it can be hard to cram all of those thoughts onto the screen in a way that doesn’t feel forced. When the character is a dog, however, it is a much more difficult feat. And here, it shows. The book is full of Cujo’s own thoughts and feelings about what is happening to him. How he is reacting to sights and sounds once the rabies takes hold of him. It’s obviously incredibly hard to do this on screen, so we don’t get any of that. We’re also missing lots of important information about characters that we learn in the book. Lots of background and context for why they act the way they do. I get stuff has to be cut to account for a reasonable run time, but so much was cut here. Performances were decent, I don’t think anyone stood out in particular apart from the dog playing Cujo. Some parts of the plot were changed, and I don’t think they worked particularly well. Overall, quite disappointed with this considering how much I enjoyed the book!
