Wenn die Langeweile zur Last wird. Um das direkt zu Beginn klar zu stellen: Ich bin kein großer Fan der Buchvorlage von Stephen King, aber dennoch habe ich versucht dem Film eine faire Chance zu geben. Allerdings ist dieser Film so hochgradig langweilig, dass mir das irgendwann einfach nicht mehr möglich war. Denn die Geschichte zieht sich und zieht sich und es hört nicht auf. Sekunden werden zu Minuten, Minuten zu Stunden. Und dann sitzt da dieser Hund vor dem kaputten Auto, in welchem eine Mutter mit ihrem Kleinkind sitzt und es passiert nichts. Selbst wenn der Hund angreift ist das kaum spannend genug, um die Minuten davor und danach noch zu retten. Ich saß knappe 90 Minuten da und habe mir eine Film angesehen, der sich wie 180 anfühlt und versucht, den Zuschauer durch die Langeweile zu erdrücken. Die Handlung fand ich im Buch schon nicht allzu spannend. Vor allem aber auch, da ein Gefühl aufgebaut wird, welches mir nicht gefällt. Dieser Zeitdruck, der geschaffen wird, da die beiden Festsitzenden langsam einfach nicht mehr durchhalten. Im Film war das auch der Fall, aber es war mir ab einem gewissen Punkt einfach egal. Ich wusste was passieren würde, auch wenn der Film in einem Fall den Schwanz einzieht, und dann war es eben so. Die Handlung hat mich einfach kalt gelassen. Den Punkt, den ich "Cujo" aber geben muss, ist der Look und die Inszenierung. Denn der Look hat mich immer wieder an Horrorfilme aus den 70ern erinnert, die einfach dreckig und räudig aussehen. Genau das schafft der Film auch hin und wieder, was mir ziemlich gut gefallen hat. Die Inszenierung ist ebenfalls nicht übel. Diese beiden Punkt habe ich dann doch noch neutral sehen können. Denn das muss ich einfach sagen. Der Film scheitert an der Prämisse und nicht an der technischen Umsetzung, da ich die Kamera und Inszenierung vollkommen solide fand. Insgesamt ist "Cujo" also ein Film, den ich aufgrund des Pacings ziemlich schwer zu ertragen fand. 2/5 Sternen.

[39] nota=2.0 estrelas:
A snoozer of a King adaptation as horror that does have a couple things going for it as a family drama. Danny Pintauro is fantastic in his role as little Tad, making me believe he was actually frightened for his life when he and his mom were stuck in the car with zombified Cujo stalking outside (the best part of the whole movie by a mile). I've also got to give the film credit for its portrayal of the male lead as a father. It's rare to see good dads in movies that aren't explicitly geared as family fare. Dee Wallace's mom character is portrayed far more negatively, the way dads are more often shown, and the script lets her contain multitudes, as she seeks selfish pleasure and ultimately protects her son when she has to. It's pretty refreshing, actually. Cujo himself is a menacing villain, but everything plays out in such a lazy, laconic way that your interest flags. It's also shot with zero panache. Passable in ways, but it lacks the humor of better adaptations like Graveyard Shift and the pure filmmaking muscle of ones like Christine .

The screenplay relies on a series of absurdly convenient oversights: a breaking car that happens to fail at the worst possible location, characters who refuse to communicate basic information to one another, and a complete lack of survival instincts. Because the script fails to establish intelligent stakes, the audience is left rooting against the human protagonists rather than fearing the antagonist. This structural ineptitude leads directly into the film's most egregious flaw: the central conflict gets boring after exactly five minutes. The novelty of a rabid St. Bernard trapping a mother and child inside a sweltering Ford Pinto wears off almost immediately. Once the physical parameters of the siege are established, the film completely runs out of ideas. The audience is subjected to endless, repetitive cycles of the dog barking at the window, the characters screaming, and the dog retreating, only to repeat the sequence moments later. Stripped of psychological depth or escalating tension, the film ceases to be scary and becomes aggressively monotonous. Compounding this boredom is the screenplay's reliance on overkill. Lacking the nuance required to sustain a feature-length film in a single location, the filmmakers substitute genuine terror with relentless, loud overstimulation. The editing becomes frantic, the score shrieks at every minor movement, and the dog is subjected to an absurd amount of cosmetic gore that feels cartoonish rather than frightening. By dialing every sensory element up to eleven without any narrative progression, the film numbs the audience. The overkill exposes the fundamental emptiness of the script; it is a short story stretched violently beyond its breaking point. Cujo is a monumental waste of time. It takes a terrifying, subtext-rich novel about family fractures and domestic terror and flattens it into a dull, repetitive creature feature. The screenplay lacks the wit to engage the mind, the pacing to hold the attention, or the restraint to build actual dread. Instead of delivering a tight, memorable thriller, Cujo leaves its audience trapped in a stagnant vehicle of poor filmmaking, praying for the credits to roll.

This was not great. A hard thing when adapting books to the screen is capturing all that rich internal narrative. Even with human characters, it can be hard to cram all of those thoughts onto the screen in a way that doesn’t feel forced. When the character is a dog, however, it is a much more difficult feat. And here, it shows. The book is full of Cujo’s own thoughts and feelings about what is happening to him. How he is reacting to sights and sounds once the rabies takes hold of him. It’s obviously incredibly hard to do this on screen, so we don’t get any of that. We’re also missing lots of important information about characters that we learn in the book. Lots of background and context for why they act the way they do. I get stuff has to be cut to account for a reasonable run time, but so much was cut here. Performances were decent, I don’t think anyone stood out in particular apart from the dog playing Cujo. Some parts of the plot were changed, and I don’t think they worked particularly well. Overall, quite disappointed with this considering how much I enjoyed the book!

Um das direkt zu Beginn klar zu stellen: Ich bin kein großer Fan der Buchvorlage von Stephen King, aber dennoch habe ich versucht dem Film eine faire Chance zu geben. Allerdings ist dieser Film so hochgradig langweilig, dass mir das irgendwann einfach nicht mehr möglich war. Denn die Geschichte zieht sich und zieht sich und es hört nicht auf. Sekunden werden zu Minuten, Minuten zu Stunden. Und dann sitzt da dieser Hund vor dem kaputten Auto, in welchem eine Mutter mit ihrem Kleinkind sitzt und es passiert nichts. Selbst wenn der Hund angreift ist das kaum spannend genug, um die Minuten davor und danach noch zu retten. Ich saß knappe 90 Minuten da und habe mir eine Film angesehen, der sich wie 180 anfühlt und versucht, den Zuschauer durch die Langeweile zu erdrücken. Die Handlung fand ich im Buch schon nicht allzu spannend. Vor allem aber auch, da ein Gefühl aufgebaut wird, welches mir nicht gefällt. Dieser Zeitdruck, der geschaffen wird, da die beiden Festsitzenden langsam einfach nicht mehr durchhalten. Im Film war das auch der Fall, aber es war mir ab einem gewissen Punkt einfach egal. Ich wusste was passieren würde, auch wenn der Film in einem Fall den Schwanz einzieht, und dann war es eben so. Die Handlung hat mich einfach kalt gelassen. Den Punkt, den ich "Cujo" aber geben muss, ist der Look und die Inszenierung. Denn der Look hat mich immer wieder an Horrorfilme aus den 70ern erinnert, die einfach dreckig und räudig aussehen. Genau das schafft der Film auch hin und wieder, was mir ziemlich gut gefallen hat. Die Inszenierung ist ebenfalls nicht übel. Diese beiden Punkt habe ich dann doch noch neutral sehen können. Denn das muss ich einfach sagen. Der Film scheitert an der Prämisse und nicht an der technischen Umsetzung, da ich die Kamera und Inszenierung vollkommen solide fand. Insgesamt ist "Cujo" also ein Film, den ich aufgrund des Pacings ziemlich schwer zu ertragen fand. 2/5 Sternen.

A snoozer of a King adaptation as horror that does have a couple things going for it as a family drama. I've also got to give the film credit for its portrayal of the male lead as a father. It's rare to see good dads in movies that aren't explicitly geared as family fare. Dee Wallace's mom character is portrayed far more negatively, the way dads are more often shown, and the script lets her contain multitudes, as she seeks selfish pleasure and ultimately protects her son when she has to. It's pretty refreshing, actually. Cujo himself is a menacing villain, but everything plays out in such a lazy, laconic way that your interest flags. It's also shot with zero panache. Passable in ways, but it lacks the humor of better adaptations like Graveyard Shift and the pure filmmaking muscle of ones like Christine .

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.

7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

I watched this because I saw a TikTok saying that Martin Scorsese called this as Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s most terrifying film. It's really not a terrifying or even traditionally disturbing film. It's like a slow-burn detective story, but even so, it doesn’t fully grip either. It doesn’t have that usual pull, no strong sense of piecing clues together or being hooked by the mystery. The pacing is deliberately slow, almost hypnotic, but instead of drawing me in, I just felt bored. I know it's how easily people can be influenced into something darker. That violence isn’t always something external, but something already sitting beneath the surface. But even if I understood all the references, it still didn't resonate with me.

[6] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Though this may controversial, I did not enjoy this film at all. I feel like there’s something i’m missing. I can appreciate its approach in blocking, lighting, and general impact on J-Horror, but it felt like Kurosawa maybe relied too much on abstract storytelling to fully convey his message. Ambiguous endings can be used in very creative ways, but it almost felt like Cure left way too many questions unanswered (to the point where it was hard to interpret every single one). All the intentional “open ended” questions throughout this film almost left a bad impression- and it kind of ruined what could have been an incredibly unique form of storytelling.

[7] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Esse filme foi a segunda decepção do ano, logo depois de "La chimera" e realmente acho, que o grande problema para eu não ter gostado foi, novamente, ter criado muita expectativa. A ideia do filme é genial e as atuações em um geral são muito boas, principalmente do ator que faz o Mamiya, porém a construção dessa ideia e o decorrer da história simplesmente não me agradaram. Tudo é muito monótono, quieto e calmo, quase toda parte do filme. Além disso, é necessário ficar batendo cabeça do início ao fim do filme para entender coisas simples e básicas, que o diretor deixa solto ou apenas disponibiliza migalhas, para que possamos pensar e ligar os pontos, mas certas coisas passam do limite do normal e quando chega ao final do filme você não entendeu grande parte do filme. Não digo que não entendi, mas sim que é um longo caminho até chegar a mensagem que o diretor realmente quer passar. Acredito que o Kurosawa tentou fazer algo tão mirabolante, genial e místico, mas que no final se perdeu um pouco, na minha concepção. Ele quis trazer muitos detalhes e certas coisas que ficam em aberto, ou pistas pequenas, que são de extrema importância para a compreensão de determinados pontos, mas que no final fica difícil ligar tantas informações e tantas pistas para formular uma linha de pensamento. Penso que, talvez, se eu ver esse filme futuramente, posso mudar de ideia, até porque, como falei, a ideia do filme é promissora e bem interessante, mas para mim neste momento, foi mal direcionada e confusa.

[33] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Un thriller psicológico que avanza con mucha calma, pero utiliza ese ritmo para construir una sensación constante de inquietud. Más que resolver un misterio, parece interesado en explorar la fragilidad de la mente humana y lo fácil que una persona puede derribar las inhibiciones de otras cuando encuentra las grietas adecuadas. La violencia no surge de la nada, sino de impulsos que ya estaban ahí, esperando ser liberados. Su final ambiguo me pareció uno de sus mayores aciertos. La idea de que la manipulación y la violencia puedan reproducirse como un ciclo, más que como un hecho aislado, resulta inquietante y deja preguntas abiertas en lugar de respuestas cómodas. En conjunto, me pareció una propuesta muy interesante y bien construida. Su mayor virtud también puede ser su mayor defecto: confía tanto en la ambigüedad que, por momentos, deja demasiado a la interpretación. Para algunos eso será parte de su encanto; para otros, una fuente de frustración.

Un thriller psicológico que avanza con mucha calma, pero utiliza ese ritmo para construir una sensación constante de inquietud. Más que resolver un misterio, parece interesado en explorar la fragilidad de la mente humana y lo fácil que una persona puede derribar las inhibiciones de otras cuando encuentra las grietas adecuadas. La violencia no surge de la nada, sino de impulsos que ya estaban ahí, esperando ser liberados. Su final ambiguo me pareció uno de sus mayores aciertos. La idea de que la manipulación y la violencia puedan reproducirse como un ciclo, más que como un hecho aislado, resulta inquietante y deja preguntas abiertas en lugar de respuestas cómodas. En conjunto, me pareció una propuesta muy interesante y bien construida. Su mayor virtud también puede ser su mayor defecto: confía tanto en la ambigüedad que, por momentos, deja demasiado a la interpretación. Para algunos eso será parte de su encanto; para otros, una fuente de frustración.

There’s either something I missed or I just wasn’t in the right mood, because this critically acclaimed ‘ masterpiece ’ was neither ‘ mesmerising ’ nor particularly ‘ powerful ’, and quite frankly I didn’t care for it all that much. Apparently kicking off the wave of late 90s J-Horror, I don't really see this as part of that canon, being a different beast entirely. I love a drawn out methodically psychological thriller, and this most definitely has those qualities in a not so short supply, but for me it borders on the miserable and gruelling with none of the chilling or foreboding tone able to pull me in, and a less than satisfying payoff, or lack thereof. I didn’t enjoy the directors later effort, the fiercely overrated Pulse, so obviously his style is just not working for me, but I’m truly surprised how much this one missed the mark in my opinion. There were elements of the cult 70s underground flick Blue Sunshine, but all it did was make me want to revisit that classic and forget about this entirely.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.

4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.

6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.

[9] nota=2.5 estrelas:
It wants to be a political movie about apartheid, so it's set in South Africa. But it doesn't have anything to say about actual, real life South African apartheid and it's legacy, so the profoundly poignant history of the setting is ignored, and South Africa just becomes a vaguely impoverished, multiracial backdrop. There are implied economic differences between the Black and white South Africans, but nothing political. The story is about an entirely fictional apartheid, with no care for how the situation would intersect with the actual history of a recently overthrown apartheid regime, and so what should have been an evocative setting winds up coming across as rather tone deff, in a way that it wouldn't have if the movie were just set in Europe. The movie is set in 2008, which means that the mothership would have landed in 1988 . . . six years before South African apartheid fucking ended. And I want it said that I like this movie! It's an interesting and entertaining work of science fiction, that inverts a lot of alien invasion tropes in a way that I find compelling. I just can't get over the superficially woke ignorance of its political framing. As much as I enjoy forwardly political movies, I feel like District 9 is at its best when it's not trying to make obviouse real-world comparisons—the premise is political enough, we don't need to see the Black South African masses marching through the streets calling for apartheid!

There’s something fascinating about the movie’s strange sense of realism. Of course, the story itself is completely unrealistic, but the movie is remarkably meticulous in its pursuit of realism. The documentary-style direction is part of it, but so are all the carefully prepared details: the derogatory terms used for the aliens, the justifications put forward by the corporations, the human-rights organizations, and so on. All of these little touches make the world feel much more real. The visual quality is excellent, too. Whether it’s the sight of a gigantic UFO hovering over the city or the scenes inside the alien settlement, everything feels surprisingly natural and never out of place. That’s actually quite an achievement. And although it’s a little grotesque, I also liked the technique of having bits of flesh occasionally splatter against the camera lens. It’s a simple but very effective touch.

This is filmslop: a terrible movie masked by good production and the illusion of progressivism. Like One Battle After Another (OBAA), this movie takes a very surface-level approach to addressing progressive issues. It uses imagery inspired by the events that took place in District Six, when 60,000 Black South Africans were forcibly removed from their homes and relocated by the Apartheid Government. Furthermore, this movie depicts police brutality, medical torture, xenophobia, segregation, corporate abuse, war profiteering, and more. However, like OBAA, its purpose is to create surface-level sympathy for the aliens and obstacles for our MC, instead of interrogating these issues, their effects, and using them to reflect the ills of our society. This film tries to pull a white-saviour story on us, but utterly fails because of how EVIL our MC is. MC is a horrible person from the get-go; he's a depraved, power-hungry psychopath who only sides with the aliens because he needs to, not because he wants to. He never grows in this story, staying the same miserable human he always was. As for the aliens, how we're meant to see them and how they're depicted are very different. On one hand, they display humanity, with relationships, worries, and feelings, but on the other hand, you can't help but understand the actions of our villains, as the aliens are only depicted as crazed maniacs, and any facts given to us only reinforce these views, instead of debunking them. Its depictions of Nigerians are very racist. This film plays into racist caricatures of Nigerians, viewing them as violent scammers who believe in nonsensical rituals, when this is clearly not the case. The tone is all over the place. I have no idea what I'm supposed to feel in any given moment, and I don't think this movie does either. For example, at the start, it tries to balance its very dark depictions of the beginnings of forced resettlement with humour, but fails miserably as it doesn't know when to stop being comedic or dark. There are also many plot holes apparent in this film, relating to the aliens, the authoritarian company that manages District 9 and more. This adds more layers of confusion to an already confusing mess of a film. In conclusion, this film is SO BAD.

I distinctly remember seeing District 9 in theaters in 2009 and disliking it. Given the overwhelming praise it received, I always wondered whether I had missed something? After finally revisiting it all these years later, I’m convinced that my initial reaction was correct: District 9 isn’t good. The film fails for me in two main areas: story and style. Narratively, it presents itself as an intelligent, original piece of high-concept science fiction, but it’s really anything but. The apartheid allegory is immediately obvious and handled with very little subtlety. Beyond that, the plot becomes repetitive and never develops into anything especially compelling. Wikus is also a weak and passive protagonist, which makes it difficult to invest in his transformation or care about what happens to him. Stylistically, the film combines documentary and found-footage techniques, but neither approach is convincing. The multiple camera angles, conspicuously scripted interviews, and constant shifts in perspective prevent it from ever feeling like an authentic documentary. It also repeatedly uses the “blood on the lens technique” every time someone gets shot, which gets old incredibly quickly. With an unsubtle and unengaging narrative, ugly visuals, unconvincing presentation, and a protagonist I couldn’t root for, I’m left wondering what the film is actually offering? Ultimately, not much.

There are things about the first half of District 9 that I found interesting. The mockumentary format works well, and the film’s depiction of bureaucracy, forced relocation, and casual dehumanization gives it a more interesting foundation than where the movie ultimately finishes. I really struggled with the apartheid allegory at the center of it. I understand the commentary the film is attempting to make, but drawing such an explicit parallel between the victims of South African apartheid and a population of literal aliens feels like a strange and uncomfortable comparison. I understand what the film is reaching for, but I could not get past the feeling that framing such a horrific and very real history through this particular comparison risks delegitimizing some of its horrors rather than meaningfully illuminating them. I also found Wikus difficult to invest in for much of the movie. His eventual empathy feels less like a genuine reckoning with the cruelty he has participated in and more like something forced upon him once he begins experiencing that cruelty himself. There are interesting ideas here, and I understand why the film has endured, but I was much more interested in the movie District 9 seemed to be during its first act. By the time it turns into a fairly conventional action sci-fi movie, a lot of what initially made it interesting gets lost. I kept wishing it would return to the questions it had raised instead of shooting its way through them.

This is filmslop: a terrible movie masked by good production and the illusion of progressivism. Like One Battle After Another (OBAA), this movie takes a very surface-level approach to addressing progressive issues. It uses imagery inspired by the events that took place in District Six, when 60,000 Black South Africans were forcibly removed from their homes and relocated by the Apartheid Government. Furthermore, this movie depicts police brutality, medical torture, xenophobia, segregation, corporate abuse, war profiteering, and more. However, like OBAA, its purpose is to create surface-level sympathy for the aliens and obstacles for our MC, instead of interrogating these issues, their effects, and using them to reflect the ills of our society. This film tries to pull a white-saviour story on us, but utterly fails because of how EVIL our MC is. MC is a horrible person from the get-go; he's a depraved, power-hungry psychopath who only sides with the aliens because he needs to, not because he wants to. He never grows in this story, staying the same miserable human he always was. As for the aliens, how we're meant to see them and how they're depicted are very different. On one hand, they display humanity, with relationships, worries, and feelings, but on the other hand, you can't help but understand the actions of our villains, as the aliens are only depicted as crazed maniacs, and any facts given to us only reinforce these views, instead of debunking them. Its depictions of Nigerians are very racist. This film plays into racist caricatures of Nigerians, viewing them as violent scammers who believe in nonsensical rituals, when this is clearly not the case. The tone is all over the place. I have no idea what I'm supposed to feel in any given moment, and I don't think this movie does either. For example, at the start, it tries to balance its very dark depictions of the beginnings of forced resettlement with humour, but fails miserably as it doesn't know when to stop being comedic or dark. There are also many plot holes apparent in this film, relating to the aliens, the authoritarian company that manages District 9 and more. This adds more layers of confusion to an already confusing mess of a film. In conclusion, this film is SO BAD.

I distinctly remember seeing District 9 in theaters in 2009 and disliking it. Given the overwhelming praise it received, I always wondered whether I had missed something? After finally revisiting it all these years later, I’m convinced that my initial reaction was correct: District 9 isn’t good. The film fails for me in two main areas: story and style. Narratively, it presents itself as an intelligent, original piece of high-concept science fiction, but it’s really anything but. The apartheid allegory is immediately obvious and handled with very little subtlety. Beyond that, the plot becomes repetitive and never develops into anything especially compelling. Wikus is also a weak and passive protagonist, which makes it difficult to invest in his transformation or care about what happens to him. Stylistically, the film combines documentary and found-footage techniques, but neither approach is convincing. The multiple camera angles, conspicuously scripted interviews, and constant shifts in perspective prevent it from ever feeling like an authentic documentary. It also repeatedly uses the “blood on the lens technique” every time someone gets shot, which gets old incredibly quickly. With an unsubtle and unengaging narrative, ugly visuals, unconvincing presentation, and a protagonist I couldn’t root for, I’m left wondering what the film is actually offering? Ultimately, not much.

There are things about the first half of District 9 that I found interesting. The mockumentary format works well, and the film’s depiction of bureaucracy, forced relocation, and casual dehumanization gives it a more interesting foundation than where the movie ultimately finishes. I really struggled with the apartheid allegory at the center of it. I understand the commentary the film is attempting to make, but drawing such an explicit parallel between the victims of South African apartheid and a population of literal aliens feels like a strange and uncomfortable comparison. I understand what the film is reaching for, but I could not get past the feeling that framing such a horrific and very real history through this particular comparison risks delegitimizing some of its horrors rather than meaningfully illuminating them. I also found Wikus difficult to invest in for much of the movie. His eventual empathy feels less like a genuine reckoning with the cruelty he has participated in and more like something forced upon him once he begins experiencing that cruelty himself. There are interesting ideas here, and I understand why the film has endured, but I was much more interested in the movie District 9 seemed to be during its first act. By the time it turns into a fairly conventional action sci-fi movie, a lot of what initially made it interesting gets lost. I kept wishing it would return to the questions it had raised instead of shooting its way through them.

Sci-fi action movie filmed primarily in a mockumentary/found footage style, but it intermittently breaks from that to a traditional 3rd person narrative and even uses news broadcast blurbs at times. The format switches work very well. The unknown cast adds realism to the mockumentary style. It’s a good story, a fresh take on first contact and a brutally honest portrayal of how humanity would probably react. Heavily themed on Apartheid and racial injustice, while also taking aim at corporate greed and the global military industrial complex. A subplot has a ruthless corporate executive openly plotting against his own son in law. The irony of the main character having to lose his humanity to become humane parallels the viewer’s transformation to rooting for the aliens by the third act. Excellent cgi effects for the aliens and alien technology, and practical body horror. While the sci-fi elements and themes are prevalent, this is first and foremost an action movie. Hardly a dull moment.

It’s an action alien movie with crazy weapons and a fair amount of gore, but it’s not your stereotypical action alien movie with crazy weapons and a fair amount of gore. I simultaneously love the story and am pretty pissed off by the story (complimentary). Like I’ve questioned before with movies, including my beloved Arrival , why is mankind so quick to assume the worst intent from those not like us? Why must we always seek self-gain at the expense of others? My main critique is the way in which our main character develops; it’s a fairly common trope that I saw coming from a mile away and didn’t add much substance for me. I have ideas on how I would’ve liked to have seen District 9 end, but we deal with what we’re dealt. Other than that, I love the action, I love the effects, I love the themes and social commentary, and I wish I hadn’t waited years to watch.

Sci-fi action movie filmed primarily in a mockumentary/found footage style, but it intermittently breaks from that to a traditional 3rd person narrative and even uses news broadcast blurbs at times. The format switches work very well. The unknown cast adds realism to the mockumentary style. It’s a good story, a fresh take on first contact and a brutally honest portrayal of how humanity would probably react. Heavily themed on Apartheid and racial injustice, while also taking aim at corporate greed and the global military industrial complex. A subplot has a ruthless corporate executive openly plotting against his own son in law. The irony of the main character having to lose his humanity to become humane parallels the viewer’s transformation to rooting for the aliens by the third act. Excellent cgi effects for the aliens and alien technology, and practical body horror. While the sci-fi elements and themes are prevalent, this is first and foremost an action movie. Hardly a dull moment.

[3] nota=0.5 estrelas:
From the uncomfortable, unappealing, ugly jig of the film's head-scratching overlong opening to the contradictory and incoherently paired quotations by MLK and Malcolm X at the end, this is an in-your-face obnoxious mess that has no clear idea of what it wants to say but is utterly convinced of its own grand importance. The film consists almost entirely of babbling losers spending the whole day aimlessly wandering back and forth on a small stretch of road. Almost without exception these are not characters but thinly drawn racist stereotypes of purposeless black idiots who are hell-bent on getting themselves into trouble but are too stupid to know how to do even that. What is supposed to pass for acting is way-the-hell over-the-top mugging by everyone except the bland and stilted phoned-in performance of the film's wannabe auteur director/screenwriter/producer Spike Lee as well as two fine performances by two of the film's three major white actors, the always excellent John Turturro and Danny Aiello. Lee loves his grandiloquent soliloquies, which consist either of lists or of outright plagiarism (or "homage," as he would dishonestly put it). There is a short montage of several actors one by one looking directly into the camera and each insulting a particular race; the insults consist of lists of nouns and adjectives; they are predicates without propositions. There is a gratuitously long list of popular black American musicians rattled off by Sam Jackson's radio host; the sole purpose here is to provide evidence that, despite what we see depicted in the film in terms of black people's behavior, many black Americans have been very successful in music; yes, that is as much of a non sequitur as it seems. Also shoehorned into the film is identification by name of to that point (1989) every black American political activist, politician, entertainer, and athlete; it is just a product placement-like in-aggregate information dump intended to serve the same purpose as the radio host's annoying list. The plagiarism is in the form of one mostly mute knuckle dragger's beat-by-beat reiteration of Robert Mitchum's love/hate soliloquy from The Night of the Hunter; it makes no sense that this individual would be familiar, certainly to the extent of memorization, with this cultural reference. This individual's sole mission is to be as irritating as possible by blaring his loud radio at everyone to provoke a response. It is all just back-and-forth yelling until a white character smashes the radio, giving this dude his pretext for attempted murder and Lee his pretext for showing the cops killing the provocateur and the mob its pretext to engage in wanton destruction. At this point the loosely knit mob of miscreants unites in its fulfilling its collective purpose of attempting to murder whitey, burning his business to the ground, and attacking the emergency responders when they arrive. These violent black thugs trying to commit suicide by cop invoke the names of real-life violent black thugs (Michael Stewart and Eleanor Bumpurs, misspelled as "Bumpers" in the end-credits dedication) who in real life did get themselves killed by the fault of their own similar recklessness. Is this hateful, insidious wreck of a movie really positing the perspective that these arsonists and would-be murderers are, or believe themselves to be, oppressed by the genial owner of the one place where they each go multiple times per day to purchase food, namely slices of pizza? What does "fight the power" (a phrase repeated about a million times in this movie) mean if not that? At the same time are we supposed to respond sympathetically when a violent mob of "fucking niggers" (to use Spike Lee's obsessively repeated choice phrase) attempt to murder the white man and then burn the place to the ground before turning on the Korean shop owner across the street and threatening him with the same fate for no reason other than that he is not black? The race riot scene is a sadistic fantasy of a racially inverted recreation of the Howard Beach incident (the mob in the film chants "Howard Beach"), the mythical attack of a black man by a white mob outside of a pizzeria in New York a few years before this movie came out. The myopic libs of 1989 America, and worldwide, were too busy drooling all over themselves and each other in competitive heaping of praise upon this work of fiction to notice or care about the world's largest democracy movement in generations, which was ongoing by the film's May 19 Cannes showing and which was weeks past its bloody finale by the film's June 30 wide release. This film's revolution around interpersonal bickering takes on a sobering context in light of the PLA's massacre of thousands, albeit thousands of miles away. The point is not that the film should be criticized with respect to an unrelated contemporaneous political event, but rather that the inordinately high critical appraisal derives not so much from a considered assessment of the film on its merits as from a conflation of the film's social consciousness with its artistic value, this conflation based in a paucity of perspective of the extent of that consciousness. At one point the graffiti'd phrase "TAWANA TOLD THE TRUTH!" appears very prominently, to put it lightly. Is this a commentary on the credulity of those who were still clinging to their desperate gang-rape fantasy, or is it a statement of sincerity? Just before the end credits why do we have MLK telling us (namely, black Americans) to be non-violent but then Malcolm X exhorting "us" to violence? Is the senseless violence depicted in the film supposed to give its community of perpetrators a sense of accomplishment for having driven out one of the vanishingly small number of businesses operating in their ghetto neighborhood? How does it make any sense that this decent guy would be an oppressor of any sort or part of "the power" to fight? The film has no idea about any of this. Like the rioters leaning in to their true calling of vicious hooliganism, Lee has heard of the names of some high-profile black people, many accomplished, some criminal, and wants to make a movie having something vaguely to do with them, but he got too wrapped up in the aimless wandering to care in the slightest about what his original objective was or where he was going, if he was ever going anywhere at all.

I was honestly prepared to give this half a star. Then the Martin Luther King Jr. quotation appeared at the end and, for a moment, I thought the film had managed to redeem itself. Two stars, perhaps. Then came the Malcolm X quotation, and I was back down to one. For me, this is a confused and frustrating film, muddled in its broader argument. The performances are strong, and the actors do what they can with the material, but the dialogue often feels artificial and overly constructed. Rather than emerging organically, the story often feels as if it has been built around a thesis the film itself has not fully worked out. My issue is not with the film’s anger at racism, police brutality or the marginalisation of black communities. Those are urgent and historically entrenched issues. My issue is with the way the film frames its central conflict, particularly around Sal’s pizzeria. Yes, it is an Italian-owned business in a Black neighbourhood, and that context matters. But it is still an Italian-American pizzeria. The demand that Sal place black public figures on his Wall of Fame is presented as a question of representation… but, representation cannot simply mean overriding the cultural identity of a space because it happens to exist within a different community. Yes, in the 1980s, the lack of black representation in American public life is a serious problem. But is the wall of an immigrant-owned pizzeria really the battleground on which that struggle should be fought? The film becomes even more troubling in its final act. Radio Raheem’s death at the hands of the police is unjust and horrifying. The police are clearly responsible for that death. But the escalation that precedes it is not morally simple either. A group enters Sal’s pizzeria aggressively, tensions rise, Sal reacts poorly, violence erupts, and then the police arrive and kill a man. That killing is the central injustice. But does that automatically make Sal responsible for what the police did? Was his business the correct object of retaliation? Spike Lee has said that only white viewers tend to ask whether Mookie “did the right thing”, arguing that the real issue is the difference between property damage and the death of a black man. I understand that distinction, and it is obviously true that a human life is worth infinitely more than a shop window. But that does not, by itself, settle the moral question. Property damage and state violence are not equivalent, but nor does the horror of one automatically justify the other. The question is not whether Sal’s window matters more than Radio Raheem’s life. Of course it does not. The question is whether destroying Sal’s pizzeria was a meaningful act of resistance, an act of misdirected rage, or something more ambiguous. This is where I find the film, and Lee’s later commentary on it, frustrating. There seems to be an almost absolute certainty about what “the right thing” is, yet the film itself ends with two quotations that appear to be in philosophical mismatch with one another. If the answer is supposed to be so obvious, why close the film with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X? Why invite that contradiction and then treat the central moral question as if it should not be asked? I would probably have appreciated Do the Right Thing more had I known less about Spike Lee’s own interpretations of it, and less about some of the troubling accounts surrounding his behaviour on set. Taken purely as a film, it has energy, anger and some visual confidence. But as a political statement, I found it far less persuasive than its reputation suggests. From the uncomfortable, unappealing, ugly jig of the film's head-scratching overlong opening to the contradictory and incoherently paired quotations by MLK and Malcolm X at the end, this is an in-your-face obnoxious mess that has no clear idea of what it wants to say but is utterly convinced of its own grand importance. The film consists almost entirely of babbling losers spending the whole day aimlessly wandering back and forth on a small stretch of road. Almost without exception these are not characters but thinly drawn racist stereotypes of purposeless black idiots who are hell-bent on getting themselves into trouble but are too stupid to know how to do even that. What is supposed to pass for acting is way-the-hell over-the-top mugging by everyone except the bland and stilted phoned-in performance of the film's wannabe auteur director/screenwriter/producer Spike Lee as well as two fine performances by two of the film's three major white actors, the always excellent John Turturro and Danny Aiello. Lee loves his grandiloquent soliloquies, which consist either of lists or of outright plagiarism (or "homage," as he would dishonestly put it). There is a short montage of several actors one by one looking directly into the camera and each insulting a particular race; the insults consist of lists of nouns and adjectives; they are predicates without propositions. There is a gratuitously long list of popular black American musicians rattled off by Sam Jackson's radio host; the sole purpose here is to provide evidence that, despite what we see depicted in the film in terms of black people's behavior, many black Americans have been very successful in music; yes, that is as much of a non sequitur as it seems. Also shoehorned into the film is identification by name of to that point (1989) every black American political activist, politician, entertainer, and athlete; it is just a product placement-like in-aggregate information dump intended to serve the same purpose as the radio host's annoying list. The plagiarism is in the form of one mostly mute knuckle dragger's beat-by-beat reiteration of Robert Mitchum's love/hate soliloquy from The Night of the Hunter; it makes no sense that this individual would be familiar, certainly to the extent of memorization, with this cultural reference. This individual's sole mission is to be as irritating as possible by blaring his loud radio at everyone to provoke a response. It is all just back-and-forth yelling until a white character smashes the radio, giving this dude his pretext for attempted murder and Lee his pretext for showing the cops killing the provocateur and the mob its pretext to engage in wanton destruction. At this point the loosely knit mob of miscreants unites in its fulfilling its collective purpose of attempting to murder whitey, burning his business to the ground, and attacking the emergency responders when they arrive. These violent black thugs trying to commit suicide by cop invoke the names of real-life violent black thugs (Michael Stewart and Eleanor Bumpurs, misspelled as "Bumpers" in the end-credits dedication) who in real life did get themselves killed by the fault of their own similar recklessness. Is this hateful, insidious wreck of a movie really positing the perspective that these arsonists and would-be murderers are, or believe themselves to be, oppressed by the genial owner of the one place where they each go multiple times per day to purchase food, namely slices of pizza? What does "fight the power" (a phrase repeated about a million times in this movie) mean if not that? At the same time are we supposed to respond sympathetically when a violent mob of "fucking niggers" (to use Spike Lee's obsessively repeated choice phrase) attempt to murder the white man and then burn the place to the ground before turning on the Korean shop owner across the street and threatening him with the same fate for no reason other than that he is not black? The race riot scene is a sadistic fantasy of a racially inverted recreation of the Howard Beach incident (the mob in the film chants "Howard Beach"), the mythical attack of a black man by a white mob outside of a pizzeria in New York a few years before this movie came out. The myopic libs of 1989 America, and worldwide, were too busy drooling all over themselves and each other in competitive heaping of praise upon this work of fiction to notice or care about the world's largest democracy movement in generations, which was ongoing by the film's May 19 Cannes showing and which was weeks past its bloody finale by the film's June 30 wide release. This film's revolution around interpersonal bickering takes on a sobering context in light of the PLA's massacre of thousands, albeit thousands of miles away. The point is not that the film should be criticized with respect to an unrelated contemporaneous political event, but rather that the inordinately high critical appraisal derives not so much from a considered assessment of the film on its merits as from a conflation of the film's social consciousness with its artistic value, this conflation based in a paucity of perspective of the extent of that consciousness. At one point the graffiti'd phrase "TAWANA TOLD THE TRUTH!" appears very prominently, to put it lightly. Is this a commentary on the credulity of those who were still clinging to their desperate gang-rape fantasy, or is it a statement of sincerity? Just before the end credits why do we have MLK telling us (namely, black Americans) to be non-violent but then Malcolm X exhorting "us" to violence? Is the senseless violence depicted in the film supposed to give its community of perpetrators a sense of accomplishment for having driven out one of the vanishingly small number of businesses operating in their ghetto neighborhood? How does it make any sense that this decent guy would be an oppressor of any sort or part of "the power" to fight? The film has no idea about any of this. Like the rioters leaning in to their true calling of vicious hooliganism, Lee has heard of the names of some high-profile black people, many accomplished, some criminal, and wants to make a movie having something vaguely to do with them, but he got too wrapped up in the aimless wandering to care in the slightest about what his original objective was or where he was going, if he was ever going anywhere at all.

I was honestly prepared to give this half a star. Then the Martin Luther King Jr. quotation appeared at the end and, for a moment, I thought the film had managed to redeem itself. Two stars, perhaps. Then came the Malcolm X quotation, and I was back down to one. For me, this is a confused and frustrating film, muddled in its broader argument. The performances are strong, and the actors do what they can with the material, but the dialogue often feels artificial and overly constructed. Rather than emerging organically, the story often feels as if it has been built around a thesis the film itself has not fully worked out. My issue is not with the film’s anger at racism, police brutality or the marginalisation of black communities. Those are urgent and historically entrenched issues. My issue is with the way the film frames its central conflict, particularly around Sal’s pizzeria. Yes, it is an Italian-owned business in a Black neighbourhood, and that context matters. But it is still an Italian-American pizzeria. The demand that Sal place black public figures on his Wall of Fame is presented as a question of representation… but, representation cannot simply mean overriding the cultural identity of a space because it happens to exist within a different community. Yes, in the 1980s, the lack of black representation in American public life is a serious problem. But is the wall of an immigrant-owned pizzeria really the battleground on which that struggle should be fought? The film becomes even more troubling in its final act. Radio Raheem’s death at the hands of the police is unjust and horrifying. The police are clearly responsible for that death. But the escalation that precedes it is not morally simple either. A group enters Sal’s pizzeria aggressively, tensions rise, Sal reacts poorly, violence erupts, and then the police arrive and kill a man. That killing is the central injustice. But does that automatically make Sal responsible for what the police did? Was his business the correct object of retaliation? Spike Lee has said that only white viewers tend to ask whether Mookie “did the right thing”, arguing that the real issue is the difference between property damage and the death of a black man. I understand that distinction, and it is obviously true that a human life is worth infinitely more than a shop window. But that does not, by itself, settle the moral question. Property damage and state violence are not equivalent, but nor does the horror of one automatically justify the other. The question is not whether Sal’s window matters more than Radio Raheem’s life. Of course it does not. The question is whether destroying Sal’s pizzeria was a meaningful act of resistance, an act of misdirected rage, or something more ambiguous. This is where I find the film, and Lee’s later commentary on it, frustrating. There seems to be an almost absolute certainty about what “the right thing” is, yet the film itself ends with two quotations that appear to be in philosophical mismatch with one another. If the answer is supposed to be so obvious, why close the film with both Martin Luther King Jr. and Malcolm X? Why invite that contradiction and then treat the central moral question as if it should not be asked? I would probably have appreciated Do the Right Thing more had I known less about Spike Lee’s own interpretations of it, and less about some of the troubling accounts surrounding his behaviour on set. Taken purely as a film, it has energy, anger and some visual confidence. But as a political statement, I found it far less persuasive than its reputation suggests. The film would be stronger if it allowed more room for doubt, rather than presenting moral certainty as though it were the same thing as moral clarity. The strongest version of this film would have understood that.

I wanted to like this movie and everyone tells you to because you see 5 stars everywhere and yes on a technical level, it's hard to argue that the cinematography is vivid, the direction confident, the performances genuinely great. Danny Aiello and Ossie Davis in particular are a masterclass in screen presence, oozing panache and charm and they've got that rare charisma where you feel their characters even when they're just standing around. But I can't get on board with the movie as a whole. Spike Lee never lets you forget this is a Statement. Every frame is turned up to eleven, the heat, the sweat, the sound design, the racial tension simmering into rage and by the midpoint it stops feeling like a story and starts feeling like a lecture. The film is soaked in anger from start to finish, and while I understand that's the point, it makes for a genuinely draining watch rather than an illuminating one. The ending with dueling quotes from Malcolm X and MLK, capped with the message that violence is bad. Thank you ….Groundbreaking. After two hours of escalating tension, the takeaway lands with all the subtlety of a PSA. I get why this movie is canonized. It's well made, it's ambitious, and Aiello and Davis alone are worth the price of admission. But important" and "enjoyable aren't the same thing, and for me, this one stays firmly in the first category….

Ventiquattro ore nel microcosmo di un quartiere di periferia nero della fine degli anni ‘80. È una giornata afosa e Samuel L. Jackson nei panni di un conduttore radiofonico pacifista che inneggia al C-H-I-L-L ci accompagna in un viaggio attraverso le semplici vite dei vari personaggi che animano l’incrocio principale del quartiere, tra una pizzeria italiana e un ventiquattrore coreano: il vecchio ubriacone soprannominato Da Major, la mother prioress, tre buontemponi che vivono sotto un ombrellone, un ragazzo autistico che vende per due dollari fotografie di Marthin Luter King e Malcom X, un omone che porta sempre con se’ il suo stereo, un iperattivo ossessionato dalle sue Jordan, l’italo-americano Sal proprietario della pizzeria con i suoi figli Vito e Pino. Il protagonista, Mookie, è osservatore di questa bomba a orologeria (non a caso è interpretato dallo stesso regista). Troppo impegnato a cercare di vivere una vita dignitosa, non si schiera né con i bianchi né con i neri, cerca di salvarsi la pelle e di porre fine agli inutili battibecchi razziali che avvengono alla pizzeria, dove lavora. Man mano che la giornata va avanti capisce che deve prendere in mano la situazione e fare la cosa giusta. Divertentissimi i dialoghi anche grazie a una regia irriverente che cita i videoclip rap di quegli anni, montaggio serrato che non lascia spazio alla metabolizzazione. Lo spettatore cerca di restare a galla in un vortice di cose che succedono una dopo l’altra, proprio come il protagonista, finché la situazione non gli sfugge completamente di mano, e necessita di una scelta netta. Meno realista pessimista e più ispirante del suo fratello parigino La Haine, Do the Right Thing riesce a trasmettere tanta insofferenza verso la questione razziale con due ore che volano via grazie a un ritmo sostenuto e dei dialoghi - ripeto - divertentissimi (altra differenza rispetto al film di Kassovitz, in cui la narrazione viene arbitrariamente interrotta per dare spazio a dei “vuoti” cosmici, a dei piani statico-estatici che mettono in risalto un ulteriore momento in cui è scandita la vita dei personaggi: la noia). Per Mookie non c’è spazio per la noia. La sua vita è frenetica, americana, una miccia innesca un esplosione di violenza nel senso opposto.

Lo spettatore cerca di restare a galla in un vortice di cose che succedono una dopo l’altra, proprio come il protagonista, finché la situazione non gli sfugge completamente di mano, e necessita di una scelta netta. Meno realista pessimista e più ispirante del suo fratello parigino La Haine, Do the Right Thing riesce a trasmettere tanta insofferenza verso la questione razziale con due ore che volano via grazie a un ritmo sostenuto e dei dialoghi - ripeto - divertentissimi (altra differenza rispetto al film di Kassovitz, in cui la narrazione viene arbitrariamente interrotta per dare spazio a dei “vuoti” cosmici, a dei piani statico-estatici che mettono in risalto un ulteriore momento in cui è scandita la vita dei personaggi: la noia). Per Mookie non c’è spazio per la noia. La sua vita è frenetica, americana, una miccia innesca un esplosione di violenza nel senso opposto.

Green Book for the arthouse crowd - Armond White Surely no masterpiece - David Stratton Reasonably happy that a 3 hour Japanese film with multiple meta-narratives which asks of some familiarity with Chekhov from the audience has proven so popular. I much preferred a very different film festival darling from 2021, the gritty and strangling Hive from Kosovo which ran a tight 80 minutes, but any increased appreciation for more challenging cinema is respectable. Whilst it would be nice for recent slow cinema diamonds like Long Day's Journey Into Night (2018) or Inside the Yellow Cocoon Shell (2023) to share in some of this success I much prefer to discuss this film over Don't Look Up or Squid Game which seemed to dominate cultural conversation that year. The strength of the film is this running theme that 'we are the love we have lost' and how that manifests in different ways for various personality types. On this, the text succeeds, it is humanist and relatable. There are moving moments, I like the smoking through the sunroof and the closing lines of Uncle Vanya delivered through sign language from a mute Sonya (Park Yu-rim) and particularly enjoyed the scene of Yūsuke (Hidetoshi Nishijima) observing his wife's infidelity then leaving quietly. I also love the Saab, great car choice. Length is not so much the issue, it is the inability for the film to stay focused which lets it down. A generation raised on meandering television series seems not to mind this but I still expect a level of purposeful refinement to writing and craft to pacing. The cinematography is also done in the modern adroit style, cuts to a still shot with an object entering the scene with speed or a slow dissolve between spinning wheels and spinning tape on a cassette. I don't mind when this style is used for intention over design ( Past Lives ) but too often the objective is the aesthetic. What to say about the connections to Chekhov? Burin described it as "both wide-of-the-mark and on-the-nose" which I like, the play material either feels abstract from the emotional malaise or stops still to show direct connection. I like that it took such a difficult shot at it though with the multilingual angle. Vanya on 42nd Street definitely handled the material better but it was a smart move to take a different approach here. Landscapes were beautiful.

I like a lot of different parts of this film. But to quickly sum up my feelings, I feel as if “The juice is not worth the squeeze” with this one.. I hate to feel that way as there’s a lot of things to like about this film, it’s just the time it takes to get there. The film has a general slow pace which I don’t mind in films, it’s the execution. There’s a lot of scene developing subtext about characters and their emotions towards one another, not a lot of dialogue and usually if it is it’s not directly saying what is true to the moment. WHICH is the point of the film, but I just never found the dialogue itself and the issues at hand to always be interesting enough to warrant this technique or development to be so prominent throughout the runtime. Then there’s portions where you are getting somewhere and….it’s….getting…there….just….keeeep……waiting……we’re…..THERE. I actually loved those moments for what it’s worth, it’s just that the pacing is already slow as molasses and the better moments in themselves is slow as well. The opening credits rolled around the 45 min mark and that just mentally did something to me, when I realized how that opening portion of the film was meant to actually start the movie. Something that I feel could have been shortened from 45 minutes to about 15-20 with effective dialogue and pacing. It’s hard to really harp on a director on pacing when most of that is intentional in this case. You can feel it’s meant to be a slow grind to the finish line for the pay off to feel that much more emotionally rewarding to see, yet I felt like the finishing beats of the film are something you can read on the characters face the entire time and a lot of the “filler” I experienced was for something I expected the whole time. There’s a few good moments throughout this run time like I said earlier, I enjoy parts. I love most scenes with the driver, this is a character that I think has good interactions with the lead to really break Yūsukes walls down. Her story really came full circle at the end which felt good, yet sometimes in certain emotional moments there’s a point where the dialogue really gets on the nose with things like “AND THIS EMOTIONAL MOMENT IN MY LIFE CAN SERVE AS A LESSON TO YOU BTW….” For a film that’s subtle throughout its entire run, it sort of blows its figurative load randomly throughout the film and seems to have a hard time finding a balance between nuance and convenient dialogue. Something I did like about the film is some of the themes in particular the overhead theme of grief and how you can grieve someone you have complicated feelings about. How hard it may be to let go of certain ideas about this person, that there isn’t going to be a reconciliation. The complexities of human relationships, how one person can never truly be understood 100% even through years and years of a relationship. There are always different sides of us as we grow and change. It’s about adapting, growing, challenging yourself and coming to grips with hard truths. The car scene between Yūsuke & Takatsuki is probably the best directed bit and best written portion of the film. It’s a payoff inside about the last hour of the film. The performances across the board are good, especially the lead, if not a little drab seeing him almost never smile and just look melancholic almost the whole film. Overall I think this just felt like overly long for myself and that could it be cutdown at least half an hour at minimum and have its emotional effectiveness still hit.

[36] nota=3.0 estrelas:
I like a lot of different parts of this film. But to quickly sum up my feelings, I feel as if “The juice is not worth the squeeze” with this one.. I hate to feel that way as there’s a lot of things to like about this film, it’s just the time it takes to get there. The film has a general slow pace which I don’t mind in films, it’s the execution. There’s a lot of scene developing subtext about characters and their emotions towards one another, not a lot of dialogue and usually if it is it’s not directly saying what is true to the moment. WHICH is the point of the film, but I just never found the dialogue itself and the issues at hand to always be interesting enough to warrant this technique or development to be so prominent throughout the runtime. Then there’s portions where you are getting somewhere and….it’s….getting…there….just….keeeep……waiting……we’re…..THERE. I actually loved those moments for what it’s worth, it’s just that the pacing is already slow as molasses and the better moments in themselves is slow as well. The opening credits rolled around the 45 min mark and that just mentally did something to me, when I realized how that opening portion of the film was meant to actually start the movie. Something that I feel could have been shortened from 45 minutes to about 15-20 with effective dialogue and pacing. It’s hard to really harp on a director on pacing when most of that is intentional in this case. You can feel it’s meant to be a slow grind to the finish line for the pay off to feel that much more emotionally rewarding to see, yet I felt like the finishing beats of the film are something you can read on the characters face the entire time and a lot of the “filler” I experienced was for something I expected the whole time. There’s a few good moments throughout this run time like I said earlier, I enjoy parts. I love most scenes with the driver, this is a character that I think has good interactions with the lead to really break Yūsukes walls down. Her story really came full circle at the end which felt good, yet sometimes in certain emotional moments there’s a point where the dialogue really gets on the nose with things like “AND THIS EMOTIONAL MOMENT IN MY LIFE CAN SERVE AS A LESSON TO YOU BTW….” For a film that’s subtle throughout its entire run, it sort of blows its figurative load randomly throughout the film and seems to have a hard time finding a balance between nuance and convenient dialogue. Something I did like about the film is some of the themes in particular the overhead theme of grief and how you can grieve someone you have complicated feelings about. How hard it may be to let go of certain ideas about this person, that there isn’t going to be a reconciliation. The complexities of human relationships, how one person can never truly be understood 100% even through years and years of a relationship. There are always different sides of us as we grow and change. It’s about adapting, growing, challenging yourself and coming to grips with hard truths. The car scene between Yūsuke & Takatsuki is probably the best directed bit and best written portion of the film. It’s a payoff inside about the last hour of the film. The performances across the board are good, especially the lead, if not a little drab seeing him almost never smile and just look melancholic almost the whole film. Overall I think this just felt like overly long for myself and that could it be cutdown at least half an hour at minimum and have its emotional effectiveness still hit.

It is a familiar trope of French cinema, yet the Japanese seem to have given it a new, lifeless interpretation. Cinema is not theatre. I was confused by the opening; relationship dynamics felt unclear, emotional beats didn’t land cleanly, and by the time the “2 years later” card and intro credits hit (40 minutes in!), I was still trying to piece together that overlong prologue I just saw. After that, it settles into a slow moving, very talky, theatre folk drama with lots of subtlety, themes of infidelity, shared grief, and not ever truly knowing someone. It never felt impactful enough to justify the length. I struggled to stay engaged, and 3hrs of subtitles felt like work rather than immersion. Some foreign films completely absorb me to the point I forget I’m reading; this wasn’t one of them. This one made me feel very outside of everything. Not bad, just not for me. Maybe I’m missing some nuance, but from my POV it feels very overrated. Of course a movie about driving a car will have some nice sweeping shots and cinematography, but it wasn’t incredible, nothing I haven’t seen before, and that plot just wasn’t very captivating. It only finally begins to open up a bit in the last stretch, but by then it’s like… that’s it? A long road to a simple idea. This could’ve been a short film.

Drive My Car shares its name with a short and fun song by The Beatles , but it’s quite the opposite. Not short, nor fun. A long, quiet, slow-burn trauma bond that never fully clicked for me. Like a melodramatic play, ‘twas grade-A crapola. Critically acclaimed, subtitled snoozefest 😴 I’ll admit, I was already burnt out on slow burns, so seeing the 3-hour runtime didn’t help, but I didn’t realize how much that would be felt. I was confused by the opening; relationship dynamics felt unclear, emotional beats didn’t land cleanly, and by the time the “2 years later” card and intro credits hit (40 minutes in!), I was still trying to piece together that overlong prologue I just saw. After that, it settles into a slow moving, very talky, theatre folk drama with lots of subtlety, themes of infidelity, shared grief, and not ever truly knowing someone. It never felt impactful enough to justify the length. I struggled to stay engaged, and 3hrs of subtitles felt like work rather than immersion. Some foreign films completely absorb me to the point I forget I’m reading; this wasn’t one of them. This one made me feel very outside of everything. Not bad, just not for me. Maybe I’m missing some nuance, but from my POV it feels very overrated. Of course a movie about driving a car will have some nice sweeping shots and cinematography, but it wasn’t incredible, nothing I haven’t seen before, and that plot just wasn’t very captivating. It only finally begins to open up a bit in the last stretch, but by then it’s like… that’s it? A long road to a simple idea. This could’ve been a short film.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.

Drive My Car no es una película sobre aprender a vivir con una pérdida. Es, quizá, una película sobre descubrir que nunca terminamos de conocer a las personas que amamos. Kafuku pasa buena parte de su vida intentando descifrar a Oto: sus silencios, sus infidelidades, las historias que inventa, aquello que calla. Pero cuando ella muere, descubre una paradoja devastadora: a veces la muerte no nos arrebata solamente a una persona, sino también la posibilidad de hacerle las preguntas que dejamos para después. Quizá amar sea convivir con esa clase de incertidumbre. La película parece decir que escuchar no siempre significa alcanzar al otro. Podemos conocer su voz, sus gestos, sus rutinas y hasta sus heridas, y aun así existir frente a una habitación interior cuya puerta nunca se abre del todo. Por eso el auto funciona como algo más que un escenario: es un espacio de confesión. Dos desconocidos avanzan durante horas sin mirarse directamente, y paradójicamente, en esa ausencia de mirada consiguen verse de verdad. Misaki y Kafuku no se salvan mutuamente; simplemente se reconocen en el lugar donde ambos están rotos. Y quizá ahí está lo más hermoso: no necesitamos resolver el dolor de alguien para acompañarlo. La película también cuestiona esa idea romántica de que amar significa conocer al otro por completo. Tal vez sea exactamente al contrario. Amar es aceptar que el otro siempre conservará una parte de sí mismo que no nos pertenece. Hay algo profundamente humano en nuestra necesidad de encontrar explicaciones: creemos que ponerle palabras a una herida hará que duela menos. Pero algunas heridas no se cierran cuando encontramos una respuesta, sino cuando dejamos de exigirla. Drive My Car me dejó pensando que el duelo no consiste solamente en extrañar a alguien, sino en aprender a vivir con todo lo que nunca sabremos de esa persona. Y quizás amar a alguien sea también hacer las paces con ese misterio. ¿Es posible conocer verdaderamente a alguien a quien amamos, o el amor exige abrazar la imposibilidad de comprenderlo por completo?

Drive My Car follows an actor and theater director, Yusuke Kafuku who get invited to direct a multilingual production of Uncle Vanya in Hiroshima, two years after his wife passed away. There, he meets Misaki, his quiet personal driver. Through long drives and theater rehearsals, he slowly confronts his grief, secrets, and inner healing. It’s a slow film, but it never feels boring to watch. The cinematography is outstanding the views of Hiroshima by the sea feel so fresh and beautiful, also the snowy scenes in Kutsukake’s hometown are stunning. I really liked how the film gives a long 40-minute prologue as background for the character, so there are no flashbacks for the rest of the movie. Even though it’s slow, the pacing feels just right. It’s interesting to follow the characters’ theater rehearsals and preparations, and how the play’s dialogues parallel the characters’ inner conflicts. The use of different languages by the actors is also very unique. The “dialogue” between Sonia and Uncle Vanya in the ending is incredibly powerful.

A film about grief, intimacy, guilt, and how little we can ever truly know another person. Loved how the red saab becomes this private space between solitude and connection, where Yusuke and Misaki slowly recognize the same guilt in each other without ever needing to completely explain themselves. Uncle vanya slowly becomes more than a play within the film. The multilingual rehearsals, repetition, sign language… all blur the line between performing and actually confronting yourself. Acting becomes another language for feelings you can’t say as yourself. Such an impressive way to weave a play through three hours where even the lines we understand seem to quietly serve the film’s message. So subtle. Grief lingers through the slow pacing and endless drives, which somehow gave me a bittersweet sense of peace. And that Hokkaido journey with the red car surrounded by snow finally gives them the space to say what they’ve been carrying. Not forgiveness, not closure, just acceptance. Then misaki inherits the saab. The same car that carried Yusuke through his grief, memories, and loneliness now carries her. Maybe that’s all there is to it sometimes. You carry what you’ve lost, you get behind the wheel and you keep the car moving.

Un périple rempli à la fois de mélancolie et de chaleur humaine, une véritable balade à l'atmosphère oscillant entre la profonde tristesse provenant de passés douloureux, et un sentiment d'apaisement. À l'intérieur de cette voiture rouge difficile à rater, nous allons assister à la rencontre de deux êtres blessés et égarés. Dans cette sorte de cocon permettant au protagoniste d'échapper au dehors, cette espèce de symbole de son intimité, de son monde intérieur où il s'est renfermé sur lui-même, une chauffeuse viendra s'y introduire, cette deuxième âme esquintée qui deviendra progressivement pour le personnage principal une compagnie précieuse, une semblable avec laquelle il développera une relation de confiance, transformant petit à petit ce qui était un environnement de solitude et d'isolement en un refuge, un lieu de partage et de guérison pour deux individus aux plaies encore ouvertes, une voiture avec laquelle ils partiront vers un voyage introspectif. Avec Drive My Car, Ryusuke Hamaguchi démontre une nouvelle fois sa capacité à fluidifier et teinter d'authenticité ses métrages. Le film se déroule lentement, soigneusement, en laissant tout le temps à son spectateur de s'imprégner de son ambiance naturelle. Je me suis vraiment complètement senti absorbé par ces silences, ces instants de calme presque aérien, cette mise en scène utilisant les espaces, les environnements, les regards ou encore de simples gestes pour illustrer l'intériorité des personnages avec subtilité, mais aussi toutes ces discussions parfois chaleureuses, et à d'autres moments beaucoup plus lourdes, quand les fêlures étouffées refont finalement surface. Il y a une profonde humanité qui se dégage de ce film, notamment lorsque Hamaguchi va, autour d'une pièce de théâtre servant de fil conducteur, présenter des personnages d'horizons distincts, certains avec des origines différentes, s'exprimant avec d'autres langues, et même un autre ayant un handicap avec lequel il parvient à vivre. On sent que le réalisateur tient à dépeindre tout ce qui fait la richesse de l'humain, que ce soit en montrant les différences apparentes, mais aussi en explorant des vécus qui n'ont rien à voir entre eux. À travers cette pièce de théâtre et les récits gravitant autour, ayant comme le dit si bien le film le pouvoir de faire ressortir toute la subtilité et la profondeur des sentiments, ainsi que les interactions entre nos deux protagonistes qui sont parfois remplies d'échanges et parfois simplement silencieuses, Hamaguchi explore les différents chemins pour espérer franchir la terrible épreuve qu'est le deuil et tenter de soulager son mal-être, un moyen d'avancer malgré ce trou béant provoqué par la perte et la culpabilité, qui se trouverait donc dans le partage, l'introspection et l'extériorisation. Faire preuve d'honnêteté et faire la paix avec soi-même, accepter ses erreurs, ses regrets, ce qui ne peut être changé, et rester malgré tout ouvert au reste du monde, c'est pour moi ce que prône Drive My Car, cette sublime parenthèse de vie pleine d'humanité qui m'aura complètement transporté.
