The first time I saw this was on release, and it remains one of my favorite moviegoing experiences. I caught a late showing in my college town, walked out around 1am, and still had time to grab a burger and a drink at one of my favorite bars. I gave it five stars then — it left me with a strange, specific peace I couldn't fully explain. About four years later, I hit play again and realized how much I'd actually forgotten. It felt almost like a first viewing, except this time I was older, a little wiser, and genuinely stunned by how good the script is. It would be easy to assume the film is simply "inspired" by Murakami's short story of the same name, but it's actually weaving together at least two more stories from the same collection — "Kino" and "Scheherazade" — alongside Chekhov's Uncle Vanya, which functions as the film's central framing device, mirroring the protagonist's emotional state and his relationship to his own grief. None of it feels clunky or bolted on — it's fully absorbed into the film's own language. What struck me most this time is how the despair on screen never too feel harsh toward the viewer — but the tension is there. It's life, distilled: that inevitable state of living and missing, of loss that doesn't resolve so much as scar over. And still — you move forward. Maybe that's the most human thing there is.

Not all three-hour movies are going to be GOATs. For every GODFATHER/GODFATHER PART II, you are going to get a MEET JOE BLACK. Happily, DRIVE MY CAR falls into the former category. The 35-minute prologue set in Tokyo is one of the greatest pieces of cinema I've ever seen. The complex relationship between Hidetoshi Nishijima's protagonist, and Reika Kirishima as his wife -- who features in three sensitive and nuanced explicit love scenes, something you don't find with 48-year-old actresses in Hollywood -- is well-written and well-directed, with a turntable playing Beethoven and a full-length hallway mirror, given Chekhovian introductions. Speaking of Chekhov, the remainder of the film involves NIshijima directing a multilingual performance of "Uncle Vanya" in Hiroshima, with young Toko MIura as a driver he didn't ask for. Six languages are utilized. The cast and theater staff (including Miura) are broken characters who use the play as therapy to explore or heal their wounds, but not every character finds their muse in Chekhov or achieves their happy ending. The three hours fly by. Long silences in a film can be deadly but here the silences invite you to think and reflect. A gorgeous work of art, and the fact that it was made during COVID, with an epilogue set at the height of the pandemic, only makes it more urgent and more interesting.

Asks the essential human question on how do we continue to choose to live in spite of everything. Drive My Car is a film of reserved stillness that rewards the patient, really fell into this one. Ambient, slow and steady yet full of humanistic integrity, Hamaguchi’s rendition lifts Murakami's 20 or so page short story about an isolated man dialoging through his past and turns it into an incredibly ambitious project concerning art, personhood, grief, transference through creation, and acceptance. The creative liberties it takes with the initial story turns it from a compelling piece about two people conversing into an incisive and engaging treatise on the anatomy of melancholy and complex yet essential human truths. The words we leave unsaid end up corroding us from the inside out; sometimes all we need is someone not to fix anything for us, but simply to hear us out. Life changes when we move away from drifting inaction and decide to choose every second. To be heard is to feel connected, to be connected is to feel alive, and to feel alive is to save ourselves. Visually gorgeous and the soundtrack had me floating… sometimes films come to you at the right time when you need them, and this one did just that. Can feel myself returning to this one a lot in years to come.

Drive My Car no es una película sobre aprender a vivir con una pérdida. Es, quizá, una película sobre descubrir que nunca terminamos de conocer a las personas que amamos. Kafuku pasa buena parte de su vida intentando descifrar a Oto: sus silencios, sus infidelidades, las historias que inventa, aquello que calla. Pero cuando ella muere, descubre una paradoja devastadora: a veces la muerte no nos arrebata solamente a una persona, sino también la posibilidad de hacerle las preguntas que dejamos para después. Quizá amar sea convivir con esa clase de incertidumbre. La película parece decir que escuchar no siempre significa alcanzar al otro. Podemos conocer su voz, sus gestos, sus rutinas y hasta sus heridas, y aun así existir frente a una habitación interior cuya puerta nunca se abre del todo. Por eso el auto funciona como algo más que un escenario: es un espacio de confesión. Dos desconocidos avanzan durante horas sin mirarse directamente, y paradójicamente, en esa ausencia de mirada consiguen verse de verdad. Misaki y Kafuku no se salvan mutuamente; simplemente se reconocen en el lugar donde ambos están rotos. Y quizá ahí está lo más hermoso: no necesitamos resolver el dolor de alguien para acompañarlo. La película también cuestiona esa idea romántica de que amar significa conocer al otro por completo. Tal vez sea exactamente al contrario. Amar es aceptar que el otro siempre conservará una parte de sí mismo que no nos pertenece. Hay algo profundamente humano en nuestra necesidad de encontrar explicaciones: creemos que ponerle palabras a una herida hará que duela menos. Pero algunas heridas no se cierran cuando encontramos una respuesta, sino cuando dejamos de exigirla. Drive My Car me dejó pensando que el duelo no consiste solamente en extrañar a alguien, sino en aprender a vivir con todo lo que nunca sabremos de esa persona. Y quizás amar a alguien sea también hacer las paces con ese misterio. ¿Es posible conocer verdaderamente a alguien a quien amamos, o el amor exige abrazar la imposibilidad de comprenderlo por completo?

Drive My Car follows an actor and theater director, Yusuke Kafuku who get invited to direct a multilingual production of Uncle Vanya in Hiroshima, two years after his wife passed away. There, he meets Misaki, his quiet personal driver. Through long drives and theater rehearsals, he slowly confronts his grief, secrets, and inner healing. It’s a slow film, but it never feels boring to watch. The cinematography is outstanding the views of Hiroshima by the sea feel so fresh and beautiful, also the snowy scenes in Kutsukake’s hometown are stunning. I really liked how the film gives a long 40-minute prologue as background for the character, so there are no flashbacks for the rest of the movie. Even though it’s slow, the pacing feels just right. It’s interesting to follow the characters’ theater rehearsals and preparations, and how the play’s dialogues parallel the characters’ inner conflicts. The use of different languages by the actors is also very unique. The “dialogue” between Sonia and Uncle Vanya in the ending is incredibly powerful.

A film about grief, intimacy, guilt, and how little we can ever truly know another person. Loved how the red saab becomes this private space between solitude and connection, where Yusuke and Misaki slowly recognize the same guilt in each other without ever needing to completely explain themselves. Uncle vanya slowly becomes more than a play within the film. The multilingual rehearsals, repetition, sign language… all blur the line between performing and actually confronting yourself. Acting becomes another language for feelings you can’t say as yourself. Such an impressive way to weave a play through three hours where even the lines we understand seem to quietly serve the film’s message. So subtle. Grief lingers through the slow pacing and endless drives, which somehow gave me a bittersweet sense of peace. And that Hokkaido journey with the red car surrounded by snow finally gives them the space to say what they’ve been carrying. Not forgiveness, not closure, just acceptance. Then misaki inherits the saab. The same car that carried Yusuke through his grief, memories, and loneliness now carries her. Maybe that’s all there is to it sometimes. You carry what you’ve lost, you get behind the wheel and you keep the car moving.

Un périple rempli à la fois de mélancolie et de chaleur humaine, une véritable balade à l'atmosphère oscillant entre la profonde tristesse provenant de passés douloureux, et un sentiment d'apaisement. À l'intérieur de cette voiture rouge difficile à rater, nous allons assister à la rencontre de deux êtres blessés et égarés. Dans cette sorte de cocon permettant au protagoniste d'échapper au dehors, cette espèce de symbole de son intimité, de son monde intérieur où il s'est renfermé sur lui-même, une chauffeuse viendra s'y introduire, cette deuxième âme esquintée qui deviendra progressivement pour le personnage principal une compagnie précieuse, une semblable avec laquelle il développera une relation de confiance, transformant petit à petit ce qui était un environnement de solitude et d'isolement en un refuge, un lieu de partage et de guérison pour deux individus aux plaies encore ouvertes, une voiture avec laquelle ils partiront vers un voyage introspectif. Avec Drive My Car, Ryusuke Hamaguchi démontre une nouvelle fois sa capacité à fluidifier et teinter d'authenticité ses métrages. Le film se déroule lentement, soigneusement, en laissant tout le temps à son spectateur de s'imprégner de son ambiance naturelle. Je me suis vraiment complètement senti absorbé par ces silences, ces instants de calme presque aérien, cette mise en scène utilisant les espaces, les environnements, les regards ou encore de simples gestes pour illustrer l'intériorité des personnages avec subtilité, mais aussi toutes ces discussions parfois chaleureuses, et à d'autres moments beaucoup plus lourdes, quand les fêlures étouffées refont finalement surface. Il y a une profonde humanité qui se dégage de ce film, notamment lorsque Hamaguchi va, autour d'une pièce de théâtre servant de fil conducteur, présenter des personnages d'horizons distincts, certains avec des origines différentes, s'exprimant avec d'autres langues, et même un autre ayant un handicap avec lequel il parvient à vivre. On sent que le réalisateur tient à dépeindre tout ce qui fait la richesse de l'humain, que ce soit en montrant les différences apparentes, mais aussi en explorant des vécus qui n'ont rien à voir entre eux. À travers cette pièce de théâtre et les récits gravitant autour, ayant comme le dit si bien le film le pouvoir de faire ressortir toute la subtilité et la profondeur des sentiments, ainsi que les interactions entre nos deux protagonistes qui sont parfois remplies d'échanges et parfois simplement silencieuses, Hamaguchi explore les différents chemins pour espérer franchir la terrible épreuve qu'est le deuil et tenter de soulager son mal-être, un moyen d'avancer malgré ce trou béant provoqué par la perte et la culpabilité, qui se trouverait donc dans le partage, l'introspection et l'extériorisation. Faire preuve d'honnêteté et faire la paix avec soi-même, accepter ses erreurs, ses regrets, ce qui ne peut être changé, et rester malgré tout ouvert au reste du monde, c'est pour moi ce que prône Drive My Car, cette sublime parenthèse de vie pleine d'humanité qui m'aura complètement transporté.

The first time I saw this was on release, and it remains one of my favorite moviegoing experiences. I caught a late showing in my college town, walked out around 1am, and still had time to grab a burger and a drink at one of my favorite bars. I gave it five stars then — it left me with a strange, specific peace I couldn't fully explain. About four years later, I hit play again and realized how much I'd actually forgotten. It felt almost like a first viewing, except this time I was older, a little wiser, and genuinely stunned by how good the script is. It would be easy to assume the film is simply "inspired" by Murakami's short story of the same name, but it's actually weaving together at least two more stories from the same collection — "Kino" and "Scheherazade" — alongside Chekhov's Uncle Vanya, which functions as the film's central framing device, mirroring the protagonist's emotional state and his relationship to his own grief. None of it feels clunky or bolted on — it's fully absorbed into the film's own language. What struck me most this time is how the despair on screen never too feel harsh toward the viewer — but the tension is there. It's life, distilled: that inevitable state of living and missing, of loss that doesn't resolve so much as scar over. And still — you move forward. Maybe that's the most human thing there is.

Not all three-hour movies are going to be GOATs. For every GODFATHER/GODFATHER PART II, you are going to get a MEET JOE BLACK. Happily, DRIVE MY CAR falls into the former category. The 35-minute prologue set in Tokyo is one of the greatest pieces of cinema I've ever seen. The complex relationship between Hidetoshi Nishijima's protagonist, and Reika Kirishima as his wife -- who features in three sensitive and nuanced explicit love scenes, something you don't find with 48-year-old actresses in Hollywood -- is well-written and well-directed, with a turntable playing Beethoven and a full-length hallway mirror, given Chekhovian introductions. Speaking of Chekhov, the remainder of the film involves NIshijima directing a multilingual performance of "Uncle Vanya" in Hiroshima, with young Toko MIura as a driver he didn't ask for. Six languages are utilized. The cast and theater staff (including Miura) are broken characters who use the play as therapy to explore or heal their wounds, but not every character finds their muse in Chekhov or achieves their happy ending. The three hours fly by. Long silences in a film can be deadly but here the silences invite you to think and reflect. A gorgeous work of art, and the fact that it was made during COVID, with an epilogue set at the height of the pandemic, only makes it more urgent and more interesting.

Asks the essential human question on how do we continue to choose to live in spite of everything. Drive My Car is a film of reserved stillness that rewards the patient, really fell into this one. Ambient, slow and steady yet full of humanistic integrity, Hamaguchi’s rendition lifts Murakami's 20 or so page short story about an isolated man dialoging through his past and turns it into an incredibly ambitious project concerning art, personhood, grief, transference through creation, and acceptance. The creative liberties it takes with the initial story turns it from a compelling piece about two people conversing into an incisive and engaging treatise on the anatomy of melancholy and complex yet essential human truths. The words we leave unsaid end up corroding us from the inside out; sometimes all we need is someone not to fix anything for us, but simply to hear us out. Visuellement bluffant, émotionnellement creux. Aie Aie Aie. Je m'attendais à BEAUCOUP mieux que la partie 1, mais à peine. Toutefois, les raisons de mon retrait sont différentes entre la partie 1 et la partie 2. À de nombreuses reprises, j'ai trouvé le film austère et glacial avec un manque de liens émotionnels avec les personnages. Par exemple, j'aurais aimé voir comment Chani et Paul se sont rapprochés car au départ elle avait quand même des doutes et lui avait ses visions prémonitoires la concernant. Enfaite, j'ai trouvé leur rapprochement hyper soudain comme précipité tout en étant assumé et c'est pas pour moi. De manière générale, je sens une certaine précipitation des évènements de la part de Villeneuve, ce qui m'a fait décroché. Des années ont l'air de passer comme des semaines là où, je peux le sentir, les livres doivent probablement bien nous le faire sentir ce temps qui passe. Autre remarque, l'expansion et la croissance de la "religion" de la mère de Paul qui est fourré au 1000e plan du film. J'aurais aimé un focus dessus parce qu'une parole de la mère qui dit "il faut commencer par ceux qui ont peurs" et puis "on a fini avec le nord, passons au sud"... mouais Denis steuplait hein. Des révélations chocs comme le fait que la mère de Paul soit la fille du baron et la mort symbolique de celui-ci part la main de son petit-fils m'ont laissé de marbre. Je soupçonne que cela s'explique par, pour moi encore une fois, un retrait de l'intrigue politique au second plan afin de polluer le premier plan du film sur le fait que tout indique que Paul est le Lisan Al-Ghaib (jeu de mot qui m'a fait croire à autre chose et je pense que c'était totalement le but). Je ne dis pas qu'il n'y a aucune intrigue politique, ce serait mentir sans vergogne. Je dis plutôt que sa place est hybride là où elle devrait être centrale. Toutefois, je comprendrais que d'autres ne pensent la même chose, et c'est OK. On retrouve des personnages qui se veulent être impactant retirer de tout leur éclat dû à un manque de place affligeant (ex: Empereur, Rautha). J'ai également du mal à croire en la relation entre Paul et sa mère. Leurs interactions me font plus penser à un frère et sa soeur plutôt qu'à un fils et sa mère. Vers la fin elle se reprend mais bon. Si on recentre notre attention sur Paul, j'ai pas compris en quoi c'était évident qu'il aille chercher la potion bleue. Pour moi c'est un peu sorti de nulle part. Oui oui sa prescience etc mais je suis pas convaincu par ce que je vois, justement parce que tout va vite et de manière très déconnecté. Et son shift ne s'explique pas tant que ça, on peut le comprendre en l'imaginant mais ce n'est jamais rien de factuel là où on comprenait celui d'Anakin par exemple. D'ailleurs, on sent que ce film est un film qui prépare le prochain. Ça m'a un peu dérangé. mais ça reste minime. Passons au positif, c'est déprimant sinon. J'ai beaucoup aimé le choix visuel de passer de la couleur au noir et blanc dans l'arène. Je n'ai pas d'explication au phénomène mais c'était sympa. De plus, les éléments du film sont présents mais mal intégré à mon avis, c'est dommage. (pff j'étais censé virer au positif) L'amourette bien que rapide est mignonne. On peut imaginer que Paul et Chani tienne énormément l'un à l'autre. De plus, j'ai bien aimé la première traversée du désert de Paul avec Chani. Les plans étaient beaux, l'ambiance était chic, les chorégraphies étaient apaisantes par leur synchronicité. Bref c'était chouette. Enfin, j'aime bien l'idée d'un faux saveur qui s'approprie les mythes pour parvenir à ses fins. C'est intéressant. On en vient même à se demander si le mythe est réellement faux ou s'il est devenu réel à force de le propager ou s'il a toujours été réel. Notre avis peut néanmoins se trouver biaisé par la mise en scène et le pdv de Paul (visions etc). Bref, c'est sympa ça. PS: Voir les idées des adaptations m'a donné envie de débuter les livres un jour. J'pense que j'apprécierai plus. Ou bien pas du tout et ça conclura ma tentative désespérée :( PS2: Niveau religion, et ce que traduit cette oeuvre, je préfère me taire sinon j'vais écrire 3 pavés supplémentaires. Pas content. Frank Herbert est un cas mais Denis Villeneuve est tout aussi en faute pour l'image qu'il renvoie. PS3: Je pense sincèrement qu'une série aurait été plus adaptée pour cette oeuvre.

Sé que la calificación puede generar preguntas pero afortunadamente tengo bastante que decir de la que me parece una de las películas más sobrevaloradas de la historia. Vi la primer película en su momento y me pareció interesante pero nada espectacular, destacaba en el elenco y en los visuales pero nada que me llevaría a repetirla. Esa película planteó la adaptación un universo el cual pude ver que tiene como eje central la política, el problema de hacer historias sobre política es que se debe tratar con extrema atención el diálogo y el conflicto en cuestión, pues si ninguno de los dos puntos es interesante, no genera un gancho para ver horas de discusiones con el motivo de llevar un conflicto a una resolución contundente. En su momento no tomé tan en cuenta eso al ser solo la primera parte de Dune, pero cuando ves la segunda parte de esa historia sabiendo que es ya la mitad de una trilogía y el interés se siente vacío, ya es preocupante. Cuando Dune parte 2 salió vi gente alabándola como una de las mejores sino que la mejor experiencia cinematográfica de los últimos años, no podría estar más en desacuerdo y sostengo mi punto en base a su carencia de identidad. Es bien sabido que Star Wars plagió en muchos aspectos (aunque sean mínimos) a los libros de Dune, sin embargo, el reconocimiento a Star Wars viene de cómo a pesar de ello se logró crear un universo con identidad, el cual no viene de una obra previa sino que directamente nació en el cine, siendo que ahora su mundo es identificable al igual que sus personajes e historias, ya es un icono de la cultura pop. Ahora parece que los papeles se han invertido y Dune que en teoría es “la obra original” pareciera que quiere replicar a Star Wars, lo cual tiene sentido, la adaptación original de Dune fue un total fracaso. Dune parte 2 no parece que haga un trabajo por sacar a relucir su concepto y su mundo, más bien parece que quiere replicar lo que su supuesta copia “la venganza de los Sith” hizo años atrás para ser el éxito que fue y es lamentable pensar como la franquicia que en teoría es la copia me parece que tiene mucha más identidad que la obra original. No me quedo con los ambientes ni escenarios de la película, no me quedo con los nombres de los personajes, el conflicto no tiene lo suyo, solo parece que quieren convertir a Paul Atreides en otro Anakin Skywalker en vez de darle valor por ser su propio personaje. Y no, no es mala película, la disfrute, me emocione, estuve atento a ella y es una mejora absoluta de la 1 en todo aspecto, principalmente en el ritmo. Pero me parece desmedido el escándalo que en su momento se hizo al nombrar Dune Parte 2 como una de las mejores películas de la historia cuando me parece una buena película más del montón que destaca únicamente por su alto presupuesto. Personalmente tampoco siento que el elenco haya dado su mejor trabajo, sentí que igual hubo un hype desmedido por varios personajes y actores que tampoco son la gran cosa. Mi conclusión es que venimos de tantas películas malas que una película decente pareció una obra maestra a los ojos de todos, porque de lo contrario no me explico el hype.

Visuellement bluffant, émotionnellement creux. Aie Aie Aie. Je m'attendais à BEAUCOUP mieux que la partie 1, mais à peine. Toutefois, les raisons de mon retrait sont différentes entre la partie 1 et la partie 2. À de nombreuses reprises, j'ai trouvé le film austère et glacial avec un manque de liens émotionnels avec les personnages. Par exemple, j'aurais aimé voir comment Chani et Paul se sont rapprochés car au départ elle avait quand même des doutes et lui avait ses visions prémonitoires la concernant. Enfaite, j'ai trouvé leur rapprochement hyper soudain comme précipité tout en étant assumé et c'est pas pour moi. De manière générale, je sens une certaine précipitation des évènements de la part de Villeneuve, ce qui m'a fait décroché. Des années ont l'air de passer comme des semaines là où, je peux le sentir, les livres doivent probablement bien nous le faire sentir ce temps qui passe. Autre remarque, l'expansion et la croissance de la "religion" de la mère de Paul qui est fourré au 1000e plan du film. J'aurais aimé un focus dessus parce qu'une parole de la mère qui dit "il faut commencer par ceux qui ont peurs" et puis "on a fini avec le nord, passons au sud"... mouais Denis steuplait hein. Des révélations chocs comme le fait que la mère de Paul soit la fille du baron et la mort symbolique de celui-ci part la main de son petit-fils m'ont laissé de marbre. Je soupçonne que cela s'explique par, pour moi encore une fois, un retrait de l'intrigue politique au second plan afin de polluer le premier plan du film sur le fait que tout indique que Paul est le Lisan Al-Ghaib (jeu de mot qui m'a fait croire à autre chose et je pense que c'était totalement le but). Je ne dis pas qu'il n'y a aucune intrigue politique, ce serait mentir sans vergogne. Je dis plutôt que sa place est hybride là où elle devrait être centrale. Toutefois, je comprendrais que d'autres ne pensent la même chose, et c'est OK. On retrouve des personnages qui se veulent être impactant retirer de tout leur éclat dû à un manque de place affligeant (ex: Empereur, Rautha). J'ai également du mal à croire en la relation entre Paul et sa mère. Leurs interactions me font plus penser à un frère et sa soeur plutôt qu'à un fils et sa mère. Vers la fin elle se reprend mais bon. Si on recentre notre attention sur Paul, j'ai pas compris en quoi c'était évident qu'il aille chercher la potion bleue. Pour moi c'est un peu sorti de nulle part. Oui oui sa prescience etc mais je suis pas convaincu par ce que je vois, justement parce que tout va vite et de manière très déconnecté. Et son shift ne s'explique pas tant que ça, on peut le comprendre en l'imaginant mais ce n'est jamais rien de factuel là où on comprenait celui d'Anakin par exemple. D'ailleurs, on sent que ce film est un film qui prépare le prochain. Ça m'a un peu dérangé. mais ça reste minime. Passons au positif, c'est déprimant sinon. J'ai beaucoup aimé le choix visuel de passer de la couleur au noir et blanc dans l'arène. Je n'ai pas d'explication au phénomène mais c'était sympa. De plus, les éléments du film sont présents mais mal intégré à mon avis, c'est dommage. (pff j'étais censé virer au positif) L'amourette bien que rapide est mignonne. On peut imaginer que Paul et Chani tienne énormément l'un à l'autre. De plus, j'ai bien aimé la première traversée du désert de Paul avec Chani. Les plans étaient beaux, l'ambiance était chic, les chorégraphies étaient apaisantes par leur synchronicité. Bref c'était chouette. Enfin, j'aime bien l'idée d'un faux saveur qui s'approprie les mythes pour parvenir à ses fins. C'est intéressant. On en vient même à se demander si le mythe est réellement faux ou s'il est devenu réel à force de le propager ou s'il a toujours été réel. Notre avis peut néanmoins se trouver biaisé par la mise en scène et le pdv de Paul (visions etc). Bref, c'est sympa ça. PS: Voir les idées des adaptations m'a donné envie de débuter les livres un jour. J'pense que j'apprécierai plus. Ou bien pas du tout et ça conclura ma tentative désespérée :( PS2: Niveau religion, et ce que traduit cette oeuvre, je préfère me taire sinon j'vais écrire 3 pavés supplémentaires. Pas content. Frank Herbert est un cas mais Denis Villeneuve est tout aussi en faute pour l'image qu'il renvoie. PS3: Je pense sincèrement qu'une série aurait été plus adaptée pour cette oeuvre.

Sé que la calificación puede generar preguntas pero afortunadamente tengo bastante que decir de la que me parece una de las películas más sobrevaloradas de la historia. Vi la primer película en su momento y me pareció interesante pero nada espectacular, destacaba en el elenco y en los visuales pero nada que me llevaría a repetirla. Esa película planteó la adaptación un universo el cual pude ver que tiene como eje central la política, el problema de hacer historias sobre política es que se debe tratar con extrema atención el diálogo y el conflicto en cuestión, pues si ninguno de los dos puntos es interesante, no genera un gancho para ver horas de discusiones con el motivo de llevar un conflicto a una resolución contundente. En su momento no tomé tan en cuenta eso al ser solo la primera parte de Dune, pero cuando ves la segunda parte de esa historia sabiendo que es ya la mitad de una trilogía y el interés se siente vacío, ya es preocupante. Cuando Dune parte 2 salió vi gente alabándola como una de las mejores sino que la mejor experiencia cinematográfica de los últimos años, no podría estar más en desacuerdo y sostengo mi punto en base a su carencia de identidad. Es bien sabido que Star Wars plagió en muchos aspectos (aunque sean mínimos) a los libros de Dune, sin embargo, el reconocimiento a Star Wars viene de cómo a pesar de ello se logró crear un universo con identidad, el cual no viene de una obra previa sino que directamente nació en el cine, siendo que ahora su mundo es identificable al igual que sus personajes e historias, ya es un icono de la cultura pop. Ahora parece que los papeles se han invertido y Dune que en teoría es “la obra original” pareciera que quiere replicar a Star Wars, lo cual tiene sentido, la adaptación original de Dune fue un total fracaso. Dune parte 2 no parece que haga un trabajo por sacar a relucir su concepto y su mundo, más bien parece que quiere replicar lo que su supuesta copia “la venganza de los Sith” hizo años atrás para ser el éxito que fue y es lamentable pensar como la franquicia que en teoría es la copia me parece que tiene mucha más identidad que la obra original. No me quedo con los ambientes ni escenarios de la película, no me quedo con los nombres de los personajes, el conflicto no tiene lo suyo, solo parece que quieren convertir a Paul Atreides en otro Anakin Skywalker en vez de darle valor por ser su propio personaje. Y no, no es mala película, la disfrute, me emocione, estuve atento a ella y es una mejora absoluta de la 1 en todo aspecto, principalmente en el ritmo. Pero me parece desmedido el escándalo que en su momento se hizo al nombrar Dune Parte 2 como una de las mejores películas de la historia cuando me parece una buena película más del montón que destaca únicamente por su alto presupuesto. Personalmente tampoco siento que el elenco haya dado su mejor trabajo, sentí que igual hubo un hype desmedido por varios personajes y actores que tampoco son la gran cosa. Mi conclusión es que venimos de tantas películas malas que una película decente pareció una obra maestra a los ojos de todos, porque de lo contrario no me explico el hype.

[1] nota=0.5 estrelas:
Somehow Dune: Part Two managed to be even longer, louder, and somehow still feel like nothing was happening. In the first film, Paul Atreides was treated like a legendary figure before I ever understood why I should care about him. Unfortunately, Part Two doubles down on that. Everyone keeps looking at Paul like he’s the greatest thing to ever walk across the desert, but the movie never really earns that feeling. We’re constantly told he’s a messiah or the chosen one but I’m still waiting for the part where I understand why. Instead of watching a character become extraordinary, it feels like watching everyone else convince themselves that he already is. The Fremen’s devotion to Paul also made the story harder to take seriously. It feels less like a believable movement and more like an entire population suddenly joining a religion because the script told them to. And the final was strangely underwhelming. A story that spends so much time preparing for greatness somehow ends on a very ordinary note. Two movies, almost five hours, and my main takeaway is still: more sand, more silence, more people telling me Paul is special.

[12] nota=1.5 estrelas:
I think this is the greatest example of a “good” movie vs. an “enjoyable/favorite” movie I’ve ever seen. I say that because this movie is GREAT from nearly all technical standpoints. Great actors doing some great acting, absolutely beautiful cinematography and special effects, insanely impressive sets, and just a sheer feeling of grandness that, I feel, is only topped by a handful of movies. All around, just a beautifully made film. Still, I didn’t enjoy myself AT ALL. I don’t think the story is nearly as impressive as the first one, or impressive at all for that matter. I find it boring, confusing, and just honestly dull. I find that they waste unreasonable amounts of time on storylines that don’t matter and/or just aren’t entertaining, and rush the very few things I actually enjoyed. I mean, and this is obviously the card they were dealt, seeing as this was based on a book, it’s all just talking and politics, but they do it so different in this land, “Arakkis,” that half the film is spent explaining all of that through boring exposition and whatnot, and the other half is not very interesting at all, as someone who enjoys stories similar to this, like Game of Thrones. The action scenes, though VERY far and few were, again, gorgeously and impressively shot, but I feel lack stakes, substance, and, again, enjoyment. Half of the scenes just felt like Neo and Agent Smith going at it, even though Neo already knows all of the moves Agent Smith will make. This was a dumb comparison, in hindsight, but what I mean to say is that they’re un-compelling and boring for the most part, besides that gladiator-type fight in the middle and the fight scene with the big tank thing near the 40-minute mark. The characters- don’t get me started on the characters. I’m guessing this is something most people actually LIKE about Dune- seeing as they are able as realistic of characters you can write given their positions, but I sincerely couldn’t name you one that I care about/ like. I mean, in the first one, I cared about Paul because he actually had a personality, I liked Jason Momoa’s character a lot, and I thought the Baron was a very intriguing villain, but this time around, there was none of that charm. Everyone was just this boring, dull, character with seemingly the same personality, unless you’re Paul or his mother, because then you have NO personality, making the finale and all of the stuff with Chani pretty uninteresting and unrewarding to be quite honest. Again; the fact that this movie even got to be made is a wonder within itself- with all of those spacecrafts, settings, character designs, buildings, etc, that they had to create, shoot, and put to film is such a tasteful way, but I just didn’t enjoy it at all. I found it to be INSANELY long, like, blood-curdlingly long in my opinion, to the point where I was just actually started to breathe heavier (coming from someone who likes longer movies) and (with zero exaggeration whatsoever) probably checked how much longer it was roughly 15-20 times, very boring and dull, lifeless if you will, and everything I “liked” about it wasn’t done any better than what I’ve seen a gazillion times before. My rating: 3.4/10

Somehow Dune: Part Two managed to be even longer, louder, and somehow still feel like nothing was happening. In the first film, Paul Atreides was treated like a legendary figure before I ever understood why I should care about him. Unfortunately, Part Two doubles down on that. Everyone keeps looking at Paul like he’s the greatest thing to ever walk across the desert, but the movie never really earns that feeling. We’re constantly told he’s a messiah or the chosen one but I’m still waiting for the part where I understand why. Instead of watching a character become extraordinary, it feels like watching everyone else convince themselves that he already is. The Fremen’s devotion to Paul also made the story harder to take seriously. It feels less like a believable movement and more like an entire population suddenly joining a religion because the script told them to. And the final was strangely underwhelming. A story that spends so much time preparing for greatness somehow ends on a very ordinary note. Two movies, almost five hours, and my main takeaway is still: more sand, more silence, more people telling me Paul is special.

I think this is the greatest example of a “good” movie vs. an “enjoyable/favorite” movie I’ve ever seen. I say that because this movie is GREAT from nearly all technical standpoints. Great actors doing some great acting, absolutely beautiful cinematography and special effects, insanely impressive sets, and just a sheer feeling of grandness that, I feel, is only topped by a handful of movies. All around, just a beautifully made film. Still, I didn’t enjoy myself AT ALL. I don’t think the story is nearly as impressive as the first one, or impressive at all for that matter. I find it boring, confusing, and just honestly dull. I find that they waste unreasonable amounts of time on storylines that don’t matter and/or just aren’t entertaining, and rush the very few things I actually enjoyed. I mean, and this is obviously the card they were dealt, seeing as this was based on a book, it’s all just talking and politics, but they do it so different in this land, “Arakkis,” that half the film is spent explaining all of that through boring exposition and whatnot, and the other half is not very interesting at all, as someone who enjoys stories similar to this, like Game of Thrones. The action scenes, though VERY far and few were, again, gorgeously and impressively shot, but I feel lack stakes, substance, and, again, enjoyment. Half of the scenes just felt like Neo and Agent Smith going at it, even though Neo already knows all of the moves Agent Smith will make. This was a dumb comparison, in hindsight, but what I mean to say is that they’re un-compelling and boring for the most part, besides that gladiator-type fight in the middle and the fight scene with the big tank thing near the 40-minute mark. The characters- don’t get me started on the characters. I’m guessing this is something most people actually LIKE about Dune- seeing as they are able as realistic of characters you can write given their positions, but I sincerely couldn’t name you one that I care about/ like. I mean, in the first one, I cared about Paul because he actually had a personality, I liked Jason Momoa’s character a lot, and I thought the Baron was a very intriguing villain, but this time around, there was none of that charm. Everyone was just this boring, dull, character with seemingly the same personality, unless you’re Paul or his mother, because then you have NO personality, making the finale and all of the stuff with Chani pretty uninteresting and unrewarding to be quite honest. Again; the fact that this movie even got to be made is a wonder within itself- with all of those spacecrafts, settings, character designs, buildings, etc, that they had to create, shoot, and put to film is such a tasteful way, but I just didn’t enjoy it at all. I found it to be INSANELY long, like, blood-curdlingly long in my opinion, to the point where I was just actually started to breathe heavier (coming from someone who likes longer movies) and (with zero exaggeration whatsoever) probably checked how much longer it was roughly 15-20 times, very boring and dull, lifeless if you will, and everything I “liked” about it wasn’t done any better than what I’ve seen a gazillion times before. My rating: 3.4/10

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,

Denis Villeneuve en su máximo esplendor. La película es una obra maestra. Realmente magistral. Es de esas películas en las que cuesta encontrar algo que no esté a la altura: el guion, la dirección, la fotografía, los efectos visuales, las actuaciones y, por supuesto, la apoteósica banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Absolutamente todo funciona. La primera vez que la vi en el cine, en IMAX, salí completamente alucinado. La amé de principio a fin. Pero después de haber leído Dune, la experiencia fue todavía mejor. Amé el libro de Frank Herbert y, precisamente por eso, una de las cosas que más me impresionó de la primera película fue su enorme fidelidad a la obra original. Sin embargo, al leer el libro y volver a Dune: Part Two, entendí que Denis Villeneuve tomó muchas más libertades para llevar la historia hacia una dirección diferente. Y, lejos de molestarme, me pareció maravilloso. Porque eso demuestra que Villeneuve no buscó simplemente trasladar el libro página por página a la pantalla. Entendió su esencia, tomó decisiones propias y construyó su propia visión de Dune. Y eso, para mí, es precisamente lo que hacen los grandes directores. Volver a ver esta película una y otra vez es un verdadero lujo. Cada visionado permite apreciar algo nuevo: la composición de cada plano, los colores, la fotografía, los detalles de los escenarios, la magnitud de Arrakis y el nivel técnico de una producción que visualmente es simplemente impresionante. Y si hablamos de sus grandes virtudes, es imposible no detenerse en la banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Personalmente, es mi compositor favorito de música para cine y aquí vuelve a entregar un trabajo extraordinario, completamente diferente al de la primera película. Hay momentos en los que basta con cerrar los ojos para sentir el desierto de Arrakis, la inmensidad del planeta y, sobre todo, cómo la tensión va aumentando poco a poco hasta convertir la historia en la promesa de una guerra santa. Las actuaciones también están a un nivel extraordinario. Era algo que podía esperarse después de una primera película con un elenco tan sólido, pero las nuevas incorporaciones elevan todavía más el conjunto. Austin Butler como Feyd-Rautha y Florence Pugh como Irulan son excelentes, pero para mí hay dos que se roban absolutamente la película: Javier Bardem como Stilgar y Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides. Chalamet, especialmente, entrega una de las mejores actuaciones de su carrera. Se puede ver en su rostro el tormento, el miedo y el dolor de un hombre que sabe perfectamente hacia dónde lo está llevando el camino que ha elegido, pero que también entiende que cada paso que da puede acercarlo cada vez más al caos que intentaba evitar. Dune: Part Two es una película maravillosa, épica y técnicamente impresionante. Una obra que consiguió conquistar tanto al público como a la crítica y que, en mi opinión, tiene absolutamente merecidos todos los elogios que recibió. Denis Villeneuve tomó una de las obras más importantes de la ciencia ficción, la llevó a la pantalla grande con una visión propia y consiguió convertirla en una experiencia cinematográfica monumental. Una verdadera obra de arte moderna.

[32] nota=5.0 estrelas:
Denis Villeneuve en su máximo esplendor. La película es una obra maestra. Realmente magistral. Es de esas películas en las que cuesta encontrar algo que no esté a la altura: el guion, la dirección, la fotografía, los efectos visuales, las actuaciones y, por supuesto, la apoteósica banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Absolutamente todo funciona. La primera vez que la vi en el cine, en IMAX, salí completamente alucinado. La amé de principio a fin. Pero después de haber leído Dune, la experiencia fue todavía mejor. Amé el libro de Frank Herbert y, precisamente por eso, una de las cosas que más me impresionó de la primera película fue su enorme fidelidad a la obra original. Sin embargo, al leer el libro y volver a Dune: Part Two, entendí que Denis Villeneuve tomó muchas más libertades para llevar la historia hacia una dirección diferente. Y, lejos de molestarme, me pareció maravilloso. Porque eso demuestra que Villeneuve no buscó simplemente trasladar el libro página por página a la pantalla. Entendió su esencia, tomó decisiones propias y construyó su propia visión de Dune. Y eso, para mí, es precisamente lo que hacen los grandes directores. Volver a ver esta película una y otra vez es un verdadero lujo. Cada visionado permite apreciar algo nuevo: la composición de cada plano, los colores, la fotografía, los detalles de los escenarios, la magnitud de Arrakis y el nivel técnico de una producción que visualmente es simplemente impresionante. Y si hablamos de sus grandes virtudes, es imposible no detenerse en la banda sonora de Hans Zimmer. Personalmente, es mi compositor favorito de música para cine y aquí vuelve a entregar un trabajo extraordinario, completamente diferente al de la primera película. Hay momentos en los que basta con cerrar los ojos para sentir el desierto de Arrakis, la inmensidad del planeta y, sobre todo, cómo la tensión va aumentando poco a poco hasta convertir la historia en la promesa de una guerra santa. Las actuaciones también están a un nivel extraordinario. Era algo que podía esperarse después de una primera película con un elenco tan sólido, pero las nuevas incorporaciones elevan todavía más el conjunto. Austin Butler como Feyd-Rautha y Florence Pugh como Irulan son excelentes, pero para mí hay dos que se roban absolutamente la película: Javier Bardem como Stilgar y Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides. Chalamet, especialmente, entrega una de las mejores actuaciones de su carrera. Se puede ver en su rostro el tormento, el miedo y el dolor de un hombre que sabe perfectamente hacia dónde lo está llevando el camino que ha elegido, pero que también entiende que cada paso que da puede acercarlo cada vez más al caos que intentaba evitar. Dune: Part Two es una película maravillosa, épica y técnicamente impresionante. Una obra que consiguió conquistar tanto al público como a la crítica y que, en mi opinión, tiene absolutamente merecidos todos los elogios que recibió. Denis Villeneuve tomó una de las obras más importantes de la ciencia ficción, la llevó a la pantalla grande con una visión propia y consiguió convertirla en una experiencia cinematográfica monumental. Una verdadera obra de arte moderna.

This is a very charming coming-of-age story that feels very magical for its modern and internet-age depiction of middle school. I was going into my senior year of high school when this came out, but youth-hood is a timeless experience all the same. In all honesty it would be unfair to compare this to a show like PEN15 because of its lack of social commentary, yes obviously they are both coming of age stories with awkward and anxious preteens, but both pieces of media are accomplishing two different goals. PEN15 has its two female leads, Maya and Anna, who bring a lot of interesting dialogue to be said about race and class in television. Usually I would label a film like this as “white people: the movie” but it would rub me the wrong way doing so as such, so I’ll make a one time exception for this film.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.

4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"

J'avais détesté ce film quand je l'avais vu ado. Le revoir maintenant n'a pas fondamentalement changé mon opinion. Formellement c'est très bien exécuté, c'est du Fincher à son prime (quoique cette surabondance de numérique verse un peu parfois dans le too much). Quoiqu'un peu trop verbeux. Cornélius ne nous laisse aucun répit avec ses pensées, ça aurait été bien de suggérer plutôt que de réciter. Avec le recul c'est un peu le point faible de Fincher, c'est un très bon illustrateur, mais tous ses films sont d'une froideur clinique - bien que, d'une certaine façon, ce soit assez adapté au sujet, un peu de subtilité sur l'exposition aurait été bienvenue. En revoyant le film en connaissant le twist, on décèle en effet les quelques indices qui sont disséminés ici et là passé la moitié. Mais ça ne me réconcilie pour autant pas avec cette fin qui reste à mes yeux une fin de petit malin. Pour moi le film tient difficilement avec ce twist - je comprends l'allégorie, le message, mais j'ai du mal à accepter tout ce qui se précède. La névrose est trop forte notamment dès qu'il est en public. Ça fait partie de ces films où l'allégorie, l'exercice de style, prime sur la narration ("qu'importe la cohérence, c'est la manière qui importe"). Je ne crois pas une seconde à l'histoire de Cornélius, et c'est trop pratique de tout mettre sous le fait que de toute façon, c'est dans sa tête. Et puis bon, même le message profond, c'est digne d'un adolescent en pleine rébellion : "fuck le capitalisme, faut tout faire péter, vive l'anarchie". Ok, cool, ça a le mérite d'être original d'arriver à être aussi jusqu'au boutiste à Hollywood. Maintenant, il serait temps de grandir. Et allez consulter si vous êtes mal dans votre peau.

|EN| Fight Club David Fincher, 1999 David Fincher is a director I consider very competent, but rarely one who truly excites me. With Fight Club , however, he certainly manages to bring the film home, helped by remarkable source material: Chuck Palahniuk's novel already provides a story with considerable impact. I think Fight Club has to be judged in two different ways: through the first viewing and through every viewing that follows. On a first watch, the film works extremely well. It captures your attention, builds its world, and successfully deceives the audience until the reveal. The production is excellent, the cinematography is distinctive, and the sound effectively supports the story. Its themes — consumerism, alienation, identity, and masculinity in crisis — also contribute to its enormous cultural impact. The problem comes with subsequent viewings. Once you know the trick, the castle slowly begins to collapse: forced elements and narrative inconsistencies become more visible, making the whole mechanism much less solid than it initially appears. This is where, for me, it loses something compared to other thrillers built around a revelation. The Usual Suspects , for example, becomes more fascinating and precise with every viewing; Fight Club , on the other hand, loses some of its magic once you already know the trick. Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Fight Club (1999) Fight Club: Violence in Place of Understanding Human Alienation On its surface, Fight Club is a film about the alienation of modern man: alienation from work, from the body, from objects, from the crowd, from the self. My thesis is that instead of building a machine for understanding this alienation, the film builds a machine for discharging it, and that this discharge is substituted for analysis through an aestheticization of violence. Contrary to the common reading that treats the film as a critique of late-twentieth-century consumerism (a reading I'll address below and show to be insufficient), my argument is that the film's formal structure, at a level deeper than the characters' explicit dialogue, presents violence not as an object of examination but as the very telos of liberation. The choice of an unreliable narrator is, at first glance, a classic device for representing the subject's internal rupture, a tradition running from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari to Taxi Driver . The key difference, however, lies in how the camera positions itself relative to that rupture. In the scene introducing Tyler on the airplane, Fincher uses a low-angle medium shot that places Tyler in a position of visual authority from the very first moment, before the narrator himself even understands his relationship to this man. This choice, unlike Scorsese's treatment of Travis Bickle, where the camera deliberately maintains a cold, alienated distance from the subject, invites the viewer into identification from the outset. The film's form makes the audience fall in love with Tyler before the narrative ever discloses that he is a hallucination. This formal-narrative contradiction is where the problem begins: the final revelation (that Tyler and the narrator are one) is shocking at the level of story, but at the level of form it has already been neutralized. The camera has been complicit with Tyler from the start, not with the narrator. Comparing two key fight scenes, the narrator's first brawl with Tyler in the parking lot and the narrator's fight with "Angel Face," reveals the film's editing pattern. In both scenes, the cutting rate accelerates as the fight continues, and the sound design shifts from realistic effects toward exaggerated sonic design (heartbeat, echo), a pattern nearly identical to the escalation used in genre action sequences. The contrast with something like the fight scenes in Scorsese's Raging Bull is instructive: there, slow, repetitive editing turns violence into an experience of attrition and meaninglessness; the blows repeat until pleasure is drained away. In Fight Club, by contrast, the editing builds toward a rhythmic climax that completes pleasure rather than dissolving it. This formal choice is not incidental; it is meaning-making. At the sensory level, the audience experiences violence not as crisis but as resolution, precisely reproducing the same psychological pattern the film claims to be exposing. The most significant objection to this reading is the common argument, made by critics such as actor Edward Norton and in academic readings including those of Ruben Austin and Henry Giroux, that the film is a self-aware critique of toxic masculine ideology: the final scene, in which the narrator shoots Tyler and stands beside Marla, is read as a symbolic rejection of the fantasy of violence. This reading is defensible at the level of plot, but it fails at the level of form. Visually, the closing scene is accompanied by a triumphant score (the song "Where Is My Mind," with its melodic swell) synchronized with images of the towers collapsing, a combination that evokes liberation and grandeur, not warning or catastrophe. If the film truly intended to reject violence, its final sound design and editing should have conveyed a sense of emptiness or horror, not an inspirational musical crescendo. In other words, the explicit language of the plot (the rejection of Tyler) contradicts the implicit language of form (the celebration of destruction). In cinema, form always has the last word. In the film's framing system, Marla is almost always shown in tight shots, from angles that place her at the margins or behind the narrator. For example, in the support-group scenes, the camera focuses on the narrator's reaction to Marla's presence rather than on Marla herself as a subject with an independent crisis. This consistent framing choice reveals that within the film's formal apparatus, alienation is understood not as a universal human problem but as a specifically masculine crisis, whose resolution is sought through the reclamation of the male body via pain. This can be contrasted with a film like Kieślowski's Three Colors: Blue , which builds a crisis of identity through a woman whose relationship to loss is tied not to the body and violence but to silence and quiet reconstruction. The absence of such a possibility in Fight Club is not accidental; it reflects the limits of the film's formal imagination. Fight Club is a film of considerable technical skill, but that skill, rather than serving an understanding of alienation, serves to aestheticize a violent solution. The contradiction between the explicit language of the plot (which claims to critique violence) and the implicit language of form (which celebrates it) is exactly what turns the film not into an analysis but into an unconscious complicity with its own subject matter. For this reason, I give half a star to a film that has put formalist craft in the service of a dangerous thesis: the replacement of understanding with violence.

é um daqueles filmes que parecem ter conquistado um status quase intocável na cultura pop, mas pra mim, essa fama é muito maior do que seus méritos. o filme é frequentemente tratado como uma obra profunda e revolucionária, porém acho uma narrativa que, apesar de começar com uma proposta interessante, termina se rendendo a um espetáculo vazio. nos primeiros atos, a história parece caminhar para uma crítica ao capitalismo, ao consumismo e à alienação da vida moderna. até há espaço para imaginar uma discussão mais complexa sobre o sistema e sobre como ele molda a identidade masculina. mo entanto, essa possibilidade logo é abandonada e em vez de aprofundar suas críticas, o filme transforma esse discurso em um pretexto para cenas de violência, caos e ação, esvaziando boa parte do potencial que havia construído. outro aspecto que me incomodou foi a forma como os personagens são apresentados. Achei todos profundamente antipáticos e difíceis de acompanhar. a impressão é de que o filme espera que o espectador admire figuras que, na prática, são dominadas pelo ego, pela agressividade e por uma visão bastante limitada das relações humanas. me parece um filme pensado prioritariamente para um público masculino. sua reflexão sobre masculinidade é quase inteiramente construída a partir da violência, da destruição e da necessidade de reafirmação do homem. falta sensibilidade para explorar outras dimensões dos personagens ou das pessoas afetadas por suas ações, o que torna a experiência emocionalmente distante. sei bem que o filme possui uma direção marcante, um ritmo envolvente e um desfecho que surpreendeu muitos espectadores. ainda assim, esses elementos não foram suficientes para me convencer. Para mim, trata-se de um filme superestimado: começa sugerindo uma crítica social promissora, mas termina reduzindo suas ideias a um espetáculo de violência que parece muito menos inteligente do que acredita ser.

Fight Club (1999) Fight Club: Violence in Place of Understanding Human Alienation On its surface, Fight Club is a film about the alienation of modern man: alienation from work, from the body, from objects, from the crowd, from the self. My thesis is that instead of building a machine for understanding this alienation, the film builds a machine for discharging it, and that this discharge is substituted for analysis through an aestheticization of violence. Contrary to the common reading that treats the film as a critique of late-twentieth-century consumerism (a reading I'll address below and show to be insufficient), my argument is that the film's formal structure, at a level deeper than the characters' explicit dialogue, presents violence not as an object of examination but as the very telos of liberation. The choice of an unreliable narrator is, at first glance, a classic device for representing the subject's internal rupture, a tradition running from The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari to Taxi Driver . The key difference, however, lies in how the camera positions itself relative to that rupture. In the scene introducing Tyler on the airplane, Fincher uses a low-angle medium shot that places Tyler in a position of visual authority from the very first moment, before the narrator himself even understands his relationship to this man. This choice, unlike Scorsese's treatment of Travis Bickle, where the camera deliberately maintains a cold, alienated distance from the subject, invites the viewer into identification from the outset. The film's form makes the audience fall in love with Tyler before the narrative ever discloses that he is a hallucination. This formal-narrative contradiction is where the problem begins: the final revelation (that Tyler and the narrator are one) is shocking at the level of story, but at the level of form it has already been neutralized. The camera has been complicit with Tyler from the start, not with the narrator. Comparing two key fight scenes, the narrator's first brawl with Tyler in the parking lot and the narrator's fight with "Angel Face," reveals the film's editing pattern. In both scenes, the cutting rate accelerates as the fight continues, and the sound design shifts from realistic effects toward exaggerated sonic design (heartbeat, echo), a pattern nearly identical to the escalation used in genre action sequences. The contrast with something like the fight scenes in Scorsese's Raging Bull is instructive: there, slow, repetitive editing turns violence into an experience of attrition and meaninglessness; the blows repeat until pleasure is drained away. In Fight Club, by contrast, the editing builds toward a rhythmic climax that completes pleasure rather than dissolving it. This formal choice is not incidental; it is meaning-making. At the sensory level, the audience experiences violence not as crisis but as resolution, precisely reproducing the same psychological pattern the film claims to be exposing. The most significant objection to this reading is the common argument, made by critics such as actor Edward Norton and in academic readings including those of Ruben Austin and Henry Giroux, that the film is a self-aware critique of toxic masculine ideology: the final scene, in which the narrator shoots Tyler and stands beside Marla, is read as a symbolic rejection of the fantasy of violence. This reading is defensible at the level of plot, but it fails at the level of form. Visually, the closing scene is accompanied by a triumphant score (the song "Where Is My Mind," with its melodic swell) synchronized with images of the towers collapsing, a combination that evokes liberation and grandeur, not warning or catastrophe. If the film truly intended to reject violence, its final sound design and editing should have conveyed a sense of emptiness or horror, not an inspirational musical crescendo. In other words, the explicit language of the plot (the rejection of Tyler) contradicts the implicit language of form (the celebration of destruction). In cinema, form always has the last word. In the film's framing system, Marla is almost always shown in tight shots, from angles that place her at the margins or behind the narrator. For example, in the support-group scenes, the camera focuses on the narrator's reaction to Marla's presence rather than on Marla herself as a subject with an independent crisis. This consistent framing choice reveals that within the film's formal apparatus, alienation is understood not as a universal human problem but as a specifically masculine crisis, whose resolution is sought through the reclamation of the male body via pain. This can be contrasted with a film like Kieślowski's Three Colors: Blue , which builds a crisis of identity through a woman whose relationship to loss is tied not to the body and violence but to silence and quiet reconstruction. The absence of such a possibility in Fight Club is not accidental; it reflects the limits of the film's formal imagination. Fight Club is a film of considerable technical skill, but that skill, rather than serving an understanding of alienation, serves to aestheticize a violent solution. The contradiction between the explicit language of the plot (which claims to critique violence) and the implicit language of form (which celebrates it) is exactly what turns the film not into an analysis but into an unconscious complicity with its own subject matter. For this reason, I give half a star to a film that has put formalist craft in the service of a dangerous thesis: the replacement of understanding with violence.

é um daqueles filmes que parecem ter conquistado um status quase intocável na cultura pop, mas pra mim, essa fama é muito maior do que seus méritos. o filme é frequentemente tratado como uma obra profunda e revolucionária, porém acho uma narrativa que, apesar de começar com uma proposta interessante, termina se rendendo a um espetáculo vazio. nos primeiros atos, a história parece caminhar para uma crítica ao capitalismo, ao consumismo e à alienação da vida moderna. até há espaço para imaginar uma discussão mais complexa sobre o sistema e sobre como ele molda a identidade masculina. mo entanto, essa possibilidade logo é abandonada e em vez de aprofundar suas críticas, o filme transforma esse discurso em um pretexto para cenas de violência, caos e ação, esvaziando boa parte do potencial que havia construído. outro aspecto que me incomodou foi a forma como os personagens são apresentados. Achei todos profundamente antipáticos e difíceis de acompanhar. a impressão é de que o filme espera que o espectador admire figuras que, na prática, são dominadas pelo ego, pela agressividade e por uma visão bastante limitada das relações humanas. me parece um filme pensado prioritariamente para um público masculino. sua reflexão sobre masculinidade é quase inteiramente construída a partir da violência, da destruição e da necessidade de reafirmação do homem. falta sensibilidade para explorar outras dimensões dos personagens ou das pessoas afetadas por suas ações, o que torna a experiência emocionalmente distante. sei bem que o filme possui uma direção marcante, um ritmo envolvente e um desfecho que surpreendeu muitos espectadores. ainda assim, esses elementos não foram suficientes para me convencer. Para mim, trata-se de um filme superestimado: começa sugerindo uma crítica social promissora, mas termina reduzindo suas ideias a um espetáculo de violência que parece muito menos inteligente do que acredita ser.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{

Lots of stuff that works and lots of stuff that doesn’t. Nice social commentary, some really sharp symbolism, and creative metaphors. Some scenes use tension really well, along with some inspired cinematography. But the tonal mess that this movie is can sometimes be simply too much. None of the comedic scenes worked for me, not even a little bit. I would cut out the TSA guy entirely. I don’t believe comedic relief is really necessary in horror movies (especially when it lacks comedy), but most importantly, the job of comedic relief is to relieve tension. Why the hell would you want to relieve tension in a horror film? It seems as though Peele’s background in comedy is hindering his potential as a serious horror director. To clarify, I don’t think you can’t mix genres; I don’t believe in limitations in art. But here, the genre-breaking doesn’t seem to serve any purpose other than wasting my time. Aside from all that, the movie was also uneven in a plethora of ways: some scenes are brilliantly written and directed (helped a lot by some exceptional performances), while others are laughably cliché and interfere with the movie’s strengths. I think a great screenplay is hidden in here but is in dire need of a rewrite. As for Mr. Peele, I can see his obvious talent and potential, and I’m interested to see whether he manages to live up to it in his later projects, which I’m intending to watch.

Der von nicht wenigen als Rassist bezeichnete Jordan Peele bekommt ein dickes Budget für sein Regie-Debüt, um in einem reinen Fantasy-Film die Realität zu verdrehen. Der Rest ist Filmgeschichte, leider derart Status. Vier „Nur-weil-ich-schwarz-bin“-Oscar-Nominierungen für eine allseits hofierte Hass-Tirade und einen Genre-Beitrag, wie er bis dahin bei derartigen Veranstaltungen gar nicht beachtet wurde. Die Frage nach dem Warum ist vermutlich einfach beantwortet, an einer herausragenden Qualität des Werkes liegt es sicher nicht: So viele Jahre indoktrinierter Komplex, meist schon seit der Wiege. Dieser Film ist das vielgesuchte feierliche Eingeständnis: Schuldig, schuldig, weiß zu sein. Wenn nicht Schuldeingeständnis, dann Schuldzuweisung. Zur Geschichte: Ein weißer junger Mann läuft abends mit seiner dunkelhäutigen Freundin durch Harlem. Nun ja, fast. Das hier ist kein Kurzfilm, er geht 105 Minuten. Sonst stört sich das vermeintlich bessere Publikum, genau das, welches hier nicht nur Unterhaltung sucht, sondern immer ein Statement findet, ja immer am billigen Kniff der Jump-Scares. Bei Peele sind jene als hochfrequentiertes Stilmittel ausnahmsweise erlaubt. Der Rest läuft auch nach Schema F: Einführung, Fragezeichen, erwarteter Plot-Twist, exzessives Ende. Dann doch eine stimmige Tour de Force, wenigstens ein einigermaßen genießbarer Genre-Happen? Wie man es nimmt: von unappetitlich („für das größere Ziel wird auch das Bett mit dem kleineren Ziel geteilt“) über unverschämt („alle Weißen wären insgeheim gern schwarz“) bis unerträglich („die weiße Bestie“). Da haben wir ihn, den „The Birth of a Nation“ unserer Zeit, allerdings einen „The Downfall of a Nation“. Nein zu Spaltung und derartigem Rassismus! ENGLISH Jordan Peele, described by quite a few as a racist, is given a hefty budget for his directorial debut to distort reality in a pure fantasy film. The rest is film history – unfortunately, that’s just the way it is. Four ‘just-because-I’m-black’ Oscar nominations for a universally fawned-over tirade of hatred and a contribution to the genre that had previously gone entirely unnoticed at such events. The question of why is probably easy to answer; it certainly isn’t down to the outstanding quality of the work: so many years of indoctrinated insecurity, mostly instilled from the cradle. This film is the much-sought-after solemn admission: guilty, guilty of being white. If not an admission of guilt, then an attribution of blame. The story goes like this: a young white man is walking through Harlem one evening with his dark-skinned girlfriend. Well, almost. This isn’t a short film; it runs for 105 minutes. Otherwise, the supposedly more discerning audience – precisely those who aren’t just looking for entertainment here, but always find a statement, and are always on the lookout for the cheap trick of jump scares – would take offence. With Peele, however, these are, for once, permitted as a frequently used stylistic device. The rest also follows a formulaic pattern: introduction, a question mark, the expected plot twist, an over-the-top ending. So is it a coherent tour de force after all, or at least a reasonably enjoyable slice of genre fare? It depends on how you look at it: ranging from distasteful (‘for the greater good, one shares the bed with the lesser good’) to outrageous (‘all white people would secretly like to be black’) to unbearable (‘the white beast’). There it is, the ‘The Birth of a Nation’ of our time – though in this case, ‘The Downfall of a Nation’. No to division and racism of this sort!
