[20] nota=2.0 estrelas:
Der von nicht wenigen als Rassist bezeichnete Jordan Peele bekommt ein dickes Budget für sein Regie-Debüt, um in einem reinen Fantasy-Film die Realität zu verdrehen. Der Rest ist Filmgeschichte, leider derart Status. Vier „Nur-weil-ich-schwarz-bin“-Oscar-Nominierungen für eine allseits hofierte Hass-Tirade und einen Genre-Beitrag, wie er bis dahin bei derartigen Veranstaltungen gar nicht beachtet wurde. Die Frage nach dem Warum ist vermutlich einfach beantwortet, an einer herausragenden Qualität des Werkes liegt es sicher nicht: So viele Jahre indoktrinierter Komplex, meist schon seit der Wiege. Dieser Film ist das vielgesuchte feierliche Eingeständnis: Schuldig, schuldig, weiß zu sein. Wenn nicht Schuldeingeständnis, dann Schuldzuweisung. Zur Geschichte: Ein weißer junger Mann läuft abends mit seiner dunkelhäutigen Freundin durch Harlem. Nun ja, fast. Das hier ist kein Kurzfilm, er geht 105 Minuten. Sonst stört sich das vermeintlich bessere Publikum, genau das, welches hier nicht nur Unterhaltung sucht, sondern immer ein Statement findet, ja immer am billigen Kniff der Jump-Scares. Bei Peele sind jene als hochfrequentiertes Stilmittel ausnahmsweise erlaubt. Der Rest läuft auch nach Schema F: Einführung, Fragezeichen, erwarteter Plot-Twist, exzessives Ende. Dann doch eine stimmige Tour de Force, wenigstens ein einigermaßen genießbarer Genre-Happen? Wie man es nimmt: von unappetitlich („für das größere Ziel wird auch das Bett mit dem kleineren Ziel geteilt“) über unverschämt („alle Weißen wären insgeheim gern schwarz“) bis unerträglich („die weiße Bestie“). Da haben wir ihn, den „The Birth of a Nation“ unserer Zeit, allerdings einen „The Downfall of a Nation“. Nein zu Spaltung und derartigem Rassismus! ENGLISH Jordan Peele, described by quite a few as a racist, is given a hefty budget for his directorial debut to distort reality in a pure fantasy film. The rest is film history – unfortunately, that’s just the way it is. Four ‘just-because-I’m-black’ Oscar nominations for a universally fawned-over tirade of hatred and a contribution to the genre that had previously gone entirely unnoticed at such events. The question of why is probably easy to answer; it certainly isn’t down to the outstanding quality of the work: so many years of indoctrinated insecurity, mostly instilled from the cradle. This film is the much-sought-after solemn admission: guilty, guilty of being white. If not an admission of guilt, then an attribution of blame. The story goes like this: a young white man is walking through Harlem one evening with his dark-skinned girlfriend. Well, almost. This isn’t a short film; it runs for 105 minutes. Otherwise, the supposedly more discerning audience – precisely those who aren’t just looking for entertainment here, but always find a statement, and are always on the lookout for the cheap trick of jump scares – would take offence. With Peele, however, these are, for once, permitted as a frequently used stylistic device. The rest also follows a formulaic pattern: introduction, a question mark, the expected plot twist, an over-the-top ending. So is it a coherent tour de force after all, or at least a reasonably enjoyable slice of genre fare? It depends on how you look at it: ranging from distasteful (‘for the greater good, one shares the bed with the lesser good’) to outrageous (‘all white people would secretly like to be black’) to unbearable (‘the white beast’). There it is, the ‘The Birth of a Nation’ of our time – though in this case, ‘The Downfall of a Nation’. No to division and racism of this sort!

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

If this movie were a hamburger (I say this because I just ate two pepperoni and bacon hamburgers that my dad made and they were absurdly amazing), the moment this afternoon when I finally saw the credits would be the moment when, more than stuffed, feeling sick, I would lean back in my chair as if about to give birth, look up, turn my neck, sigh, and closing my eyes briefly, put my hand to my forehead as if in despair or regret for having eaten something bigger than I could handle. I think this comparison would be much better if I remembered exactly what I would say afterwards, today I'm not feeling well. "Happy Hour," being the Japanese classic that it is, was on my list and I randomly picked the name and went looking for it. I pressed play and damn, 5 hours of film made me think like it was a vital decision whether I would embark on this journey or live in peace, and perhaps fortunately (or unfortunately) I chose to watch, and now I just want to go home, sleep and make my mind think that this will regulate my sleep, but at least it will give me the rest I need. I should clarify that I didn't watch the whole movie in one sitting, not even in a single day, of course, and something tells me that some fanatics will comment that this was the reason I didn't like it so much, but damn, I'm not going to do that, I'm sorry. I watched about 3 hours of the movie today to finish it and I can't say if it was good or bad, but actually something in me makes me want to be sure that it wasn't enjoyable, and I agree with that something. I wanted to stop watching the movie several times and I don't know why I didn't. I think for some reason I expected it to be as good as "Eureka," which has a similar vibe, but this one is something much more distinct. Affairs, slice of life, the drama of constantly dissatisfied adult life and friendships—all of this makes up "Happy Hour" and the narratives of the four characters. I think this is an attempt to immerse us as much as possible in everyone's lives and the melancholy that pervades the entire film, which is why it's so long. In fact, the character development and the acting (including amateur performances, but still very good) are very good elements, but at the same time, I felt like I was traveling and traveling and didn't reach a destination with the plot. It's not that "Happy Hour" is necessarily bad; I understand that it's so acclaimed not only because cinephiles love a tediously long film (I say this respectfully, okay?) and, on top of that, a Japanese one, but because it's clearly a strong, well-made work with a unique approach; truly impressive. But personally, I can't like it. The story didn't grab my attention, I lost interest at numerous points, and despite appreciating several aspects like the well-done production, I couldn't connect with the film and I think I wasted my time watching the whole thing. I'm sorry.

Mis bout à bout, le projet impressionne : une narration audacieuse, un regard déjà singulier sur le monde, porté par une foi dans la puissance de la poésie, de l'écoute, des trajectoires personnelles. Comment se connaître et s'aimer soi-même, comment composer avec l'autre ? Hamaguchi est un cinéaste profondément philosophique, et qui l'assume — sa grâce est de rendre cette philosophie accessible. Il aime aussi inviter d'autres œuvres dans son cinéma, avec exigence : le théâtre dans "Drive My Car" ou "Soudain", et ici la lecture intégrale d'un texte intime signé d'une jeune romancière, suivie d'un débat avec elle. Postures clivantes, qu'on pourra juger anti cinématographiques, mais qui définissent son geste. Les moments les plus forts sont sans doute les affrontements. Je pense à cette soirée, après un atelier étrange où les quatre amies apprennent à écouter le corps des autres, où le divorce tenu secret de l'une d'elles finit par affleurer et fait éclater les tensions pour des raisons parfaitement inattendues, qui tiennent à la susceptibilité, à la jalousie. À partir de là, ce groupe qu'on imaginait uni vole en éclats, puis tente de se reformer sans jamais vraiment y parvenir. Beaucoup diront que le format tient davantage de la série ; je dirais simplement que "Senses" est un film trop long, parce que l'émotion s'y dilue sur une durée qu'il ne parvient pas à tenir. Les ramifications montent si haut qu'on finit par perdre de vue le tronc : l'amitié et ses perceptions divergentes au sein d'un groupe de femmes, la solidarité, l'amour, bref la vie, ou comment la reconstruire dans le Japon d'aujourd'hui, entre famille, amitié et travail. Dans ses œuvres suivantes, même plus courtes comme "Contes du hasard et autres fantaisies", l'artisan Hamaguchi devient orfèvre : l'émotion se densifie de film en film sans rien sacrifier des audaces de mise en scène. "Senses" n'atteint pas encore cette puissance. J'y vois pourtant la matrice de "Soudain", si différent dans son sujet mais si proche dans sa foi en la conversation comme événement : en resserrant sur deux personnages ce que "Senses" dispersait sur quatre trajectoires, Hamaguchi parvient enfin à tenir l'émotion sur la durée. Reste qu’il compose dans "Senses" avec une galerie de femmes complexes, autrement plus fines que les clichés dont se contentent la plupart des fictions, et touche à une vérité profonde dans la représentation de l'humain. On sent l'artiste au travail. Parler de brouillon serait injuste tant il contient de belles choses ; disons plutôt que les films qu'il signera ensuite, avec des ingrédients similaires, seront encore plus émotionnels, profonds, évocateurs.

While I love long films, there are times I'm daunted by the runtime depending on the film itself. 'Happy Hour' is a 5+ hour drama around the small lives of four women. That's right: just when you finished a 2 1/2 hour movie, you got another 2 1/2 hour movie to watch plus an additional seventeen minutes of your choice. Despite the praise, I'm rather mixed, but I can understand both opinionated sides, even if I lean a bit more on one. It's rather a visual novel: exploring their lives in full detail, every scene taking its time with its slower pacing, making sure the audience is living with them, details hidden till revealed, and really loves the leads by delaying the conflict till around the eighty-minute mark. My favorite would be Akari; she's a nurse and I found her more interesting in personality, although Sakurako's storyline kicks in gear around the three-hour mark, and Jun is the one with her conflict; Fumi's show comes in later. While I appreciate its commitment in itself, did it really need to be 317 minutes long? I don't think so. Cutting two hours or so would make it an abridged version, sure, but there were several times I felt unengaged and even bored because it felt rather dry and tedious, in my opinion. The length basically doesn't earn itself from its script, and I felt something rich and beautiful was missing. At least it wasn't sappy - far from it. 'Yi Yi' is almost three hours, but I never thought it was a bog as it manages to tell its epic slice-of-life story without sacrificing too much; 'Happy Hour', on the other hand, is too precious of its memories all the time. Some don't think it's a big deal, but I thought the cinematography was kinda boring. Let me say this: the framing and composition are well-done, but the lack of color grading and using only the white balance, I assume, got tiring and plain after a while. Also, the sound editing isn't amazing, but I imagine the budget was much smaller, and I've heard editing is expensive. I can see both sides defending for what they stand: either a reflective, human masterpiece or a bloated, self-indulgent movie. As for me, it's a risky experiment that doesn't fully pay off for me, where I see a great three-hour film hidden within what I thought was the editor's cut. A minor recommendation.

During the latter half of the expedition that is Happy Hour , there is a scene where a young author named Ms. Nose is criticized for having read her book to an audience in a monotone voice. She answers that since she knew the characters she wrote so well, and all of the emotions are on the page, no matter what vocal inflections she adds, the importance is found in the words. Happy Hour hinges on words and communication. For what's basically a five-hour-long monologue how could it not be about these things? The story follows four women who vocalize their anxieties to everyone except the people who these actual anxieties originate, mostly their husbands. The story becomes how communication gets lost in a marriage. Saying a couple of words as a husband and wife pass by each other around the breakfast table is not the kind of interaction that can sustain a marriage. Before long the important needs of these women go unaddressed and they realize they could do better. I like where Hamaguchi takes the story. In a very Bergman-esque fashion, he captures the female perspective with confidence. However, to draw on how Ms. Nose reads her book in a monotone way, the rest of the movie features the most unemotive acting I've ever seen. I believe this was done purposefully to show the true emptiness behind each woman's marriage. None of the cast are trained actors either for this reason. The scene I brought up basically literalizes the intent of emphasizing the dialogue. For my personal enjoyment of this film, I couldn't get compelled to care about any of these characters for the lack of them feeling like people I know or acting like actual people at all. A character would be told about how their partner wants a divorce and they would wear an awkward blank stare. Outside of the film's length showcasing an incremental decline of each character's relationship with their spouse, I did not see the need for a five-hour project. I would've settled for three. I think for anything dialogue-heavy, talented actors really go a long way to sell key emotional moments. A lot of the time I couldn't read what emotion a character was showing, rendering the point of the scene mute. Hamaguchi builds a believable world around its characters, but there was so much more to explore, things that were left unsaid, which makes me think that the five hour runtime could've been used more effectively.

I enjoyed this dialogue-driven flick in bursts and flashes -- more than I can say Hamaguchi's other big hit, Drive My Car -- whenever it really productively explored the ways we do or don't communicate with one another. I just wish it wasn't five-plus bloody hours. I know, I know: the entire movie is fundamentally about the ways we do or don't communicate, so my statement above can seem silly. The kick is that it does so with varying degrees of clarity or focus throughout its painful runtime, and I found myself rapt in those stretches where it really was tackling the concepts head-on. So yes, then this thing gets into the meaning of what it is to be in a relationship, and how we center ourselves while also supporting other people? Brilliant. I wasn't sold on its tactics at first, but the way Hamaguchi puts you through these trust exercises, seemingly without purpose, and then has a participant criticize the instructor with the same thoughts as I had, only to have the purpose hinted at a bit more firmly -- well, let's just say it helped crystallize the point of the film. It's not that I'm an idiot; I understand and appreciate some artistic metaphor and allusion. It's when people are staring in silence for five minutes, or moving into much less direct tangents that I find myself being pulled into areas of the film that work for me much less well, and that I think is where the majority of this thing spends its time. I don't need to be spoonfed, as I love when movies trust the viewer; but this also means the movie sometimes meeting me halfway. I value its quiet, austere, calm take, and that it's able to produce great tension in the most silent of conversations. I especially value the core concepts it's working with, and I was sucked into the movie when it really knuckled down. But as someone who cared a lot less for the meandering bits about infidelity, or gender roles in parenting, or career aspirations, I drifted in this thing a lot more than I'd like. In short, a bit too long and a bit too all-encompassing for the energy I was willing to put in. Still, an impressive beast, and one I'll be thinking about -- in pieces, at least.

The story of four friends in Kobe and their disintegrating relationships amidst endless and varied attempts to communicate. Akari is divorced and outspoken, a strong nurse with an empathy deficit. Sakurako is a put-upon housewife with an ungenerous husband and a teenager (who in turn has a unexpectedly pregnant girlfriend). Fumi is a childless curator with a husband who's more a roommate than a romantic (or, at least, his romantic affections are directed elsewhere). And Jun is divorcing her spouse, a cold blooded scientist who hasn't harmed her but won't ever let her go, even if she has to fly into hiding with her unborn child. I've seen "Happy Hour" described as novelistic and that's true, but also a coded way of excusing its 317-minute run time. Just as much of a novel, however, the film reminds me of a workshop, and indeed two very long stretches of the movie are centered around performances of sorts at Fumi's arts space, PORTO (not to mention the extended, fractious discussions after both). Perhaps fitting as I understand that Ryusuke Hamaguchi developed the script through improvisational exercises with his non-professional actresses. Not entirely successful in its own right, as the dyads can feel a bit obvious and the pacing languorous, but I'm convinced that this work is a rehearsal for a compelling cinematic voice.

If this movie were a hamburger (I say this because I just ate two pepperoni and bacon hamburgers that my dad made and they were absurdly amazing), the moment this afternoon when I finally saw the credits would be the moment when, more than stuffed, feeling sick, I would lean back in my chair as if about to give birth, look up, turn my neck, sigh, and closing my eyes briefly, put my hand to my forehead as if in despair or regret for having eaten something bigger than I could handle. I think this comparison would be much better if I remembered exactly what I would say afterwards, today I'm not feeling well. "Happy Hour," being the Japanese classic that it is, was on my list and I randomly picked the name and went looking for it. I pressed play and damn, 5 hours of film made me think like it was a vital decision whether I would embark on this journey or live in peace, and perhaps fortunately (or unfortunately) I chose to watch, and now I just want to go home, sleep and make my mind think that this will regulate my sleep, but at least it will give me the rest I need. I should clarify that I didn't watch the whole movie in one sitting, not even in a single day, of course, and something tells me that some fanatics will comment that this was the reason I didn't like it so much, but damn, I'm not going to do that, I'm sorry. I watched about 3 hours of the movie today to finish it and I can't say if it was good or bad, but actually something in me makes me want to be sure that it wasn't enjoyable, and I agree with that something. I wanted to stop watching the movie several times and I don't know why I didn't. I think for some reason I expected it to be as good as "Eureka," which has a similar vibe, but this one is something much more distinct. Affairs, slice of life, the drama of constantly dissatisfied adult life and friendships—all of this makes up "Happy Hour" and the narratives of the four characters. I think this is an attempt to immerse us as much as possible in everyone's lives and the melancholy that pervades the entire film, which is why it's so long. In fact, the character development and the acting (including amateur performances, but still very good) are very good elements, but at the same time, I felt like I was traveling and traveling and didn't reach a destination with the plot. It's not that "Happy Hour" is necessarily bad; I understand that it's so acclaimed not only because cinephiles love a tediously long film (I say this respectfully, okay?) and, on top of that, a Japanese one, but because it's clearly a strong, well-made work with a unique approach; truly impressive. But personally, I can't like it. The story didn't grab my attention, I lost interest at numerous points, and despite appreciating several aspects like the well-done production, I couldn't connect with the film and I think I wasted my time watching the whole thing. I'm sorry.

Mis bout à bout, le projet impressionne : une narration audacieuse, un regard déjà singulier sur le monde, porté par une foi dans la puissance de la poésie, de l'écoute, des trajectoires personnelles. Comment se connaître et s'aimer soi-même, comment composer avec l'autre ? Hamaguchi est un cinéaste profondément philosophique, et qui l'assume — sa grâce est de rendre cette philosophie accessible. Il aime aussi inviter d'autres œuvres dans son cinéma, avec exigence : le théâtre dans "Drive My Car" ou "Soudain", et ici la lecture intégrale d'un texte intime signé d'une jeune romancière, suivie d'un débat avec elle. Postures clivantes, qu'on pourra juger anti cinématographiques, mais qui définissent son geste. Les moments les plus forts sont sans doute les affrontements. Je pense à cette soirée, après un atelier étrange où les quatre amies apprennent à écouter le corps des autres, où le divorce tenu secret de l'une d'elles finit par affleurer et fait éclater les tensions pour des raisons parfaitement inattendues, qui tiennent à la susceptibilité, à la jalousie. À partir de là, ce groupe qu'on imaginait uni vole en éclats, puis tente de se reformer sans jamais vraiment y parvenir. Beaucoup diront que le format tient davantage de la série ; je dirais simplement que "Senses" est un film trop long, parce que l'émotion s'y dilue sur une durée qu'il ne parvient pas à tenir. Les ramifications montent si haut qu'on finit par perdre de vue le tronc : l'amitié et ses perceptions divergentes au sein d'un groupe de femmes, la solidarité, l'amour, bref la vie, ou comment la reconstruire dans le Japon d'aujourd'hui, entre famille, amitié et travail. Dans ses œuvres suivantes, même plus courtes comme "Contes du hasard et autres fantaisies", l'artisan Hamaguchi devient orfèvre : l'émotion se densifie de film en film sans rien sacrifier des audaces de mise en scène. "Senses" n'atteint pas encore cette puissance. J'y vois pourtant la matrice de "Soudain", si différent dans son sujet mais si proche dans sa foi en la conversation comme événement : en resserrant sur deux personnages ce que "Senses" dispersait sur quatre trajectoires, Hamaguchi parvient enfin à tenir l'émotion sur la durée. Reste qu’il compose dans "Senses" avec une galerie de femmes complexes, autrement plus fines que les clichés dont se contentent la plupart des fictions, et touche à une vérité profonde dans la représentation de l'humain. On sent l'artiste au travail. Parler de brouillon serait injuste tant il contient de belles choses ; disons plutôt que les films qu'il signera ensuite, avec des ingrédients similaires, seront encore plus émotionnels, profonds, évocateurs.

[21] nota=3.0 estrelas:
While I love long films, there are times I'm daunted by the runtime depending on the film itself. 'Happy Hour' is a 5+ hour drama around the small lives of four women. That's right: just when you finished a 2 1/2 hour movie, you got another 2 1/2 hour movie to watch plus an additional seventeen minutes of your choice. Despite the praise, I'm rather mixed, but I can understand both opinionated sides, even if I lean a bit more on one. It's rather a visual novel: exploring their lives in full detail, every scene taking its time with its slower pacing, making sure the audience is living with them, details hidden till revealed, and really loves the leads by delaying the conflict till around the eighty-minute mark. My favorite would be Akari; she's a nurse and I found her more interesting in personality, although Sakurako's storyline kicks in gear around the three-hour mark, and Jun is the one with her conflict; Fumi's show comes in later. While I appreciate its commitment in itself, did it really need to be 317 minutes long? I don't think so. Cutting two hours or so would make it an abridged version, sure, but there were several times I felt unengaged and even bored because it felt rather dry and tedious, in my opinion. The length basically doesn't earn itself from its script, and I felt something rich and beautiful was missing. At least it wasn't sappy - far from it. 'Yi Yi' is almost three hours, but I never thought it was a bog as it manages to tell its epic slice-of-life story without sacrificing too much; 'Happy Hour', on the other hand, is too precious of its memories all the time. Some don't think it's a big deal, but I thought the cinematography was kinda boring. Let me say this: the framing and composition are well-done, but the lack of color grading and using only the white balance, I assume, got tiring and plain after a while. Also, the sound editing isn't amazing, but I imagine the budget was much smaller, and I've heard editing is expensive. I can see both sides defending for what they stand: either a reflective, human masterpiece or a bloated, self-indulgent movie. As for me, it's a risky experiment that doesn't fully pay off for me, where I see a great three-hour film hidden within what I thought was the editor's cut. A minor recommendation.

[24] nota=3.0 estrelas:
During the latter half of the expedition that is Happy Hour , there is a scene where a young author named Ms. Nose is criticized for having read her book to an audience in a monotone voice. She answers that since she knew the characters she wrote so well, and all of the emotions are on the page, no matter what vocal inflections she adds, the importance is found in the words. Happy Hour hinges on words and communication. For what's basically a five-hour-long monologue how could it not be about these things? The story follows four women who vocalize their anxieties to everyone except the people who these actual anxieties originate, mostly their husbands. The story becomes how communication gets lost in a marriage. Saying a couple of words as a husband and wife pass by each other around the breakfast table is not the kind of interaction that can sustain a marriage. Before long the important needs of these women go unaddressed and they realize they could do better. I like where Hamaguchi takes the story. In a very Bergman-esque fashion, he captures the female perspective with confidence. However, to draw on how Ms. Nose reads her book in a monotone way, the rest of the movie features the most unemotive acting I've ever seen. I believe this was done purposefully to show the true emptiness behind each woman's marriage. None of the cast are trained actors either for this reason. The scene I brought up basically literalizes the intent of emphasizing the dialogue. For my personal enjoyment of this film, I couldn't get compelled to care about any of these characters for the lack of them feeling like people I know or acting like actual people at all. A character would be told about how their partner wants a divorce and they would wear an awkward blank stare. Outside of the film's length showcasing an incremental decline of each character's relationship with their spouse, I did not see the need for a five-hour project. I would've settled for three. I think for anything dialogue-heavy, talented actors really go a long way to sell key emotional moments. A lot of the time I couldn't read what emotion a character was showing, rendering the point of the scene mute. Hamaguchi builds a believable world around its characters, but there was so much more to explore, things that were left unsaid, which makes me think that the five hour runtime could've been used more effectively.

I enjoyed this dialogue-driven flick in bursts and flashes -- more than I can say Hamaguchi's other big hit, Drive My Car -- whenever it really productively explored the ways we do or don't communicate with one another. I just wish it wasn't five-plus bloody hours. I know, I know: the entire movie is fundamentally about the ways we do or don't communicate, so my statement above can seem silly. The kick is that it does so with varying degrees of clarity or focus throughout its painful runtime, and I found myself rapt in those stretches where it really was tackling the concepts head-on. So yes, then this thing gets into the meaning of what it is to be in a relationship, and how we center ourselves while also supporting other people? Brilliant. I wasn't sold on its tactics at first, but the way Hamaguchi puts you through these trust exercises, seemingly without purpose, and then has a participant criticize the instructor with the same thoughts as I had, only to have the purpose hinted at a bit more firmly -- well, let's just say it helped crystallize the point of the film. It's not that I'm an idiot; I understand and appreciate some artistic metaphor and allusion. It's when people are staring in silence for five minutes, or moving into much less direct tangents that I find myself being pulled into areas of the film that work for me much less well, and that I think is where the majority of this thing spends its time. I don't need to be spoonfed, as I love when movies trust the viewer; but this also means the movie sometimes meeting me halfway. I value its quiet, austere, calm take, and that it's able to produce great tension in the most silent of conversations. I especially value the core concepts it's working with, and I was sucked into the movie when it really knuckled down. But as someone who cared a lot less for the meandering bits about infidelity, or gender roles in parenting, or career aspirations, I drifted in this thing a lot more than I'd like. In short, a bit too long and a bit too all-encompassing for the energy I was willing to put in. Still, an impressive beast, and one I'll be thinking about -- in pieces, at least.

Instead, while I wasn't truly wowed by it like seemingly all of my mutuals on here were, I was at least impressed by it more often than not. It's conversational and almost scarily like watching genuine interactions between people that, despite how clearly so much effort is put into each exchange between its characters, the film with time starts to feel less like a narrative work and more like documentary. It's through these moments that the characters share, and what they talk about, that they are able to work through the woes of their lives. It is through talking that they will seemingly be taking a new path towards being better. Do I think Hamaguchi has portrayed that better in his other films at a much shorter length? Absolutely. I do also think that being able to make the ending to a film that's this long feel in some way cathartic, and it's not because you are in relief that it's finally over, that's still an achievement. I think also especially with intense family drama going on with myself currently, the moments reflecting on love and divorce had extra poignancy. I'll do my best to take from what Ryûsuke offers here and know that when darker feelings seem more fruitful, it's taking a breath and being able to communicate with others that's more valuable. 6/10

The story of four friends in Kobe and their disintegrating relationships amidst endless and varied attempts to communicate. Akari is divorced and outspoken, a strong nurse with an empathy deficit. Sakurako is a put-upon housewife with an ungenerous husband and a teenager (who in turn has a unexpectedly pregnant girlfriend). Fumi is a childless curator with a husband who's more a roommate than a romantic (or, at least, his romantic affections are directed elsewhere). And Jun is divorcing her spouse, a cold blooded scientist who hasn't harmed her but won't ever let her go, even if she has to fly into hiding with her unborn child. I've seen "Happy Hour" described as novelistic and that's true, but also a coded way of excusing its 317-minute run time. Just as much of a novel, however, the film reminds me of a workshop, and indeed two very long stretches of the movie are centered around performances of sorts at Fumi's arts space, PORTO (not to mention the extended, fractious discussions after both). Perhaps fitting as I understand that Ryusuke Hamaguchi developed the script through improvisational exercises with his non-professional actresses. Not entirely successful in its own right, as the dyads can feel a bit obvious and the pacing languorous, but I'm convinced that this work is a rehearsal for a compelling cinematic voice.

I ordered a region-free DVD player just so I could watch this intimate, five-hour-plus epic of domestic life from Ryusuke Hamaguchi, who’s quickly become one of my favorite working directors (and quite possibly my very favorite). Two discs, three viewing sessions, and one day of rumination later, I can say that Happy Hour is an essential part of Hamaguchi’s filmography, thoroughly imbued with the intelligence and humanity that mark his extraordinary recent work ( Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy , Drive My Car , Evil Does Not Exist ). I have a few hesitations about some recurring elements that, despite the massive runtime, feel less consequential than I’d like them to be (guy who runs the New Age workshop that we experience in full, I’m looking at you). But on the whole, I was happy to be immersed in a film that values the mundane but that, in its very form, departs so strikingly from ordinary moviegoing experience. A few areas of thought: * Loved how completely female friendship permeates the film, even through some long stretches in which Akari, Jun, Sakurako, and Fumi remain apart. I thought from time to time about Virginia Woolf’s The Waves , in which the friendship between six characters who meet as children and interact only intermittently as adults forms a vessel that gives life meaning, a structure of belonging that has no official sanction or force but remains a continuous source of identity. The slow pace of the film’s first two hours comes in part from how the women, preoccupied by and/or attempting to cover up unhappiness related to marriage, family life, and work, don’t communicate very openly with one another, but one senses how their bond might offer a framework for disruption or renewal. I found the middle hour, leading up to and immediately following the trip to the hot springs resort, most compelling for precisely this reason, as the women begin to prod each other—lovingly, but not always pleasantly—to speak beyond their learned inhibitions, to risk a more radical, unsettling kind of honesty with one another. * As for what the film has to say about gender, sex and sexuality, and Japan’s still conservative mores and laws around marriage and divorce: forceful stuff, appropriately stamped with the texture and complication of actual life. None of the heterosexual relationships in Happy Hour are satisfying in any way, and Jun’s refusal to submit herself to a marriage she’s come to experience as deadly—as she attests in court, he’s killed her by lack of conversation—acts as a catalyst for some of the other women to ask themselves questions about desire, need, and sacrifice that would otherwise remain encased in the “cotton wool” of the ordinary (I’m borrowing from Woolf again). Nevertheless, it’s not apparent that there are right or wrong choices for each of the women, merely that there are choices: whether one seeks a separation or a strategy for marital repair, one can do and say things beyond the routine and reassert a right to happiness, even when the path to happiness remains elusive. * On the related topic of expressivity: I understand that the stolid reserve of the women has a cultural element and that it makes key moments of breakdown or decisiveness all the more poignant. At times, though, the performances verge on illegibility, and in some of the more charged stretches of the last two hours, I couldn’t quite work out what the film was suggesting about self-possession under duress. It occurred to me that the restrained affect might be related to the film’s understanding of itself as a kind of literary text, too. The visiting writer who reads her short story aloud at the cultural institute where Fumi works is herself asked why she performs with so little emotion, and the answer is a fascinating one: she doesn’t want to pretend that she can inhabit all of her characters, and she thinks that a sort of presentational truth, one that simply delivers the words themselves, still carries all the requisite feeling. A version of this idea may apply to the film, too. In the relative absence of histrionics, perhaps we are better able to understand and internalize the accrued weight of what these women have carried in their lives, the unspectacular ways they have been subsumed into (but thankfully not consumed by) the everyday. * Lastly, about duration: yes, I do think this could be an hour or two shorter and it would work nearly as well. And yet, I think it’s important to say that this isn’t a miniseries in disguise. It’s a novelistic film, just as Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy is a filmic collection of short stories. Although I watched in installments, I felt the continuous logic of the film’s development, the way the friendship group’s warm, complex, fraught tangle shifted and reconstituted, and how it informed the dramas in the women’s individual lives. Though I found some parts of the film too languorous, a bit too repetitive or restrained, I also didn’t want to leave these characters in the end, with their understanding of themselves and the impact of some of their bolder, pattern-breaking choices still very much in progress. But that’s the truth in which I suspect Hamaguchi is most invested: whatever span of time one chooses for a story, markers like beginnings and endings are arbitrary impositions, creations dictated by narrative. Life doesn’t work that way, and neither does friendship. letterboxd.com/cinemapoodle/list/ryusuke-hamaguchi-ranked-so-far/

It has been a joy and quite a chance experiment to follow Hamaguchi’s career backwards from Evil Does not Exist, Drive my Car, to Wheels of Fortune and Fantasy, and Happy Hour. Recently got a sneak peak of All of a Sudden as well. I’m dying to watch his even earlier films like Passion and Asako, and I don’t know how he can surprise me more. As you get more into his filmography you tap on your forehead and have this realization that this is a director who knows what he’s best at and keeps mastering his craft. His talent of scene construction, script writing, character building, momentum continuity just shines through the screen from the beginning like no other. Massive thanks to French New Wave, to Kurosawa, and Locarno film festival for providing the inspiration and stage for Hamaguchi to leave marks in film history. I wonder if the title Happy Hour is the exact translation from the Japanese title or if there’s nuance. I hate that in American (?) culture it has a rather superficial meaning. The length of the film… I think I felt it was halfway after two hours ish, the typical length for an entire feature film, which was so surprising, you can’t resist your urge to check on time when the movie’s bad, and this one I even needed to calculate a bathroom break (when are they not talking!!? Haha). Hamaguchi has the ability of writing dialogue that run smoothly, you would speak like that in daily life, they can be philosophical but have the sprinkle of mundane. And when they are going they struck you, when they stop they linger. They are not fast words with volume like maybe Linklater films, and the characters speak in a flat tone, with breaks, it’s really interesting I wonder how much of it is directors decision. Cinematographer has easy time with Hamaguchi project maybe haha, shots are so simple not dreamy flowy etc, they can even be problematic by the industry standards? Especially in the workshop scene (much of time the window light overpower and you can’t see faces at all, it’s dark). But it serves Hamaguchi’s style so well. Clocking in at over five hours, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Happy Hour (Happī Ā) is a quiet, monumental masterpiece of slow-cinema intimacy that feels less like watching a scripted movie and more like observing real lives unfold in unhurried, real time. Set in Kobe, the film follows a tight-knit circle of four women in their late 30s whose long-standing dynamics fracture when one of them suddenly reveals she is undergoing a messy divorce prompting the remaining three to re-examine their own stifled desires, marriages, and personal truths. What makes the film so uniquely captivating is Hamaguchi’s extraordinary process: developed through acting workshops with non-professional actors, the performances possess an astonishing, naturalistic grace (jointly earning all four lead actresses the Best Actress award at Locarno). Extended sequences like a fascinating body-listening workshop or a literary reading are allowed to breathe so fully that minor shifts in conversation carry the emotional impact of major plot twists. It’s an epic, exquisitely patient exploration of female friendship, emotional honesty, and the quiet compromises of adulthood.

Two discs, three viewing sessions, and one day of rumination later, I can say that Happy Hour is an essential part of Hamaguchi’s filmography, thoroughly imbued with the intelligence and humanity that mark his extraordinary recent work ( Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy , Drive My Car , Evil Does Not Exist ). I have a few hesitations about some recurring elements that, despite the massive runtime, feel less consequential than I’d like them to be (guy who runs the New Age workshop that we experience in full, I’m looking at you). But on the whole, I was happy to be immersed in a film that values the mundane but that, in its very form, departs so strikingly from ordinary moviegoing experience. A few areas of thought: * Loved how completely female friendship permeates the film, even through some long stretches in which Akari, Jun, Sakurako, and Fumi remain apart. I thought from time to time about Virginia Woolf’s The Waves , in which the friendship between six characters who meet as children and interact only intermittently as adults forms a vessel that gives life meaning, a structure of belonging that has no official sanction or force but remains a continuous source of identity. The slow pace of the film’s first two hours comes in part from how the women, preoccupied by and/or attempting to cover up unhappiness related to marriage, family life, and work, don’t communicate very openly with one another, but one senses how their bond might offer a framework for disruption or renewal. I found the middle hour, leading up to and immediately following the trip to the hot springs resort, most compelling for precisely this reason, as the women begin to prod each other—lovingly, but not always pleasantly—to speak beyond their learned inhibitions, to risk a more radical, unsettling kind of honesty with one another. * As for what the film has to say about gender, sex and sexuality, and Japan’s still conservative mores and laws around marriage and divorce: forceful stuff, appropriately stamped with the texture and complication of actual life. None of the heterosexual relationships in Happy Hour are satisfying in any way, and Jun’s refusal to submit herself to a marriage she’s come to experience as deadly—as she attests in court, he’s killed her by lack of conversation—acts as a catalyst for some of the other women to ask themselves questions about desire, need, and sacrifice that would otherwise remain encased in the “cotton wool” of the ordinary (I’m borrowing from Woolf again). Nevertheless, it’s not apparent that there are right or wrong choices for each of the women, merely that there are choices: whether one seeks a separation or a strategy for marital repair, one can do and say things beyond the routine and reassert a right to happiness, even when the path to happiness remains elusive. * On the related topic of expressivity: I understand that the stolid reserve of the women has a cultural element and that it makes key moments of breakdown or decisiveness all the more poignant. At times, though, the performances verge on illegibility, and in some of the more charged stretches of the last two hours, I couldn’t quite work out what the film was suggesting about self-possession under duress. It occurred to me that the restrained affect might be related to the film’s understanding of itself as a kind of literary text, too. The visiting writer who reads her short story aloud at the cultural institute where Fumi works is herself asked why she performs with so little emotion, and the answer is a fascinating one: she doesn’t want to pretend that she can inhabit all of her characters, and she thinks that a sort of presentational truth, one that simply delivers the words themselves, still carries all the requisite feeling. A version of this idea may apply to the film, too. In the relative absence of histrionics, perhaps we are better able to understand and internalize the accrued weight of what these women have carried in their lives, the unspectacular ways they have been subsumed into (but thankfully not consumed by) the everyday. * Lastly, about duration: yes, I do think this could be an hour or two shorter and it would work nearly as well. And yet, I think it’s important to say that this isn’t a miniseries in disguise. It’s a novelistic film, just as Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy is a filmic collection of short stories. Although I watched in installments, I felt the continuous logic of the film’s development, the way the friendship group’s warm, complex, fraught tangle shifted and reconstituted, and how it informed the dramas in the women’s individual lives. Though I found some parts of the film too languorous, a bit too repetitive or restrained, I also didn’t want to leave these characters in the end, with their understanding of themselves and the impact of some of their bolder, pattern-breaking choices still very much in progress. But that’s the truth in which I suspect Hamaguchi is most invested: whatever span of time one chooses for a story, markers like beginnings and endings are arbitrary impositions, creations dictated by narrative. Life doesn’t work that way, and neither does friendship. letterboxd.com/cinemapoodle/list/ryusuke-hamaguchi-ranked-so-far/

Clocking in at over five hours, Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Happy Hour (Happī Ā) is a quiet, monumental masterpiece of slow-cinema intimacy that feels less like watching a scripted movie and more like observing real lives unfold in unhurried, real time. Set in Kobe, the film follows a tight-knit circle of four women in their late 30s whose long-standing dynamics fracture when one of them suddenly reveals she is undergoing a messy divorce prompting the remaining three to re-examine their own stifled desires, marriages, and personal truths. What makes the film so uniquely captivating is Hamaguchi’s extraordinary process: developed through acting workshops with non-professional actors, the performances possess an astonishing, naturalistic grace (jointly earning all four lead actresses the Best Actress award at Locarno). Extended sequences like a fascinating body-listening workshop or a literary reading are allowed to breathe so fully that minor shifts in conversation carry the emotional impact of major plot twists. It’s an epic, exquisitely patient exploration of female friendship, emotional honesty, and the quiet compromises of adulthood.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.

Братья Стругацкие хотели чтобы экранизировать свою повесть,  Алексею Герману, режиссер решил снимать «Трудно быть богом» еще в 1968 году, через 4 года после выхода книги. Вместе с Борисом Стругацким они написали первый вариант сценария. В августе Герман получил разрешение на съёмки, но вскоре началась операция «Дунай» — вторжение в Чехословакию войск СССР и других стран Варшавского договора, поэтому режиссеру не разрешили снимать фильм. Производство картины затянулось по причине трудностей с финансированием и сложности озвучания. Когда же финансирование нашлось, снимали картину в 2000 году и закончились в 2006 году. С тех пор, Алексей Герман работал в основном над звуком. К сожалению, он умер в феврале 2013 года, не успев доработать звуковую составляющую. Завершали работу над картиной его сын, Алексей Герман мл., и Светлана Кармалита. Самих же братьев тоже уже не стало. Сама же картина вышла в 2013 г., долго делали эту картину, очень долго, но стоило ли овчинка выделки? А вот и нет, то что Стругацкими использовалось редко и умело, в фильме гипертрофированно до немыслимых масштабов и превратилось в самоцель, идея здесь исключительно одна, мол, все люди коричневая субстанция, коричневая субстанция на них, вокруг них и внутри них, субстанцией люди были всегда и навеки им и останутся, ибо такова их природа, так себе мысль конечно, но это как говорится  “У кого что болит?” Однако донести свою точку зрения можно куда менее блевотными способами, чем строить трёхчасовой фильм вокруг одной банальной идеи залитой литрами жидкой грязи и коричневой субстанцией, иногда вообще закрадывается крамольная мысль, что целью режиссёра как раз и было заснять тонны грязи и коричневой субстанции, чтобы потом посмеяться с того, как люди будут находить в этой смрадной клоаке космической глубины философский подтекст. Разумеется тут же нашлись толпы не быдла объявившие картину гениальной, мол, всё так и есть, только они такие волшебные выходят на улицу, чтобы прикупить очередной IPhone или баночку фуагра, как их тут же окружает грязное вонючее быдло, само собой сами они при этом себя такими не считают, пусть эти товарищи продолжают искать жемчуг в море поноса хоть до скончания времён, нам же как это странно не звучало нужны внятный сюжет, логика, нормальная игра актёров и приемлемая картинка, а не сферичная шизофреничная блевотная ерунда, какой именитый режиссёр её не снимал и сколько бы лет он на это не потратил, король то голый Господа. “I’d rather be happy over liking Hard to Be a God.” - COOP, 2025 I watched this movie almost three years ago and called this dreadful, uncomfortable, and drawn out figurative “snuff film” a masterpiece. Then I never watched it again, and I deeply regret not revisiting it sooner. I have to ask… what the hell did I even see in this movie? A deep character study? Clearly something. I know that not every great film is supposed to be “enjoyable”, but I don’t think a good movie should give me absolutely nothing to enjoy at all, like this one does. Seriously, I could barely even finish it. The only good thing I can say is that the cinematography reflects the movie's tone perfectly. It’s very atmospheric, but that can’t salvage how genuinely uncomfortable it made me feel throughout. And not even in a good, thought provoking way. I got to a scene in the dungeon with only 35 minutes left and just decided to skip to the end… which I know is cheating, but how am I supposed to stay invested in something I already hate watching? Watching this movie again was legitimately one of the most dreadful viewing experiences I’ve ever had. The first time I saw it, I was 15, at a point in my life when I wanted to be a “true cinema nerd” and get into more “absurd cinema.” In doing so, I guess I convinced myself that I loved this movie way more than I actually did. Okay fine; that’s the understatement of the century. The worst thing you can do as a movie fan is convince yourself that you like something you really don’t. I really do want to love these kinds of movies, okay? I think movies like “Stalker” and “Werkmeister Harmonies” are very thought provoking, and masterfully made films that were made with a greater intention than to be slow and enduring for the sake of it. They’re also movies I haven’t seen in a while, but can confirm I’ve seen more than once in less than three years,  and have taken actual time to think down. But this one just feels like an endurance test and never feels like it has anything meaningful to say. It’s nothing more than one big drag of a watch.

Hard to Be a God is impossible to follow. In a way that I know is intentional but nonetheless made the film a laborious watch. Also, come ON having your lead look at the camera and say “It’s Hard for a God” is the most pretentious, heavy-handed, and unearned moment I’ve seen in a movie in a long while. You go hours barely engaging with the awesome concept the movie is premised on, then just have a character say it to the viewer??? I think if this were a better movie that scene could maybe work, as a Shakespearean aside kind of moment, but it definitely doesn’t do that in this film. ESPECIALLY because they do another title drop in a more traditionally shot scene with the exact same context 15 minutes later! There’s cool ideas buried in It’s Hard to be a God, but overall this is a messy, slog of a film. Sidenote: Why do a substantial number of this film’s shots look like a Hype Williams music video? Background guys jump into the center of the fish-eye lens like they’re Missy Elliot. I like the use of that perspective but some of the scenes legitimately looked too similar to influential music videos be taken as intended in this context. An odd issue to have. Two totally different artworks from different ends of the globe, but one came first so the other now carries the tonality of the other, at least for me.

A logikátlan dolgokkal telezsúfolt terek ügyesen elhitetik a nézőkkel, hogy amit látnak az egy alternatív univerzum, de igazából olyanok ezek a díszletek, mintha nem lenne ott semmi, mert funkciótlan és felesleges. Egy világ építéséhez szükség lenne arra is, hogy a szereplőket néha lássuk nevetni, tudjuk mit találnak esetleg szépnek, milyen amikor nem ölik egymást, vagy épp nincsenek iszonyatosan bebaszva. Ja, és esetleg a nők és a gyerekek is komolyabb szerephez jutnának, de legalább egynél többnek lehetne szöveges szerepe, amiből jellemet tud építeni magának. Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

This film is 3 hours of absolute mayhem and carnage. The film is about a group of humans who get sent to another planet with humans, but these ones are stuck in the Middle Ages basically. So the Earth humans have to integrate themselves with the populous and make sure that they are able to get through these dark times. We follow one of these Earth humans know has ‘Don Rumata’. At no point did I feel like the Don Rumata was doing his job and why he came to the planet in the first place. To help this civilization evolve. It felt like he was just abusing everyone and being a complete menace. He takes method acting to a whole new level 😂. It’s quite clear that he has immersed himself so much that he’s really living the lie. Leonid Yarmolnik, the actor who plays Don Rumata, gives a phenomenally true and outlandish performance. He was great. I could see an argument for watching this with subtitles OFF. They provided basically no help in terms of what was happening. The only upside is that quite a bit of the dialogue is funny and some of it can be surprisingly profound. Honestly I got more understanding of the story from one of the old Lego games, where there’s no dialogue and just grunting. It’s like the actors were told the beginning and the end of a scene and then told to just improvise the rest. To be honest, to begin with, it was a tough watch because of how nonsensical it is. The production is crazy good and completely immersive. There are few films that are at this level in terms of that aspect. It’s muddy and mucky everywhere, everyone is covered in piss and shit. Every part of the film feels so alive. As if they really created a fully fictional medieval village and told all the extras to go about their jobs whilst the film was happening. There’s a part where someone’s guts get spilled out and then his whole chest comes away and you see a still beating heart. Some guy literally gets dragged by a horse during a scene. There are also so many times where someone will just get shat on midway through a scene 😂 The film is shot in a documentary style. The amount of times a scene will be happening and some dude will just walk across the frame, looking directly down the lens the whole time. So funny. Because of the documentary hand held style the camera work is really interesting. The camera is constantly moving and it feels like the film has very few cuts. The editing is pretty good in that regard too. There isn’t really any worrying about if something is slightly obscuring the shot or if the lens is covered in blood or crap. That being said though, towards the end, during a pivotal scene, someone is blocking the majority of the fame. I think someone from behind the camera calls out (not heard) the actors look, wait (someone says wait), the person blocking the frame moves slightly and then the actors continue with the scene. Like nothing happened 😂. I watched this in two sittings. I don’t know whether the second half is better or, if me having a sleep made me enjoy it more. Honestly though, once you just accept it for what is it, there’s so much humour in its wackyness and uniqueness. Below is just a few of my favourite quotes/passages of dialogue from this film: “Don Rumata, the empires best swordsman. 186 duals but not a single kill. Only their ears. 372 ears in total.” “Maybe the Abyss belched you out? Maybe you’re the son of god?” “The fact that I’m talking to you… doesn’t necessarily mean we’re having a conversation” “Don’t get mad Don. Have a potato” - “What would you do if you were a god?” - “I wouldn’t have any problems urinating” (Don proceeds to pour out his water flask to help the man - the man later urinates on Don) “Creator, if you exist, blow us away like dust or pus. Or leave us to rot like we are. Destroy us all. Destroy everyone.” “Get out, everyone. I’m going to wash my arse” “I saw you blowing snot today” “If you write about me, and you’ll probably have to… write that… it’s hard to be a god”

383/500 Aleksei German’s Hard to Be a God is an immersive and miasmic experience that chooses textural storytelling over traditional narrative. Within the first few minutes, excrement has been thrown, and you must decide for yourself whether you’re in or out. The filth doesn’t end there: German’s entropic odyssey festers with pestilence, decay, rot, and offal, all caught within the claustrophobic framework of Ilin and Klimenko’s somnambulant cinematography. Hands in the camera; piss, shit, and spit just being thrown at you for three hours straight—it’s a complete indifference to the audience and to the film’s subjects. But that indifference is the point. Ilin, Klimenko, and German visualize an authoritarian society where there is no personal space; life clambers on top of itself, everyone preying on everyone else just to survive. It’s a direct reflection of the Stalinism that German’s family lived through. Hard to Be a God is constantly reminding us that there is no dignity in authoritarian societies. Rumata starts the film as a passive observer, believing he can watch the cruelty and stupidity around him without joining it, hoping to influence society through behavior modification. By the end, he realizes he can’t, and that he’s as guilty as everyone else of contributing to the moral rot of Arkanar society. In a world devoid of purpose and meaning, ennui and cruelty consume everyone and everything; and passivity becomes its own sort of violence.

Não demora muito para que, vendo É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS (2013), a gente desista logo de entender a trama e se permita viajar na força onírica de suas imagens. Há quem diga que é porque o livro no qual o filme é baseado é de difícil adaptação, mas é possível que o cineasta russo Aleksey German não tenha se preocupado muito com esse tipo de detalhe. Seu filme-testamento, em nenhum momento, procura ser fácil para o espectador, foi feito como que numa delírio. O fato de ter quase três horas de duração também não ajuda muito o trabalho a ser apreciado por espectadores apressados e impacientes. É preciso paciência e uma reeducação do olhar para que essas imagens poderosas sejam não só apreciadas, mas recebidas com maravilhamento e assombro, misturado também a algum asco provocado por cenas violentas ou de causar repulsa mesmo, como pessoas com o nariz pingando, com feridas expostas ou imagens de cadáveres pendurados ou vísceras à mostra, num espetáculo tão perturbador que esquece-se que são efeitos especiais. Talvez o preto e branco das imagens passe essa impressão de verdade. É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS é um dos trabalhos mais importantes da carreira de German, contemporâneo de Andrei Tarkovski, e que morreu antes de ver sua obra finalizada. German passou quatro décadas idealizando, doze anos filmando e faleceu em 2013, deixando a edição e a finalização para seu filho e sua esposa, ambos colaboradores de longa data da produção. Felizmente é um desses trabalhos bem especiais, que oferecem ao espectador uma experiência única, que vai além do gostar ou do não gostar. Independentemente disso, saímos da sessão diferentes. É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS se passa em um universo semelhante à nossa Idade Média em alguns países da Europa, mas há algo de muito estranho que nos leva a acreditar que se trata de um mundo novo e estranho. E na verdade se trata de um outro planeta, como é dito no início, nos letreiros de apresentação. Ver o filme no cinema ou ao menos em uma tela maior é essencial para que os vários planos gerais e os ricos detalhes da direção de arte e a bela fotografia em preto e branco sejam vistos com mais clareza. É, definitivamente, um filme para ser assistido no cinema, por mais difícil que seja sua exibição comercial. Tanto é que até agora ele permanece inédito em nosso circuito. Pude vê-lo em uma mostra dedicada a filmes ousados esteticamente e arriscados comercialmente, a Mostra Cinema em Transe, exibida em Fortaleza no mês de janeiro. O curioso de ler a sinopse de É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS é não encontrar exatamente o que é descrito na tela. Na trama, um grupo de cientistas é enviado ao planeta Arkanar para ajudar a civilização local, que está passando por uma fase ainda muito rudimentar de sua história, a encontrar o seu caminho para o progresso. A missão é difícil, já que eles não podem interferir violentamente e nem matar aquelas pessoas. O cientista Rumata tenta salvar os intelectuais locais de uma punição. Essa é mais ou menos a sinopse meio maluca e resumida que aparece no IMDB. Na confusa história que acompanhamos na tela, que é o que importa, afinal, já que a obra cinematográfica precisa ser analisada de modo independente da obra literária, vemos um homem de aparência quase gigante e considerado um deus pelos demais. Aos nossos olhos ele só parece superior aos demais por ser maior, mais forte, se vestir diferente e principalmente por não estar coberto de lama. Os demais mais parecem porcos vivendo em um chiqueiro. A lama é uma constante e está presente em quase todo o filme. Ainda que adaptado da obra literária dos mestres da ficção científica russa Arkady e Boris Strugatsky, que também serviram de inspiração para uma das obras mais aclamadas de Tarkovski, STALKER, o filme de German brinca muito com as possibilidades que só o cinema é capaz, como a aproximação um tanto exagerada da câmera nos rostos e corpos dos atores, ou a própria maneira como eles lidam com essa câmera, chegando, em alguns momentos, a falar com ela. É o tipo de obra que cobra muito do espectador, mas que recompensa muito bem aqueles dispostos a irem até o fim em sua difícil travessia. Hard to Be a God takes you through a world where people look directly into the camera and objects are constantly dangled in front of it, while faces and hands appear from nowhere like the lens is another person trying to make its way through each brutal scene. I absolutely love it and these are some Sunday morning ramblings as to why. The main character, Rumata, goes through a constant bombardment of requests and threats, alongside the filth and brutality of the society he is in. But for most of the film he takes almost everything in his stride, like he's super calm regardless of what mess is happening. He knows another kind of civilisation is possible and knows that something needs to change, but that doesn't mean he can do anything on his own. So he's kind of stuck in a perpetual cycle of guts and grime; back and forth with piss, snot and puddles and random machines and spikes and musical instruments and fog. But in spite of that, I never felt the film lacked 'progress' because I never really got why 'progress' needs to mean moving in a tidy way from one point to another. Life doesn't really work that way, or maybe it does for some folks, but it doesn't for social and technological development, despite how we might think that it does. Rumata basically continues living in this world where everything is interrupted and familiar problems return, with the Renaissance he knows could happen staying somewhere on the horizon beyond the moonshine, zits and donkey penises. The filthiness is probably pushed a bit too far, and 3 hours of hawking and traipsing through sludge, alongside lacerated butt cheeks and dead fish, totally becomes an endurance test - but that was also part of the fun. I didn't find it repetitive because the filmmaker finds so many different ways of presenting this world, particularly through the movement of the camera and the awesome use of props. It is disgusting and obscene, but it also has moments of despair and grief for characters whose lives I got interested in without necessarily identifying with them. The Baron, for instance, waving his sword around like a raging loon before ending up face down with arrows in his back was especially brutal. He had so much more to give! The film also left me thinking about a society where few people seem capable of imagining that things could be different, while Rumata knows that they can be and still can't work out how to make that change happen. His knowledge and his $$$ distinguishes him from the people around him, but he's not really superior cos he still spits and flings donkey poop, increasingly behaving like someone who belongs in that time and place. The thing that makes him different is that he knows another world is possible, while the film gradually tests how much that knowledge is worth when he can't create it himself. By the time he goes berserk and loses his restraint, the hours beforehand validate his spree, and I found the whole thing fascinating and totally unforgettable.

383/500 Aleksei German’s Hard to Be a God is an immersive and miasmic experience that chooses textural storytelling over traditional narrative. Within the first few minutes, excrement has been thrown, and you must decide for yourself whether you’re in or out. The filth doesn’t end there: German’s entropic odyssey festers with pestilence, decay, rot, and offal, all caught within the claustrophobic framework of Ilin and Klimenko’s somnambulant cinematography. Hands in the camera; piss, shit, and spit just being thrown at you for three hours straight—it’s a complete indifference to the audience and to the film’s subjects. But that indifference is the point. Ilin, Klimenko, and German visualize an authoritarian society where there is no personal space; life clambers on top of itself, everyone preying on everyone else just to survive. It’s a direct reflection of the Stalinism that German’s family lived through. Hard to Be a God is constantly reminding us that there is no dignity in authoritarian societies. Rumata starts the film as a passive observer, believing he can watch the cruelty and stupidity around him without joining it, hoping to influence society through behavior modification. By the end, he realizes he can’t, and that he’s as guilty as everyone else of contributing to the moral rot of Arkanar society. In a world devoid of purpose and meaning, ennui and cruelty consume everyone and everything; and passivity becomes its own sort of violence.

Não demora muito para que, vendo É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS (2013), a gente desista logo de entender a trama e se permita viajar na força onírica de suas imagens. Há quem diga que é porque o livro no qual o filme é baseado é de difícil adaptação, mas é possível que o cineasta russo Aleksey German não tenha se preocupado muito com esse tipo de detalhe. Seu filme-testamento, em nenhum momento, procura ser fácil para o espectador, foi feito como que numa delírio. O fato de ter quase três horas de duração também não ajuda muito o trabalho a ser apreciado por espectadores apressados e impacientes. É preciso paciência e uma reeducação do olhar para que essas imagens poderosas sejam não só apreciadas, mas recebidas com maravilhamento e assombro, misturado também a algum asco provocado por cenas violentas ou de causar repulsa mesmo, como pessoas com o nariz pingando, com feridas expostas ou imagens de cadáveres pendurados ou vísceras à mostra, num espetáculo tão perturbador que esquece-se que são efeitos especiais. Talvez o preto e branco das imagens passe essa impressão de verdade. É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS é um dos trabalhos mais importantes da carreira de German, contemporâneo de Andrei Tarkovski, e que morreu antes de ver sua obra finalizada. German passou quatro décadas idealizando, doze anos filmando e faleceu em 2013, deixando a edição e a finalização para seu filho e sua esposa, ambos colaboradores de longa data da produção. Felizmente é um desses trabalhos bem especiais, que oferecem ao espectador uma experiência única, que vai além do gostar ou do não gostar. Independentemente disso, saímos da sessão diferentes. É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS se passa em um universo semelhante à nossa Idade Média em alguns países da Europa, mas há algo de muito estranho que nos leva a acreditar que se trata de um mundo novo e estranho. E na verdade se trata de um outro planeta, como é dito no início, nos letreiros de apresentação. Ver o filme no cinema ou ao menos em uma tela maior é essencial para que os vários planos gerais e os ricos detalhes da direção de arte e a bela fotografia em preto e branco sejam vistos com mais clareza. É, definitivamente, um filme para ser assistido no cinema, por mais difícil que seja sua exibição comercial. Tanto é que até agora ele permanece inédito em nosso circuito. Pude vê-lo em uma mostra dedicada a filmes ousados esteticamente e arriscados comercialmente, a Mostra Cinema em Transe, exibida em Fortaleza no mês de janeiro. O curioso de ler a sinopse de É DIFÍCIL SER UM DEUS é não encontrar exatamente o que é descrito na tela. Na trama, um grupo de cientistas é enviado ao planeta Arkanar para ajudar a civilização local, que está passando por uma fase ainda muito rudimentar de sua história, a encontrar o seu caminho para o progresso. A missão é difícil, já que eles não podem interferir violentamente e nem matar aquelas pessoas. O cientista Rumata tenta salvar os intelectuais locais de uma punição. Essa é mais ou menos a sinopse meio maluca e resumida que aparece no IMDB. Na confusa história que acompanhamos na tela, que é o que importa, afinal, já que a obra cinematográfica precisa ser analisada de modo independente da obra literária, vemos um homem de aparência quase gigante e considerado um deus pelos demais. Aos nossos olhos ele só parece superior aos demais por ser maior, mais forte, se vestir diferente e principalmente por não estar coberto de lama. Os demais mais parecem porcos vivendo em um chiqueiro. A lama é uma constante e está presente em quase todo o filme. Ainda que adaptado da obra literária dos mestres da ficção científica russa Arkady e Boris Strugatsky, que também serviram de inspiração para uma das obras mais aclamadas de Tarkovski, STALKER, o filme de German brinca muito com as possibilidades que só o cinema é capaz, como a aproximação um tanto exagerada da câmera nos rostos e corpos dos atores, ou a própria maneira como eles lidam com essa câmera, chegando, em alguns momentos, a falar com ela. É o tipo de obra que cobra muito do espectador, mas que recompensa muito bem aqueles dispostos a irem até o fim em sua difícil travessia.
