And my personal taste, also controversially, still rates the OG Mad Max as the one that means the most to me. I watched it on first release in London with my old man, and it was of course unlike anything I'd seen before. So bleak, such an unfamiliar backdrop, as I'd basically only seen Hollywood or old British movies up to then, such a scary film. And no familiar actors to feel safe with. I also have a soft spot for number 2, the Road Warrior, a great follow up. And like many I was deeply disappointed with Thunder Dome. Fury Road is a definite improvement over that last entry, absolutely no doubt. But call me an old reactionary or simply a fuddy-duddy, I need something more than an extended chase to wow me, however frenetic or visually resplendent. I appreciate great stunts, but I miss the days when CGI wasn't a thing, however much it 'enhances' the action. And lastly, as much as I usually love Tom Hardy he's no Mel Gibson, he's not the Max I grew up with, he's completely different, and I'd have less problem if his character had not been named Max. [13] nota=1.5 estrelas:
Reminds me a lot of Star Wars Episode 1 in the way the film is focused on self-important lore and world-building above all else, turning its back on the fizzy melodramatic fun of the original works. None of the characters are engaging, little of the action is exciting, everything is so transparently in service of delivering lame jargon and iconography, which all has a smug 1960s hippie vibe to it that I find totally insufferable. The extent to which it is impossible to give a shit about Max or Furiosa is remarkable, they're not cool, charming, funny, self-reflective or in possession of any other potentially humanising traits, just relentless grim stoicism. Perhaps if the film were not saddled with one of Tom Hardy's most moronically misjudged performances and Max had some kind of charisma, like Mel Gibson achieved without sacrificing intensity, the viewer would have had some kind of way in to the film on an emotional level, shame no one reigned him in. Also remarkable is how unexpectedly slow it is, both dialogue and action scenes dragging terribly - take the scene where Max first holds Furiosa and the wives at gunpoint, it goes on so long with so little of any significance happening that it starts to become awkward, the characters just standing and looking at eachother. This absolutely feels like it was directed by a 70 year old and edited by someone with no prior action film experience. Of course there's a lot of spectacle, but you mainly consume it with a dispassionate appreciation of the scale and detail of the production design and the work that must have gone into realising it, rarely approaching the edge of your seat. Miller just isn't a good enough action director to cope with the scale he's aiming for here - within the huge road-fleets there's no real sense of where the active characters are in relation to eachother, of who is in which samey vehicle or where the danger will be coming from, so the feeling that the baddies are just popping into existence to fulfil a quota for action within an artificial entertainment becomes too nagging. Would also help if this hadn't aimed for a PG-13 rating, more graphic violence would at least provoke a visceral reaction to what's happening on screen that you don't get when the film is constantly shying away from the reality of people getting shot in the head or blown up or crushed by huge trucks. A lot of people seem to be very passionate fans of Fury Road and yet the follow-up was a huge financial flop, so why didn't they turn up for it in droves? I think the reality is that it's easy to make this film sound conceptually cool on paper, but on a more nuts-and-bolts level it is let down by weak direction - the idea of the film is better than the reality.

A ver, primero que nada: no llegué a terminar la película. Pero si soy completamente sincera, los primeros 40 minutos fueron suficientes. Para muestra, basta un botón. Igual voy a ser buena y darle una oportunidad y terminarla, porque sé que tiene una cantidad absurda de críticas positivas y probablemente haya algo que todavía no estoy viendo. Pero si tengo que sacar una primera conclusión es que me está resultando muy difícil tomarme en serio lo que estoy viendo. No porque la propuesta sea exagerada (esa es parte de su identidad) sino porque muchas de las situaciones me resultan poco verosímiles incluso dentro de la lógica que plantea la propia historia. Lo que más me llama la atención es que se nota que tiene muchísimo presupuesto, pero pareciera que se olvidaron de ponerlo en el guion. Desde el principio me hice millones de preguntas sobre la lógica de esta peli: decisiones sin sentido, situaciones que parecen contradecir las propias reglas que plantea la película e inconsistencias de los personajes. Y creo que ese es mi principal problema: No logra hacerte entrar en su mundo. Es una distopía en la que casi no hay agua, el sol parece querer quemar a todo el mundo y solo lo mas importante para mostrar es como una sociedad decide resolver sus problemas manejando vehículos a toda velocidad por un desierto. Esta premisa puede ser completamente delirante, es justamente por eso q necesitás construir muy bien la trama y las reglas de ese universo para que el espectador diga “okay, esto está loco pero tiene sentido dentro de este mundo” y pueda empatizarrr. Además todo ocurre a una velocidad tan frenética y fría que lo hace todavía más difícil de procesar y así de apoco deja de impresionarte lo que ves. Todo está puesto al servicio de la acción, mientras que la trama y los personajes principales quedan bastante relegados. Y hablando de personajes, tampoco están tan buenos. El protagonista: tipo sensillo, fuerte, misterioso, sarcástico, antihéroe, con pasado trágico y prácticamente todas las características clásicas para que un hombre conecte. El villano es una cosa cochina no se que más decir. Y después están los personajes femeninos. Acá me costó mucho comprar el supuesto mensaje de empoderamiento. Tenemos un grupo de mujeres que son literalmente modelos, todas extremadamente atractivas, vestidas con muy poca ropa, ingenuas e indefensas. Incluso mantienen una actitud cariñosa con una persona que les hizo daño. Hay un personaje femenino que sí se presenta como fuerte y capaz, pero incluso no termina de despegarse de ciertos clichés. Visualmente la película es espectacular. Probablemente sea lo que más puedo rescatar hasta ahora. Tiene una estética muy original y extremadamente reconocible. Todo es exagerado y artificial, pero creo que justamente esa artificialidad es parte de su identidad. El mundo se siente quemado por el sol, los colores son súper contrastantes, los vehículos y personajes tienen diseños increíbles y cada plano parece pensado para ser visualmente muy impactante y llamativo. La música también acompaña muy bien toda esta locura. Si querés una película superficial, no tenés ganas de analizar demasiado la lógica de lo que estás viendo, querés acción prácticamente constante, paisajes increíbles, personajes visualmente muy llamativos y poco interés por el lore o la construcción del mundo, probablemente esta sea tu película. Pero bueno, en cuanto a la trama, se podría haber hecho y aprovechado muchísimo más (y sin hacer falta sacrificar acción) Hacer una película de 2 horas que básicamente trata sobre vehículos peleando en un desierto es una idea muy arriesgada. Para que funcione, hay que saber atrapar al espectador y hacer que le importe lo que está pasando no solo entretenerlo con explosiones y colores. Igual, voy a terminarla. Capaz dentro de una hora vuelvo acá a borrar absolutamente todo esto. Ojalá...

Reminds me a lot of Star Wars Episode 1 in the way the film is focused on self-important lore and world-building above all else, turning its back on the fizzy melodramatic fun of the original works. None of the characters are engaging, little of the action is exciting, everything is so transparently in service of delivering lame jargon and iconography, which all has a smug 1960s hippie vibe to it that I find totally insufferable. The extent to which it is impossible to give a shit about Max or Furiosa is remarkable, they're not cool, charming, funny, self-reflective or in possession of any other potentially humanising traits, just relentless grim stoicism. Perhaps if the film were not saddled with one of Tom Hardy's most moronically misjudged performances and Max had some kind of charisma, like Mel Gibson achieved without sacrificing intensity, the viewer would have had some kind of way in to the film on an emotional level, shame no one reigned him in. Also remarkable is how unexpectedly slow it is, both dialogue and action scenes dragging terribly - take the scene where Max first holds Furiosa and the wives at gunpoint, it goes on so long with so little of any significance happening that it starts to become awkward, the characters just standing and looking at eachother. This absolutely feels like it was directed by a 70 year old and edited by someone with no prior action film experience. Of course there's a lot of spectacle, but you mainly consume it with a dispassionate appreciation of the scale and detail of the production design and the work that must have gone into realising it, rarely approaching the edge of your seat. Miller just isn't a good enough action director to cope with the scale he's aiming for here - within the huge road-fleets there's no real sense of where the active characters are in relation to eachother, of who is in which samey vehicle or where the danger will be coming from, so the feeling that the baddies are just popping into existence to fulfil a quota for action within an artificial entertainment becomes too nagging. Would also help if this hadn't aimed for a PG-13 rating, more graphic violence would at least provoke a visceral reaction to what's happening on screen that you don't get when the film is constantly shying away from the reality of people getting shot in the head or blown up or crushed by huge trucks. A lot of people seem to be very passionate fans of Fury Road and yet the follow-up was a huge financial flop, so why didn't they turn up for it in droves? I think the reality is that it's easy to make this film sound conceptually cool on paper, but on a more nuts-and-bolts level it is let down by weak direction - the idea of the film is better than the reality.

A ver, primero que nada: no llegué a terminar la película. Pero si soy completamente sincera, los primeros 40 minutos fueron suficientes. Para muestra, basta un botón. Igual voy a ser buena y darle una oportunidad y terminarla, porque sé que tiene una cantidad absurda de críticas positivas y probablemente haya algo que todavía no estoy viendo. Pero si tengo que sacar una primera conclusión es que me está resultando muy difícil tomarme en serio lo que estoy viendo. No porque la propuesta sea exagerada (esa es parte de su identidad) sino porque muchas de las situaciones me resultan poco verosímiles incluso dentro de la lógica que plantea la propia historia. Lo que más me llama la atención es que se nota que tiene muchísimo presupuesto, pero pareciera que se olvidaron de ponerlo en el guion. Desde el principio me hice millones de preguntas sobre la lógica de esta peli: decisiones sin sentido, situaciones que parecen contradecir las propias reglas que plantea la película e inconsistencias de los personajes. Y creo que ese es mi principal problema: No logra hacerte entrar en su mundo. Es una distopía en la que casi no hay agua, el sol parece querer quemar a todo el mundo y solo lo mas importante para mostrar es como una sociedad decide resolver sus problemas manejando vehículos a toda velocidad por un desierto. Esta premisa puede ser completamente delirante, es justamente por eso q necesitás construir muy bien la trama y las reglas de ese universo para que el espectador diga “okay, esto está loco pero tiene sentido dentro de este mundo” y pueda empatizarrr. Además todo ocurre a una velocidad tan frenética y fría que lo hace todavía más difícil de procesar y así de apoco deja de impresionarte lo que ves. Todo está puesto al servicio de la acción, mientras que la trama y los personajes principales quedan bastante relegados. Y hablando de personajes, tampoco están tan buenos. El protagonista: tipo sensillo, fuerte, misterioso, sarcástico, antihéroe, con pasado trágico y prácticamente todas las características clásicas para que un hombre conecte. El villano es una cosa cochina no se que más decir. Y después están los personajes femeninos. Acá me costó mucho comprar el supuesto mensaje de empoderamiento. Tenemos un grupo de mujeres que son literalmente modelos, todas extremadamente atractivas, vestidas con muy poca ropa, ingenuas e indefensas. Incluso mantienen una actitud cariñosa con una persona que les hizo daño. Hay un personaje femenino que sí se presenta como fuerte y capaz, pero incluso no termina de despegarse de ciertos clichés. Visualmente la película es espectacular. Probablemente sea lo que más puedo rescatar hasta ahora. Tiene una estética muy original y extremadamente reconocible. Todo es exagerado y artificial, pero creo que justamente esa artificialidad es parte de su identidad. El mundo se siente quemado por el sol, los colores son súper contrastantes, los vehículos y personajes tienen diseños increíbles y cada plano parece pensado para ser visualmente muy impactante y llamativo. La música también acompaña muy bien toda esta locura. Si querés una película superficial, no tenés ganas de analizar demasiado la lógica de lo que estás viendo, querés acción prácticamente constante, paisajes increíbles, personajes visualmente muy llamativos y poco interés por el lore o la construcción del mundo, probablemente esta sea tu película. Pero bueno, en cuanto a la trama, se podría haber hecho y aprovechado muchísimo más (y sin hacer falta sacrificar acción) Hacer una película de 2 horas que básicamente trata sobre vehículos peleando en un desierto es una idea muy arriesgada. Para que funcione, hay que saber atrapar al espectador y hacer que le importe lo que está pasando no solo entretenerlo con explosiones y colores. Igual, voy a terminarla. Capaz dentro de una hora vuelvo acá a borrar absolutamente todo esto. Ojalá...

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

I read bell hooks' critical essay about this film right after watching it, so I might be biased toward criticism here. But I think her points are important. She points out that key details of Malcolm's story have been changed, such as the role of his siblings in his conversion to Islam. She also points out that (Black) women in general are portrayed rather superficially, as "either virgins or whores, madonnas or prostitutes— and that’s Hollywood". And that Malcolm's criticisms of colonialism and capitalism are almost absent from the film – likely to make the film more palatable to white audiences. That said, it's still a powerful biopic. It's beautifully shot and powerfully acted. But it's also too Hollywood for its own sake.

skillsで鑑賞。リアペの課題が出ていたのでそれを添付 I watched the movie “Malcolm X”, and I was surprised and impressed by the way Malcolm’s identity changed over time. In his early life, his identity was deeply shaped by racism. However, in the end, he came to see himself as he truly was, without viewing himself through the lens of skin color. In this essay, I will discuss this transformation through three aspects that his name, institutional discrimination, and his experience in prison. Firstly, I was surprised that his name, Malcolm Little, is actually the named from white plantation owner. This was revealed when Malcolm was in prison and taught about black is not wrong via many things. His name, “Little” was not Malcolm’s family name, and it was taken from the name of his ancestor’s plantation owner. I think this was shocking because it shows how slavery took away people’s identity as they did not give the name from the very beginning, and it continues after many decades. Secondly, I was surprised that there is some invisible discrimination. When I hear “discrimination problems,” I always come up with some violent problems. Of course, Malcolm was a victim of physical violence due to discrimination, such as his father being killed by white people, but he was also affected by more subtle, mental discrimination. For example, he was a good student at school, despite being the only colored in his school, and he dreamed of becoming a lawyer. However, when he told his teacher, he was discouraged simply because he was Black. Another example, he always tried to straighten his curly hair to look more like a white person. He thought this made him better than other Black people. But later, he realized this way of thinking actually showed how much he had been influenced by white standards. This part was very interesting to me because there are some examples of invisible discrimination. Lastly, I was surprised that he finally found himself in “prison”. I had no expectation that an important figure like Malcolm X had once been a criminal, and it was also during his time that motivated to learn and proud of being black. He started to read some books and knew that words related to “black” had negative meanings while words related to “white” had positive ones, or that the first humans on Earth were in prison. These discoveries made him prouder as a black and triggered him to see himself without the perspective of white. In conclusion, Malcolm X’s story shows that identity can change through experience, knowledge, and reflection. Through his name, his experiences with discrimination, and his time in prison, he gradually freed himself from the influence of racism and came to understand his true self.

In his early life, his identity was deeply shaped by racism. However, in the end, he came to see himself as he truly was, without viewing himself through the lens of skin color. In this essay, I will discuss this transformation through three aspects that his name, institutional discrimination, and his experience in prison. For example, he was a good student at school, despite being the only colored in his school, and he dreamed of becoming a lawyer. Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Malcolm X had his phones tapped, was stalked by the FBI, and had informants surround him under the COINTELPRO program. MLK Jr. had the FBI sending him anonymous letters blackmailing him and telling him to kill himself. Not 30 years later, they greenlight movies portraying these people in tailored, Hollywood lights. You tell me what's more plausible: that America had a radical ideological shift in a couple of decades, or that they decided it would be more effective for them to hijack these incredibly nuanced movements borne of blood and bones, and turn them into just another story of revolution. We normally only make movies for and tell the stories of revolutionaries who had their visions come to life. Those who failed are forgotten; they'll probably have their name uttered for the last time by a family members a few decades after they're buried. Is this the world Malcolm X imagined? Malcolm X failed, as admirable as he may have been. America is the only place where the dead bodies of revolutionaries are exhumed, dressed up, and paraded around as if their visions have come to life. America is the only place where they can get away with not changing by making their revolutionaries dance on stage, dead or alive, to make it seem like something has changed. They put them through the school curriculum criterion. Rosa Parks didn't give up her seat? She's through. MLK had a dream? Let him through. Nat Turner led an incredibly violent slave rebellion? Nah, make him wait 2 centuries instead of 2 decades before we give him a story; he did too much. It is because of this facade of change that I have an inherent mistrust of anything that comes out of Hollywood. The American film industry has become a monster of unfathomable proportions, and it would be crazy naïve not to entertain (or accept entirely) the idea that it is used to push whatever political narrative Western civilization wants perpetuated at that specific point in time. I love this movie. It is amazing, but I would rather approach it with a cautious hate than with open arms just to be one of the many victims seeded with America's culture machine. Malcolm X, you tha goat.

To be fair to Lee, and I think Baldwin vocalized this suspicion as well, a Malcolm movie is probably undoable: how can one conceivably imagine  Hollywood allowing a movie to do justice to Malcolm, as an individual life and a microcosm of black life and revolutionary politics in America, in an honest way? This movie is a perfectly fine drama if one wants to ignore the history or the political significance of its subject, but it’s bad history, and not even in a pedantic, fact-checking sort of way. It’s predicated on a book which itself failed to capture Malcolm’s politics or the changes he underwent toward the end of his life (see George Breitman’s excellent 1967 The Last Year of Malcolm X, or the excellent collection Malcolm X Speaks , as a corrective to the Haley autobiography which came out before the script for this movie was even finished). This script was itself famously lambasted by Baldwin as a terrible white Hollywood bastardization of his vision (the movie literally includes a scene Baldwin attacked as an egregious distortion of his vision in a co-writer’s “revision” of his work, instead of the scene Baldwin envisioned. Nell Irvin Painter and Gerald Horne have spilled enough ink on how the script and Lee distorts Malcolm’s historical legacy and political significance. While I won’t go so far as to fully endorse Kwame Ture’s harsh judgement that Lee is a “petit bourgeois who took the choice of selling out of his people for a fistful of dollars” by failing to show that “Malcolm X was a revolutionary”, I think it’s fair to say that Lee doesn’t capture what Baldwin saw in Malcolm, the revolutionary spirit, what he called “a virile impulse long since fled from the American way of life”, a virility which neither Lee’s skillful direction nor Denzel’s tremendous performance evoke. Aside from the formal skill in the movie’s direction, and the great acting, Lee is refreshingly bold in connecting Malcolm to ‘92 at the beginning of the movie, and it’s a shame the rest of thet movie isn’t animated by that same polarizing political charge: Malcolm was a political revolutionary, and by the end of the movie he ceased to be a calculating, political man and is elevated into a depoliticized symbol of Black cultural pride. He counts for color and attitude—for a temperament, much as King and Malcolm represent dueling temperaments at the end of Do the Right Thing— without the substantial content of his political trajectory (e.g. we could also take Karenga’s complaint of the lack of engagement of Malcolm with Africans in the movie, i.e. his internationalism, one of the vital elements of his later political evolution). You can’t capture everything in a life, but to capture someone truthfully , one must engage with the essential aspects of one’s life and work. Malcolm was too great a man, Lee too great a director and Denzel too great an actor for this movie to come together like this.

This movie was all over the place. It did a terrible job getting his political views across and failed to show how his upbringing shaped who he became. Malcolm X was a self-critic. He constantly challenged his own beliefs and was humble enough to admit when he was wrong. He was nicknamed Satan during one period of his life, before joining the Nation of Islam and later converting to Sunni Islam. He disagreed with many of Martin Luther King’s views and shared a well-known friendship with Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay). Before he entered the criminal world, he frequented music gigs and rubbed shoulders with some of the major blues musicians of the era. The film touches on none of this. It could have focused on one chapter of his life and explored it with real depth. Instead, it scatters across everything and lands on nothing. The film does show his Hajj, and to its credit, the pilgrimage sequence is depicted with some care. But it fails to follow through on what the Hajj meant. The transformation it triggered — his rejection of the Nation of Islam’s racial theology, his embrace of Sunni Islam, and his decision to challenge Elijah Muhammad — is barely explored. That’s the consequence that put a target on his back, and the film treats it as background noise rather than the pivotal turning point it was. The film also completely flattens his relationship with Martin Luther King. Malcolm was openly critical of the civil rights movement’s direction. He argued that political movements tend to get whitewashed, diluted, and commodified. The film makes it seem as though the two men were broadly aligned. They weren’t, and that tension matters. If you’re watching this to understand Malcolm X and his politics, skip it and read the autobiography instead. If you want to watch Denzel Washington play Malcolm X, this is your film because his performance is genuinely excellent. But as a portrait of the man? Three hours, and they left out almost everything that made him who he was.

Avec Malcolm X, Spike Lee signe un film qui se veut à la fois ambitieux et nécessaire. Il est évident que ce projet lui tient à cœur et que son importance pour la communauté afro-américaine ne fait aucun doute. Le film est complet, documenté, et témoigne d’un véritable engagement. On comprend pourquoi il a été réalisé et pourquoi il est considéré comme un jalon du cinéma engagé. Pourtant, malgré la force du sujet et l’évidence du travail fourni, le film peine à captiver. Trois heures de récit font parfois sentir le poids de la longueur, et le rythme manque de dynamisme. À certains moments, on a l’impression de parcourir une encyclopédie visuelle plutôt que de vivre une expérience cinématographique. Les séquences s’enchaînent avec fidélité aux événements historiques, mais sans toujours offrir de point de vue nouveau ou d’élan dramatique capable de captiver le spectateur non averti. Le problème n’est pas le sujet, qui est passionnant et chargé d’une intensité politique et humaine indéniable, mais la manière dont il est traité. Malcolm X ressemble parfois à un biopic « Wikipédia » : tout est là, rien n’est oublié, mais la narration peine à provoquer l’émotion ou à stimuler l’esprit. On ressent une impression de distance, comme si le film voulait tout raconter plutôt que raconter quelque chose. En résumé, Malcolm X est un film important, admirable dans son ambition et sa sincérité, mais qui, pour moi, échoue à captiver pleinement. La richesse du matériau historique ne suffit pas à transformer le film en une expérience cinématographique fascinante. Mon jugement repose moins sur le fond que sur la forme : malgré tout le respect que j’ai pour le sujet, je me suis ennuyé, et le film ne m’a pas accroché.

[16] nota=2.0 estrelas:
To be fair to Lee, and I think Baldwin vocalized this suspicion as well, a Malcolm movie is probably undoable: how can one conceivably imagine  Hollywood allowing a movie to do justice to Malcolm, as an individual life and a microcosm of black life and revolutionary politics in America, in an honest way? This movie is a perfectly fine drama if one wants to ignore the history or the political significance of its subject, but it’s bad history, and not even in a pedantic, fact-checking sort of way. It’s predicated on a book which itself failed to capture Malcolm’s politics or the changes he underwent toward the end of his life (see George Breitman’s excellent 1967 The Last Year of Malcolm X, or the excellent collection Malcolm X Speaks , as a corrective to the Haley autobiography which came out before the script for this movie was even finished). This script was itself famously lambasted by Baldwin as a terrible white Hollywood bastardization of his vision (the movie literally includes a scene Baldwin attacked as an egregious distortion of his vision in a co-writer’s “revision” of his work, instead of the scene Baldwin envisioned. Nell Irvin Painter and Gerald Horne have spilled enough ink on how the script and Lee distorts Malcolm’s historical legacy and political significance. While I won’t go so far as to fully endorse Kwame Ture’s harsh judgement that Lee is a “petit bourgeois who took the choice of selling out of his people for a fistful of dollars” by failing to show that “Malcolm X was a revolutionary”, I think it’s fair to say that Lee doesn’t capture what Baldwin saw in Malcolm, the revolutionary spirit, what he called “a virile impulse long since fled from the American way of life”, a virility which neither Lee’s skillful direction nor Denzel’s tremendous performance evoke. Aside from the formal skill in the movie’s direction, and the great acting, Lee is refreshingly bold in connecting Malcolm to ‘92 at the beginning of the movie, and it’s a shame the rest of thet movie isn’t animated by that same polarizing political charge: Malcolm was a political revolutionary, and by the end of the movie he ceased to be a calculating, political man and is elevated into a depoliticized symbol of Black cultural pride. He counts for color and attitude—for a temperament, much as King and Malcolm represent dueling temperaments at the end of Do the Right Thing— without the substantial content of his political trajectory (e.g. we could also take Karenga’s complaint of the lack of engagement of Malcolm with Africans in the movie, i.e. his internationalism, one of the vital elements of his later political evolution). You can’t capture everything in a life, but to capture someone truthfully , one must engage with the essential aspects of one’s life and work. Malcolm was too great a man, Lee too great a director and Denzel too great an actor for this movie to come together like this.

[18] nota=2.0 estrelas:
This movie was all over the place. It did a terrible job getting his political views across and failed to show how his upbringing shaped who he became. Malcolm X was a self-critic. He constantly challenged his own beliefs and was humble enough to admit when he was wrong. He was nicknamed Satan during one period of his life, before joining the Nation of Islam and later converting to Sunni Islam. He disagreed with many of Martin Luther King’s views and shared a well-known friendship with Muhammad Ali (then Cassius Clay). Before he entered the criminal world, he frequented music gigs and rubbed shoulders with some of the major blues musicians of the era. The film touches on none of this. It could have focused on one chapter of his life and explored it with real depth. Instead, it scatters across everything and lands on nothing. The film does show his Hajj, and to its credit, the pilgrimage sequence is depicted with some care. But it fails to follow through on what the Hajj meant. The transformation it triggered — his rejection of the Nation of Islam’s racial theology, his embrace of Sunni Islam, and his decision to challenge Elijah Muhammad — is barely explored. That’s the consequence that put a target on his back, and the film treats it as background noise rather than the pivotal turning point it was. The film also completely flattens his relationship with Martin Luther King. Malcolm was openly critical of the civil rights movement’s direction. He argued that political movements tend to get whitewashed, diluted, and commodified. The film makes it seem as though the two men were broadly aligned. They weren’t, and that tension matters. If you’re watching this to understand Malcolm X and his politics, skip it and read the autobiography instead. If you want to watch Denzel Washington play Malcolm X, this is your film because his performance is genuinely excellent. But as a portrait of the man? Three hours, and they left out almost everything that made him who he was.

[26] nota=2.0 estrelas:
Avec Malcolm X, Spike Lee signe un film qui se veut à la fois ambitieux et nécessaire. Il est évident que ce projet lui tient à cœur et que son importance pour la communauté afro-américaine ne fait aucun doute. Le film est complet, documenté, et témoigne d’un véritable engagement. On comprend pourquoi il a été réalisé et pourquoi il est considéré comme un jalon du cinéma engagé. Pourtant, malgré la force du sujet et l’évidence du travail fourni, le film peine à captiver. Trois heures de récit font parfois sentir le poids de la longueur, et le rythme manque de dynamisme. À certains moments, on a l’impression de parcourir une encyclopédie visuelle plutôt que de vivre une expérience cinématographique. Les séquences s’enchaînent avec fidélité aux événements historiques, mais sans toujours offrir de point de vue nouveau ou d’élan dramatique capable de captiver le spectateur non averti. Le problème n’est pas le sujet, qui est passionnant et chargé d’une intensité politique et humaine indéniable, mais la manière dont il est traité. Malcolm X ressemble parfois à un biopic « Wikipédia » : tout est là, rien n’est oublié, mais la narration peine à provoquer l’émotion ou à stimuler l’esprit. On ressent une impression de distance, comme si le film voulait tout raconter plutôt que raconter quelque chose. En résumé, Malcolm X est un film important, admirable dans son ambition et sa sincérité, mais qui, pour moi, échoue à captiver pleinement. La richesse du matériau historique ne suffit pas à transformer le film en une expérience cinématographique fascinante. Mon jugement repose moins sur le fond que sur la forme : malgré tout le respect que j’ai pour le sujet, je me suis ennuyé, et le film ne m’a pas accroché.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):

Watched this for my spring of 2026 college course: cinema director: Spike Lee (think that was the course name). Theme/Subject: transformation Cinematic aspect: cinematography One expressive cinematography is the three different color pallets to paint the historical transformation Malcolm X had. Each color pallet reflects the three acts in the film. The first one (Act I) is shown to be warm and rich which represents his youth and his drug addiction since there was a crack epidemic ravaging  the black population. Then we move to Act II which contains one cool shade color that represents Malcolm X’s time in prison. When serving his time in prison Malcolm found his faith, Islam, and we get to Act III which is to be seen as more of the earthy type of color to represent him joining the National of Islam (NOI) and eventually Malcolm X left and went to Mecca he took the name of el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz. Each color shows different stages of his life. I think the opening montage really sets the mood for the film. It was an interesting way of incorporating history of violence against the black population mixed with the audio of Malcolm X along with the American flag slowly burning up and turning into the letter X. Right there and then you get a sense of what the movie will be about. When reading the textbook (pg 203-207) it was important that Lee wanted to shoot the Middle Eastern scenes in Africa rather than New Jersey. “It was a life-changing experience for Spike” (pg 204). Lee felt an instant connection where he saw the pyramid and the sphinx for the first time and thought those were his ancestors who built them. Scientists to this day don’t know how it was built. Scavenger Hunt #138 Film 1 of 30 Category: A film about activism. The Film *Malcolm X* is not simply a biography of an important man. It is the story of a person repeatedly destroying an old version of himself in order to become someone greater. Spike Lee refuses to present Malcolm as though he entered the world already prepared to become a leader. We see his anger, vanity, criminality, discipline, faith, pride, mistakes, and eventual willingness to reconsider beliefs that once defined him. The different names he carries represent those transformations. Malcolm Little is the child born into a family terrorized by racism. Detroit Red is the young man attempting to bury that pain beneath style, excitement, and crime. Malcolm X rejects the name inherited through slavery and replaces it with the unknown history stolen from him. El Hajj Malik El Shabazz emerges after Mecca with a larger understanding of humanity. Each name belongs to the same man, but none contains him completely. The early scenes are energetic and entertaining, but that energy hides enormous insecurity. Malcolm straightens his hair, changes the way he dresses, and performs a version of himself designed to survive and feel powerful. The conk becomes more than a hairstyle. It shows how racism can teach someone to reject features of his own body before he even realizes he is doing it. Prison becomes the place where physical confinement produces intellectual freedom. Malcolm begins reading, questioning language, and recognizing how history has been written by people with the power to define everyone else. Education does not merely give him information. It gives him a new understanding of himself. He discovers that controlling language means controlling the boundaries of what people believe is possible. The Nation of Islam gives Malcolm discipline, purpose, and a community, but the same organization that helps rebuild him eventually attempts to control him. His devotion to Elijah Muhammad is sincere, which makes the betrayal deeply personal. Malcolm realizes that replacing one form of dependence with another is not true liberation. He must be willing to question the person who taught him how to question everything else. His journey to Mecca becomes the film’s final great transformation. Malcolm does not abandon his understanding of racism in America, but he recognizes that his previous beliefs about race were incomplete. What makes him extraordinary is not that he was always correct. It is that he was willing to change publicly after building his identity around certainty. Many people would rather protect their pride than admit that experience has expanded their understanding. The Direction Spike Lee directs the film with the scale and confidence of an epic while keeping Malcolm’s personal evolution at its center. The opening immediately connects Malcolm’s life to the America that continued after his death. Images of the American flag burning into the shape of an X are combined with footage of Rodney King being beaten, making it clear that this is not a safely contained history lesson. The conditions Malcolm confronted did not disappear with him. Each period of Malcolm’s life has its own visual identity. The early sequences are colorful, playful, and alive with movement. Prison removes that freedom and replaces it with hard lines, shadows, and confined spaces. As Malcolm becomes a public figure, the compositions grow larger and more controlled, reflecting the authority he has developed. By the final section, that control begins collapsing under surveillance, threats, and betrayal. Lee never allows Malcolm’s speeches to become interruptions in the story. Speaking is the action. The film understands that Malcolm’s voice was his greatest instrument because he could transform private anger into a shared political consciousness. The crowds do not simply admire him. They recognize experiences that society repeatedly told them to endure quietly. The march to the hospital is one of the clearest demonstrations of his power. Malcolm controls the movement of an entire crowd with small gestures, revealing the discipline behind his leadership. The police see danger because they are witnessing a Black man exercise authority that does not depend upon their permission. The final movement carries an unavoidable sense of dread. Malcolm knows that death is approaching, but he continues speaking because fear can no longer determine the value of his work. The famous shot of him moving toward the ballroom makes him appear almost separated from the ground, as though history is carrying him toward a fate both he and the audience already understand. At more than three hours, the film is long, but that length mostly feels earned. Malcolm’s transformation would lose its meaning if any major stage were treated as a brief montage. Some supporting relationships are compressed because the film has so much history to contain, yet the overall scale allows Malcolm to feel like a full human being rather than a collection of famous speeches. The Acting Denzel Washington gives one of the greatest performances ever placed in a biographical film. He does not simply imitate Malcolm’s voice and physical mannerisms. He captures the intelligence, humor, anger, confidence, vulnerability, and constant mental movement beneath them. His performance changes with every stage of Malcolm’s life. Detroit Red moves with youthful arrogance, constantly trying to appear larger than he feels. The imprisoned Malcolm becomes quieter as his mind awakens. The public speaker controls rooms through rhythm and precision. The later Malcolm appears calmer but also more exposed because he is no longer protected by the certainty or organization that once surrounded him. Denzel is especially powerful during the speeches because he communicates why people followed Malcolm. The words are important, but so is the feeling that every sentence has been sharpened by personal experience. Malcolm does not speak about racism as an abstract political subject. He speaks as someone whose family, childhood, body, opportunities, and identity were all shaped by it. Angela Bassett brings strength and emotional clarity to Betty Shabazz. Betty is not merely the supportive wife waiting outside Malcolm’s public life. She understands the danger surrounding him and the cost his mission places on their family. Bassett shows the love between them while never pretending that loving someone with a historical purpose is easy. Delroy Lindo is also excellent as West Indian Archie, particularly when Malcolm encounters him years later. Archie’s decline becomes a vision of the future Malcolm escaped. Albert Hall gives Baines the calm authority necessary to make Malcolm’s religious transformation believable, while Al Freeman Jr. portrays Elijah Muhammad with enough warmth to make Malcolm’s eventual disillusionment feel genuinely painful. Conclusion *Malcolm X* succeeds because it refuses to freeze Malcolm into a simple symbol. He was not one thing for his entire life. He was a man capable of growth, contradiction, anger, tenderness, discipline, and change. The film respects him enough to show the journey rather than only celebrating the final image. His evolution does not weaken his legacy. It is the legacy. Malcolm teaches that identity does not have to remain confined by the name, history, or beliefs handed to us. A person can examine himself, reject what no longer serves the truth, and continue becoming someone new. The assassination is devastating because Malcolm dies at the moment his understanding is becoming widest. Scavenger Hunt #138 Film 1 of 30 Category: A film about activism. The Film *Malcolm X* is not simply a biography of an important man. It is the story of a person repeatedly destroying an old version of himself in order to become someone greater. Spike Lee refuses to present Malcolm as though he entered the world already prepared to become a leader. We see his anger, vanity, criminality, discipline, faith, pride, mistakes, and eventual willingness to reconsider beliefs that once defined him. The different names he carries represent those transformations. Malcolm Little is the child born into a family terrorized by racism. Detroit Red is the young man attempting to bury that pain beneath style, excitement, and crime. Malcolm X rejects the name inherited through slavery and replaces it with the unknown history stolen from him. El Hajj Malik El Shabazz emerges after Mecca with a larger understanding of humanity. Each name belongs to the same man, but none contains him completely. The early scenes are energetic and entertaining, but that energy hides enormous insecurity. Malcolm straightens his hair, changes the way he dresses, and performs a version of himself designed to survive and feel powerful. The conk becomes more than a hairstyle. It shows how racism can teach someone to reject features of his own body before he even realizes he is doing it. Prison becomes the place where physical confinement produces intellectual freedom. Malcolm begins reading, questioning language, and recognizing how history has been written by people with the power to define everyone else. Education does not merely give him information. It gives him a new understanding of himself. He discovers that controlling language means controlling the boundaries of what people believe is possible. The Nation of Islam gives Malcolm discipline, purpose, and a community, but the same organization that helps rebuild him eventually attempts to control him. His devotion to Elijah Muhammad is sincere, which makes the betrayal deeply personal. Malcolm realizes that replacing one form of dependence with another is not true liberation. He must be willing to question the person who taught him how to question everything else. His journey to Mecca becomes the film’s final great transformation. Malcolm does not abandon his understanding of racism in America, but he recognizes that his previous beliefs about race were incomplete. What makes him extraordinary is not that he was always correct. It is that he was willing to change publicly after building his identity around certainty. Many people would rather protect their pride than admit that experience has expanded their understanding. The Direction Spike Lee directs the film with the scale and confidence of an epic while keeping Malcolm’s personal evolution at its center. The opening immediately connects Malcolm’s life to the America that continued after his death. Images of the American flag burning into the shape of an X are combined with footage of Rodney King being beaten, making it clear that this is not a safely contained history lesson. The conditions Malcolm confronted did not disappear with him. Each period of Malcolm’s life has its own visual identity. The early sequences are colorful, playful, and alive with movement. Prison removes that freedom and replaces it with hard lines, shadows, and confined spaces. As Malcolm becomes a public figure, the compositions grow larger and more controlled, reflecting the authority he has developed. By the final section, that control begins collapsing under surveillance, threats, and betrayal. Lee never allows Malcolm’s speeches to become interruptions in the story. Speaking is the action. The film understands that Malcolm’s voice was his greatest instrument because he could transform private anger into a shared political consciousness. The crowds do not simply admire him. They recognize experiences that society repeatedly told them to endure quietly. The march to the hospital is one of the clearest demonstrations of his power. Malcolm controls the movement of an entire crowd with small gestures, revealing the discipline behind his leadership. The police see danger because they are witnessing a Black man exercise authority that does not depend upon their permission. The final movement carries an unavoidable sense of dread. Malcolm knows that death is approaching, but he continues speaking because fear can no longer determine the value of his work. The famous shot of him moving toward the ballroom makes him appear almost separated from the ground, as though history is carrying him toward a fate both he and the audience already understand. At more than three hours, the film is long, but that length mostly feels earned. Malcolm’s transformation would lose its meaning if any major stage were treated as a brief montage. Some supporting relationships are compressed because the film has so much history to contain, yet the overall scale allows Malcolm to feel like a full human being rather than a collection of famous speeches. The Acting Denzel Washington gives one of the greatest performances ever placed in a biographical film. He does not simply imitate Malcolm’s voice and physical mannerisms. He captures the intelligence, humor, anger, confidence, vulnerability, and constant mental movement beneath them. His performance changes with every stage of Malcolm’s life. Detroit Red moves with youthful arrogance, constantly trying to appear larger than he feels. The imprisoned Malcolm becomes quieter as his mind awakens. The public speaker controls rooms through rhythm and precision. The later Malcolm appears calmer but also more exposed because he is no longer protected by the certainty or organization that once surrounded him. Denzel is especially powerful during the speeches because he communicates why people followed Malcolm. The words are important, but so is the feeling that every sentence has been sharpened by personal experience. Malcolm does not speak about racism as an abstract political subject. He speaks as someone whose family, childhood, body, opportunities, and identity were all shaped by it. Angela Bassett brings strength and emotional clarity to Betty Shabazz. Betty is not merely the supportive wife waiting outside Malcolm’s public life. She understands the danger surrounding him and the cost his mission places on their family. Bassett shows the love between them while never pretending that loving someone with a historical purpose is easy. Delroy Lindo is also excellent as West Indian Archie, particularly when Malcolm encounters him years later. Archie’s decline becomes a vision of the future Malcolm escaped. Albert Hall gives Baines the calm authority necessary to make Malcolm’s religious transformation believable, while Al Freeman Jr. portrays Elijah Muhammad with enough warmth to make Malcolm’s eventual disillusionment feel genuinely painful. Conclusion *Malcolm X* succeeds because it refuses to freeze Malcolm into a simple symbol. He was not one thing for his entire life. He was a man capable of growth, contradiction, anger, tenderness, discipline, and change. The film respects him enough to show the journey rather than only celebrating the final image. His evolution does not weaken his legacy. It is the legacy. Malcolm teaches that identity does not have to remain confined by the name, history, or beliefs handed to us. A person can examine himself, reject what no longer serves the truth, and continue becoming someone new. The assassination is devastating because Malcolm dies at the moment his understanding is becoming widest. He has separated from the institution that once gave him power, broadened his view of humanity, and begun building something independently. The tragedy is not only that a great man was killed. It is that we will never know what his next transformation might have become. The final sequence expands Malcolm beyond one body. When people across generations declare themselves Malcolm X, they are not claiming to replace him. They are recognizing that his struggle for dignity, knowledge, and self definition belongs to everyone denied the right to define themselves. Spike Lee created something far greater than a standard biopic. He made a film about the courage required to confront the world and the even greater courage required to confront yourself. Malcolm’s power did not come from never changing. It came from refusing to stop.

No other visual rendition of a public figure can even approximate the effect of its testament to the significance of not just this individual life, but every individual life. It magnetizes with its ambition only to pull the viewer in further, further into its sweeping crevices that envelop the harrowing volatility of souls. Still so early in their illustrious careers, Denzel Washington and Spike Lee demonstrate a drive here that it’s difficult to say they ever had again (if anyone else has ever had it at all); their particular fortitude, courage, confidence, and determination as artists harmonize perfectly with their subject. Just please watch this movie.

Inizio col dire che sono contento che Chalamet non abbia vinto l'oscar, per quanto valore abbia, con questo film. Perché? Perché sarebbe stata un'ingiustizia verso le altre GIGANTI performance che non sono state prese in considerazione tanto quanto Marty Supreme. Non fraintendete, qui è incredibile, ma probabilmente non si avvicina alla sua top 3. Sono dell'opinione che la pubblicità ed il marketing, abbiano reso iconico questo film, perché altrimenti non se ne sarebbe parlato così tanto. Safdie fa un lavoro sublime, il personaggio di Marty è scritto e messo in scena in un modo quasi unico. Mi è pesato particolarmente stargli dietro, più volte ho provato fastidio nel sentirlo parlare o anche solo respirare guardando le espressioni. E' proprio quel tipo di persona che non dovrebbe nascere, nemmeno per sbaglio. Narcisista, manipolatore, adulatore, ladro, bugiardo, truffatore, egoista. A livello tecnico con Diamanti Grezzi, che trovo superiore a Marty Supreme, ha già fatto vedere di cosa è capace. Qui ha comunque tenuto l'asticella alta, nonostante non abbia apprezzato alcune cose. Secondo me ci sono delle "problematiche" che sotto certi aspetti lo rendono debole: - il personaggio di Marty sovrasta completamente ogni altro personaggio all'interno del film. Sicuramente è una cosa voluta, ne sono certo, ma rende la visione troppo piatta in alcuni momenti. L'unico personaggio, che ha probabilmente un pò di risalto, è Kletzki. Ma solamente perché Safdie gli dedica 5 minuti di screenplay e gli da un'identità ben definita; - qual è il topic principale di questo film? è un (non)biopic, è un film sullo sport, è un film drammatico, è un film sull'ossessione. E' tutto, ma non è niente. Non è carne né pesce. Quindi cos'è? L'ho trovato senza identità. Trovo davvero ironico che alla fine della visione, l'unica cosa che mi abbia davvero colpito, è l'unica cosa che mi portava a non vedere Marty Supreme, Chalamet. La cosa che mi ricorderà di questo film è la pallina da ping pong, brandizzata ovviamente, che mi è stata regalata da mio nipote. Lo guarderò di nuovo però, questo è certo.

Doch anstatt authentischer Atmosphäre dröhnen im Minutentakt Synthesizer Melodien oder Pop-Hits aus den 80ern durch die Boxen. Was soll das? Und dann Timothée Chalamet. Mein Gott. Die Bälle fliegen mit einer Physik durchs Bild, die eher an ein kaputtes Retro-Videospiel erinnert als an echten Sport. Kein einziger Charakter besitzt Tiefe, Sympathie oder auch nur den Ansatz einer Persönlichkeit. Marty Supreme ist lauter, belangloser Schrott, der sich nach dem Abspann zum Glück von selbst aus dem Gedächtnis löscht. 2/5 oder auch 4/10 Punkten —————————————————————————— Marty Suprem e is a film that, from the very first minute, feels like tinnitus – in other words, just plain annoying. The film is set in the 1950s. But instead of an authentic atmosphere, synthesiser tunes or 80s pop hits blare out of the speakers every minute. What on earth is that about? And then there’s Timothée Chalamet. My God. After five minutes, you just want to force a tranquilliser and a cup of chamomile tea down his throat. Ninety per cent of it is frantic running about, shrill screaming and utter hysteria. The tournament scenes look quite stylish at first glance, but quickly turn out to be nothing more than a CGI spectacle. The balls fly across the screen with physics that are more reminiscent of a broken retro video game than of real sport. Not a single character possesses any depth, likeability or even the slightest hint of a personality. Marty Supreme is nothing but loud, meaningless rubbish which, thankfully, fades from memory of its own accord once the credits roll. 2/5 or 4/10 Points

Before anyone gets on me, stops reading, or decides they hate this take: I understand why so many people like this movie. I can see why it scores so high. For me, it wasn’t even a decent film and here’s why. The core problem is that Marty Supreme seems to want both things at once: a portrait of an arrogant, self-absorbed climber, and a hero you’re supposed to root for. That tension never really resolves, and a lot of the film’s weaker choices come from it. Most of the characters are flat enough that it’s hard to attach to them. The ones that stay interesting are Marty Mauser, Wally, and the dog Moses. Rachel is the clearest miss. The character could have worked, but Odessa A’zion’s performance rarely holds attention. Her only decent moment is the argument with Marty after they come back from looking for the dog. Kay Stone is the reverse: a thin character lifted by Gwyneth Paltrow. Even then, it’s frustrating how aware Kay is of Marty’s real intentions, yet she falls for him anyway including with the necklace she gives him, which then disappears because of what they do. Too often the film has better performances than character writing, or better ideas than performances. Several side plots also do little for the whole. Ezra Mishkin arrives like a random gangster fragment: a boss who wants his dog back, as if a John Wick got stuck in this one. That thread might have supported Marty if Ezra had simply stayed a rich old man attached to a shelter dog. The Auschwitz material is worse. It functions more like a bad joke than character development. It adds nothing to the plot, and using a story like that just to land a cheap beat feels unnecessary. If it had shaped someone in a real way, it could have earned its place. It doesn’t. What does work is Marty himself as a construction. The arrogant, ego-driven hustler chasing greatness is a strong idea, and Timothée Chalamet makes him watchable. The ambition is clear and often compelling. The problem is the film’s posture toward him. It keeps nudging you to root for Marty. Wanting the opposite waiting for consequences to finally catch him would have made his wins hit harder. The character is interesting; the film’s protection of him is not. The direction is similarly uneven. Some moments are sharp Marty running from the police has real energy, the movement and framing actually matching his panic and momentum. Then other stretches turn heavy without payoff, like the escape with Wally from the gas station, where the scene feels chaotic and overbearing rather than controlled. Marty Supreme has a creative premise and a few strong pieces, but more that doesn’t land than that does. I went in with high hopes and left disappointed. Tyler was good tho. Before anyone gets on me, stops reading, or decides they hate this take: I understand why so many people like this movie. I can see why it scores so high. For me, it wasn’t even a decent film and here’s why. The core problem is that Marty Supreme seems to want both things at once: a portrait of an arrogant, self-absorbed climber, and a hero you’re supposed to root for. That tension never really resolves, and a lot of the film’s weaker choices come from it. Most of the characters are flat enough that it’s hard to attach to them. The ones that stay interesting are Marty Mauser, Wally, and the dog Moses. Rachel is the clearest miss. The character could have worked, but Odessa A’zion’s performance rarely holds attention. Her only decent moment is the argument with Marty after they come back from looking for the dog. Kay Stone is the reverse: a thin character lifted by Gwyneth Paltrow. Even then, it’s frustrating how aware Kay is of Marty’s real intentions, yet she falls for him anyway including with the necklace she gives him, which then disappears because of what they do. Too often the film has better performances than character writing, or better ideas than performances. Several side plots also do little for the whole. Ezra Mishkin arrives like a random gangster fragment: a boss who wants his dog back, as if a John Wick got stuck in this one. That thread might have supported Marty if Ezra had simply stayed a rich old man attached to a shelter dog. The Auschwitz material is worse. It functions more like a bad joke than character development. It adds nothing to the plot, and using a story like that just to land a cheap beat feels unnecessary. If it had shaped someone in a real way, it could have earned its place. It doesn’t. What does work is Marty himself as a construction. The arrogant, ego-driven hustler chasing greatness is a strong idea, and Timothée Chalamet makes him watchable. The ambition is clear and often compelling. The problem is the film’s posture toward him. It keeps nudging you to root for Marty. Wanting the opposite waiting for consequences to finally catch him would have made his wins hit harder. The character is interesting; the film’s protection of him is not. The direction is similarly uneven. Some moments are sharp Marty running from the police has real energy, the movement and framing actually matching his panic and momentum. Then other stretches turn heavy without payoff, like the escape with Wally from the gas station, where the scene feels chaotic and overbearing rather than controlled. Marty Supreme has a creative premise and a few strong pieces, but more that doesn’t land than that does. I went in with high hopes and left disappointed. Tyler was good tho. Also, that sperm race: another weak joke in a movie that already has too many, and a pretty clear sign of a scene the film did not need.

Wishing for his success despite loathing his actions. In Marty Supreme, the movie is more or less split into two separate and distinct tracks. One a fairly typical, but brilliantly shot, short sports movie.  The other, a scrabbling descent into layers and layers of cons, dodges, grifts, and hustles weaving in and out of one another for nearly two hours.  All of it wonderfully acted, with cameos galore, but utterly draining and seemingly endless. I find myself at a strange impasse as a result. Wishing for his success despite loathing his actions. In Marty Supreme, the movie is more or less split into two separate and distinct tracks. One a fairly typical, but brilliantly shot, short sports movie.  The other, a scrabbling descent into layers and layers of cons, dodges, grifts, and hustles weaving in and out of one another for nearly two hours.  All of it wonderfully acted, with cameos galore, but utterly draining and seemingly endless. I find myself at a strange impasse as a result. [26] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Tratto da eventi storici realmente accaduti, ovvero gli omicidi seriali avvenuti a Hwaseong in una provincia rurale della Corea del Sud. "Memories of Murder" è stato uno dei maggior successi commerciali dell'apprezzato regista coreano Bong Joon-ho. Anche se l'incipit della narrazione e il modus operandi del serial killer vengono descritti in modo del tutto ordinario. Memories of Murder si discosta dal solito poliziesco per quel ricordo, un frammento di eventi autoctoni svaniti nel tempo che tornano alla mente solo nel finale, capace di trasportare lo spettatore occidentale in un mondo parzialmente estraneo. L'opera di Bong Joo-ho è dunque degna di interesse perchè porta alla superficie una concreta denuncia sociale, una pertinente e aspra critica alla società, nello specifico quella delle forze di Polizia, fondata sul concetto autartico dell'ego. Un ego smisurato che non si preoccupa minimamente del concetto di variabilità dell'ipotesi. Ciò che conta di più è portare a termine le indagini ad ogni costo, e insabbiare alla stampa certe pratiche ortodosse adottate a discapito dei sospettati. Tipiche pratiche fra l'altro molto diffuse nella cultura asiatica.. Il film cattura l'interesse già da subito grazie all'ottimo cast, Sang Kang-ho (Parasite), Park Ha-il, Kim Roi-ha, Kim Sang-Kyung, Jung In-sun etc, e all'ambientazione rurale piovosa e a una fotografia degna di nota. Aimé non mancano delle forzature per "incanalare" la sceneggiatura negli eventi voluti, e l'importante minutaggio evidenzia dei dettagli di trama superflui. Ma la soggettiva peculiarità della trama sta tutta racchiusa nel finale amaro quanto drammaticamente evocativo. La curiosità, e il rammarico di aver sbagliato scuotono i sensi del protagonista e dello spettatore.. Dove il cinismo del passato riemerge e si impadronisce di nuovo della ragione, ma quello che ne rimane e soltanto l'immaginazione di un volto comune. Troppo comune.. Visione consigliatissima. Voto: più che sufficiente.

Une œuvre qui reprend l'histoire vraie d'un mystérieux tueur en série national aux manies étranges qui n'a jamais été démasqué. C'est un film d'enquête qui ne se prend pas au sérieux tout du long, sauf à la fin où il essaye de faire passer un message sur les stéréotypes de l'apparence d'un tueur en série dans l'imaginaire collectif (ce que Cure faisait beaucoup mieux avec beaucoup plus de poésie). Le film reste sympathique, bien présenté et cohérent. Mais bon sang pourquoi il est aussi vide et énervant tout du long ? Les personnages sont insupportables, et vu que le film ne propose rien d'autre on se retrouve seul face à eux. Cet aspect ridicule marche en tant que comédie à certains moments, mais le revirement sérieux à la fin offre au film une situation inconsistante inconfortable. É aquilo: se a gente não gosta dos protagonistas, dificilmente consegue se envolver com a história. E aqui aconteceu justamente isso. Agora, uma coisa que gostei bastante foi a ambientação, mostrando a transição de um regime autoritário para uma democracia funcional e como esse contexto influencia a investigação. No final, senti como se o filme tivesse sido feito pensando justamente no serial killer. Quando o detetive quebra a quarta parede e olha diretamente para a câmera, dizendo que o assassino tem um rosto normal e que pode ser qualquer pessoa, parece quase um aviso à população: ele ainda está à solta e pode estar em qualquer lugar.

[26] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Tratto da eventi storici realmente accaduti, ovvero gli omicidi seriali avvenuti a Hwaseong in una provincia rurale della Corea del Sud. "Memories of Murder" è stato uno dei maggior successi commerciali dell'apprezzato regista coreano Bong Joon-ho. Anche se l'incipit della narrazione e il modus operandi del serial killer vengono descritti in modo del tutto ordinario. Memories of Murder si discosta dal solito poliziesco per quel ricordo, un frammento di eventi autoctoni svaniti nel tempo che tornano alla mente solo nel finale, capace di trasportare lo spettatore occidentale in un mondo parzialmente estraneo. L'opera di Bong Joo-ho è dunque degna di interesse perchè porta alla superficie una concreta denuncia sociale, una pertinente e aspra critica alla società, nello specifico quella delle forze di Polizia, fondata sul concetto autartico dell'ego. Un ego smisurato che non si preoccupa minimamente del concetto di variabilità dell'ipotesi. Ciò che conta di più è portare a termine le indagini ad ogni costo, e insabbiare alla stampa certe pratiche ortodosse adottate a discapito dei sospettati. Tipiche pratiche fra l'altro molto diffuse nella cultura asiatica.. Il film cattura l'interesse già da subito grazie all'ottimo cast, Sang Kang-ho (Parasite), Park Ha-il, Kim Roi-ha, Kim Sang-Kyung, Jung In-sun etc, e all'ambientazione rurale piovosa e a una fotografia degna di nota. Aimé non mancano delle forzature per "incanalare" la sceneggiatura negli eventi voluti, e l'importante minutaggio evidenzia dei dettagli di trama superflui. Ma la soggettiva peculiarità della trama sta tutta racchiusa nel finale amaro quanto drammaticamente evocativo. La curiosità, e il rammarico di aver sbagliato scuotono i sensi del protagonista e dello spettatore.. Dove il cinismo del passato riemerge e si impadronisce di nuovo della ragione, ma quello che ne rimane e soltanto l'immaginazione di un volto comune. Troppo comune.. Visione consigliatissima. Voto: più che sufficiente.

Deux flics de province tellement dépassés par leur enquête qu'ils préfèrent frapper des suspects au hasard et consulter une voyante plutôt que suivre une vraie méthode scientifique, l'académie de police coréenne n'a visiblement jamais entendu parler de la scène de crime qu'on ne piétine pas à dix personnes. Bong Joon-ho enchaîne les scènes qui devraient installer une tension glaçante mais qui basculent sans prévenir dans un comique presque slapstick, comme cette poursuite ridicule dans les champs de riz où l'un des flics dégringole une pente en pleine filature. Pissed me off. I get it, I understand why it ends the way it ends but it was so immensely frustrating it ruined the movie for me. And I get that that is the point!!! Admittedly, I didn’t know that this movie was based on a true story and that it was a cold case in 2003 until it ended and my brother told me, so know that I know that, I get it even more. And so I don’t necessarily dislike the idea of a no-answer (the final shot is amazing, yeah) — especially if that was the ‘truth’ at the time — and of course I get that the cops are meant to be corrupt and that the desperation of an unsolvable crime drives people to the brink, but I had a very hard time caring about men with power abusing it while women were being brutally murdered, seemingly in the background. I like Bong Joon Ho, and I didn’t think that this was a hyper misogynistic movie, but the brutality of the crimes felt so commonplace. The victims were consistently treated as a narrative afterthought and I just couldn’t bring myself to care about it at all. The cops torture men to get a confession for their own sake. Of course they don’t care about the women being raped and murdered with their own clothes, why would they? All they want is a confession, which is what the movie makes us care about. The women are an afterthought to the corruption. They are victims twice over, once in ‘practice’ (for lack of a better term), and for a second time when they are effectively forgotten about during the course of the investigation. And I get that that is sadly the way it almost always seems to be in real life, and perhaps the movie does it so well, it portrays that calloused, misogynistic corruption that seeps into everything so well that I couldn’t stand it. I felt like this meme while attempting to laugh at the dropkicks. How can I care about anything in the face of such brutality, especially when that brutality seems to be barely relevant? I don’t think it’s a bad movie, but I rarely write searching for objectivity, so I can only say that I hated it. Not for me at all. Once again, I understand why it does all that it does, and I guess I understand why it’s hailed as a Great, but I couldn’t look past how cavalier it was towards women being consistently brutalized. And I understand that perhaps that’s the way it’s meant to be, I guess it is a critique on that very calloused misogynistic corruption, but it feels a bit like the idea of an anti war movie. How can a movie not be misogynistic when most of its female characters are shown with their limbs splayed out on the ground? I’ve been very angry lately and I just can’t bring myself to ignore misogyny more than any woman does every day.

Let’s be honest: if you strip away all the pseudo-intellectual interpretations people have of this movie, it’s literally about nothing. It feels like everything that happens was made solely to build up to the ending. And yes, the ending is interesting in its own way, but it’s nowhere near as groundbreaking, revolutionary, or profound as people try to make it out to be. Movies like this existed before, were being made around the same time, and continued to be made afterward. There’s nothing particularly new here, other than the fact that this specific movie was made by Koreans. And if you take the ending away, there’s basically nothing left. The movie doesn’t stand out in any other way. There’s no particularly interesting detective element, no characters you actually want to follow, and no dialogue that’s especially engaging. Just exaggerated emotional reactions that start getting annoying after a while. It’s an incredibly boring movie. Yes, it has an idea, and yes, that idea is expressed reasonably well, but it’s hardly some extraordinary concept that magically makes up for everything else. It’s simply a mediocre movie about nothing that people seem to worship way too much — and, honestly, the only real reason I can see for that is that it was made in Korea. [13] nota=1.5 estrelas:
Pissed me off. I get it, I understand why it ends the way it ends but it was so immensely frustrating it ruined the movie for me. And I get that that is the point!!! Admittedly, I didn’t know that this movie was based on a true story and that it was a cold case in 2003 until it ended and my brother told me, so know that I know that, I get it even more. And so I don’t necessarily dislike the idea of a no-answer (the final shot is amazing, yeah) — especially if that was the ‘truth’ at the time — and of course I get that the cops are meant to be corrupt and that the desperation of an unsolvable crime drives people to the brink, but I had a very hard time caring about men with power abusing it while women were being brutally murdered, seemingly in the background. I like Bong Joon Ho, and I didn’t think that this was a hyper misogynistic movie, but the brutality of the crimes felt so commonplace. The victims were consistently treated as a narrative afterthought and I just couldn’t bring myself to care about it at all. The cops torture men to get a confession for their own sake. Of course they don’t care about the women being raped and murdered with their own clothes, why would they? All they want is a confession, which is what the movie makes us care about. The women are an afterthought to the corruption. They are victims twice over, once in ‘practice’ (for lack of a better term), and for a second time when they are effectively forgotten about during the course of the investigation. And I get that that is sadly the way it almost always seems to be in real life, and perhaps the movie does it so well, it portrays that calloused, misogynistic corruption that seeps into everything so well that I couldn’t stand it. I felt like this meme while attempting to laugh at the dropkicks. How can I care about anything in the face of such brutality, especially when that brutality seems to be barely relevant? I don’t think it’s a bad movie, but I rarely write searching for objectivity, so I can only say that I hated it. Not for me at all. Once again, I understand why it does all that it does, and I guess I understand why it’s hailed as a Great, but I couldn’t look past how cavalier it was towards women being consistently brutalized. And I understand that perhaps that’s the way it’s meant to be, I guess it is a critique on that very calloused misogynistic corruption, but it feels a bit like the idea of an anti war movie. How can a movie not be misogynistic when most of its female characters are shown with their limbs splayed out on the ground? I’ve been very angry lately and I just can’t bring myself to ignore misogyny more than any woman does every day.
