Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Nolan set out to make a film about the atomic bomb, working inside a framework that all but guarantees certain choices: the female characters stay thin, and the American establishment — despite building and deploying the most destructive weapon ever used — ends up framed as the aggrieved party. Three hours built around one event, and we never see that event’s human cost. No Hiroshima, no Nagasaki. What we get is Trinity shot with dread, and a hallucination of burned bodies mid-celebration — real craft, but it’s guilt filtered through Oppenheimer’s psychology, not the people who actually died. “We only see what we’re shown” isn’t a defence, it’s the problem — every war film would look blameless in its own cinema by that logic. This isn’t unique to Nolan either; American war films (Iraq, Korea, Vietnam) keep casting the US as victim in wars it started, the same way some WWII films let American soldiers alone liberate the camps and quietly cut the Soviets out. To be fair, the film’s real subject is different: Oppenheimer devoured by the establishment that used him. That’s honest, documented history. But it’s a different casualty from the nation, and the two blur together too easily. Even on its own terms, the pacing fails its nerve. The security hearing eats up the runtime; the actual moral reckoning gets compressed into mood and sound design instead of a position the film is willing to hold. A question this big — was this justified? — can’t be answered by half. Beautiful score, exceptional editing, a flawless cast. None of it amounts to an argument.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ Oppenheimer is a technically extraordinary film that ultimately keeps its most serious question at arm's length. It flirts with self-criticism through the psychology of one man while leaving the nation's — and the weapon's — actual victims outside the frame entirely. Craft of this level deserves an equally serious answer to the question it raises, not an atmosphere of unease standing in for one.

I’m still yet to see The Odyssey, but it’s basically impossible to read anything related to film right now and not find an essay on how Christoper Nolan has finally completed his accidental reverse  triptych on tracing the evolution of man's relationship to power and evil, on the heroes who mistake intelligence for virtue. The Odyssey imagines the mythic birth of strategic violence, to be cunning is to acquire the status of a moral good. Tenet imagines something much later and much more bleak, the bureaucratisation of the apocalypse. While Oppenheimer is found somewhere in the middle, the shift from strategy to science, the genius who acquires the capacity to destroy the world. History, read backwards, starts to echo a series of increasingly sophisticated excuses of exceptional men. It’s a very stylish and neat way to view the films, more stylish and neat, perhaps, then the films themselves. And while these film’s three leads, Odysseus, Oppenheimer, and the Protagonist may be from different centuries, experiencing different crises, each man crosses a threshold that cannot be uncrossed, each inheriting history itself as both burden and the very justification for existence.  And I don’t know if I fully agree, Nolan doesn’t quite seem the type of filmmaker to spend over a decade silently remaking the same film; but the reading makes one thing feel clear to me, that Oppenheimer is much more a clear symptom of Nolan’s work than his masterpiece. I’m not exactly a fan of Tenet, a film less intellectually rigorous than hermetically sealed, so completely fascinated by its own narrative mechanisms, smugly constructing its timeloop as an axiom, that it never stops to ask if it is mistaking opacity for complexity. For a film that is supposed to feel like human agency is being dissolved into infrastructure, it’s strangely legible, the end was always written into the beginning, it all makes sense in the end, there’s always a hero to its story, even if we only see the consequences of actions already chosen. If I wanted cinema like that then I’d much rather take Assayas’s Demonlover, or Denis’s Bastards every time, at least those films see something Nolan never can bring into sight; those systems become frightening because no one can comprehend them. The very forms of those films do not ask us to admire their architectures, but they ask us to live inside the consequences, never becoming legible because the modern world does not allow for it; these are stories of networks, not heroes. But with Oppenheimer I find my feelings more disjointed; it doesn’t help that the public reaction to the film seems to proclaim it as the grand brilliant masterpiece to define the 2020s American cinema. It’s obviously an accomplished film on most technical levels, and I can appreciate a lot of it’s editing, and a genuine fantastic lead performance; but any admiration I have turns to stone by the time its greatest irony has come to light; a film about the invention of systems capacity of escaping our control (nuclear winter) is so convinced that history is driven by the great man. How can one singular consciousness make us feel the weight of such horrors? The Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings show up not as straight realities but as subjective events that disturb Oppenheimer’s own interior life. Is the film refusal to depict these events an ethical one to stop atrocity turning into aesthetics? I’m not convinced, we leave so much knowing about what it feels to invent the bomb, but we feel so little about what that means for… everyone else, including those who lived beneath it. The limits of making a biopic about a man’s guilt is failing to be a statement on how humanity doomed itself with his invention, you either make us understand catastrophe, or how it feels to be ‘great’ but ‘cursed’. Nolan’s films have always been fascinated by guilt, exceptional men have to be crushed eventually by the weight of their exceptional decisions, too heavy for ‘normal people’ to understand; but guilt is not morality, and Nolan’s guilt more resembles proof of one’s exceptional depth than functioning as their own ethical reckoning. Oppenheimer must suffer so intensely through his mind that his suffering becomes the film’s moral inquiry. Are we ‘really’ confronting evil? Or just watching a man’s conscience work as usual? (I feel like those TikToks about men where it’s like ‘men are just now having the thoughts we have at a sleepover at nine’). Again and again, in Nolan’s cinema, civilisation persists because one extraordinary man discovers that one’s intelligence can allow them to suspend morality. Splitting the atom, the Trojan Horse, controlling time itself. Different myths that share the fundamental conviction, history depends on the men who act when everyone else cannot. But that’s the rancid conservative impulse at the heart of his filmmaking, maybe not quite in the partisan sense (although we’ve all seen the think pieces on Dark Knight and Interstellar), but in the shape of his histories. This nineteenth century imagination being recycled back into contemporary culture, a world now ruled by invisible systems and anonymous power, it’s ironically, a very romantic vision of a lost past disguised as modernity. Carlyle’s influence is exhausting, the ending of two geniuses talking about the future of the nuclear age might be even worse. Don’t forget, it was a Nazi who said that sovereignty is revealed in the exception, Nolan might as well endorse it through his fantasies. Of course, there is an obvious objection to my claims, Odysseus devises the Horse; the Protagonist orchestrates events from both ends of time, but Oppenheimer doesn’t drop the bomb, he just invents it. Power has already migrated elsewhere; into the invisible machinery of Cold War America. The point isn’t that Oppenheimer controls history, it’s that Nolan insists on making him the center of it. The film shows that history’s decisive moral drama is located at the moment of invention, not administration. As if Oppenheimer becomes the last individual capable of containing this history with any moral imagination, the bomb no longer belongs to him, but the film behaves as if the bomb’s only meaning does. However history does not have a centre, catastrophe cannot be understood through the conscience of one man, however remarkable they might have been. Oppenheimer mistakes the scale of its subject for the depth of its thought. This perhaps explains why I left Oppenheimer remaining untouched by its very indifferent ideas on the means of humanity’s own destruction. Nolan wants to imagine a world transformed by things too powerful for any one individual to contain. But his imagination cannot stop returning to the individual who started it all, however powerless they might be. A filmmaker who dreams of networks but still believes in heroes that even his tragedies preserve the mythology of exceptional men. That might have worked for the Greeks, but it works less for the bomb.

This nineteenth century imagination being recycled back into contemporary culture, a world now ruled by invisible systems and anonymous power, it’s ironically, a very romantic vision of a lost past disguised as modernity. Carlyle’s influence is exhausting, the ending of two geniuses talking about the future of the nuclear age might be even worse. Don’t forget, it was a Nazi who said that sovereignty is revealed in the exception, Nolan might as well endorse it through his fantasies. Of course, there is an obvious objection to my claims, Odysseus devises the Horse; the Protagonist orchestrates events from both ends of time, but Oppenheimer doesn’t drop the bomb, he just invents it. Power has already migrated elsewhere; into the invisible machinery of Cold War America. The point isn’t that Oppenheimer controls history, it’s that Nolan insists on making him the center of it. The film shows that history’s decisive moral drama is located at the moment of invention, not administration. As if Oppenheimer becomes the last individual capable of containing this history with any moral imagination, the bomb no longer belongs to him, but the film behaves as if the bomb’s only meaning does. However history does not have a centre, catastrophe cannot be understood through the conscience of one man, however remarkable they might have been. Oppenheimer mistakes the scale of its subject for the depth of its thought. This perhaps explains why I left Oppenheimer remaining untouched by its very indifferent ideas on the means of humanity’s own destruction. Nolan wants to imagine a world transformed by things too powerful for any one individual to contain. But his imagination cannot stop returning to the individual who started it all, however powerless they might be. A filmmaker who dreams of networks but still believes in heroes that even his tragedies preserve the mythology of exceptional men. That might have worked for the Greeks, but it works less for the bomb.

Nolan set out to make a film about the atomic bomb, working inside a framework that all but guarantees certain choices: the female characters stay thin, and the American establishment — despite building and deploying the most destructive weapon ever used — ends up framed as the aggrieved party. Three hours built around one event, and we never see that event’s human cost. No Hiroshima, no Nagasaki. What we get is Trinity shot with dread, and a hallucination of burned bodies mid-celebration — real craft, but it’s guilt filtered through Oppenheimer’s psychology, not the people who actually died. “We only see what we’re shown” isn’t a defence, it’s the problem — every war film would look blameless in its own cinema by that logic. This isn’t unique to Nolan either; American war films (Iraq, Korea, Vietnam) keep casting the US as victim in wars it started, the same way some WWII films let American soldiers alone liberate the camps and quietly cut the Soviets out. To be fair, the film’s real subject is different: Oppenheimer devoured by the establishment that used him. That’s honest, documented history. But it’s a different casualty from the nation, and the two blur together too easily. Even on its own terms, the pacing fails its nerve. The security hearing eats up the runtime; the actual moral reckoning gets compressed into mood and sound design instead of a position the film is willing to hold. A question this big — was this justified? — can’t be answered by half. Beautiful score, exceptional editing, a flawless cast. None of it amounts to an argument.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​ Oppenheimer is a technically extraordinary film that ultimately keeps its most serious question at arm's length. It flirts with self-criticism through the psychology of one man while leaving the nation's — and the weapon's — actual victims outside the frame entirely. Craft of this level deserves an equally serious answer to the question it raises, not an atmosphere of unease standing in for one.

I’m still yet to see The Odyssey, but it’s basically impossible to read anything related to film right now and not find an essay on how Christoper Nolan has finally completed his accidental reverse  triptych on tracing the evolution of man's relationship to power and evil, on the heroes who mistake intelligence for virtue. The Odyssey imagines the mythic birth of strategic violence, to be cunning is to acquire the status of a moral good. Tenet imagines something much later and much more bleak, the bureaucratisation of the apocalypse. While Oppenheimer is found somewhere in the middle, the shift from strategy to science, the genius who acquires the capacity to destroy the world. History, read backwards, starts to echo a series of increasingly sophisticated excuses of exceptional men. It’s a very stylish and neat way to view the films, more stylish and neat, perhaps, then the films themselves. And while these film’s three leads, Odysseus, Oppenheimer, and the Protagonist may be from different centuries, experiencing different crises, each man crosses a threshold that cannot be uncrossed, each inheriting history itself as both burden and the very justification for existence.  And I don’t know if I fully agree, Nolan doesn’t quite seem the type of filmmaker to spend over a decade silently remaking the same film; but the reading makes one thing feel clear to me, that Oppenheimer is much more a clear symptom of Nolan’s work than his masterpiece. I’m not exactly a fan of Tenet, a film less intellectually rigorous than hermetically sealed, so completely fascinated by its own narrative mechanisms, smugly constructing its timeloop as an axiom, that it never stops to ask if it is mistaking opacity for complexity. For a film that is supposed to feel like human agency is being dissolved into infrastructure, it’s strangely legible, the end was always written into the beginning, it all makes sense in the end, there’s always a hero to its story, even if we only see the consequences of actions already chosen. If I wanted cinema like that then I’d much rather take Assayas’s Demonlover, or Denis’s Bastards every time, at least those films see something Nolan never can bring into sight; those systems become frightening because no one can comprehend them. The very forms of those films do not ask us to admire their architectures, but they ask us to live inside the consequences, never becoming legible because the modern world does not allow for it; these are stories of networks, not heroes. But with Oppenheimer I find my feelings more disjointed; it doesn’t help that the public reaction to the film seems to proclaim it as the grand brilliant masterpiece to define the 2020s American cinema. It’s obviously an accomplished film on most technical levels, and I can appreciate a lot of it’s editing, and a genuine fantastic lead performance; but any admiration I have turns to stone by the time its greatest irony has come to light; a film about the invention of systems capacity of escaping our control (nuclear winter) is so convinced that history is driven by the great man. How can one singular consciousness make us feel the weight of such horrors? The Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings show up not as straight realities but as subjective events that disturb Oppenheimer’s own interior life. Is the film refusal to depict these events an ethical one to stop atrocity turning into aesthetics? I’m not convinced, we leave so much knowing about what it feels to invent the bomb, but we feel so little about what that means for… everyone else, including those who lived beneath it. The limits of making a biopic about a man’s guilt is failing to be a statement on how humanity doomed itself with his invention, you either make us understand catastrophe, or how it feels to be ‘great’ but ‘cursed’. Nolan’s films have always been fascinated by guilt, exceptional men have to be crushed eventually by the weight of their exceptional decisions, too heavy for ‘normal people’ to understand; but guilt is not morality, and Nolan’s guilt more resembles proof of one’s exceptional depth than functioning as their own ethical reckoning. Oppenheimer must suffer so intensely through his mind that his suffering becomes the film’s moral inquiry. Are we ‘really’ confronting evil? Or just watching a man’s conscience work as usual? (I feel like those TikToks about men where it’s like ‘men are just now having the thoughts we have at a sleepover at nine’). Again and again, in Nolan’s cinema, civilisation persists because one extraordinary man discovers that one’s intelligence can allow them to suspend morality. Splitting the atom, the Trojan Horse, controlling time itself. Different myths that share the fundamental conviction, history depends on the men who act when everyone else cannot. But that’s the rancid conservative impulse at the heart of his filmmaking, maybe not quite in the partisan sense (although we’ve all seen the think pieces on Dark Knight and Interstellar), but in the shape of his histories. This nineteenth century imagination being recycled back into contemporary culture, a world now ruled by invisible systems and anonymous power, it’s ironically, a very romantic vision of a lost past disguised as modernity. Carlyle’s influence is exhausting, the ending of two geniuses talking about the future of the nuclear age might be even worse. Don’t forget, it was a Nazi who said that sovereignty is revealed in the exception, Nolan might as well endorse it through his fantasies. Of course, there is an obvious objection to my claims, Odysseus devises the Horse; the Protagonist orchestrates events from both ends of time, but Oppenheimer doesn’t drop the bomb, he just invents it. Power has already migrated elsewhere; into the invisible machinery of Cold War America. The point isn’t that Oppenheimer controls history, it’s that Nolan insists on making him the center of it. The film shows that history’s decisive moral drama is located at the moment of invention, not administration. As if Oppenheimer becomes the last individual capable of containing this history with any moral imagination, the bomb no longer belongs to him, but the film behaves as if the bomb’s only meaning does. However history does not have a centre, catastrophe cannot be understood through the conscience of one man, however remarkable they might have been. Oppenheimer mistakes the scale of its subject for the depth of its thought. This perhaps explains why I left Oppenheimer remaining untouched by its very indifferent ideas on the means of humanity’s own destruction. Nolan wants to imagine a world transformed by things too powerful for any one individual to contain. But his imagination cannot stop returning to the individual who started it all, however powerless they might be. A filmmaker who dreams of networks but still believes in heroes that even his tragedies preserve the mythology of exceptional men. That might have worked for the Greeks, but it works less for the bomb.

Oppenheimer est symptomatique de la filmographie de Cristopher Nolan. Il réinterprète des sujets passionnants et complexes avec des moyens colossaux et une capacité rare de créer un engouement massif auprès du grand public. Cependant, Oppenheimer, tout comme Interstellar ou Tenet, tombe toujours dans les mêmes travers qui font de ses œuvres des gâchis bien tristes. Des temporalités mélangées, où on aime faire des bonds dans le futur pour inlassablement revenir en arrière, des twists de merde artificiellement complexifiés et des personnages qui aiment s'écouter parler. Un cinéma "intelligent" ou un cinéma balourd qui impose à son public de se concentrer pendant 3 heures jusqu'à ne plus rien comprendre tant on est surchargés d'information pour se convaincre de la supériorité cérébrale de son scénario. Volontairement fatiguant, rien n'est développé si sa mise en scène ne sert pas l'histoire, le film passe son temps à expliquer ce qu'il ne filme pas. On apprend pas grand chose de Oppenheimer, de ce qu'il est, de ce qu'il fait, de ce qu'il le motive, de l'homme de science qu'il a été, de l'homme de pouvoir qu'il est devenu, de ses états d'âme, des conséquences de ses actions. Mais on préfère s'étendre sur un procès qui se passe on ne sait pas trop quand exactement, parce que Robert Downey Jr. est on se sait pas trop qui, qui souhaite empêcher à Cilian Murphy on ne sait pas trop quoi qui permettrait à ce dernier de faire quelque chose de sûrement important. Et c'est pas le film qui va nous aider à y voir beaucoup plus clair, profitant de la confusion pour mieux cacher les lacunes de Nolan. Au final, on finit par s'extasier sur le moindre acteur un peu connu ou sur des scènes bien américaines comme le namedrop de JFK vers la fin du film comme si c'était une scène post crédit Marvel. Mais peut-être que les histoires de cul intéressent plus Nolan que le tragique des bombardements atomiques d'Hiroshima et de Nagasaki dont tout semblait faux (et ce n'est pas la faute à Cilian Murphy) puisque le film n'avait cœur à rien. Spectacle du rien, psychologie de comptoir. Politiquement inconséquent, gâchis complet pour un film qui aurait mérité d'être plus digeste si Nolan ne faisait pas tout pour plomber sa mise en scène.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

"When I came to you with those calculations, we thought we might start a chain reaction that would destroy the entire world." Oppenheimer is a movie with a message... but the message is far more memorable than the movie itself. Make no mistake: Christopher Nolan's film, which won seven Academy Awards including best picture and best director, is an impressive technical milestone, particularly for its score, sound design, and maybe editing. I say "maybe" editing because though Jennifer Lame has overall succeeded in condensing an encyclopedia of information into a three hour film and making it (mostly) involving, the story is extremely hard to follow. Not just sequences, but individual scenes look disjointed. There may have been a stronger sense of setup and payoff if the footage was differently arranged, and better shot (more on that later). I also wonder how much of the material we actually needed to understand the film's main point, which is that the invention of a divinely powerful weapon will destroy the world in one way or another. The first two hours of the film detail the creation and testing of the atomic bomb, while the last hour focuses on Admiral Strauss manipulating the 1954 Gray Board hearing to ruin Oppenheimer's reputation. This latter event felt extremely petty and trivial in comparison to the tragedies of World War II, but as the final scene reveals, maybe that was the point. Strauss's egotism is like a bomb that, when ignited, wrecks the dignity of those who are the unfortunate target. But I still did not care about this subplot, despite it being historically accurate (I think), and I would have been more interested in the drama between Oppenheimer and his former assistant, Edward Teller. Then there is Nolan's typical lack of camera direction; most of the dialogue scenes (which constitute maybe 90 percent of the film) simply cut back and forth between actors who dump exposition and scientific formulas in monotonous voices in front of plain-looking backgrounds. Films like Inception are similarly guilty, but Nolan's best films are often redeemed by his imaginative premises (e.g. a dream within a dream). But once Nolan began to direct stories that weren't his own, his films - at least for me - lost their flavor. It is the main criticism that I have against The Odyssey and, to a marginally lesser extent, Oppenheimer . Nevertheless, Oppenheimer forces viewers to think critically about the moral implications of using such dangerous weapons at will. Should we play with fire just because we can? It is an extremely important message in today's world, and that alone makes the film worth watching at least once. As a piece of entertainment, however, the film falters. This was my third viewing, and I still zoned out several times throughout the movie. Most people seem to love Oppenheimer , but for me, it does not "take in the sheets."

This is my third time watching this film, and it gets better with every watch. From the moment the opening frame of raindrops shows, I was captivated. The rain being a motif for the consequences and troubles of Oppenheimer is a beautiful decision, and it executed perfectly throughout the entire film. It shows the weight that Oppenheimer has to carry with the decisions that he made, even if he appears to not be fully set on his emotions. Murphy absolutely deserved the Oscar for this masterful, career-defining performance. The way he able to play an anti-hero by showing regret through his voice and emotional restraint at times is done in a way only a few actors can do. I’d like to applaud the successful writing as well. Oppenheimer is one of the most complex characters Nolan has written. He has many moral flaws throughout, and even more contradictions to his actions, but yet the audience is made to feel for him emotionally, as we see the weight he carries, and the regret he holds, even if it’s too late. The cinematography in this film is also superb. The use of frequent, quick flashes throughout helps create the overall story, and sets the tone for what is going on. It allows for complex story telling, well-rounded characters, and sophisticated story telling. This helps create the great structure and pacing that this film has, which many argue is a problem in other Nolan movies. I can’t write this review without giving praise to Ludwig, and his amazing score for this film. It’s his best work, and I think he’ll have a hard time ever topping this string carried melody. I’d also like to shoutout Emily blunt. Her performance is already very famous for what she does with such little screen time, but the praise is warranted. Her face acting is a masterclass in show don’t tell. If she had more screen time, she’d have an Oscar for this role, which she might’ve deserved even with the little time she had to show off her talent. This is Nolan’s second best film. It has become very clear to me after debating this for a long time. This watch was necessary for me to determine where this ranks in his filmography. It is also the best film of the 2020s so far. There’s an argument for Dune 2, but Oppenheimer still clears. Now I am become death, destroyer of worlds.

Wanted to check that my perception of this film was not clouded by me being 17 and fairly new to IMAX at release. Those checks have cleared. The greatest lead acting performance ever. Greatest VFX and SFX ever, and would-be greatest score if Ludwig didn’t top it with Sinners. The perfection of Nolan’s exposition and weird editing of dialogue panning to everyone but the speaker’s face. Everyone involved in this film was born to play their role in it. The build and release of tension (much like how the movie presents fission) is masterful, using gorgeous visuals of subatomic warfare and sonic booms of egotism to represent the fractured genius of Oppenheimer’s mind and conscience in both the physical and moral sense in the lead-up, execution and conclusion of his most important moments. The Trinity Test remains my favourite scene ever crafted. What separates this from other biopics, or even The Odyssey, is the ambiguity that Nolan allows the viewer to cherish. Your view of Oppenheimer’s morality and consequentiality is entirely up to your reading of events - with clear view of the Red Scare, of America’s myths, of human history; you are the jury.

I remember when my Grandmother used to speak with me on the phone about Harry Truman's speech indicating the end of World War II. She would start to tear up when he spoke about how not one more American would be killed. It used to be very powerful to hear. There was, however, a missing part of this story I never knew about, the man who had to live with creating the bomb that ended the war. The film takes us from the opening credits to the kangaroo court of J. Robert Oppenheimer. Due to his past associations with communists, he never stood a chance. It was amazing to watch his brilliance be taken over by a man who was no more loyal to him than the communists he once befriended. Oppenheimer was the main architect who built the atomic bomb and he lived with the guilt long after it dropped. This guilt and a petty grudge gave Lewis Strauss all the ammunition he needed. Strauss got what he wanted from Oppenheimer. Strauss takes down Oppenheimer by sticking him in a kangaroo court. Afterwards, Strauss doesn't realize he's sitting in his own version of a kangaroo court until it's too late. I remember walking out of the theater and my friend and I both agreed how amazing it was. In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan used IMAX cameras for the entire film. In Oppenheimer, he used them for a majority of the film. This made it a visual spectacle that looked as good on a 4K TV as it did when I saw it in theaters. Cillian Murphy was an actor I knew of before this film. As Oppenheimer, he became the emotional center of the film regardless of time or destination. I could look in his eyes and know the highs and lows of being the man who received far more credit than he wanted. Beyond Nolan's directing, my friend and I discussed Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss extensively. I thought he was going to have a good chance at winning the Oscar, but he stole the film in every scene he was in. I saw Oppenheimer 3 years ago on the anniversary of the bomb dropping in Hiroshima in 1945. It was a moment that hit me after I left the theater. A few weeks later, I watched the film again in theaters, and then a few months later again with my Mom. Each time I thought to myself about how Oppenheimer had to live with what he did. Lewis Strauss had to live with unnecessary pettiness that cost him what he worked so hard for. Harry Truman may have taken responsibility, but guilt has to fall on someone's shoulders. Oppenheimer wasn't wrong for taking on the guilt, but just like his other mistakes, decisions are very hard to take back once they've been made. "When I came to you with those calculations, we thought we might start a chain reaction that would destroy the entire world." Oppenheimer is a movie with a message... but the message is far more memorable than the movie itself. Make no mistake: Christopher Nolan's film, which won seven Academy Awards including best picture and best director, is an impressive technical milestone, particularly for its score, sound design, and maybe editing. I say "maybe" editing because though Jennifer Lame has overall succeeded in condensing an encyclopedia of information into a three hour film and making it (mostly) involving, the story is extremely hard to follow. Not just sequences, but individual scenes look disjointed. There may have been a stronger sense of setup and payoff if the footage was differently arranged, and better shot (more on that later). I also wonder how much of the material we actually needed to understand the film's main point, which is that the invention of a divinely powerful weapon will destroy the world in one way or another. The first two hours of the film detail the creation and testing of the atomic bomb, while the last hour focuses on Admiral Strauss manipulating the 1954 Gray Board hearing to ruin Oppenheimer's reputation. This latter event felt extremely petty and trivial in comparison to the tragedies of World War II, but as the final scene reveals, maybe that was the point. Strauss's egotism is like a bomb that, when ignited, wrecks the dignity of those who are the unfortunate target. But I still did not care about this subplot, despite it being historically accurate (I think), and I would have been more interested in the drama between Oppenheimer and his former assistant, Edward Teller. Then there is Nolan's typical lack of camera direction; most of the dialogue scenes (which constitute maybe 90 percent of the film) simply cut back and forth between actors who dump exposition and scientific formulas in monotonous voices in front of plain-looking backgrounds. Films like Inception are similarly guilty, but Nolan's best films are often redeemed by his imaginative premises (e.g. a dream within a dream). But once Nolan began to direct stories that weren't his own, his films - at least for me - lost their flavor. It is the main criticism that I have against The Odyssey and, to a marginally lesser extent, Oppenheimer . Nevertheless, Oppenheimer forces viewers to think critically about the moral implications of using such dangerous weapons at will. Should we play with fire just because we can? It is an extremely important message in today's world, and that alone makes the film worth watching at least once. As a piece of entertainment, however, the film falters. This was my third viewing, and I still zoned out several times throughout the movie. Most people seem to love Oppenheimer , but for me, it does not "take in the sheets."

This is my third time watching this film, and it gets better with every watch. From the moment the opening frame of raindrops shows, I was captivated. The rain being a motif for the consequences and troubles of Oppenheimer is a beautiful decision, and it executed perfectly throughout the entire film. It shows the weight that Oppenheimer has to carry with the decisions that he made, even if he appears to not be fully set on his emotions. Murphy absolutely deserved the Oscar for this masterful, career-defining performance. The way he able to play an anti-hero by showing regret through his voice and emotional restraint at times is done in a way only a few actors can do. I’d like to applaud the successful writing as well. Oppenheimer is one of the most complex characters Nolan has written. He has many moral flaws throughout, and even more contradictions to his actions, but yet the audience is made to feel for him emotionally, as we see the weight he carries, and the regret he holds, even if it’s too late. The cinematography in this film is also superb. The use of frequent, quick flashes throughout helps create the overall story, and sets the tone for what is going on. It allows for complex story telling, well-rounded characters, and sophisticated story telling. This helps create the great structure and pacing that this film has, which many argue is a problem in other Nolan movies. I can’t write this review without giving praise to Ludwig, and his amazing score for this film. It’s his best work, and I think he’ll have a hard time ever topping this string carried melody. I’d also like to shoutout Emily blunt. Her performance is already very famous for what she does with such little screen time, but the praise is warranted. Her face acting is a masterclass in show don’t tell. If she had more screen time, she’d have an Oscar for this role, which she might’ve deserved even with the little time she had to show off her talent. This is Nolan’s second best film. It has become very clear to me after debating this for a long time. This watch was necessary for me to determine where this ranks in his filmography. It is also the best film of the 2020s so far. There’s an argument for Dune 2, but Oppenheimer still clears. Now I am become death, destroyer of worlds.

Oppenheimer was the main architect who built the atomic bomb and he lived with the guilt long after it dropped. This guilt and a petty grudge gave Lewis Strauss all the ammunition he needed. Strauss got what he wanted from Oppenheimer. Strauss takes down Oppenheimer by sticking him in a kangaroo court. Afterwards, Strauss doesn't realize he's sitting in his own version of a kangaroo court until it's too late. I remember walking out of the theater and my friend and I both agreed how amazing it was. In The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan used IMAX cameras for the entire film. In Oppenheimer, he used them for a majority of the film. This made it a visual spectacle that looked as good on a 4K TV as it did when I saw it in theaters. Cillian Murphy was an actor I knew of before this film. As Oppenheimer, he became the emotional center of the film regardless of time or destination. I could look in his eyes and know the highs and lows of being the man who received far more credit than he wanted. Beyond Nolan's directing, my friend and I discussed Robert Downey Jr. as Lewis Strauss extensively. I thought he was going to have a good chance at winning the Oscar, but he stole the film in every scene he was in. I saw Oppenheimer 3 years ago on the anniversary of the bomb dropping in Hiroshima in 1945. It was a moment that hit me after I left the theater. A few weeks later, I watched the film again in theaters, and then a few months later again with my Mom. Each time I thought to myself about how Oppenheimer had to live with what he did. Lewis Strauss had to live with unnecessary pettiness that cost him what he worked so hard for. Harry Truman may have taken responsibility, but guilt has to fall on someone's shoulders. Oppenheimer wasn't wrong for taking on the guilt, but just like his other mistakes, decisions are very hard to take back once they've been made. I write longer reflections about life and film here: filmsthatstay.substack.com/

Bong Joon-ho didn't just direct a movie; he orchestrated a sleek, parasitic masterclass in late-stage capitalism that completely shatters your worldview before you even realize you're bleeding. It is a gloriously unhinged, darkly hilarious, and utterly ruthless fever dream that takes a sharp, aesthetic scalpel to class warfare and leaves you wildly entertained yet profoundly disturbed. Call Me by Your Name’s cum peach walked so Parasite’s killer peach could absolute-fuckin-run, and I need everyone to start treating Bong Joon-ho’s allergic weaponization of stone fruit with the cinematic reverence it genuinely deserves. This movie is a hyper-slick, brilliantly depraved masterclass in social divide that completely reshuffled my brain chemistry. Crazy Rich Asians walked with its pristine, gilded wealth fantasy so that the outrageously out-of-touch Park family could literally get stabbed in the backyard, proving that the absolute peak of modern cinema is watching the ultra-rich get their delicate, expensive bubble shattered by the raw, suffocating reality of the working class. The absolute chokehold this film has on me is permanent, and I swear to god I be in the club requesting "Jessica, only child, Illinois, Chicago, classmate of Kim Jin-mo, he's your cousin, ding dong" like it’s the hottest track on the charts. Park So-dam flicking that lighter on top of the overflowing toilet in the middle of a catastrophic flood is officially my eternal mood board, capturing that exact, unbothered IT-girl energy even when the world is literally drowning in sewage. It’s a breathtakingly sharp, wildly chaotic masterpiece that lures you in with scammer-family comedy only to leave you paralyzed by the tragic, impossible illusion of upward mobility. 10/10, no notes, permanently playing that door-chime jingle on loop in my mind forever.

Bong Joon-ho didn't just direct a movie; he orchestrated a sleek, parasitic masterclass in late-stage capitalism that completely shatters your worldview before you even realize you're bleeding. It is a gloriously unhinged, darkly hilarious, and utterly ruthless fever dream that takes a sharp, aesthetic scalpel to class warfare and leaves you wildly entertained yet profoundly disturbed. Call Me by Your Name’s cum peach walked so Parasite’s killer peach could absolute-fuckin-run, and I need everyone to start treating Bong Joon-ho’s allergic weaponization of stone fruit with the cinematic reverence it genuinely deserves. This movie is a hyper-slick, brilliantly depraved masterclass in social divide that completely reshuffled my brain chemistry. Crazy Rich Asians walked with its pristine, gilded wealth fantasy so that the outrageously out-of-touch Park family could literally get stabbed in the backyard, proving that the absolute peak of modern cinema is watching the ultra-rich get their delicate, expensive bubble shattered by the raw, suffocating reality of the working class. The absolute chokehold this film has on me is permanent, and I swear to god I be in the club requesting "Jessica, only child, Illinois, Chicago, classmate of Kim Jin-mo, he's your cousin, ding dong" like it’s the hottest track on the charts. Park So-dam flicking that lighter on top of the overflowing toilet in the middle of a catastrophic flood is officially my eternal mood board, capturing that exact, unbothered IT-girl energy even when the world is literally drowning in sewage. It’s a breathtakingly sharp, wildly chaotic masterpiece that lures you in with scammer-family comedy only to leave you paralyzed by the tragic, impossible illusion of upward mobility. 10/10, no notes, permanently playing that door-chime jingle on loop in my mind forever.

Parasite feels so far removed from the formulaic Hollywood drivel continually thrust upon us that I’d almost forgotten films were allowed to behave like this. I loved the pacing. The patience of it. The way the camera just lingers and lets you look. Framing the entire outside world through that little ground-level basement window. People pissing outside it. Fumigation drifting through it. There’s something about making a window both your view of the world and a constant reminder of your place in it that really got me. And I loved the father. That quiet, almost performative resilience of a man the world simply will not give a fucking break. He’s funny and pathetic and dignified and increasingly broken, sometimes all at once. Actually, that might be what I love about Korean cinema in general. Everyone can feel slightly larger than life while simultaneously behaving like the sanest person in the room. Parasite can be hilarious, then sad, then horrifying, and apparently nobody told it those things are supposed to take turns. Brilliant film. And proof that, given sufficient context, even a pair of drying socks can have more screen presence than most Hollywood leads.

Je comprends totalement la hype autour de Parasite . C'est un film qui explore avec une incroyable modernité les inégalités sociales et la lutte des classes. Cette question dépasse de loin le cas de la Corée du Sud. Toute la mise en scène repose sur un véritable champ lexical visuel du parasite. Les personnages s'infiltrent, se cachent, occupent des espaces qui ne sont pas les leurs, jusqu'à devenir eux-mêmes des êtres jugés indésirables par la société. Pourtant, ils restent indispensables au fonctionnement de celle-ci. C'est une idée simple mais qui est montré comme je ne l'avais jamais vu. Le fait d'opposer deux familles est également très pertinent, car il permet de les comparer sous tous les angles. Le film est réalisé avec une telle maîtrise qu'il nous place dans une position de spectateur presque neutre. Il n'idéalise jamais la famille pauvre et ne diabolise pas non plus la famille riche. Malgré cela, les actions des personnages nous poussent naturellement à éprouver davantage d'empathie pour les plus démunis. Bien que (je me répète) ils sont loin d'être parfait. Cette satire sociale est, selon moi, bien plus aboutie que celle de Mickey 17 , pourtant réalisée par le même cinéaste. Elle est plus subtile, plus mature et laisse davantage de place à l'interprétation. Visuellement, le film est très réussi. Les jeux de lumière, notamment dans la nuit, sont magnifiques. J'aime beaucoup le contraste entre l'aspect lisse et presque irréel de la maison des riches et l'image plus texturée des rues où vit la famille Kim. On a presque l'impression que la famille Park évolue dans une publicité, coupée du monde réel. Cette idée est d'ailleurs renforcée par l'affiche du film, que je trouve excellente. Elle m'a rappelé, sans doute involontairement, celle de La Zone d'intérêt . Les deux œuvres partagent cette manière de montrer des personnages vivant dans un confort presque hermétique, au point d'ignorer ce qui se déroule juste à côté d'eux. Le parallèle est pertinent je trouve. Bref, un film incroyable. Une satire brillante, portée par des personnages d'une grande subtilité et un récit capable d'être aussi drôle que cru.

Parasite was a strong and memorable film that genuinely surprised me. The story felt different from what I usually watch, yet it remained consistently interesting. The characters were very well written, making it easy to get attached to them especially the Kim family. I also really liked the film’s message and the way it was delivered. It doesn’t lecture the audience about inequality; instead, it shows how deeply class divides shape people’s lives, choices, and even their sense of dignity, often in quiet, painful, and sometimes darkly funny ways. One of the most impressive aspects was the shift into thriller territory. It never felt sudden or forced. Instead, the tension kept building gradually, and you could almost feel the emotions accumulating until they finally exploded. That careful preparation made the transition land with real impact. I connected with the entire Kim family, but the relationship that stayed with me the most was the one between Moon-gwang and her husband Geun-sae. There was something powerful in her loyalty and sacrifice that left a lasting impression. The film portrays the theme of social class with striking clarity. The contrast between the Kims’ semi-basement existence and the Parks’ spacious, sunlit house constantly reminds you how differently the same world can look depending on where you stand. The ending, especially the visualization of Ki-woo’s goal earning enough money to one day buy the house and reunite with his father felt particularly strong and emotional. My only real issue was with Ki-jung. At times she is presented as intelligent and capable, but then in certain moments (like the scene where she nervously repeats the made-up formula with her brother before the first lesson) she suddenly feels much weaker. Right after that she becomes tough and composed again. Because of these shifts, I never quite got a clear sense of who she was supposed to be, and her character ended up feeling inconsistent. Overall, a powerful and memorable film.

Vamos começar com o maestro da obra, Bong Joon-ho dirige o filme com uma maestria cirúrgica, não tem uma sequência ruim aqui, todas são extremamente a inventivas e incríveis, a direção fica o tempo inteiro brincando com o público, seja com planos mais cômicos ou tensos a primeira vista, mas que está subvertendo seus temas e até enganando o espectador. Vale dizer que o filme está CHEIO de rimas visuais, parece que cada take do filme está inserido ali de forma muito inteligente e cada composição presente conta alguma coisa. Outra obra prima desse filme é o seu enredo e seu roteiro, a trama guia e engana o espectador de maneira brilhante. O jeito que as coisas vão acontecendo é espetacular e o jeito que ele vai escalonando de uma maneira tão irreal mas ao mesmo tempo extremamente real. As atuações aqui são incríveis, todo mundo manda muito bem em seus devidos papéis, mas um em específico me chamou a atenção, Song Kang-ho transmite tudo apenas pelo olhar, ele apresenta uma atuação simplesmente maravilhosa. Parasite feels so far removed from the formulaic Hollywood drivel continually thrust upon us that I’d almost forgotten films were allowed to behave like this. I loved the pacing. The patience of it. The way the camera just lingers and lets you look. Framing the entire outside world through that little ground-level basement window. People pissing outside it. Fumigation drifting through it. There’s something about making a window both your view of the world and a constant reminder of your place in it that really got me. And I loved the father. That quiet, almost performative resilience of a man the world simply will not give a fucking break. He’s funny and pathetic and dignified and increasingly broken, sometimes all at once. Actually, that might be what I love about Korean cinema in general. Everyone can feel slightly larger than life while simultaneously behaving like the sanest person in the room. Parasite can be hilarious, then sad, then horrifying, and apparently nobody told it those things are supposed to take turns. Brilliant film. And proof that, given sufficient context, even a pair of drying socks can have more screen presence than most Hollywood leads.

Je comprends totalement la hype autour de Parasite . C'est un film qui explore avec une incroyable modernité les inégalités sociales et la lutte des classes. Cette question dépasse de loin le cas de la Corée du Sud. Toute la mise en scène repose sur un véritable champ lexical visuel du parasite. Les personnages s'infiltrent, se cachent, occupent des espaces qui ne sont pas les leurs, jusqu'à devenir eux-mêmes des êtres jugés indésirables par la société. Pourtant, ils restent indispensables au fonctionnement de celle-ci. C'est une idée simple mais qui est montré comme je ne l'avais jamais vu. Le fait d'opposer deux familles est également très pertinent, car il permet de les comparer sous tous les angles. Le film est réalisé avec une telle maîtrise qu'il nous place dans une position de spectateur presque neutre. Il n'idéalise jamais la famille pauvre et ne diabolise pas non plus la famille riche. Malgré cela, les actions des personnages nous poussent naturellement à éprouver davantage d'empathie pour les plus démunis. Bien que (je me répète) ils sont loin d'être parfait. Cette satire sociale est, selon moi, bien plus aboutie que celle de Mickey 17 , pourtant réalisée par le même cinéaste. Elle est plus subtile, plus mature et laisse davantage de place à l'interprétation. Visuellement, le film est très réussi. Les jeux de lumière, notamment dans la nuit, sont magnifiques. J'aime beaucoup le contraste entre l'aspect lisse et presque irréel de la maison des riches et l'image plus texturée des rues où vit la famille Kim. On a presque l'impression que la famille Park évolue dans une publicité, coupée du monde réel. Cette idée est d'ailleurs renforcée par l'affiche du film, que je trouve excellente. Elle m'a rappelé, sans doute involontairement, celle de La Zone d'intérêt . Les deux œuvres partagent cette manière de montrer des personnages vivant dans un confort presque hermétique, au point d'ignorer ce qui se déroule juste à côté d'eux. Le parallèle est pertinent je trouve. Bref, un film incroyable. Une satire brillante, portée par des personnages d'une grande subtilité et un récit capable d'être aussi drôle que cru.

Parasite was a strong and memorable film that genuinely surprised me. The story felt different from what I usually watch, yet it remained consistently interesting. The characters were very well written, making it easy to get attached to them especially the Kim family. I also really liked the film’s message and the way it was delivered. It doesn’t lecture the audience about inequality; instead, it shows how deeply class divides shape people’s lives, choices, and even their sense of dignity, often in quiet, painful, and sometimes darkly funny ways. One of the most impressive aspects was the shift into thriller territory. It never felt sudden or forced. Instead, the tension kept building gradually, and you could almost feel the emotions accumulating until they finally exploded. That careful preparation made the transition land with real impact. I connected with the entire Kim family, but the relationship that stayed with me the most was the one between Moon-gwang and her husband Geun-sae. There was something powerful in her loyalty and sacrifice that left a lasting impression. The film portrays the theme of social class with striking clarity. The contrast between the Kims’ semi-basement existence and the Parks’ spacious, sunlit house constantly reminds you how differently the same world can look depending on where you stand. The ending, especially the visualization of Ki-woo’s goal earning enough money to one day buy the house and reunite with his father felt particularly strong and emotional. My only real issue was with Ki-jung. At times she is presented as intelligent and capable, but then in certain moments (like the scene where she nervously repeats the made-up formula with her brother before the first lesson) she suddenly feels much weaker. Right after that she becomes tough and composed again. Because of these shifts, I never quite got a clear sense of who she was supposed to be, and her character ended up feeling inconsistent. Overall, a powerful and memorable film.

Parasite is one of those movies that I've always wanted to watch but never got around to for whatever reason until last night (this is one of the first movies I added to my watchlist iirc) and I'm so glad that I finally did 🥹. I normally don't give something a 5 unless it's something I deeply resonate with emotionally and I don't get much out of that from Parasite if I'm being honest, but this is just such a technical marvel in every sense of the word that I can't help but give it the rating it deserves. Totally deserving of it's modern classic status and one of my new favourite movies (even if I'm not quite sure where it ranks yet). SPOILERS I'm definitely going to come back to this and give it a longer review some time in the future but for now I want to get some of my general thoughts out there. For one, this is one of the most entertaining movies of all time. Pretty much everything from that montage towards the start to the very end of the movie is filled with so many intense sequences, great dialogue, and fantastic moments that the film had me going crazy for most of the runtime. It's just such an entertaining movie front to back that I had an amazing time with. Another great aspect of this film is the symbolism but I don't have much to say in this regard as of now. It's clear that the rock for example symbolises something and I don't know what yet but things like that throughout the movie are so fascinating that I felt like I had to mention it. The main thing that makes this film stand out is it's messaging and depiction of class struggle and I found it super compelling. The way the Kim family compromises all of their morals just for financial stability shows just how much poverty can destroy your very essence as a person which is such a compelling idea. One review on here suggested that the line from Ki-Woo towards the end of the film about how his doctor and lawyer didn't look anything like a doctor or lawyer could suggest that these people are also pretending which is astounding. The capitalist society we live in forces EVERYONE to play a part just so they can live somewhat comfortably. As of now my only real complaint was how Ki-Woo getting brain damage played out. The scene of it happening and the ensuing scenes of him constantly laughing were absolutely shocking but then he's pretty much back to normal and I do think this works for the ending scene and his promise to help his father (which is a phenomenal ending btw) but I still felt that the quick change was a bit odd but that's more of a nitpick than anything. Por que esse filme aí tem nada a ver com o anime? Parasita é uma poesia visual e é até difícil falar o porque esse filme é tão perfeito sem dar spoiler, mas vamos lá. Vamos começar com o maestro da obra, Bong Joon-ho dirige o filme com uma maestria cirúrgica, não tem uma sequência ruim aqui, todas são extremamente a inventivas e incríveis, a direção fica o tempo inteiro brincando com o público, seja com planos mais cômicos ou tensos a primeira vista, mas que está subvertendo seus temas e até enganando o espectador. Vale dizer que o filme está CHEIO de rimas visuais, parece que cada take do filme está inserido ali de forma muito inteligente e cada composição presente conta alguma coisa. Outra obra prima desse filme é o seu enredo e seu roteiro, a trama guia e engana o espectador de maneira brilhante. O jeito que as coisas vão acontecendo é espetacular e o jeito que ele vai escalonando de uma maneira tão irreal mas ao mesmo tempo extremamente real. As atuações aqui são incríveis, todo mundo manda muito bem em seus devidos papéis, mas um em específico me chamou a atenção, Song Kang-ho transmite tudo apenas pelo olhar, ele apresenta uma atuação simplesmente maravilhosa. Tematicamente o filme é muito forte, o tema tratado aqui já é forte por si só, mas esse filme não fica na mesmisse de obras que tratam desse tema, ele vai além, ele compara, ele mostra, ele rima a situação dos personagens com situações reais, ele sai do preto e branco e nós traz algo novo e esse "novo" é genial. A cinematografia do filme é linda linda linda, tem takes maravilhosamente doloridos, mas muitos takes aqui tem uma beleza mórbida. Queria chamar atenção pra montagem do filme que faz um trabalho incrível, tudo é muito bem encaixado e torna o filme extremamente fluido. Em suma, Parasita é uma obra prima do cinema, o filme todo além de possuir um enredo e um roteiro maravilhoso, uma direção espetacular, uma temática forte e o filme tem tantas rimas visuais que o filme por si só se torna uma poesia visual.

I’m not sure this film should be classified as horror; to me it was more of a disturbing drama sprinkled with a handful of gory murders. Just as with “X”, the previous film that kicked off the trilogy of which “Pearl” is the second entry, a great deal of the film was spent building plot and the first murder occurred exactly at the one-hour mark. I don’t think anyone can deny that this film looks REALLY good. Other reviewers who note a resemblance to “The Wizard of Oz” are not to be commended on their keen perception; the director made it absolutely clear that is what he was going for. From the opening shot which mirrors Dorothy‘s arrival in Oz to the vintage title fonts and styles to the sumptuous colors throughout, one half expects a group of Munchkins to emerge from the cornfield at any time. While I felt that Jenna Ortega might have possessed greater screen presence in the first movie despite her smaller part, there is no rival to Mia Goth in this one. She owns the screen and creates a complex and (almost) sympathetic character in Pearl. It would be interesting to rewatch “X” with an eye on the older version of the character, which I did not even realize on the first viewing was played by Mia Goth. That shows you how keen my perception is. The conventional wisdom of all reviews I have seen is that “Maxxxine”, the third film in the trilogy, is the weakest of the three. But as “X” was good enough to get me to watch “Pearl”, so “Pearl” is good enough to carry me through to finish the trilogy.

[19] nota=3.0 estrelas:
I’m not sure this film should be classified as horror; to me it was more of a disturbing drama sprinkled with a handful of gory murders. Just as with “X”, the previous film that kicked off the trilogy of which “Pearl” is the second entry, a great deal of the film was spent building plot and the first murder occurred exactly at the one-hour mark. I don’t think anyone can deny that this film looks REALLY good. Other reviewers who note a resemblance to “The Wizard of Oz” are not to be commended on their keen perception; the director made it absolutely clear that is what he was going for. From the opening shot which mirrors Dorothy‘s arrival in Oz to the vintage title fonts and styles to the sumptuous colors throughout, one half expects a group of Munchkins to emerge from the cornfield at any time. While I felt that Jenna Ortega might have possessed greater screen presence in the first movie despite her smaller part, there is no rival to Mia Goth in this one. She owns the screen and creates a complex and (almost) sympathetic character in Pearl. It would be interesting to rewatch “X” with an eye on the older version of the character, which I did not even realize on the first viewing was played by Mia Goth. That shows you how keen my perception is. The conventional wisdom of all reviews I have seen is that “Maxxxine”, the third film in the trilogy, is the weakest of the three. But as “X” was good enough to get me to watch “Pearl”, so “Pearl” is good enough to carry me through to finish the trilogy.

What captivated me most was its deliberately old-fashioned style - the theatrical performances, exaggerated emotions, and long takes that feel lifted straight out of classic Hollywood. Mia Goth is unquestionably the film's greatest strength. Her extended monologue is emotionally devastating, but the ending lingers in my mind just as much - nearly two minutes of her desperately holding a smile as the end credits roll over cheerful, almost quaint music. It's the perfect closing note for a film built on the contrast between its bright, nostalgic aesthetic and its steadily growing psychological horror. It's rare to see a horror film that draws so confidently from cinema's past while using that style to tell such an unsettling character study. Mia Goth keeps marching toward the horror queen's crown with unwavering confidence -perhaps with just a touch too much arrogance, but it fits her well.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

[1] nota=3.5 estrelas:
Siempre he sido amante de los clásicos de Disney y disfruto muchísimo de los Live Actions. De todos los clásicos de Disney, uno de mis favoritos siempre ha sido Pinocho. Creo que es una historia muy linda, conmovedora y, por sobre todo, con muchísimo corazón. Una historia que tiene un sinfín de enseñanzas, partiendo por adquirir todo desde la inocencia y aprendiendo poco a poco a distinguir entre lo correcto y lo incorrecto. Este Live Action tuvo muchísimo odio incluso antes de estrenarse, en especial porque ese mismo año se estrenaba otra historia de Pinocho, pero esta vez contada desde el punto de vista de Guillermo del Toro. En lo personal, me gustó muchísimo esta película. Siento que logró capturar muchas cosas de la historia original de muy buena manera. Obviamente, no todo es tal como lo vimos en la película original, ya que hay ciertos cambios y ajustes que se hicieron a la historia, pero en general sentí que mantuvo muy bien su esencia. Lo primero que más amé fue el diseño. Encuentro que es muy fiel al original y, en una época en la que muchas veces se opta por modificar elementos de los clásicos, se agradece muchísimo que hayan decidido mantener la apariencia de los personajes tan cercana a lo que conocíamos. Lo otro que me encantó es que las canciones clásicas se mantienen, en especial uno de los temas más hermosos de Pinocho: “La Estrella Azul”, o su versión en inglés, “When You Wish Upon a Star”, que de hecho terminó convirtiéndose en uno de los temas más representativos de Disney. En términos de actuaciones, encuentro que estuvo bien. La verdad es que me gustó el trabajo que hizo cada uno con su personaje. Ahí, en especial, celebro a Benjamin Evan Ainsworth como Pinocho, que si bien principalmente pone la voz al personaje, encuentro que logró transmitir perfectamente el encanto y la inocencia que representa Pinocho. Hay mucho debate respecto al cambio que le hicieron al final de la historia y, la verdad, a mí también me gustó. Siento que deja espacio para que cada persona pueda darle su propio vuelco mágico al desenlace y, al mismo tiempo, encuentro que está completamente ad hoc con lo que representa la historia: que los deseos se pueden volver realidad. La guinda de la torta fue que todos los relojes de Geppetto eran referencias a muchísimos clásicos de Disney. Encontré que eso fue un broche de oro y un detalle muy lindo, especialmente por todas las referencias que escondía y por lo que representa para los amantes de los clásicos de Disney. Una película muy linda que, aunque entiendo que no todos la hayan disfrutado, a mí me dejó encantado. Una historia con muchísimas enseñanzas acerca de escuchar a nuestra conciencia, hacer el bien y tomar buenas decisiones. Una película que, a mi gusto, prometía mucho y cumplió lo que prometía: mantener la esencia de un clásico que quiero muchísimo, entregándonos una historia llena de magia, inocencia y corazón. Para disfrutar solo o en familia.

Yes they changed a few things but minor, maybe should have turned him into a real boy but, who knows maybe he does after walking home. I really enjoyed it regardless! My summary: Pinocchio (2022) is about Geppetto, a lonely woodcarver whose wish brings his puppet Pinocchio to life, and the Blue Fairy tells him he can become a real boy by being brave, truthful, and selfless while Jiminy Cricket serves as his conscience. Pinocchio is tricked by Honest John into joining Stromboli’s puppet show, escapes with the help of a girl named Fabiana, and later is lured to Pleasure Island, where he watches Lampwick turn into a donkey and even begins growing donkey ears and a tail before escaping. When Geppetto sails out to rescue him, he is swallowed by Monstro, so Pinocchio finds him inside the sea monster and comes up with a plan to make Monstro sneeze by lighting a fire. After Monstro spits them out and chases them, they crash onto shore, and Geppetto appears to die, but Pinocchio’s magical tear falls onto him and brings him back to life. In the end, Geppetto realizes Pinocchio has already proven himself to be a true boy through his courage and love, and although the movie leaves it ambiguous whether he physically becomes a real human, Jiminy explains that in his heart, Pinocchio is already a real boy.

Yes, I'm finally doing it. I'm finally reviewing one of these godforsaken remakes after all this time. It's not that I didn't want to do it in the first place, I just had difficulty picking which one to go with hence why it took so long to get to it. So with that said, let's rip into 2022's Pinocchio! No, not the Netflix masterpiece nor that stupid Paulie Shore one. I'm talking about the Disney+ exclusive live-action remake of the 1940s animated classic based on the novel by Carlo Collodi. Directed by Robert Zemeckis of Back to the Future fame, this is yet another one of those remakes that has been met with scorn and disgust from reveal to release. Nobody I knew enjoyed it and it's often regarded as one of Disney's lamest films in recent years. Especially didn't help matters when it came to Zemeckis' current track record compared to the stuff he made back in the day. As for me, I'm in the group of people that isn't so overly-offended whenever I hear a remake announced. I acknowledge that very few of them actually match up to the originals and there are some that undeniably sucked but I don't go around the internet screaming bloody rape every time Disney reveals a new remake. With that said, I get that this rendition of Pinocchio is a bit of a mess but screw me, was it a fun mess. The story remains the same as in the original but plenty of changes were made so that it doesn't feel like a bit-by-bit copy. A few ideas were pretty interesting such as Pinoc befriending a ballerina puppet but there are some that either had me scratching my head or misses the point of certain moments. Having Pinoc go to school only to get kicked out as well the removal of cigars and ACTUAL beer at Pleasure Island only serves to negate the purposes behind the themes of the story and were only done out of fear of pissing off a bunch of politically-correct retards and brain-dead soccer moms. The moments that were supposed to be scary came off as goofy not helped by the cartoony CGI, alot of the pop-culture jokes felt forced and made no sense within the film's time period and yes, this is the film that started the unusual trend of family films where a character would stop to smell literal feces left on the ground, it's practically the next screaming goat for some fucking reason. Even the acting felt over-the-top, while there are a few genuine standouts like Benjamin Evan Ainsworth as Pinocchio and even an unrecognisable Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Jiminy Cricket, alot of the actors were trying way too hard to elevate the material. Don't get me wrong, I appreciate that it doesn't take itself too seriously compared to other remakes and it's able to embrace it's original's animated roots but man, when they ham it up, they really fucking ham it up. Probably the best example I can think of is Tom Hanks as Gepetto, there's just no telling what the hell he's even doing, it's one of the most odd performances I've ever seen from this guy. He acts like a drunk mumbling buffoon that makes the robbers featured on World's Dumbest Criminals look subtle by comparison, it's so weird that it's too hard to look away. But I guess that's kinda why I enjoyed this one. It is odd and cartoony and it doesn't even try to force any of that realism bullshit that some of the other remakes tried to do and failed. Plus, there are some elements that are genuinely pretty good. Alan Silvestri does a nice job on the soundtrack, the Pleasure Island sequence does look inventive and cool, there's a few bits of slapstick that got a good laugh, the overall scenery looks neat and despite my jab at the ridiculous-looking CGI, both Pinoc and Jiminy actually look pretty good in live-action. So even if I didn't think it was a good movie, it wasn't at least boring. The original will always be better and of course the Netflix film is undeniably the superior version of the story to go for but for what it's worth, I consider this a guilty pleasure. It's definitely more than I can say for the actual bad remakes like Mulan and Peter Pan & Wendy. *shudders* Fuck those movies.

[1] nota=3.5 estrelas:
Siempre he sido amante de los clásicos de Disney y disfruto muchísimo de los Live Actions. De todos los clásicos de Disney, uno de mis favoritos siempre ha sido Pinocho. Creo que es una historia muy linda, conmovedora y, por sobre todo, con muchísimo corazón. Una historia que tiene un sinfín de enseñanzas, partiendo por adquirir todo desde la inocencia y aprendiendo poco a poco a distinguir entre lo correcto y lo incorrecto. Este Live Action tuvo muchísimo odio incluso antes de estrenarse, en especial porque ese mismo año se estrenaba otra historia de Pinocho, pero esta vez contada desde el punto de vista de Guillermo del Toro. En lo personal, me gustó muchísimo esta película. Siento que logró capturar muchas cosas de la historia original de muy buena manera. Obviamente, no todo es tal como lo vimos en la película original, ya que hay ciertos cambios y ajustes que se hicieron a la historia, pero en general sentí que mantuvo muy bien su esencia. Lo primero que más amé fue el diseño. Encuentro que es muy fiel al original y, en una época en la que muchas veces se opta por modificar elementos de los clásicos, se agradece muchísimo que hayan decidido mantener la apariencia de los personajes tan cercana a lo que conocíamos. Lo otro que me encantó es que las canciones clásicas se mantienen, en especial uno de los temas más hermosos de Pinocho: “La Estrella Azul”, o su versión en inglés, “When You Wish Upon a Star”, que de hecho terminó convirtiéndose en uno de los temas más representativos de Disney. En términos de actuaciones, encuentro que estuvo bien. La verdad es que me gustó el trabajo que hizo cada uno con su personaje. Ahí, en especial, celebro a Benjamin Evan Ainsworth como Pinocho, que si bien principalmente pone la voz al personaje, encuentro que logró transmitir perfectamente el encanto y la inocencia que representa Pinocho. Hay mucho debate respecto al cambio que le hicieron al final de la historia y, la verdad, a mí también me gustó. Siento que deja espacio para que cada persona pueda darle su propio vuelco mágico al desenlace y, al mismo tiempo, encuentro que está completamente ad hoc con lo que representa la historia: que los deseos se pueden volver realidad. La guinda de la torta fue que todos los relojes de Geppetto eran referencias a muchísimos clásicos de Disney. Encontré que eso fue un broche de oro y un detalle muy lindo, especialmente por todas las referencias que escondía y por lo que representa para los amantes de los clásicos de Disney. Una película muy linda que, aunque entiendo que no todos la hayan disfrutado, a mí me dejó encantado. Una historia con muchísimas enseñanzas acerca de escuchar a nuestra conciencia, hacer el bien y tomar buenas decisiones. Una película que, a mi gusto, prometía mucho y cumplió lo que prometía: mantener la esencia de un clásico que quiero muchísimo, entregándonos una historia llena de magia, inocencia y corazón. Para disfrutar solo o en familia.
