If there was a 4.25 rating, that’s probably where I’d put this. I really liked how dark and uncomfortable this movie felt pretty much the whole time. Hugh Jackman was great, especially because his character keeps making decisions where you understand why he’s doing it, but at the same time you know he’s going way too far. Jake Gyllenhaal was also really good and I liked how his side of the story felt more like a slow detective movie. The rain, darker colors, and overall setting made everything feel even more depressing and tense. I also liked that the movie didn’t make everything obvious and actually made me question who I trusted throughout it. It is pretty long and there were a few slower parts, but the ending made a lot of it worth it for me.

Lived up to my expectations. Denis Villeneuve’s Prisoners is a very well crafted thriller that undoubtedly needs to be watched at night to fit the vibe of the movie. Crime thrillers are one of my favourite movie genres so i was bound to enjoy this. Hugh Jackman in my opinion has his best ever performance in this film. His character Keller Dover is the father of one of the kidnapped children and as the movie goes along, day by day you can see his rage increase and his reliance on humanity fades. In many scenes you can hear his voice break and your dragged into his broken psyche. This performance was stellar. Jake Gyllenhaal played Detective Loki, a detective who boasts his history of solving every crime he has previously met. However the one he is about to tackle, challenges and eats away at his mind. In many ways his mind is imprisoned in the maze of the case mystery. Paul Dano plays the kidnapper suspect and watching this film, it makes absolute sense why Dano was chosen to play the Riddler. Such a chilling and subtle creepiness he brings to the screen. David Dastmalchian was a suprise addition to the cast and he was a treat to see. He aswell fit the creepy and dark vibe of his character. The final third of the film was goddamn great. A plot twist that really makes you locked in on what happens next. And question what you previously watched. Bravo Denis Villeneuve 👏

The Prisoners is one of those movies that stays with you even after the ending credits. This movie is dark, intense, and very well written, with a plot that always makes you wonder who to trust. This movie deals with issues like desperation, justice, morality, and how much one can do when all they have left to fight for is on the line. The film is superbly directed by Denis Villeneuve, and the actors Hugh Jackman and Jake Gyllenhaal give amazing performances. 9.5/10 — dark, intelligent, and unnerving.

Went under the radar for me for a while and a buddy and I, seeing nothing else of interest in the theater decided to give it a shot. [32] nota=5.0 estrelas:
This film might be one of my most favourite films of all time. It is so creative. The movie follows a father whom is played by Hugh Jackman, the film is centred around his daughter and her friend being kidnapped/going missing. He takes matters into his own hands to find her or gather any information/evidence on her whereabouts so he gets closer to figuring out what happened to her. Detective Loki, played by Jake Gyllenhaal, is the main detective who is put on this case. Each performance in this film is all done extremely well. There’s so much depth and meaning in each and every character. This might be one of Hugh Jackman and Paul Dano’s best performances. The story is also very interesting and well written. “Prisoners” is highly praised feature that portrays the concept of a profoundly unsettling, emotional, and suspenseful investigation of a missing child in such an incredible and distinctive way. It portrays the anger and rage of a dad who is just trying to find his daughter and the feared feeling towards the suspected with unique story telling. It reveals the plot twist in a way that is quite unpredictable and many first-time watchers would not be able to figure out. The acting from each actor/actress is in done in an oscar worthy performance. Hugh Jackman absolutely stands out in this film because of how well he shows the realistic anger of a parent whose is daughter was kidnapped and he’s just carrying the pain of almost losing a child. Paul Dano feels more and more unsettling everytime he’s on screen because of how insane his character is and the brilliant performance he put on as a truly mind-twisted antagonist. The pacing is very important in this film and it really shows it with how well directed this film is. It’s a film that doesn’t necessarily have any confusing scenes and is easily understood. In terms of violence and gore in this film, there’s more than a few scenes that contain some gore but it actually makes sense and it’s properly placed. The cinematography stays true to the plot and every scene is well filmed. The ending itself is a major plot twist that is understandable because it gives the viewers a sense of what had happened after the film’s ending. Denis Villeneuve did quite well with the directing of this film. I have watched this film more than once and it just gets better after every rewatch.

[1] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Overly long, pessimistic nonsense. This one sentence is more than enough to rate this film and the source material as well. This work is a supposed love letter from Tarr to his great friend, Laszlo Krasznahorkai, who managed to come up with the original novel. Tarr was always very observant of Krasznahorkai' body of work, the two frequently collaborated. The major flaw of this movie is that Tarr decided to adapt one of the most boring and uninspired works of Hungarian literature. Krasznahorkai' personal philosophy is devoid of external references to our shared experiences, his overly pessimistic and oftentimes nihilistic outlook never managed to capture the historical and geographical context of everyday Hungarian life. His novel, and Tarr' subsequent movie thus feel alien and completely isolated, they only exist and thrive within their perverted and twisted minds. The characters are grossly oversimplified and generalized versions of everyday folk people, the plot and narrative paint a harsh, hopeless picture, but ultimately fail to capture any semblence of reality. The core premise of the movie can be interesting for outside observers, people who never familiarised themselves with the end of the century sociopolitical climate in Hungary, but the message gets lost for native viewers. People suffer just to suffer, struggle just to struggle. Misery can be captivating, but these two can never portray it adequately, which is an overarching critique of 20th century Hungarian literature and filmmaking in general. Watch this mess at your own risk, but I'd suggest everyone to simply read the novel, that alone is a mind-numbingly painful intellectual excercise. The runtime serves as ample justification for the worst people you know to call anyone who dislikes this work a brainless maggot, further fueling their pretentious nature.

I understand if a movie doesn't have to be cohesive, but I'm willing to let that slide if the runtime is under, say, 2.5 hours. For å holde meg i stil med både filmen og boken velger jeg å skrive denne anmeldelsen uten bruk av linjeskift. Dette er første gang jeg har sett en så lang film. Et riktig heldagsprosjekt som startet i kø på Cinemateket rundt 14:00 og endte etter klokken hadde bikket 22, og hodet var utkjørt. Åpningsscenen i filmen er en ~10 minutters lang scene med kuer som går rundt på en gjørmete gårdsplass og gjør som kuer gjør. Det er uventet, og kanskje på grensen til provoserende å ha så lange scener i en film når man er vant til å se tradisjonelle spillefilmer hvor hvert sekund i en scene på en måte må rettferdiggjøre sin eksistens i filmen. Satantango oppleves nesten som en protest mot dette. Videre i filmen blir publikum eksponert for flere slike scener. Når scenene varer i over 5 minutter med ting som rytmisk monoton gange, litt rar tangodansing, eller mennesker som ligger på gulvet og sover, blir man overrasket når scenen plutselig skifter. Mildt komiske eller pinlige scener blir forsterket når de bare varer og varer, og det blir etter hvert absurd. Etter hvert som noen av scenene drar på, glir blikket over bildet på jakt etter noe - helt til det er umulig å finne flere detaljer. Man går gjerne over til å tenke på middagsplaner for uken, eller at man angrer på at man tok morgenflyet fra Bergen og bare sov 6 timer akkurat denne dagen. At denne søvnigheten man kjenner på sikkert ikke er på grunn av filmen, men bare det at man har hatt en lang dag. Jeg innser etter hvert at jeg ikke kan skylde på dette; det er mange andre i salen som også tilsynelatende sliter med tretthet, og noen sover skamløst i stolene. Man flytter seg i stolen, lener seg litt fram, så tilbake. Forsøker å stramme leggmusklene. Lener seg fram igjen. Ruller litt på skuldrene, for så å lene seg tilbake igjen. Alt for å våkne til litt, men så fokuserer man igjen på skjermen, og det er vanskelig å si om scenen av en jente som løper over en åker i det hele tatt har endret seg. Man lukker øynene litt lenge og merker søvnen komme krypende, før man tar seg i det og nok en gang skifter positur. En scene i filmen er spesielt forstyrrende. Den involverer dyreplaging og en katt. Per forsikret meg i ettertid om at internett forsikret ham om at det var filmtriks. Håper endelig det. Filmen er utrolig gjørmete. Den er delt inn i tre akter, og når man kommer ut i pausen er det uvant at det ikke er gjørme overalt. Så inn igjen. Mer gjørme. Ubehagelige lyder fra en alkoholisert og utflytende doktor. Lyder som får det til å høres ut som bare det å eksistere er en strevsom affære. Det er på mange måter en dystopisk film, og handler i bunn og grunn om oppløsningen av et kollektivbruk etter Sovjets fall. Det eneste som kan minne om en lykkelig slutt ved denne filmen er vel egentlig at den er ferdig, og at man ikke lenger er fastlåst i en stol. Filmen er forresten i svart-hvitt. Etter seks timer med dette begynner hjernen å legge inn farger der det ikke er noen. Luen til den ene karakteren syntes jeg liksom var litt gul. For øvrig er boken kun i overkant av 300 sider. Dette betyr at fortellingen muligens kan formidles like raskt i begge medier. Jeg slet litt med å skulle gi denne filmen en karakter. Til visse tider synes jeg filmen er dårlig og blir bare frustrert, mens andre ting oppleves veldig flotte, og jeg tenker at det er gjerne et poeng bak lengden på filmen. Etter en uke betenkningstid har jeg imidlertid klart å lande på en slags karakter, men å skulle sette et nummer på noe som dette blir litt som å putte julemiddagen i en blender og forvente at mottakeren får inntrykk av om middagen var god eller dårlig. Uansett, anbefaler å se filmen hvis du først er lang-film-curious. Hvis du kjenner deg selv så godt at du vet at dette blir for mye, hold deg unna!

At this point you've already suffered 6 1/2 hours of this fucking piece of shit film. I sat with clenched fists and prayed it would be over, but no, you still have to see the village doctor take a fucking stroll for forty minutes. When the credits rolled, I laughed a black laugh and was devastated. This is an evil film made by an evil, nihilistic and godless man. A solid hour of this is just a kid torturing a cat. You see people drink their plum brandy and dance and sleep and eat and stare mindlessly. I'm certain Béla Tarr wants to psychotically frustrate his audience with boredom, that he hates everyone, and that he thinks its funny that some cinephile beret people pretend to love his film. It's not made to be loved. But it is beautiful. It's one of the most profound experiences I've had with a film, profound in the same way it's profound to move into an apartment on the eighth floor without an elevator. This is a film you suffer through. I still highly recommend it. It's like going into some weird trance. I defend the runtime, because I'm glad it exists, but the masterpiece cut would be two hours shorter. Next time I'll see it with subway surfers underneath. No film can ever phase me again.

Overly long, pessimistic nonsense. This one sentence is more than enough to rate this film and the source material as well. This work is a supposed love letter from Tarr to his great friend, Laszlo Krasznahorkai, who managed to come up with the original novel. Tarr was always very observant of Krasznahorkai' body of work, the two frequently collaborated. The major flaw of this movie is that Tarr decided to adapt one of the most boring and uninspired works of Hungarian literature. Krasznahorkai' personal philosophy is devoid of external references to our shared experiences, his overly pessimistic and oftentimes nihilistic outlook never managed to capture the historical and geographical context of everyday Hungarian life. His novel, and Tarr' subsequent movie thus feel alien and completely isolated, they only exist and thrive within their perverted and twisted minds. The characters are grossly oversimplified and generalized versions of everyday folk people, the plot and narrative paint a harsh, hopeless picture, but ultimately fail to capture any semblence of reality. The core premise of the movie can be interesting for outside observers, people who never familiarised themselves with the end of the century sociopolitical climate in Hungary, but the message gets lost for native viewers. People suffer just to suffer, struggle just to struggle. Misery can be captivating, but these two can never portray it adequately, which is an overarching critique of 20th century Hungarian literature and filmmaking in general. Watch this mess at your own risk, but I'd suggest everyone to simply read the novel, that alone is a mind-numbingly painful intellectual excercise. The runtime serves as ample justification for the worst people you know to call anyone who dislikes this work a brainless maggot, further fueling their pretentious nature.

For å holde meg i stil med både filmen og boken velger jeg å skrive denne anmeldelsen uten bruk av linjeskift. Dette er første gang jeg har sett en så lang film. Et riktig heldagsprosjekt som startet i kø på Cinemateket rundt 14:00 og endte etter klokken hadde bikket 22, og hodet var utkjørt. Åpningsscenen i filmen er en ~10 minutters lang scene med kuer som går rundt på en gjørmete gårdsplass og gjør som kuer gjør. Det er uventet, og kanskje på grensen til provoserende å ha så lange scener i en film når man er vant til å se tradisjonelle spillefilmer hvor hvert sekund i en scene på en måte må rettferdiggjøre sin eksistens i filmen. Satantango oppleves nesten som en protest mot dette. Videre i filmen blir publikum eksponert for flere slike scener. Når scenene varer i over 5 minutter med ting som rytmisk monoton gange, litt rar tangodansing, eller mennesker som ligger på gulvet og sover, blir man overrasket når scenen plutselig skifter. Mildt komiske eller pinlige scener blir forsterket når de bare varer og varer, og det blir etter hvert absurd. Etter hvert som noen av scenene drar på, glir blikket over bildet på jakt etter noe - helt til det er umulig å finne flere detaljer. Man går gjerne over til å tenke på middagsplaner for uken, eller at man angrer på at man tok morgenflyet fra Bergen og bare sov 6 timer akkurat denne dagen. At denne søvnigheten man kjenner på sikkert ikke er på grunn av filmen, men bare det at man har hatt en lang dag. Jeg innser etter hvert at jeg ikke kan skylde på dette; det er mange andre i salen som også tilsynelatende sliter med tretthet, og noen sover skamløst i stolene. Man flytter seg i stolen, lener seg litt fram, så tilbake. Forsøker å stramme leggmusklene. Lener seg fram igjen. Ruller litt på skuldrene, for så å lene seg tilbake igjen. Alt for å våkne til litt, men så fokuserer man igjen på skjermen, og det er vanskelig å si om scenen av en jente som løper over en åker i det hele tatt har endret seg. Man lukker øynene litt lenge og merker søvnen komme krypende, før man tar seg i det og nok en gang skifter positur. En scene i filmen er spesielt forstyrrende. Den involverer dyreplaging og en katt. Per forsikret meg i ettertid om at internett forsikret ham om at det var filmtriks. Håper endelig det. Filmen er utrolig gjørmete. Den er delt inn i tre akter, og når man kommer ut i pausen er det uvant at det ikke er gjørme overalt. Så inn igjen. Mer gjørme. Ubehagelige lyder fra en alkoholisert og utflytende doktor. Lyder som får det til å høres ut som bare det å eksistere er en strevsom affære. Det er på mange måter en dystopisk film, og handler i bunn og grunn om oppløsningen av et kollektivbruk etter Sovjets fall. Det eneste som kan minne om en lykkelig slutt ved denne filmen er vel egentlig at den er ferdig, og at man ikke lenger er fastlåst i en stol. Filmen er forresten i svart-hvitt. Etter seks timer med dette begynner hjernen å legge inn farger der det ikke er noen. Luen til den ene karakteren syntes jeg liksom var litt gul. For øvrig er boken kun i overkant av 300 sider. Dette betyr at fortellingen muligens kan formidles like raskt i begge medier. Jeg slet litt med å skulle gi denne filmen en karakter. Til visse tider synes jeg filmen er dårlig og blir bare frustrert, mens andre ting oppleves veldig flotte, og jeg tenker at det er gjerne et poeng bak lengden på filmen. Etter en uke betenkningstid har jeg imidlertid klart å lande på en slags karakter, men å skulle sette et nummer på noe som dette blir litt som å putte julemiddagen i en blender og forvente at mottakeren får inntrykk av om middagen var god eller dårlig. Uansett, anbefaler å se filmen hvis du først er lang-film-curious. Hvis du kjenner deg selv så godt at du vet at dette blir for mye, hold deg unna!

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

The pinnacle of pretentious bullshit. I wasted my entire Sunday on this shit. Fuck you, Tarr Béla. Fuck you and all your sycophants. The people who love this movie will tell you that it's a revolutionary thing, a deconstruction (or outright rejection) of cinema laden with symbolism, metaphor, and parable. They are EXTREMELY wrong and COPING like a motherfuckers. If you go your entire life hearing "horse shit tastes delicious, when I first ate horse shit it changed my life, horse shit is actually the food of the gods" then when you consume horse shit you are going to search for that brilliance and meaning which simply isn't there and you will find it because you are expecting it. The people who think Sátántangó is one of the greatest films of all time are similarly deluded. To get the obvious out of the way, my issue is not simply that the film is 7.5 hours long. I can absolutely seeing myself loving a movie that long. The issue is that in this prodigious runtime, Tarr accomplishes what most semi-competent directors do in a third of that time. Every scene in Sátántangó is long, every action is filmed in one take along with a hundred other actions, every exterior scene must involve characters walking in wide shots for ten minutes at a time. What does it add to the narrative, to my immersion, to the meaning? Fuck all. There are absolutely reasons to include the mundane in your story, to include scenes where little happens, to let a moment linger. What anyone who's seen three movies before can tell you, though, is that when every scene is like that, it loses all impact. The audience gets bored because they are just watching some morbidly obese alcoholic lie on the floor of his room for five minutes and it means nothing to them. Any piece of media that simulates reality is just that: simulation. When you play a video game, read a book, watch a show, you are not looking to exist in the 1:1 moments of life. Why the fuck would you? When you experience those moments in your own life your mind is usually elsewhere, so why would it be any different when you are being presented the same moments but in an obviously fictional story with fictional characters doing fictional shit that, above all else, is just plain not fucking interesting. Anyway, I know I'm not going to win over any die-hard Tarr fans. All I can do is warn people away from this movie. It is the biggest waste of time movie I've ever seen and it masquerades as meaningful and impactful cinema, a far worse crime.

But after all this movie creates this oppressive, suffocating feeling where everything seems doomed, very dirty, cold and somehow spiritually dead. My understanding of slow cinema is that it's slow to give you time to contemplate the ideas in the film — to give the viewer a sort of meditative experience. But when there doesn't seem much depth to contemplate, sometimes the slow pace just feels dull or tedious or annoying. Never-ending scenes of drunken dancing or people walking or a drunk yelling wore out their welcome. I couldn't stand the cat sequence. Even if the cat was safely drugged and the yowling was from a sound effects library, as Tarr has said, it seemed an awful ordeal to put a live animal through. Horrible. And even if they swapped out the live cat at certain rough moments — in fact, even if the cat was never harmed at all — it was distressing and distracting enough to take me completely out of the movie. I wasn't thinking about the character hurting the cat, I was thinking about the actor and the filmmaker. Sátántangó lost me there, in chapter 4 or 5 of 12. I had been okay with the film until then. Following that chapter with the interminable drunken yelling and dancing sequences kept me pretty sour on the rest of the film. The story was extremely thin, the nonlinear structure was slightly interesting but ultimately felt pointless, and I didn't care about any of the characters. If there's a point to be made about someone tricking people, it feels undercooked and unconnected to the first few chapters. I don't mind slow or long, and I love some films that are both (some Tarkovsky, for example), but this material didn't feel like it earned its length or pace to me. The cinematography and sound design were excellent. And I loved the textures of the locations/sets — all the crumbling walls, etc. I saw the 4k restoration from 2019 in the theater as part of Bleak Week 2026 at AFI Silver. After the screening, they gave us each a cinephile certificate for braving the entire seven hours, which was a fun idea. I wish I loved the movie like most people who sit through it do. I liked Werckmeister Harmonies okay. I don't know if I'll bother with another Tarr film.

The people who love this movie will tell you that it's a revolutionary thing, a deconstruction (or outright rejection) of cinema laden with symbolism, metaphor, and parable. They are EXTREMELY wrong and COPING like a motherfuckers. If you go your entire life hearing "horse shit tastes delicious, when I first ate horse shit it changed my life, horse shit is actually the food of the gods" then when you consume horse shit you are going to search for that brilliance and meaning which simply isn't there and you will find it because you are expecting it. The people who think Sátántangó is one of the greatest films of all time are similarly deluded. To get the obvious out of the way, my issue is not simply that the film is 7.5 hours long. I can absolutely seeing myself loving a movie that long. The issue is that in this prodigious runtime, Tarr accomplishes what most semi-competent directors do in a third of that time. Every scene in Sátántangó is long, every action is filmed in one take along with a hundred other actions, every exterior scene must involve characters walking in wide shots for ten minutes at a time. What does it add to the narrative, to my immersion, to the meaning? Fuck all. There are absolutely reasons to include the mundane in your story, to include scenes where little happens, to let a moment linger. What anyone who's seen three movies before can tell you, though, is that when every scene is like that, it loses all impact. The audience gets bored because they are just watching some morbidly obese alcoholic lie on the floor of his room for five minutes and it means nothing to them. Any piece of media that simulates reality is just that: simulation. When you play a video game, read a book, watch a show, you are not looking to exist in the 1:1 moments of life. Why the fuck would you? When you experience those moments in your own life your mind is usually elsewhere, so why would it be any different when you are being presented the same moments but in an obviously fictional story with fictional characters doing fictional shit that, above all else, is just plain not fucking interesting. Anyway, I know I'm not going to win over any die-hard Tarr fans. All I can do is warn people away from this movie. It is the biggest waste of time movie I've ever seen and it masquerades as meaningful and impactful cinema, a far worse crime.

The whole experience after the first 2 and a half hours was just so agonizing at times... sometimes the incredibly long, slow and eeriee scenes felt like torture towards the end. I feel bad for giving this movie such a bad rating even tho i acknowlege the beauty and passion put into this and I don't think it's a bad movie in any conventional sense... but I just cannot give this a good review if the experience as a whole was agonizing. The enviroment, style and characters created such a deeply depressive atmosphere that when there was even a tiiiny bit of humor it felt like a blessing, like i wanted to cry of laughter. (pondling, pondling x1000) In those moments i realized how actually hard this was for my mental state while watching this. The experience in a nuthsell:  "I understand what you're doing. I see the beauty. I see the intention. Please just let me leave." The amount of patience, precision and dedication required to make something like this is insane, but at the end of the day I just can't give a movie a good rating purely because I can recognize how brilliant it is. The experience itself matters to me! Sometimes it even felt like interactions were unnaturally slow. Like why did almost everything have to be so incredibly stretched and slow. The repeating soundtrack, the loud sound of footsteps in the slow walking scenes, the slow hungarian language spoken in poetry, the fucking bell ringing scene in the end, the loud clock ticking, DOCTORS 30 MINUTE OF CONSTANT MOANING, DRINKING AND SPEAKING LIKE ALL OF IT WAS A CHORE (It was funny for the first 5 minutes), constant raining, the incredibly long bar dancing scene with the 15 second accordion playing on loop, you name it.. i felt like i was going mad:D BUT even with all these miserable moments, there were individual scenes here that I think were really incredible and I will probably remember certain images and sequences for a very long time (The camerawork is breathtaking). But after all this movie creates this oppressive, suffocating feeling where everything seems doomed, very dirty, cold and somehow spiritually dead. The endless walking, the rain, the mud, the miserable people, the bleak landscapes, the constant feeling that nothing is ever going to change... after hours of it I felt like the movie had actually drained every last drop of happiness out of me. And lastly, when the movie was reaching towards the end and things actually started to happen, i was already too drained... I admire the hell out of it. I just didn't enjoy being trapped inside it.

My understanding of slow cinema is that it's slow to give you time to contemplate the ideas in the film — to give the viewer a sort of meditative experience. But when there doesn't seem much depth to contemplate, sometimes the slow pace just feels dull or tedious or annoying. Never-ending scenes of drunken dancing or people walking or a drunk yelling wore out their welcome. I couldn't stand the cat sequence. Even if the cat was safely drugged and the yowling was from a sound effects library, as Tarr has said, it seemed an awful ordeal to put a live animal through. Horrible. And even if they swapped out the live cat at certain rough moments — in fact, even if the cat was never harmed at all — it was distressing and distracting enough to take me completely out of the movie. I wasn't thinking about the character hurting the cat, I was thinking about the actor and the filmmaker. Sátántangó lost me there, in chapter 4 or 5 of 12. I had been okay with the film until then. Following that chapter with the interminable drunken yelling and dancing sequences kept me pretty sour on the rest of the film. The story was extremely thin, the nonlinear structure was slightly interesting but ultimately felt pointless, and I didn't care about any of the characters. If there's a point to be made about someone tricking people, it feels undercooked and unconnected to the first few chapters. I don't mind slow or long, and I love some films that are both (some Tarkovsky, for example), but this material didn't feel like it earned its length or pace to me. The cinematography and sound design were excellent. And I loved the textures of the locations/sets — all the crumbling walls, etc. I saw the 4k restoration from 2019 in the theater as part of Bleak Week 2026 at AFI Silver. After the screening, they gave us each a cinephile certificate for braving the entire seven hours, which was a fun idea. I wish I loved the movie like most people who sit through it do. I liked Werckmeister Harmonies okay. I don't know if I'll bother with another Tarr film.

[15] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Se7en is a film which attempts to wear many hats. On one hand you have attempts at a highly interesting and flashy serial murder case which operates as the major stopping points of the story. Each of the murders is extreme and profane, crafted with this kind of blunt detail that’s certainly entertaining, but ultimately surface level and less well thought out than they likely intended. On the other you have an extremely standard buddy cop framework between the two main characters which makes no real attempt at straying away from convention. Both of these central building blocks are joined together by this phenomenal, nearly noir, presentation which sets up the film as something which is both easily entertaining and contains more for those who are willing to seek it out. Unfortunately, I found Se7en ultimately ends up confused in this crossroad of seriousness and entertainment, ultimately ending up lingering at the surface level and only utilizing these bigger ideas as window dressing rather than something which builds towards something greater. Unfortunately the signs are there from the beginning. The characters in this film are prototypical to a degree which ends up being serviceable but lacking both in terms of story progression and intrapersonal drama. Brad Pitt plays a standard hotshot new detective, willing to prove himself and reeking in overconfidence by his supposed credentials. Rather than demonstrating his actual abilities, Pitt prefers to crack one liners and sneer at his partner’s persistence to do his job properly rather than quickly give up the moment he faces the first sign of abstraction. Likewise, his partner, Morgan Freeman, is his polar opposite. An old blood detective who just wants to retire out of the force because of the toxic apathy of society which has eroded his sense of goodwill. He’s ultimately pragmatic about his job and knows that their efforts are more likely than not to be pointless in the grand scheme of things. This is about as standard of a setup as you can get, but the film never really causes it to head in any sort of meaningful direction. Pitt and Freeman very rarely actually interact for the first quarter of the film, and due to the extremely short timeframe of the plot, their inevitable destination as uncommon allies mere days later is unnatural and unconvincing. The two of them lack chemistry, and their lack of substantial interaction makes the buddy cop presentation lose traction as a whole. Pitt’s more than willing to speak his mind, and the film is more than willing to utilize him as the main source of entertainment, but because Freeman isn’t willing to ever give him an inch these moments end up falling flatter than they had to. This is representative of how the film handles the crux of their characters as well. Pitt and Freeman represent opposite ends of the same coin. Being detectives and thoroughly entrenched in the toxicity of low society, Pitt’s optimism and Freeman’s pragmatism could represent some kind of clash of ideals. But instead, Se7en chooses to merely float these ideas rather than tackle them directly. This is most blatantly presented in a scene in a bar about halfway through the film. Freeman is telling Pitt about how he’s fed up with all of the apathy of society, how people are so willing to take the easy way out rather than work through their problems, which ultimately is the source of their misfortune. Society does not care about itself and so Freeman does not care about society. Pitt rejects this idea, not for any actual stated reason or counterargument, but merely because he cannot accept this line of thought. He states that Freeman himself is also taking the easy way out, which is true, but does little to shift his perspective in any meaningful way. This idea remains a loose thread rather than being properly explored, and this trend can be observed with much of the rest of what Se7en aims to accomplish. The other core principle of Se7en is, of course, the murders. This aspect is where the film really shines. Se7en is already a visually impressive film, perfectly capturing the kind of grime which makes up this low society by operating primarily with low blues and greys. This is a very dark film, but the main attribute I would give the visual quality is dirty. The murders primarily take place in these low income locations, even the apartment buildings are worn down and damaged. Despite the primary weather condition being rain this ends up reminding me of mud more so than dirt being washed away. This translates to the murders perfectly. Each of which are immensely brutal and highly creative, making use of the sin motif more as a suggestion for a gory creative artpiece than anything. My favorite ended up being the first of the murders, representing gluttony you have this obese man who was forced to eat himself to death, but not before cutting off an entire pound worth of meat off his body. This is far and away the most visually stimulating of any of the murders, and perfectly builds up the case as something which is equal parts sadistic and incredible. While grotesque, the visual quality makes it more entertaining than disgusting, and the absurdity of the murders themselves adds to this feeling. Of course, the problem lies with how these murders are presented. For the first half of the film, the duo is convinced that the murders are inspired by famous literary works such as The Divine Comedy and The Canterbury Tales due to them representing the titular seven sins. The film spends a significant amount of time showcasing them researching and discussing these ideas leading you to believe that these would be significant details to the case. Unfortunately, this ends up being nothing more than a wild goose chase, and these details are nothing more than window dressing than any kind of greater idea. Once you reach the halfway point, the film is more than willing to abandon this idea and pivot back towards the cops stumbling in the right direction rather than solving the murders from their own ideas. Of course, the books do end up being brought up again as a key plot point, but it’s only done so to a superficial degree rather than being an integral aspect of how the murders are conducted. This wouldn’t be so much of a problem had the film not spent as much time as it did during the set up period showcasing these works and explaining how they relate to the case. It makes their investigation seem even more like a wild goose chase rather than an intellectual process, a feeling which is only amplified as the film progresses as they never manage to make it off the back foot. Much like the murders, the person who’s leading them along is equally disappointing. John Doe’s reveal in the finale of the film is nothing short of abrupt, and what he actually manages to accomplish once he reveals himself is middling at best. While the ultimate climax, the psychological destruction of Pitt’s character, is certainly very entertaining (and brought forth one of the most iconic lines in modern cinema) John leaves a lot to be desired in terms of actually being a villain. He comes across as a caricature of Hannibal Lecture but without the raw intimidation or presence. He speaks in this very monotone and vague way as a way of demonstrating his control over the situation, only truly losing his temper when he begins to speak about his victims and their respective sins. Unfortunately, he offers little additional support to the foundation of the murders, only confirming that they were executed for superficial means rather than any kind of actual greater purpose or meaning. It’s easy to see that, yes, the people he murdered are representations of the seven sins in some way, but they aren’t carried out as a result of any sort of conviction or greater purpose, but rather just as a means of “higher punishment” administered through his own means. Pitt rightfully calls him out on this, but due to the shallow nature of his character he’s unable to capitalize on this point, mirroring his lack of ability to counter Freeman. My issues with Se7en are not due to a lack of entertainment. The movie excels when it comes to simply fun, the basic nature of its core elements, which are elevated due to the higher quality of its premise, is enough to make sitting through the film worthwhile. However, the film insists that it includes higher ideas in an attempt to nudge itself into something more without properly committing. Each of its greater elements: the character’s opposite personalities, the higher purpose of the murders/how the murders are actually solved are merely thrown out and left unresolved for the viewer to take at face value rather than leaving much room for thought. The ideas being unresolved isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but they end up feeling cheap because of how little foundation they’re given, rather than the lack of a concrete conclusion. Se7en seems to present itself as a movie which is more than your standard buddy cop serial murder mystery film, but while it’s certainly higher quality than your run of the mill flick it just can’t seem to escape its simplistic roots. In the end, it chose entertainment over truly committing to what it wants to say, it takes the easy way out, though I can’t blame them for it.

Se7en is a film which attempts to wear many hats. On one hand you have attempts at a highly interesting and flashy serial murder case which operates as the major stopping points of the story. Each of the murders is extreme and profane, crafted with this kind of blunt detail that’s certainly entertaining, but ultimately surface level and less well thought out than they likely intended. On the other you have an extremely standard buddy cop framework between the two main characters which makes no real attempt at straying away from convention. Both of these central building blocks are joined together by this phenomenal, nearly noir, presentation which sets up the film as something which is both easily entertaining and contains more for those who are willing to seek it out. Unfortunately, I found Se7en ultimately ends up confused in this crossroad of seriousness and entertainment, ultimately ending up lingering at the surface level and only utilizing these bigger ideas as window dressing rather than something which builds towards something greater. Unfortunately the signs are there from the beginning. The characters in this film are prototypical to a degree which ends up being serviceable but lacking both in terms of story progression and intrapersonal drama. Brad Pitt plays a standard hotshot new detective, willing to prove himself and reeking in overconfidence by his supposed credentials. Rather than demonstrating his actual abilities, Pitt prefers to crack one liners and sneer at his partner’s persistence to do his job properly rather than quickly give up the moment he faces the first sign of abstraction. Likewise, his partner, Morgan Freeman, is his polar opposite. An old blood detective who just wants to retire out of the force because of the toxic apathy of society which has eroded his sense of goodwill. He’s ultimately pragmatic about his job and knows that their efforts are more likely than not to be pointless in the grand scheme of things. This is about as standard of a setup as you can get, but the film never really causes it to head in any sort of meaningful direction. Pitt and Freeman very rarely actually interact for the first quarter of the film, and due to the extremely short timeframe of the plot, their inevitable destination as uncommon allies mere days later is unnatural and unconvincing. The two of them lack chemistry, and their lack of substantial interaction makes the buddy cop presentation lose traction as a whole. Pitt’s more than willing to speak his mind, and the film is more than willing to utilize him as the main source of entertainment, but because Freeman isn’t willing to ever give him an inch these moments end up falling flatter than they had to. This is representative of how the film handles the crux of their characters as well. Pitt and Freeman represent opposite ends of the same coin. Being detectives and thoroughly entrenched in the toxicity of low society, Pitt’s optimism and Freeman’s pragmatism could represent some kind of clash of ideals. But instead, Se7en chooses to merely float these ideas rather than tackle them directly. This is most blatantly presented in a scene in a bar about halfway through the film. Freeman is telling Pitt about how he’s fed up with all of the apathy of society, how people are so willing to take the easy way out rather than work through their problems, which ultimately is the source of their misfortune. Society does not care about itself and so Freeman does not care about society. Pitt rejects this idea, not for any actual stated reason or counterargument, but merely because he cannot accept this line of thought. He states that Freeman himself is also taking the easy way out, which is true, but does little to shift his perspective in any meaningful way. This idea remains a loose thread rather than being properly explored, and this trend can be observed with much of the rest of what Se7en aims to accomplish. The other core principle of Se7en is, of course, the murders. This aspect is where the film really shines. Se7en is already a visually impressive film, perfectly capturing the kind of grime which makes up this low society by operating primarily with low blues and greys. This is a very dark film, but the main attribute I would give the visual quality is dirty. The murders primarily take place in these low income locations, even the apartment buildings are worn down and damaged. Despite the primary weather condition being rain this ends up reminding me of mud more so than dirt being washed away. This translates to the murders perfectly. Each of which are immensely brutal and highly creative, making use of the sin motif more as a suggestion for a gory creative artpiece than anything. My favorite ended up being the first of the murders, representing gluttony you have this obese man who was forced to eat himself to death, but not before cutting off an entire pound worth of meat off his body. This is far and away the most visually stimulating of any of the murders, and perfectly builds up the case as something which is equal parts sadistic and incredible. While grotesque, the visual quality makes it more entertaining than disgusting, and the absurdity of the murders themselves adds to this feeling. Of course, the problem lies with how these murders are presented. For the first half of the film, the duo is convinced that the murders are inspired by famous literary works such as The Divine Comedy and The Canterbury Tales due to them representing the titular seven sins. The film spends a significant amount of time showcasing them researching and discussing these ideas leading you to believe that these would be significant details to the case. Unfortunately, this ends up being nothing more than a wild goose chase, and these details are nothing more than window dressing than any kind of greater idea. Once you reach the halfway point, the film is more than willing to abandon this idea and pivot back towards the cops stumbling in the right direction rather than solving the murders from their own ideas. Of course, the books do end up being brought up again as a key plot point, but it’s only done so to a superficial degree rather than being an integral aspect of how the murders are conducted. This wouldn’t be so much of a problem had the film not spent as much time as it did during the set up period showcasing these works and explaining how they relate to the case. It makes their investigation seem even more like a wild goose chase rather than an intellectual process, a feeling which is only amplified as the film progresses as they never manage to make it off the back foot. Much like the murders, the person who’s leading them along is equally disappointing. John Doe’s reveal in the finale of the film is nothing short of abrupt, and what he actually manages to accomplish once he reveals himself is middling at best. While the ultimate climax, the psychological destruction of Pitt’s character, is certainly very entertaining (and brought forth one of the most iconic lines in modern cinema) John leaves a lot to be desired in terms of actually being a villain. He comes across as a caricature of Hannibal Lecture but without the raw intimidation or presence. He speaks in this very monotone and vague way as a way of demonstrating his control over the situation, only truly losing his temper when he begins to speak about his victims and their respective sins. Unfortunately, he offers little additional support to the foundation of the murders, only confirming that they were executed for superficial means rather than any kind of actual greater purpose or meaning. It’s easy to see that, yes, the people he murdered are representations of the seven sins in some way, but they aren’t carried out as a result of any sort of conviction or greater purpose, but rather just as a means of “higher punishment” administered through his own means. Pitt rightfully calls him out on this, but due to the shallow nature of his character he’s unable to capitalize on this point, mirroring his lack of ability to counter Freeman. My issues with Se7en are not due to a lack of entertainment. The movie excels when it comes to simply fun, the basic nature of its core elements, which are elevated due to the higher quality of its premise, is enough to make sitting through the film worthwhile. However, the film insists that it includes higher ideas in an attempt to nudge itself into something more without properly committing. Each of its greater elements: the character’s opposite personalities, the higher purpose of the murders/how the murders are actually solved are merely thrown out and left unresolved for the viewer to take at face value rather than leaving much room for thought. The ideas being unresolved isn’t necessarily a bad thing, but they end up feeling cheap because of how little foundation they’re given, rather than the lack of a concrete conclusion. Se7en seems to present itself as a movie which is more than your standard buddy cop serial murder mystery film, but while it’s certainly higher quality than your run of the mill flick it just can’t seem to escape its simplistic roots. In the end, it chose entertainment over truly committing to what it wants to say, it takes the easy way out, though I can’t blame them for it.

A little disappointment for me. I am not a huge fan of classic police thrillers, even though I have watched many of them, and Se7en is in line with stereotypical American thrillers. Indeed, it’s about two investigators conducting an investigation into a crazy serial killer, except there is nothing original here; it’s too bland. Moreover, all the cases are foreseeable and expected, as the killer openly shows the detectives that his victims represent a specific deadly sin. It seems as if David Fincher wanted his thriller to be a global success, as he adds all the easy elements for his film to be broadly appreciated. Moreover, Brad Pitt doesn’t play that well here, according to me. The setup and the first act are also way too long. How many scenes of small talk do we have to undergo before the plot starts to get exciting ? Nevertheless, the turning point, although late, is good. The final confrontation is also decent but not that shocking or surprising for the spectator. I can’t help comparing Se7en with Prisoners . I think that Prisoners is a textbook example of what a thriller should be: it’s refined, visually soothing, and the plot is just perfect. On the contrary, Se7en is weak. To conclude, the “seven deadly sins” that John Doe follows aren’t from the Bible, as many could think. The concept traces back to Evagrius Ponticus, a Christian monk living in the Egyptian desert in the late 4th century. He wasn’t trying to build a moral code for everyone, he was writing practical guidance for monks trying to master their own minds during long stretches of solitude and temptation. He identified eight “evil thoughts” that troubled the ascetic life (he added “sadness,” which was removed later). Dante's Purgatory cemented the seven deadly sins in Western moral imagination. In the poem, Mount Purgatory is shaped like a mountain with seven terraces, one for each sin, stacked in order of severity (worst to least severe). Souls climb the mountain, working through one terrace at a time, purging themselves of that particular sin before moving up to the next. The order is : Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, Lust.

Tengo opiniones bastante encontradas con Se7en porque realmente me gustó muchísimo el desarrollo de la película, la investigación, las pistas y la forma en la que vamos conociendo a John Doe, me parecía que la película estaba construyendo algo con muchísimas posibilidades narrativas y durante gran parte de ella sentía que cada detalle tenía una razón para estar ahí. Doe claramente quería que alguien lo encontrara y que alguien pudiera observar su obra, incluso cuando Somerset y Mills llegan a su departamento se siente que Doe está impresionado por haber sido encontrado y que realmente existía una construcción alrededor de la investigación que me parecía excelente. El problema para mí aparece principalmente en el final y no porque no entienda lo que la película quiere hacer, de hecho entiendo perfectamente la intención de que Mills termine representando la ira y que Doe construya las condiciones necesarias para que Mills termine matándolo. El problema es que siento que la película justifica el final pero no lo desarrolla de la mejor manera posible. Para mí existe una diferencia muy importante entre que un acontecimiento pueda ser justificado dentro de la historia y que realmente haya sido construido narrativamente para que ese acontecimiento sea una consecuencia natural de todo lo anterior. El caso de Tracy es el ejemplo más importante. El plan de John Doe comenzó antes de que Mills fuera asignado como compañero de Somerset, por lo que Mills aparece dentro de la historia de una manera bastante circunstancial y posteriormente Doe adapta su obra alrededor de él. Contextualmente se puede justificar que Doe envidia la vida de Mills, que ve en él aquello que él mismo no tiene y que por eso decide convertirlo en la representación de la ira, pero narrativamente siento que la película no construyó suficientemente la relación de Mills con Tracy para que su muerte tuviera el peso que necesitaba tener. Tracy termina siendo fundamental para el final pero durante gran parte de la película no existe un desarrollo suficiente de ella como para sentir que estamos llegando inevitablemente a esa tragedia. Por eso también me parece extraño cuando Doe habla de su “obra maestra” como si todo lo que ocurrió hubiera estado construido específicamente alrededor de Mills, cuando realmente la película nos muestra un plan que existía antes de que Mills estuviera involucrado. La explicación existe, pero siento que aparece principalmente para poder justificar el desenlace que la película ya necesita. Para mí una revelación puede ser algo que jamás vi venir, pero cuando finalmente aparece debería poder mirar hacia atrás y pensar que todo estaba ahí, que las acciones anteriores de los personajes y las circunstancias de la historia produjeron naturalmente ese resultado. En Se7en yo no tuve completamente esa sensación, tuve más la sensación de que entiendo por qué Doe decidió hacerlo pero no siento que la película haya construido suficientemente las condiciones para que tuviera que hacerlo de esa manera. También me sucede algo parecido con Somerset durante la escena final. Somerset entiende perfectamente lo que está ocurriendo, intenta convencer a Mills de que no mate a Doe porque sabe que hacerlo significa que Doe gana, pero la forma en la que responde durante la escena me parece extraña respecto a su propia motivación. Si realmente quiere impedir que Mills lo mate, esperaba una reacción mucho más desesperada y física, intentando acercarse a él, detenerlo o ponerse entre ambos, porque Mills tiene varios segundos para tomar una decisión mientras Somerset simplemente intenta convencerlo. No digo que solamente exista una manera realista de reaccionar, pero dentro de lo que la película había construido de Somerset, su comportamiento me pareció demasiado conveniente para que Mills pudiera llegar exactamente al resultado que la historia necesitaba. Y esto es lo que más me decepciona porque la tesis de la película me parece excelente. El problema no es el nihilismo, ni que el final sea oscuro, ni siquiera que Doe consiga ganar. El problema es que siento que la tesis está mucho mejor construida conceptualmente que dramáticamente. La película sabe perfectamente qué quiere decir con Mills convirtiéndose en ira, pero siento que tuvo que acomodar algunas decisiones de los personajes para poder llegar a esa conclusión. Para mí la profundidad narrativa está mucho más relacionada con la relación entre la motivación de un personaje y las acciones que produce esa motivación. Un personaje tiene determinados valores, deseos, miedos y circunstancias, y a partir de eso debería tomar decisiones que produzcan el desarrollo de la historia. Cuando ocurre así, el final no solamente se justifica, sino que se siente como una consecuencia de todo lo que vimos. En Se7en siento que en algunos momentos ocurre lo contrario, que el final necesita que determinados personajes hagan determinadas cosas y posteriormente la película encuentra una explicación para que esas cosas tengan sentido. Me hubiera gustado muchísimo más que la película desarrollara a Mills como el protagonista central, que conociéramos mucho más su vida, su relación con Tracy, su personalidad y sobre todo su obsesión con demostrar que puede ser un buen detective. Que la investigación de Doe fuera progresivamente convirtiéndose en una obsesión personal y profesional, que Mills comenzara sacrificando aspectos de su vida por resolver el caso y que finalmente esa obsesión terminara produciendo la pérdida de Tracy y su transformación en ira. De esa manera la muerte de Tracy no sería solamente el elemento necesario para completar los siete pecados, sino la consecuencia de una relación que nosotros ya conocemos y que hemos visto desarrollarse durante toda la película. Incluso siento que Somerset podría no haber sido necesario como protagonista secundario si la película hubiera profundizado mucho más en Mills. Su presencia funciona muy bien para contrastar dos formas de entender el mundo y la investigación, pero al mismo tiempo divide el protagonismo y hace que Mills no tenga todo el desarrollo psicológico que para mí necesitaba tener para que el final realmente me destruyera. Se7en es una película que me parece muy buena durante gran parte de su desarrollo y cuya idea final me parece incluso excelente, pero para mí existe una diferencia entre tener una conclusión interesante y construir perfectamente el camino hacia ella. El final se puede explicar, se puede justificar y tiene una tesis muy clara, pero siento que la película no consiguió desarrollar todas las condiciones necesarias para que yo sintiera que ese final era una consecuencia inevitable de los personajes y no solamente la conclusión que la historia necesitaba alcanzar. Me hubiera gustado ver una película donde la profesión, la obsesión, la familia, el sacrificio y finalmente la pérdida de Mills fueran construyendo poco a poco su transformación en ira. Creo que con ese desarrollo Se7en podría haber sido una de mis películas favoritas, porque la investigación de John Doe y la tesis que plantea tienen muchísimo potencial, pero para mí la construcción narrativa del final se siente demasiado impuesta y eso termina quitándole profundidad a una película que conceptualmente tenía muchísimo más para desarrollar. Gracias

A little disappointment for me. I am not a huge fan of classic police thrillers, even though I have watched many of them, and Se7en is in line with stereotypical American thrillers. Indeed, it’s about two investigators conducting an investigation into a crazy serial killer, except there is nothing original here; it’s too bland. Moreover, all the cases are foreseeable and expected, as the killer openly shows the detectives that his victims represent a specific deadly sin. It seems as if David Fincher wanted his thriller to be a global success, as he adds all the easy elements for his film to be broadly appreciated. Moreover, Brad Pitt doesn’t play that well here, according to me. The setup and the first act are also way too long. How many scenes of small talk do we have to undergo before the plot starts to get exciting ? Nevertheless, the turning point, although late, is good. The final confrontation is also decent but not that shocking or surprising for the spectator. I can’t help comparing Se7en with Prisoners . I think that Prisoners is a textbook example of what a thriller should be: it’s refined, visually soothing, and the plot is just perfect. On the contrary, Se7en is weak. To conclude, the “seven deadly sins” that John Doe follows aren’t from the Bible, as many could think. The concept traces back to Evagrius Ponticus, a Christian monk living in the Egyptian desert in the late 4th century. He wasn’t trying to build a moral code for everyone, he was writing practical guidance for monks trying to master their own minds during long stretches of solitude and temptation. He identified eight “evil thoughts” that troubled the ascetic life (he added “sadness,” which was removed later). Dante's Purgatory cemented the seven deadly sins in Western moral imagination. In the poem, Mount Purgatory is shaped like a mountain with seven terraces, one for each sin, stacked in order of severity (worst to least severe). Souls climb the mountain, working through one terrace at a time, purging themselves of that particular sin before moving up to the next. The order is : Pride, Envy, Wrath, Sloth, Greed, Gluttony, Lust.

[30] nota=2.0 estrelas:
Tengo opiniones bastante encontradas con Se7en porque realmente me gustó muchísimo el desarrollo de la película, la investigación, las pistas y la forma en la que vamos conociendo a John Doe, me parecía que la película estaba construyendo algo con muchísimas posibilidades narrativas y durante gran parte de ella sentía que cada detalle tenía una razón para estar ahí. Doe claramente quería que alguien lo encontrara y que alguien pudiera observar su obra, incluso cuando Somerset y Mills llegan a su departamento se siente que Doe está impresionado por haber sido encontrado y que realmente existía una construcción alrededor de la investigación que me parecía excelente. El problema para mí aparece principalmente en el final y no porque no entienda lo que la película quiere hacer, de hecho entiendo perfectamente la intención de que Mills termine representando la ira y que Doe construya las condiciones necesarias para que Mills termine matándolo. El problema es que siento que la película justifica el final pero no lo desarrolla de la mejor manera posible. Para mí existe una diferencia muy importante entre que un acontecimiento pueda ser justificado dentro de la historia y que realmente haya sido construido narrativamente para que ese acontecimiento sea una consecuencia natural de todo lo anterior. El caso de Tracy es el ejemplo más importante. El plan de John Doe comenzó antes de que Mills fuera asignado como compañero de Somerset, por lo que Mills aparece dentro de la historia de una manera bastante circunstancial y posteriormente Doe adapta su obra alrededor de él. Contextualmente se puede justificar que Doe envidia la vida de Mills, que ve en él aquello que él mismo no tiene y que por eso decide convertirlo en la representación de la ira, pero narrativamente siento que la película no construyó suficientemente la relación de Mills con Tracy para que su muerte tuviera el peso que necesitaba tener. Tracy termina siendo fundamental para el final pero durante gran parte de la película no existe un desarrollo suficiente de ella como para sentir que estamos llegando inevitablemente a esa tragedia. Por eso también me parece extraño cuando Doe habla de su “obra maestra” como si todo lo que ocurrió hubiera estado construido específicamente alrededor de Mills, cuando realmente la película nos muestra un plan que existía antes de que Mills estuviera involucrado. La explicación existe, pero siento que aparece principalmente para poder justificar el desenlace que la película ya necesita. Para mí una revelación puede ser algo que jamás vi venir, pero cuando finalmente aparece debería poder mirar hacia atrás y pensar que todo estaba ahí, que las acciones anteriores de los personajes y las circunstancias de la historia produjeron naturalmente ese resultado. En Se7en yo no tuve completamente esa sensación, tuve más la sensación de que entiendo por qué Doe decidió hacerlo pero no siento que la película haya construido suficientemente las condiciones para que tuviera que hacerlo de esa manera. También me sucede algo parecido con Somerset durante la escena final. Somerset entiende perfectamente lo que está ocurriendo, intenta convencer a Mills de que no mate a Doe porque sabe que hacerlo significa que Doe gana, pero la forma en la que responde durante la escena me parece extraña respecto a su propia motivación. Si realmente quiere impedir que Mills lo mate, esperaba una reacción mucho más desesperada y física, intentando acercarse a él, detenerlo o ponerse entre ambos, porque Mills tiene varios segundos para tomar una decisión mientras Somerset simplemente intenta convencerlo. No digo que solamente exista una manera realista de reaccionar, pero dentro de lo que la película había construido de Somerset, su comportamiento me pareció demasiado conveniente para que Mills pudiera llegar exactamente al resultado que la historia necesitaba. Y esto es lo que más me decepciona porque la tesis de la película me parece excelente. El problema no es el nihilismo, ni que el final sea oscuro, ni siquiera que Doe consiga ganar. El problema es que siento que la tesis está mucho mejor construida conceptualmente que dramáticamente. La película sabe perfectamente qué quiere decir con Mills convirtiéndose en ira, pero siento que tuvo que acomodar algunas decisiones de los personajes para poder llegar a esa conclusión. Para mí la profundidad narrativa está mucho más relacionada con la relación entre la motivación de un personaje y las acciones que produce esa motivación. Un personaje tiene determinados valores, deseos, miedos y circunstancias, y a partir de eso debería tomar decisiones que produzcan el desarrollo de la historia. Cuando ocurre así, el final no solamente se justifica, sino que se siente como una consecuencia de todo lo que vimos. En Se7en siento que en algunos momentos ocurre lo contrario, que el final necesita que determinados personajes hagan determinadas cosas y posteriormente la película encuentra una explicación para que esas cosas tengan sentido. Me hubiera gustado muchísimo más que la película desarrollara a Mills como el protagonista central, que conociéramos mucho más su vida, su relación con Tracy, su personalidad y sobre todo su obsesión con demostrar que puede ser un buen detective. Que la investigación de Doe fuera progresivamente convirtiéndose en una obsesión personal y profesional, que Mills comenzara sacrificando aspectos de su vida por resolver el caso y que finalmente esa obsesión terminara produciendo la pérdida de Tracy y su transformación en ira. De esa manera la muerte de Tracy no sería solamente el elemento necesario para completar los siete pecados, sino la consecuencia de una relación que nosotros ya conocemos y que hemos visto desarrollarse durante toda la película. Incluso siento que Somerset podría no haber sido necesario como protagonista secundario si la película hubiera profundizado mucho más en Mills. Su presencia funciona muy bien para contrastar dos formas de entender el mundo y la investigación, pero al mismo tiempo divide el protagonismo y hace que Mills no tenga todo el desarrollo psicológico que para mí necesitaba tener para que el final realmente me destruyera. Se7en es una película que me parece muy buena durante gran parte de su desarrollo y cuya idea final me parece incluso excelente, pero para mí existe una diferencia entre tener una conclusión interesante y construir perfectamente el camino hacia ella. El final se puede explicar, se puede justificar y tiene una tesis muy clara, pero siento que la película no consiguió desarrollar todas las condiciones necesarias para que yo sintiera que ese final era una consecuencia inevitable de los personajes y no solamente la conclusión que la historia necesitaba alcanzar. Me hubiera gustado ver una película donde la profesión, la obsesión, la familia, el sacrificio y finalmente la pérdida de Mills fueran construyendo poco a poco su transformación en ira. Creo que con ese desarrollo Se7en podría haber sido una de mis películas favoritas, porque la investigación de John Doe y la tesis que plantea tienen muchísimo potencial, pero para mí la construcción narrativa del final se siente demasiado impuesta y eso termina quitándole profundidad a una película que conceptualmente tenía muchísimo más para desarrollar. Gracias

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Feels like one of those Pixar films that displays so much potential in the first 20 minutes in setting up some poignant message about grappling with our own sense of mortality, and Reznor and Ross' soundtrack accompanied with Jon Batiste is a worthy companion. But the movie stumbles over its own footing as it gets lost trying to narrow down and convey what exactly the underlying message of its story is. Is finding your "spark" supposed to be about realizing that your lifelong passion isn't actually lucrative and you should find something more sustainable if you can't make a living off it? Or is it about coming to terms with the idea that your lifelong ambition isn't always what it turns out to be and it's okay to just start anew? Or that your life still has purpose even if you feel like you haven't fulfilled what it is you thought you were meant to do? It becomes so convuluted by the end and these questions still go unanswered, so the emotional baggage you're left with doesn't feel nearly wrapped up as well as it could've been. Ultimately comes off as a visually and sonically captivating Pixar installment (still thought the "Great Beyond" looked and sounded cool af) but with a lot of unfulfilled potential in its central storyline and main character arc — coupled with an antagonist that's honestly not very memorable either. I liked it enough to stay entertained on my flight, but given the overall content and musical appreciation prevalent throughout its runtime, I do wish I ended up loving it more.

Is finding your "spark" supposed to be about realizing that your lifelong passion isn't actually lucrative and you should find something more sustainable if you can't make a living off it? Or that your life still has purpose even if you feel like you haven't fulfilled what it is you thought you were meant to do? It becomes so convuluted by the end and these questions still go unanswered, so the emotional baggage you're left with doesn't feel nearly wrapped up as well as it could've been. Docter matérialise des concepts abstraits avec une aisance hallucinante. Le Grand Avant, le Grand Bazar, l'océan des âmes égarées, et ces entités en charge de l'au-delà représentées par de simples traits en mouvement. On reproduit l'exploit de Vice-versa. La musique fait énormément, et le film a deux univers sonores : le jazz de Jon Batiste pour la Terre, ce sont ses mains qu'on voit jouer, rotoscopées  et les nappes éthérées de Trent Reznor et Atticus Ross pour le monde des âmes. Everything about life is just « meh », I’ve slowly been loosing passion for my hobbies and passions, just kinda stopped caring overall about everything, becoming more cynical by the minute. When Joe stands on the sidewalk after the performance - the one he always wanted, the one that would change everything - he simply appears normal, or rather empty. As he plays the piano all by himself in his dark apartment, he remembers the joyful moments of his life and yes music and jazz is there, but that’s not all there is. It’s the mundane things of everyday life. I also really liked the story of his barber friend, how he wanted to be veterinarian but bc he needed money for his daughter hospital bills, he took up barber lessons and he’s now the best there is. Becoming a barber wasn’t in his plans, as he said so himself, but he’s still happy being one bc isn’t that the whole point anyway? [15] nota=4.0 estrelas:
Très bien, et vraiment beau. Joe Gardner est professeur de musique à New York et ne vit que pour le jazz. Le jour où il décroche enfin le concert de sa vie, il tombe dans une bouche d'égout et se retrouve dans l'au-delà. Il refuse d'y aller, et se retrouve associé à une âme qui, elle, refuse de naître. Ce qui rend le film remarquable, c'est son sujet. Pixar demande si une vie qui ne réalise pas sa vocation est une vie ratée, et répond non. Le film déplace la question de la passion vers celle de ce qui nous anime vraiment au quotidien, et c'est un propos rare pour un film familial. Docter matérialise des concepts abstraits avec une aisance hallucinante. Le Grand Avant, le Grand Bazar, l'océan des âmes égarées, et ces entités en charge de l'au-delà représentées par de simples traits en mouvement. On reproduit l'exploit de Vice-versa. La musique fait énormément, et le film a deux univers sonores : le jazz de Jon Batiste pour la Terre, ce sont ses mains qu'on voit jouer, rotoscopées  et les nappes éthérées de Trent Reznor et Atticus Ross pour le monde des âmes. Ma réserve : il y a quelques égarements scénaristiques au milieu, notamment le long passage dans un corps de chat. Premier Pixar avec un héros de couleur. Oscars du film d'animation et de la musique.

As many have already noted, Speak No Evil is torture-porn cinema, but what struck the wrong note for me was the fact that it feels as though the creators thought they were cleverly and slyly subverting a Michael Haneke-like premise, while having absolutely nothing to say. I was occasionally engaged, mostly during the first half. Entering the second one, film started to ask for increasingly large suspensions of disbelief. And in the final act, film went down as fast as a speeding car goes off a cliff. And it ended in an explosion, too. The dialogue was bad for the most part, but I could have turned a blind eye to that if the characters hadn't been written as the world's ultimate idiots. On top of that, these "unexpected" villains had zero motivation for what they were doing, nor did they have anything interesting added to their backgrounds. Not to be a big bad wolf all of the time, I'll say that the film does have some merit; there are a few intriguing scenes and couple of note-worthy filmmaking choices... But, at the end, I tend to believe the filmmakers were a bit pretentious here in thinking that a muffled orchestral score could somehow turn a poorly written screenplay into an important picture, and that a controversial, shocking ending could serve as a good substitute for meaning.

I’m very annoyed with myself that I watched the American remake of Speak No Evil before this, because I didn’t even know the Danish film existed until after I finished watching it. I think knowing exactly where the story was going inevitably changed the experience for me, especially because so much of the film’s effectiveness comes from gradually realising that something is deeply wrong with this seemingly ordinary couple. Even knowing the destination, though, I thought the original handled that progression much better. It takes its time letting the discomfort build, with little moments that initially seem harmless becoming increasingly sinister. The social awkwardness is painful in the best way. Every meal, conversation and attempt at politeness feels like a negotiation where everyone knows something is wrong but nobody wants to be the person who actually says it. That aspect of the film worked really well for me. Speak No Evil understands how horrifying it can be to find yourself trapped in a social situation where basic manners start working against your survival instincts. The parents are constantly making excuses for behaviour that should immediately set off alarm bells, partly because they don’t want to appear rude, and that makes the whole thing so uncomfortable to watch. But their survival instincts made me so frustrated. There is nothing that takes me out of the immersion in a horror film quicker than watching characters voluntarily walk back into a situation they already know is dangerous. These people have so many opportunities to do something. Run. Fight. Make a scene. Literally anything. Instead, they repeatedly return to the same nightmare. I understand the film is deliberately exploring passivity, but I wasn't frightened for them. I was angry at them. The parents are spineless. And even though Agnes is just a kid, I hate her and her stupid bunny. I also think knowing the ending from the remake made some of this even more frustrating. I wasn’t experiencing the mystery in the same way someone going in completely blind would. I knew what the couple were capable of, so I spent a lot of the runtime waiting for the parents to realise what was obvious to me. That probably made their decisions feel even more ridiculous. Still, I prefer this version. It feels much more interested in letting the dread accumulate rather than rushing towards conventional horror beats. It’s not constantly trying to scare you. The story feels nastier and more hopeless, and the whole premise becomes less about a conventional monster and more about the consequences of refusing to trust your own instincts. I definitely think I would have experienced this differently if I’d seen it first. I probably spent too much of the film comparing the two in my head. But even with that handicap, Speak No Evil captures the feeling of being trapped in a deeply uncomfortable social situation and slowly realising that you're in danger so well. 5.6/10
