I’m very annoyed with myself that I watched the American remake of Speak No Evil before this, because I didn’t even know the Danish film existed until after I finished watching it. I think knowing exactly where the story was going inevitably changed the experience for me, especially because so much of the film’s effectiveness comes from gradually realising that something is deeply wrong with this seemingly ordinary couple. Even knowing the destination, though, I thought the original handled that progression much better. It takes its time letting the discomfort build, with little moments that initially seem harmless becoming increasingly sinister. The social awkwardness is painful in the best way. Every meal, conversation and attempt at politeness feels like a negotiation where everyone knows something is wrong but nobody wants to be the person who actually says it. That aspect of the film worked really well for me. Speak No Evil understands how horrifying it can be to find yourself trapped in a social situation where basic manners start working against your survival instincts. The parents are constantly making excuses for behaviour that should immediately set off alarm bells, partly because they don’t want to appear rude, and that makes the whole thing so uncomfortable to watch. But their survival instincts made me so frustrated. There is nothing that takes me out of the immersion in a horror film quicker than watching characters voluntarily walk back into a situation they already know is dangerous. These people have so many opportunities to do something. Run. Fight. Make a scene. Literally anything. Instead, they repeatedly return to the same nightmare. I understand the film is deliberately exploring passivity, but I wasn't frightened for them. I was angry at them. The parents are spineless. And even though Agnes is just a kid, I hate her and her stupid bunny. I also think knowing the ending from the remake made some of this even more frustrating. I wasn’t experiencing the mystery in the same way someone going in completely blind would. I knew what the couple were capable of, so I spent a lot of the runtime waiting for the parents to realise what was obvious to me. That probably made their decisions feel even more ridiculous. Still, I prefer this version. It feels much more interested in letting the dread accumulate rather than rushing towards conventional horror beats. It’s not constantly trying to scare you. The story feels nastier and more hopeless, and the whole premise becomes less about a conventional monster and more about the consequences of refusing to trust your own instincts. I definitely think I would have experienced this differently if I’d seen it first. I probably spent too much of the film comparing the two in my head. But even with that handicap, Speak No Evil captures the feeling of being trapped in a deeply uncomfortable social situation and slowly realising that you're in danger so well. 5.6/10

This whole movie is basically a masterclass in watching a grown ass man fail every survival check imaginable. The whole “Yes, yes… let’s turn around just to get some stupid stuffed animal” moment isn’t just bad decision making, it’s the thesis of the entire movie. This dad is so painfully clueless, so desperate to be polite, that he drags his entire family straight into hell with a smile and a nod. I wasn’t even frustrated with the bad guys. I was frustrated with him. Every red flag is practically screaming in his face, and he still chooses the most socially awkward, self destructive option possible. It’s like he’s allergic to self preservation. By the time things go bad, I wasn’t shocked I was exhausted. You can’t feel bad for people who refuse to help themselves… The movie is effective, sure. It’s tense, it’s uncomfortable, it’s bleak. But it’s also infuriating, because you’re stuck watching a dad who would rather die than be rude. And honestly? That’s the real horror…

Speak No Evil mostra como, às vezes, seguir as convenções sociais apenas para evitar um constrangimento pode nos conduzir a um destino irreversível. Quantas vezes ignoramos os avisos da própria consciência e dizemos “sim” simplesmente para não contrariar alguém? É impossível não se identificar em algum nível. Concordamos com um motorista de Uber falando besteira apenas para não gastar energia discutindo, nos colocamos em situações desconfortáveis para não parecermos rígidos demais, flexibilizamos momentaneamente nossos próprios valores para não sermos vistos como chatos ou mal-educados. Speak No Evil pega algo absolutamente cotidiano e apenas o extrapola até transformá-lo em um terror desconfortável. Assistimos aos protagonistas caminharem lentamente em direção ao abismo. E o mais angustiante é perceber que não existe uma grande decisão responsável por levá-los até lá. São pequenas concessões, uma após a outra. Para não provocar desconforto, tornam-se progressivamente mais permissivos, até o momento em que aquilo que poderia ter sido evitado parece inevitável. No fim, Speak No Evil talvez seja um terror comportamental antes de qualquer outra coisa. Não precisa investir em jump scares, ameaças sobrenaturais ou grandes estímulos visuais. Seu terror está no comportamento humano e da facilidade com que reconhecemos aquelas pequenas concessões em nós mesmos. O filme apenas leva às últimas consequências uma armadilha na qual entramos todos os dias: o medo de contrariar o próximo.

When I was younger I had no issue visiting my friends in different cities and countries and sleeping on a floor or if I’m lucky, a couch. As I’ve gotten older I still visit and stay over at friends houses but these days I get weirdly anxious about it, especially when trying to sleep. So much so that I’ll often just book a hotel instead. With that in mind it seems this film has been tailor made to torture me and twist the knife right where it hurts. So much so that I considered multiple times just switching it off. Glad I could see it through tho, this was fantastic; Psychological horror at its best. I don’t know what it is about Scandinavian films but they are so good at tapping into the minutia of social norms and what happens when you break them. Probably the area of the world with the highest ratio of bangers to flops- in fact I’m not sure I’ve ever seen a bad Scandi film. Add Christian Tafdrup to the list of Osterland, Trier, Vinterberg et al, cos this guy can cook.

[2] nota=3.5 estrelas:
This whole movie is basically a masterclass in watching a grown ass man fail every survival check imaginable. The whole “Yes, yes… let’s turn around just to get some stupid stuffed animal” moment isn’t just bad decision making, it’s the thesis of the entire movie. This dad is so painfully clueless, so desperate to be polite, that he drags his entire family straight into hell with a smile and a nod. I wasn’t even frustrated with the bad guys. I was frustrated with him. Every red flag is practically screaming in his face, and he still chooses the most socially awkward, self destructive option possible. It’s like he’s allergic to self preservation. By the time things go bad, I wasn’t shocked I was exhausted. You can’t feel bad for people who refuse to help themselves… The movie is effective, sure. It’s tense, it’s uncomfortable, it’s bleak. But it’s also infuriating, because you’re stuck watching a dad who would rather die than be rude. And honestly? That’s the real horror…

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Something only a handful of horror movies is able to bring out in me, the sense of dread that lingers inside you throughout the film. My one complaint though is with some of the characters being a little underbaked, where they feel a little pointless. Talk to Me é um daqueles raros filmes de terror que compreende que o género não precisa de escolher entre a substância e o entretenimento. Pode ser profundamente alegórico sem deixar de ser genuinamente assustador. Pode falar sobre luto, dependência e autodestruição sem sacrificar a tensão em nome da mensagem. E é precisamente esse equilíbrio que faz do filme uma das obras mais marcantes do terror contemporâneo. À primeira vista, a sua premissa não parece particularmente inovadora. A possessão enquanto metáfora para o vício, a procura desesperada por uma fuga ao sofrimento e a sedução exercida por forças que prometem alívio imediato são temas que o cinema de terror tem explorado há décadas. No entanto, Talk to Me nunca depende da originalidade da ideia, depende da excelência da sua execução. Os irmãos Philippou demonstram uma confiança invulgar na realização, construindo uma atmosfera opressiva onde cada movimento de câmara, cada corte e cada silêncio contribuem para uma crescente sensação de inevitabilidade. O terror não nasce apenas daquilo que vemos, mas sobretudo da certeza de que a tragédia já começou muito antes de as personagens se aperceberem disso. O maior triunfo do filme reside na forma como recusa transformar a alegoria no seu principal espetáculo. Nos últimos anos, o chamado "elevated horror" tornou-se tão obcecado pelas suas leituras simbólicas que, muitas vezes, se esqueceu de provocar medo. Filmes excessivamente preocupados em explicar o trauma acabam frequentemente por neutralizar aquilo que torna o terror tão poderoso, a irracionalidade, a ansiedade e o desconhecido. Talk to Me faz exatamente o contrário. Primeiro assusta. Só depois convida à interpretação. A metáfora nunca sufoca a experiência, emerge naturalmente dela. A mão funciona como um objeto profundamente simbólico. Não representa apenas o contacto com os mortos, mas também a sedução de qualquer mecanismo de evasão que ofereça prazer imediato à custa da própria destruição. É impossível não estabelecer um paralelo com a dependência, a primeira experiência surge como uma curiosidade, transforma-se rapidamente num ritual coletivo e termina por consumir completamente quem já não consegue distinguir o controlo da ilusão de controlo. O filme evita qualquer moralismo simplista, preferindo mostrar como o sofrimento emocional cria terreno fértil para esse tipo de dependência. Grande parte da força dramática deve-se à extraordinária interpretação de Sophie Wilde. A sua performance nunca procura o exagero característico do cinema de possessão, pelo contrário, assenta numa vulnerabilidade constante que torna a deterioração psicológica da personagem devastadoramente convincente. Wilde consegue transmitir medo, culpa, isolamento, desespero e alienação com uma subtileza impressionante. Mesmo nos momentos mais extremos, nunca sentimos que estamos perante uma personagem, mas perante alguém que perdeu progressivamente a capacidade de distinguir a realidade daquilo que deseja desesperadamente acreditar. Também merece destaque a maturidade visual do filme. A fotografia utiliza uma paleta aparentemente banal para criar um universo onde o sobrenatural invade lentamente a normalidade quotidiana. Os efeitos práticos são utilizados com enorme inteligência, nunca como mero espetáculo grotesco, mas como extensões físicas do sofrimento psicológico das personagens. O design sonoro, por sua vez, torna-se quase uma personagem invisível, amplificando a tensão através de silêncios desconfortáveis e de uma presença constante que parece contaminar todos os espaços. Talvez o aspeto mais admirável seja a forma como os Philippou compreendem a essência do terror. O medo nunca é tratado como uma recompensa momentânea entre cenas de exposição, é uma atmosfera permanente. O filme recusa a estrutura previsível do susto fácil e opta por uma ansiedade lenta, quase insuportável, onde o espectador sente que cada decisão aproxima inevitavelmente as personagens da sua destruição. Infelizmente, existe hoje uma tendência para reduzir qualquer filme de terror que aborde o luto ou o trauma a uma simples tentativa de imitar Hereditary. Essa leitura ignora décadas de história do género. Muito antes disso, obras como Don't Look Now, The Changeling, Pet Sematary, The Orphanage ou The Descent já utilizavam o sobrenatural para explorar o peso da perda. O terror sempre foi uma linguagem privilegiada para falar do sofrimento humano. A diferença está na forma como cada filme escolhe fazê-lo. E Talk to Me escolhe fazê-lo através do medo. Medo genuíno. Daquele que não desaparece quando as luzes da sala se acendem. Daquele que permanece porque compreendemos que os verdadeiros demónios do filme nunca foram apenas os espíritos invocados, mas a facilidade com que o vazio emocional nos leva a abrir a porta a qualquer coisa que prometa preenchê-lo. Poucos filmes recentes conseguiram equilibrar de forma tão elegante o horror visceral, a tragédia íntima e a sofisticação formal. Sem reinventar completamente o género, Talk to Me demonstra que o terror continua a ser um dos meios mais poderosos para explorar aquilo que existe de mais frágil na condição humana. É um filme que assusta primeiro, pensa depois e permanece muito tempo connosco depois dos créditos terminarem.

Não representa apenas o contacto com os mortos, mas também a sedução de qualquer mecanismo de evasão que ofereça prazer imediato à custa da própria destruição. É impossível não estabelecer um paralelo com a dependência, a primeira experiência surge como uma curiosidade, transforma-se rapidamente num ritual coletivo e termina por consumir completamente quem já não consegue distinguir o controlo da ilusão de controlo. O filme evita qualquer moralismo simplista, preferindo mostrar como o sofrimento emocional cria terreno fértil para esse tipo de dependência. Grande parte da força dramática deve-se à extraordinária interpretação de Sophie Wilde. A sua performance nunca procura o exagero característico do cinema de possessão, pelo contrário, assenta numa vulnerabilidade constante que torna a deterioração psicológica da personagem devastadoramente convincente. Wilde consegue transmitir medo, culpa, isolamento, desespero e alienação com uma subtileza impressionante. Mesmo nos momentos mais extremos, nunca sentimos que estamos perante uma personagem, mas perante alguém que perdeu progressivamente a capacidade de distinguir a realidade daquilo que deseja desesperadamente acreditar. Também merece destaque a maturidade visual do filme. A fotografia utiliza uma paleta aparentemente banal para criar um universo onde o sobrenatural invade lentamente a normalidade quotidiana. Os efeitos práticos são utilizados com enorme inteligência, nunca como mero espetáculo grotesco, mas como extensões físicas do sofrimento psicológico das personagens. O design sonoro, por sua vez, torna-se quase uma personagem invisível, amplificando a tensão através de silêncios desconfortáveis e de uma presença constante que parece contaminar todos os espaços. Talvez o aspeto mais admirável seja a forma como os Philippou compreendem a essência do terror. O medo nunca é tratado como uma recompensa momentânea entre cenas de exposição, é uma atmosfera permanente. O filme recusa a estrutura previsível do susto fácil e opta por uma ansiedade lenta, quase insuportável, onde o espectador sente que cada decisão aproxima inevitavelmente as personagens da sua destruição. Infelizmente, existe hoje uma tendência para reduzir qualquer filme de terror que aborde o luto ou o trauma a uma simples tentativa de imitar Hereditary. Essa leitura ignora décadas de história do género. Muito antes disso, obras como Don't Look Now, The Changeling, Pet Sematary, The Orphanage ou The Descent já utilizavam o sobrenatural para explorar o peso da perda. O terror sempre foi uma linguagem privilegiada para falar do sofrimento humano. A diferença está na forma como cada filme escolhe fazê-lo. E Talk to Me escolhe fazê-lo através do medo. Medo genuíno. Daquele que não desaparece quando as luzes da sala se acendem. Daquele que permanece porque compreendemos que os verdadeiros demónios do filme nunca foram apenas os espíritos invocados, mas a facilidade com que o vazio emocional nos leva a abrir a porta a qualquer coisa que prometa preenchê-lo. Poucos filmes recentes conseguiram equilibrar de forma tão elegante o horror visceral, a tragédia íntima e a sofisticação formal. Sem reinventar completamente o género, Talk to Me demonstra que o terror continua a ser um dos meios mais poderosos para explorar aquilo que existe de mais frágil na condição humana. É um filme que assusta primeiro, pensa depois e permanece muito tempo connosco depois dos créditos terminarem.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

“The Brutalist”, de Brady Corbet, sigue a László Tóth, arquitecto húngaro y sobreviviente del Holocausto, cuando intenta reconstruir su vida en Estados Unidos. El sueño americano pronto se convierte en una incómoda relación entre arte, dinero y poder. Corbet construye un drama de época monumental, fotografiado por Lol Crawley con una textura áspera y elegante. La puesta en escena impresiona, aunque su extensa duración y cambios de género terminan dispersando el relato. La película habla de migración, pertenencia, explotación y del precio de perseguir una idea. Sin embargo, su discurso sobre el sionismo resulta problemático, especialmente por una mirada que presenta Israel como único refugio seguro para los judíos. A eso se suma una caracterización algo esquemática de sus posturas políticas y religiosas. Quiere ser película de época, drama familiar, relato de artista, thriller y tragedia, pero esa mezcla no siempre encuentra equilibrio. Adrien Brody y Guy Pearce sostienen buena parte del conjunto. Su relación mezcla dependencia, protección y amenaza con una química convincente. El apartado artístico es extraordinario, pero su irregular narrativa esta demasiado convencida de sus propias ideas.

I wasn’t as blown away by Adrien Brody as a Best Actor award should make me feel. Parts of it were riveting, and other long stretches started to feel like a chore to stay locked in. I did appreciate its thesis about the American upper class’s condescension & fetishization of talented immigrant workers, though there are other films capable of speaking to that message more concisely. “The Brutalist”, de Brady Corbet, sigue a László Tóth, arquitecto húngaro y sobreviviente del Holocausto, cuando intenta reconstruir su vida en Estados Unidos. El sueño americano pronto se convierte en una incómoda relación entre arte, dinero y poder. Corbet construye un drama de época monumental, fotografiado por Lol Crawley con una textura áspera y elegante. La puesta en escena impresiona, aunque su extensa duración y cambios de género terminan dispersando el relato. La película habla de migración, pertenencia, explotación y del precio de perseguir una idea. Sin embargo, su discurso sobre el sionismo resulta problemático, especialmente por una mirada que presenta Israel como único refugio seguro para los judíos. A eso se suma una caracterización algo esquemática de sus posturas políticas y religiosas. Quiere ser película de época, drama familiar, relato de artista, thriller y tragedia, pero esa mezcla no siempre encuentra equilibrio. Adrien Brody y Guy Pearce sostienen buena parte del conjunto. Su relación mezcla dependencia, protección y amenaza con una química convincente. El apartado artístico es extraordinario, pero su irregular narrativa esta demasiado convencida de sus propias ideas.

Unfortunately, "The Brutalist" is a boring, sometimes confusing if not erratic movie that lost me when after a sudden timeskip of unknown time in the second half Laszlow's niece Zsofia, who we only saw as a young girl that was mute from the war trauma she had experienced, all of sudden was talking like it is the most normal thing. The movie never explains what happened, why the girl suddenly gained the ability to talk again, it's just something that happened. And that's true for the entire second half of the movie: Things happen. Are they exciting? Interesting? Fun? No. But they happen. And then the credits started running. I know this is from a different director (and a heartfelt "fuck you" to rapist Roman Polanski), but it's hard not to wish for a direct sequel to "The Pianist" when seeing Adrian Brody playing the role of a post-WW2 jew. There's a lot that could have been portrayed in such sequel. Instead, we're following Lazslow who flees from Europe to America to start a new life. And that is interesting. We see how he arrives, how he struggles, how cruel this unknown world is to him. We see how he rises up, gets chances and takes them. This is when this movie is at its best. This is the fantastic first half. And then his wife arrives and the movie gets worse and worse from there. Instead of focusing on the building of the ... building and the struggles that come with such work, we only ever get a surface-level look at his work. Instead, more and more time is spent on family issues, trauma and drug abuse. And sex. Lots of sex scenes. Those are important for reasons. The final 20 minutes or so would have been the moment where I would have walked out of the theater hadn't I watched the movie at  home. Without spoiling much, "The Brutalist" pulls a "Joker: Folie a Deux" and completely torpedos everything that came before. Absolute baffeling choice. Uma Bela Propaganda Ainda é Propaganda: A Perversidade do Cinema Pró-Genocídio 1. Propaganda Sionista Travestida de Cinema Uma peça de propaganda sionista travestida de cinema: assim podemos definir a experiência maçante de pouco mais de três horas que objetivam uma única mensagem: os judeus não são capazes de se assimilar a qualquer nação; portanto, sua única alternativa é a colonização da região Palestina. Essa mensagem perversa é incutida subliminarmente através de um voice-over nos primeiros 20 minutos de filme. O som que narra através das ondas do rádio a resolução que criou o Estado Genocida de Israel prepara o espectador para o inevitável caminho do povo judeu, e o filme irá trabalhar intensamente para justificar a aliá (migração dos judeus para colonizar a Palestina). 2. O Paralelo com Leni Riefenstahl Esse conteúdo já seria perverso em qualquer período histórico, mas, em tempos de um Holocausto promovido por Israel, ganha contornos semelhantes aos de O Triunfo da Vontade, de Leni Riefenstahl, com duas diferenças básicas: Leni era profundamente mais dominante em sua técnica e, naquele momento, o Holocausto judeu ainda não havia se consolidado, como o dos palestinos na atualidade. 3. A Fachada Progressista e a Supremacia Judaica O filme tenta levianamente travestir-se de progressista e anticapitalista para vender sua mensagem. Mas falha justamente em seu juízo moral e na evocação velada da supremacia judaica, afinal, como é citado pela personagem de Felicity Jones: "todos nesse país são podres". Deixando claro que não se trata de uma crítica ao sistema e sim aos gentios de modo geral. 4. Hollywood e a Tradição do Cinema Pró-Genocídio Não há novidades na relação entre o Estado de Israel e Hollywood. Aliás, isso sempre foi pauta em muitas discussões sobre a parcialidade do cinema estadunidense para com os diversos extermínios orquestrados pelo Estado Ilegítimo. Desde Exodus, de Otto Preminger, que desumaniza os árabes vítimas da Nakba, até produções mais recentes, como Setembro 5, Hollywood toma parte do opressor, assim como o cinema alemão o fez nos anos 30 e 40. 5. Méritos Técnicos e a Atuação de Adrien Brody Como pontos positivos do filme, podemos destacar a fotografia e a direção de arte, que tornam o filme um belo e ordinário exemplar de propaganda. Há também a grande atuação de Adrien Brody, vencedor do Oscar pelo longa, mas cuja extensão exagerada do filme acaba em alguns momentos saturando o espectador. 6. Conclusão: O Brilho Técnico Ofuscado pela Podridão Narrativa O Brutalista é uma perversidade envolta em erros e que tem poucos acertos em sua construção. Há o brilho técnico, porém ofuscado pela absorvente podridão narrativa e tentativa de ludibriar os olhos que veem a história ser escrita com lágrimas e sangue inocente.

I can't remember having seen a movie with this many entirely unnecessary sex-scenes. "The Pianist" is one of my favorite movies of all times and Adrian Brody is a magnificent actor. Unfortunately, "The Brutalist" is a boring, sometimes confusing if not erratic movie that lost me when after a sudden timeskip of unknown time in the second half Laszlow's niece Zsofia, who we only saw as a young girl that was mute from the war trauma she had experienced, all of sudden was talking like it is the most normal thing. The movie never explains what happened, why the girl suddenly gained the ability to talk again, it's just something that happened. And that's true for the entire second half of the movie: Things happen. Are they exciting? Interesting? Fun? No. But they happen. And then the credits started running. I know this is from a different director (and a heartfelt "fuck you" to rapist Roman Polanski), but it's hard not to wish for a direct sequel to "The Pianist" when seeing Adrian Brody playing the role of a post-WW2 jew. There's a lot that could have been portrayed in such sequel. Instead, we're following Lazslow who flees from Europe to America to start a new life. And that is interesting. We see how he arrives, how he struggles, how cruel this unknown world is to him. We see how he rises up, gets chances and takes them. This is when this movie is at its best. This is the fantastic first half. And then his wife arrives and the movie gets worse and worse from there. Instead of focusing on the building of the ... building and the struggles that come with such work, we only ever get a surface-level look at his work. Instead, more and more time is spent on family issues, trauma and drug abuse. And sex. Lots of sex scenes. Those are important for reasons. The final 20 minutes or so would have been the moment where I would have walked out of the theater hadn't I watched the movie at  home. Without spoiling much, "The Brutalist" pulls a "Joker: Folie a Deux" and completely torpedos everything that came before. Absolute baffeling choice. Not a movie I want to watch again and not a movie that felt like it was telling an important story. The gimmicky use of loud sound effects during certain scenes felt desperate.

Uma Bela Propaganda Ainda é Propaganda: A Perversidade do Cinema Pró-Genocídio 1. Propaganda Sionista Travestida de Cinema Uma peça de propaganda sionista travestida de cinema: assim podemos definir a experiência maçante de pouco mais de três horas que objetivam uma única mensagem: os judeus não são capazes de se assimilar a qualquer nação; portanto, sua única alternativa é a colonização da região Palestina. Essa mensagem perversa é incutida subliminarmente através de um voice-over nos primeiros 20 minutos de filme. O som que narra através das ondas do rádio a resolução que criou o Estado Genocida de Israel prepara o espectador para o inevitável caminho do povo judeu, e o filme irá trabalhar intensamente para justificar a aliá (migração dos judeus para colonizar a Palestina). 2. O Paralelo com Leni Riefenstahl Esse conteúdo já seria perverso em qualquer período histórico, mas, em tempos de um Holocausto promovido por Israel, ganha contornos semelhantes aos de O Triunfo da Vontade, de Leni Riefenstahl, com duas diferenças básicas: Leni era profundamente mais dominante em sua técnica e, naquele momento, o Holocausto judeu ainda não havia se consolidado, como o dos palestinos na atualidade. 3. A Fachada Progressista e a Supremacia Judaica O filme tenta levianamente travestir-se de progressista e anticapitalista para vender sua mensagem. Mas falha justamente em seu juízo moral e na evocação velada da supremacia judaica, afinal, como é citado pela personagem de Felicity Jones: "todos nesse país são podres". Deixando claro que não se trata de uma crítica ao sistema e sim aos gentios de modo geral. 4. Hollywood e a Tradição do Cinema Pró-Genocídio Não há novidades na relação entre o Estado de Israel e Hollywood. Aliás, isso sempre foi pauta em muitas discussões sobre a parcialidade do cinema estadunidense para com os diversos extermínios orquestrados pelo Estado Ilegítimo. Desde Exodus, de Otto Preminger, que desumaniza os árabes vítimas da Nakba, até produções mais recentes, como Setembro 5, Hollywood toma parte do opressor, assim como o cinema alemão o fez nos anos 30 e 40. 5. Méritos Técnicos e a Atuação de Adrien Brody Como pontos positivos do filme, podemos destacar a fotografia e a direção de arte, que tornam o filme um belo e ordinário exemplar de propaganda. Há também a grande atuação de Adrien Brody, vencedor do Oscar pelo longa, mas cuja extensão exagerada do filme acaba em alguns momentos saturando o espectador. 6. Conclusão: O Brilho Técnico Ofuscado pela Podridão Narrativa O Brutalista é uma perversidade envolta em erros e que tem poucos acertos em sua construção. Há o brilho técnico, porém ofuscado pela absorvente podridão narrativa e tentativa de ludibriar os olhos que veem a história ser escrita com lágrimas e sangue inocente.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Cinema and Architecture in a Single Film? Yes. The Brutalist definitely brings together my two greatest passions to present an extremely dense drama about pain, desire, obsession, and deep trauma, expressed through an art form as abstract as architectural design. The details and finishing touches, the straight lines, the play of light, and the raw concrete masterfully convey the pain of an artist destroyed by war, broken by a foreign country, and obsessed with a work that, in reality, belongs to someone else. I suppose The Brutalist is one of those extremely difficult films to watch. Nearly three and a half hours of runtime will scare many people away, and its slow, methodical, subtext-heavy plot will drive away whatever few have decided to stay. But if one has enough patience and openness to let themselves be absorbed by the generational drama presented by the film, The Brutalist will fly by and eventually become a masterful study, not only of a character, but of an entire generation forced to carry on with their lives in a postwar period almost as unreal as the war itself. People as privileged as László Tóth can express that uncertainty, that fear, that anger, and even their darkest desires through a building almost as monumental as it is exorbitant. Others, on the other hand, are forced to self-destruct through drugs, sexual violence, and a love relationship strong enough to survive a war, but incapable of enduring its aftermath. No. The Brutalist is not for everyone. And I will not say that it is perfect either. But it is precisely what it needs to be to become a cinematic landmark: living proof that many of us are willing to endure a slow and meditative story in order to reach a thesis that is powerful, devastating, and, above all, honest. By the way, Brutalism is an architectural movement hated by many because of its simplicity and, as its name suggests, its sordid brutality. To me, however, it is the most beautiful style in architecture. Even with its simplicity, the rawness of its materials, and its violent forms, it manages to achieve a pure kind of beauty without the need for ornamentation or retouching. Almost in the same way we humans are made. 4.5 out of 5

“Is there a better description of a cube than that of its construction?” The Brutalist is an ambitious, visually stunning epic about art, ambition, trauma, and the complicated price of the American Dream. Brady Corbet creates a film that feels deliberately monumental, mirroring its main character’s obsession with architecture through its enormous scale and imposing visual language. Adrien Brody gives a remarkable performance as László Tóth , a Hungarian-Jewish architect rebuilding his life in post-war America. His character is deeply flawed, and often difficult to understand, but Brody gives him a quiet intensity that makes his struggles compelling. Felicity Jones and Guy Pearce are equally strong, adding layers to the film’s complicated relationships and power dynamics. The architecture is arguably the film’s greatest achievement. The brutalist structures are cold, imposing, and beautiful, functioning almost like another character. The cinematography and Daniel Blumberg’s haunting score give the film a weight that makes even its quieter moments feel significant. At nearly four hours, however, The Brutalist can feel a little prolonged. Some scenes linger longer than necessary, and its deliberately slow pace demands patience. The film also occasionally leans so heavily into its symbolism and grandeur that its emotional impact becomes slightly less immediate. Still, these aren’t huge criticisms. The Brutalist is the kind of film that feels increasingly rare now: visually bold, and genuinely interested in exploring difficult ideas rather than simply telling a straightforward story. It won’t work for everyone, but for viewers willing to surrender to its pace and scale, it is an unforgettable cinematic experience. Really didn’t expect to like this going in as I’d heard it’s both “Oscar bait” and AI fuled garbage. Where the hell did those rumours even come from? This is a magnificent film and reserved every bit of credibility it received.

Cinema and Architecture in a Single Film? Yes. The Brutalist definitely brings together my two greatest passions to present an extremely dense drama about pain, desire, obsession, and deep trauma, expressed through an art form as abstract as architectural design. The details and finishing touches, the straight lines, the play of light, and the raw concrete masterfully convey the pain of an artist destroyed by war, broken by a foreign country, and obsessed with a work that, in reality, belongs to someone else. I suppose The Brutalist is one of those extremely difficult films to watch. Nearly three and a half hours of runtime will scare many people away, and its slow, methodical, subtext-heavy plot will drive away whatever few have decided to stay. But if one has enough patience and openness to let themselves be absorbed by the generational drama presented by the film, The Brutalist will fly by and eventually become a masterful study, not only of a character, but of an entire generation forced to carry on with their lives in a postwar period almost as unreal as the war itself. People as privileged as László Tóth can express that uncertainty, that fear, that anger, and even their darkest desires through a building almost as monumental as it is exorbitant. Others, on the other hand, are forced to self-destruct through drugs, sexual violence, and a love relationship strong enough to survive a war, but incapable of enduring its aftermath. No. The Brutalist is not for everyone. And I will not say that it is perfect either. But it is precisely what it needs to be to become a cinematic landmark: living proof that many of us are willing to endure a slow and meditative story in order to reach a thesis that is powerful, devastating, and, above all, honest. By the way, Brutalism is an architectural movement hated by many because of its simplicity and, as its name suggests, its sordid brutality. To me, however, it is the most beautiful style in architecture. Even with its simplicity, the rawness of its materials, and its violent forms, it manages to achieve a pure kind of beauty without the need for ornamentation or retouching. Almost in the same way we humans are made. 4.5 out of 5

“Is there a better description of a cube than that of its construction?” The Brutalist is an ambitious, visually stunning epic about art, ambition, trauma, and the complicated price of the American Dream. Brady Corbet creates a film that feels deliberately monumental, mirroring its main character’s obsession with architecture through its enormous scale and imposing visual language. Adrien Brody gives a remarkable performance as László Tóth , a Hungarian-Jewish architect rebuilding his life in post-war America. His character is deeply flawed, and often difficult to understand, but Brody gives him a quiet intensity that makes his struggles compelling. Felicity Jones and Guy Pearce are equally strong, adding layers to the film’s complicated relationships and power dynamics. The architecture is arguably the film’s greatest achievement. The brutalist structures are cold, imposing, and beautiful, functioning almost like another character. The cinematography and Daniel Blumberg’s haunting score give the film a weight that makes even its quieter moments feel significant. At nearly four hours, however, The Brutalist can feel a little prolonged. Some scenes linger longer than necessary, and its deliberately slow pace demands patience. The film also occasionally leans so heavily into its symbolism and grandeur that its emotional impact becomes slightly less immediate. Still, these aren’t huge criticisms. The Brutalist is the kind of film that feels increasingly rare now: visually bold, and genuinely interested in exploring difficult ideas rather than simply telling a straightforward story. It won’t work for everyone, but for viewers willing to surrender to its pace and scale, it is an unforgettable cinematic experience. Really didn’t expect to like this going in as I’d heard it’s both “Oscar bait” and AI fuled garbage. Where the hell did those rumours even come from? Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

[1] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Ghatak has a good eye for compositions, no doubt about that, but he really struggles with staging human interactions. The casual cruelty, contempt and callousness with which the protagonist is treated come across as ridiculous, probably because the personality traits and behaviours of her family members do not extend beyond anger, vanity and self-pity.

[2] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Beautiful cinematography, probably surpassing anything by Ray at this point. Ghatak really uses his compositions to their fullest potential, frequently with something going on the foreground, middleground, and background. Unfortunately, the story ended up being this typical endless suffering, female martyrdom that Indian cinema seemed to love so much. Genuinely don’t know what I am meant to come away with by the end. I’m sure there are cultural critiques embedded in this, but I think excessive suffering of one person is a very limiting premise that is used too much.

The production quality is somewhat low for coming out in the 60's, but it is a film that broke new ground for its film culture, so of course it needs some credit for that. Watching it today, it does not hold up fantastically, but perhaps in the right mood it becomes more watchable.

The score is good on its own but the coordination with the sequences felt off to me. Moreover, the way the character Nita was portrayed was so exhausting- no developmental arc or multidimensionality, only full of misery and being a punching bag for her family members. The Cloud-Capped Star (1960) 🇮🇳 Sight & Sound's Greatest Of All Time 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die #898/1001 Wieder geht es um die Teilung Indiens. Hier steht eine junge Frau im Mittelpunkt die versucht ihre Familie zusammenzuhalten. Der Film wirkt für mich stärker, direkter und emotional klarer als The Golden Thread . Das persönliche Opfer der Hauptfigur steht im Zentrum und wird fast unerträglich greifbar. Ghatak macht hier ein Melodram, allerdings mit formalen Brüchen. Und gerade diese stilistischen Mittel; abrupte Schnitte, überhöhte Soundeffekte machen den Film eindringlich. Tief traurig, kraftvoll und für mich intensiver und geschlossener als sein späteres Werk. __________________ Once again, it deals with the Partition of India. Here, a young woman stands at the center, trying to hold her family together. The film feels stronger, more direct, and emotionally clearer to me than The Golden Thread . The personal sacrifice of the main character is at the core and becomes almost unbearably tangible. Ghatak creates a melodrama here, but with formal ruptures. And it is precisely these stylistic devices—abrupt cuts, heightened sound effects—that make the film so striking. Deeply sad, powerful, and for me more intense and cohesive than his later work.

[21] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Director- Ritwik Ghatak. This is the first film I have seen of his. The first thing I faced while watching this film was comparing it with other films of the year that were released in the world. However, doing that is a folly, as India, unlike other countries, didn't have a dedicated Cinematic Canon before the generation of Satyajit Ray, Bimal Roy, Ritwik Ghatak, etc. Or so is my opinion, as I have watched seldom of India before the 60s. The music of the film is a highlight for me, and I also appreciated the way the shots were framed. The premise reminded me of Rocco and his Brothers, and I found this film to be a lot better than it because of my hatred for this type of martyrdom. Meghe Dhaka Tara has no clear antagonist, except maybe the intellect of the protagonist for the most part. I chuckled every time she made another dumb decision of self-sacrifice, and then felt sad or cried about it. Folks might watch the film and consider the sister to be evil, but I just find her opportunistic and not a complete narcissist, as she so said that Sanat, the protagonist's boyfriend, has his limits too. Why would he wile away his life waiting for a person who so vehemently tries to lie on the ground and be trampled by others? This time around, I saw it to be much more on the side of anti-martyrdom due to some sequences in the second half. Particularly, the ending where she screams repeatedly, "I want to live". I also liked some scenes where the protagonist talks back at those who have made it their life's mission to screw her over after drying her of everything she has, including her soul and will to live. I liked how the oldest freeloader sibling got verbally thrashed by the younger brother and the shopkeeper. The family indeed mostly comprised of beggars, with the oldest sibling being the main one. He indeed turns his life around later on, but it was too late as the protagonist succumbed to the pressure that was not only loaded on her but which she took enthusiastically. After a point, it indeed felt like this is another run-of-the-mill Pro Martyrdom Selfless Woman suffering for the whole of the runtime slop, as I so believed during my first watch, which made me hate it. But some aspects that offer a more meta view made me look more favorably towards it. I loved the ending where the shopkeeper tells the oldest brother that the family, now living in their second-story house, has completely forgotten the protagonist, because of which their financial progress could happen. This is the fate deserving of those who are dumb enough to fall for such martyrdom. The way she chose a slow and painful process of dying from TB, if not for the oldest brother finding it out, shows us that even after all this time, she really did find pleasure in her dumb behaviour. Her suffering from TB could be considered as a meta commentary too, as TB affected her breathing, and she indeed felt suffocated with her family. One could even view this film through the lens of Giri, responsibility and Ninjo, human desire, where Giri, which dominated her whole life, is the cause of her suffering. She never pursued her Ninjo, and hence her life was devoid of any joy whatsoever. What I really liked about the film is that Ghatak never sensationalises her plight, instead choosing to show the situation as it is. I can see how this would have been groundbreaking for its time but it doesn't age as well as some other films of that era. Such as Waqt, Pyaasa, Kaagaz ke Phool, Awara, Chalti ka naam Gaadi, etc. Overall, a good film, but not something I see myself ever revisiting in the future for the third time.

Hay mucho virtuosismo en la puesta en escena; las imagenes de Ghatak son potentes, complejas. Se atreve a manipular el sonido de manera expresionista, agregando ecos a las voces o incorporando sonidos extradiegéticos casi de cincia ficción, e un intento interesante pero algo tosco y que parece quedar a medio camino. La actriz que interpreta a Nita sorprende en su calma, en un estoicismo que parece convertirse en resignación, parece habitar en una frecuencia distinta a la del resto, su sacrificio la eleva y le da un aire de santidad. Los insertos musicales son bellos, modernos, momentos de escape de la realidad tan cruda. La película es devastadora pero la insistencia en su martirio es tal que se vuelve burda, casi sádica, son todos tan egoístas, tan insensilbles. Esta redundancia en el dolor hace que narrativamente se pierda el rumbo, y se llega en punto en que solo ruego que esto se acabe y que ojalá Nita tenga alguna recompensa, algún atisbo de felicidad. El final es demoledor: con una sencilla rima visual expande el alcance de la historia y la convierte en el drama de muchas otras mujeres.

In The Cloud-Capped Star , director Ritwik Ghatak is interested in how larger social-economic backgrounds impact the daily personal lives and social intimacies of the average person. The life of the individual acts as the catalyst towards these large-scale industrial changes underlying society. The rapid motion of the train in one of the earliest sequences of the film, which travels in the direction of Neeta (the protagonist), mirrors the rapid advancements that industrialization (a catalyst from India’s newfound independence given the context this film was released in) act as a means of rapidly changing the dynamics of the characters’ lives (if only present in the background). The use of music and general sound design functions as an on-the-nose connection between how the characters feel, especially on the metaphorical or metaphysical level. Juxtaposing their personal familial struggles to that of the mythical lyrics of the songs creates the notion that musical numbers function in two contrasting, yet complimentary ways. On the one hand, they harm the overall sense of realism that the film exhibits, but at the same time also work to express the repressed emotional sentiments of the interpersonal relationships of the film's characters that could not otherwise be depicted without music. The aesthetic close-up shots are very prominent, especially in the melodrama which of course allows for the intrigue of personal depth and insight into the emotions of the characters in this film, especially in the scene where Neeta and her brother sing together. This reflects an earlier scene in which Neeta is asked if her and her brother will be singing together, prompting her to say that she gave it up. We later see in the scene where they sing together in the dark room that she is only able to sing in these moments of intimacy and overall personal time. The presence of her brother then, indicates a closeness that she only shares with him as opposed to the rest of her family. Melodrama also functions as a political critique as it focuses on these internal struggles of family that are exacerbated by the advent of rapid industrialization around them.  Melodrama seems to exist in these extreme opposites of who is good and who is bad, but there also exists the historical contradictions within the film. For instance, her father recognizes all the ways in which Neeta is being exploited, but is inevitably the one to kick her out.  This creates a contrast to her internal struggles and the context she exists in. In this way, the film also bears similarities to the Italian Neo-realism film movement, but also cranks the realism up to a heightened level that can only be found in melodrama. Given this understanding we can look back to the train and understand it as a creation with the propensity to bring about Sysiphian repercussions. The train may represent progress, but the fact that the people keep repeating or perpetuating their condition, whether it be asking for donation money or treating Neeta poorly demonstrates that progress must come from both the individuals and society.

THE CLOUD-CAPPED STAR is an Indian melodrama from 1960, filmed in gorgeous black and white.  It's an interesting story about the long-suffering eldest daughter in a formerly genteel Hindu family that has been displaced by the Partition in 1947.  In this family education and "white-collar" employment had been taken for granted, but they are now in a small house in what is basically a refugee camp.  The eldest daughter, Nita, makes some money tutoring, and seems to be the main (or even only) bread-winner.  She is stoic and dutiful to a fault, and spends nothing on herself so her family can scrape by and keep up appearances. Nita reminded me somewhat of George Bailey from IT'S A WONDERFUL LIFE or even Eleanor Dashwood from "Sense and Sensibility."  Except there's no guarantee that things will turn out for the best, or even that Nita's family will be grateful.  CLOUD-CAPPED STAR explores the idea that letting people walk all over you may not do them or you any good. I love that idea, but the style of this movie kept me from loving it on the whole.  It is melodramatic in style as well as substance, and some of the flamboyant, on-the-nose dialog and music detracted from my enjoyment.  There were also many instances where I could tell from the dramatic scoring that something significant had happened, but I didn't have the cultural or historical understanding to know what.  But obviously the way a certain person was dressed in one scene (for instance) was a big deal for some reason, and in another scene a character laughed and smiled at what seemed like a jarringly inappropriate moment.  I'm sure the intended audience would know what was going on, but I was sometimes at a loss.  I didn't even know the importance of the Partition to these characters--I found that out from Wikipedia. I liked this film, and it was certainly interesting throughout, but I was never involved enough emotionally for me to call it great.

Director- Ritwik Ghatak. This is the first film I have seen of his. The first thing I faced while watching this film was comparing it with other films of the year that were released in the world. However, doing that is a folly, as India, unlike other countries, didn't have a dedicated Cinematic Canon before the generation of Satyajit Ray, Bimal Roy, Ritwik Ghatak, etc. Or so is my opinion, as I have watched seldom of India before the 60s. The music of the film is a highlight for me, and I also appreciated the way the shots were framed. The premise reminded me of Rocco and his Brothers, and I found this film to be a lot better than it because of my hatred for this type of martyrdom. Meghe Dhaka Tara has no clear antagonist, except maybe the intellect of the protagonist for the most part. I chuckled every time she made another dumb decision of self-sacrifice, and then felt sad or cried about it. Folks might watch the film and consider the sister to be evil, but I just find her opportunistic and not a complete narcissist, as she so said that Sanat, the protagonist's boyfriend, has his limits too. Why would he wile away his life waiting for a person who so vehemently tries to lie on the ground and be trampled by others? This time around, I saw it to be much more on the side of anti-martyrdom due to some sequences in the second half. Particularly, the ending where she screams repeatedly, "I want to live". I also liked some scenes where the protagonist talks back at those who have made it their life's mission to screw her over after drying her of everything she has, including her soul and will to live. I liked how the oldest freeloader sibling got verbally thrashed by the younger brother and the shopkeeper. The family indeed mostly comprised of beggars, with the oldest sibling being the main one. He indeed turns his life around later on, but it was too late as the protagonist succumbed to the pressure that was not only loaded on her but which she took enthusiastically. After a point, it indeed felt like this is another run-of-the-mill Pro Martyrdom Selfless Woman suffering for the whole of the runtime slop, as I so believed during my first watch, which made me hate it. But some aspects that offer a more meta view made me look more favorably towards it. I loved the ending where the shopkeeper tells the oldest brother that the family, now living in their second-story house, has completely forgotten the protagonist, because of which their financial progress could happen. This is the fate deserving of those who are dumb enough to fall for such martyrdom. The way she chose a slow and painful process of dying from TB, if not for the oldest brother finding it out, shows us that even after all this time, she really did find pleasure in her dumb behaviour. Her suffering from TB could be considered as a meta commentary too, as TB affected her breathing, and she indeed felt suffocated with her family. One could even view this film through the lens of Giri, responsibility and Ninjo, human desire, where Giri, which dominated her whole life, is the cause of her suffering. She never pursued her Ninjo, and hence her life was devoid of any joy whatsoever. What I really liked about the film is that Ghatak never sensationalises her plight, instead choosing to show the situation as it is. I can see how this would have been groundbreaking for its time but it doesn't age as well as some other films of that era. Such as Waqt, Pyaasa, Kaagaz ke Phool, Awara, Chalti ka naam Gaadi, etc. Overall, a good film, but not something I see myself ever revisiting in the future for the third time.

In The Cloud-Capped Star , director Ritwik Ghatak is interested in how larger social-economic backgrounds impact the daily personal lives and social intimacies of the average person. The life of the individual acts as the catalyst towards these large-scale industrial changes underlying society. The rapid motion of the train in one of the earliest sequences of the film, which travels in the direction of Neeta (the protagonist), mirrors the rapid advancements that industrialization (a catalyst from India’s newfound independence given the context this film was released in) act as a means of rapidly changing the dynamics of the characters’ lives (if only present in the background). The use of music and general sound design functions as an on-the-nose connection between how the characters feel, especially on the metaphorical or metaphysical level. Juxtaposing their personal familial struggles to that of the mythical lyrics of the songs creates the notion that musical numbers function in two contrasting, yet complimentary ways. On the one hand, they harm the overall sense of realism that the film exhibits, but at the same time also work to express the repressed emotional sentiments of the interpersonal relationships of the film's characters that could not otherwise be depicted without music. The aesthetic close-up shots are very prominent, especially in the melodrama which of course allows for the intrigue of personal depth and insight into the emotions of the characters in this film, especially in the scene where Neeta and her brother sing together. This reflects an earlier scene in which Neeta is asked if her and her brother will be singing together, prompting her to say that she gave it up. We later see in the scene where they sing together in the dark room that she is only able to sing in these moments of intimacy and overall personal time. The presence of her brother then, indicates a closeness that she only shares with him as opposed to the rest of her family. Melodrama also functions as a political critique as it focuses on these internal struggles of family that are exacerbated by the advent of rapid industrialization around them.  Melodrama seems to exist in these extreme opposites of who is good and who is bad, but there also exists the historical contradictions within the film. For instance, her father recognizes all the ways in which Neeta is being exploited, but is inevitably the one to kick her out.  This creates a contrast to her internal struggles and the context she exists in. In this way, the film also bears similarities to the Italian Neo-realism film movement, but also cranks the realism up to a heightened level that can only be found in melodrama. Given this understanding we can look back to the train and understand it as a creation with the propensity to bring about Sysiphian repercussions. The train may represent progress, but the fact that the people keep repeating or perpetuating their condition, whether it be asking for donation money or treating Neeta poorly demonstrates that progress must come from both the individuals and society.

THE CLOUD-CAPPED STAR is an Indian melodrama from 1960, filmed in gorgeous black and white.  It's an interesting story about the long-suffering eldest daughter in a formerly genteel Hindu family that has been displaced by the Partition in 1947.  In this family education and "white-collar" employment had been taken for granted, but they are now in a small house in what is basically a refugee camp.  The eldest daughter, Nita, makes some money tutoring, and seems to be the main (or even only) bread-winner.  She is stoic and dutiful to a fault, and spends nothing on herself so her family can scrape by and keep up appearances. Nita reminded me somewhat of George Bailey from IT'S A WONDERFUL LIFE or even Eleanor Dashwood from "Sense and Sensibility."  Except there's no guarantee that things will turn out for the best, or even that Nita's family will be grateful.  CLOUD-CAPPED STAR explores the idea that letting people walk all over you may not do them or you any good. I love that idea, but the style of this movie kept me from loving it on the whole.  It is melodramatic in style as well as substance, and some of the flamboyant, on-the-nose dialog and music detracted from my enjoyment.  There were also many instances where I could tell from the dramatic scoring that something significant had happened, but I didn't have the cultural or historical understanding to know what.  But obviously the way a certain person was dressed in one scene (for instance) was a big deal for some reason, and in another scene a character laughed and smiled at what seemed like a jarringly inappropriate moment.  I'm sure the intended audience would know what was going on, but I was sometimes at a loss.  I didn't even know the importance of the Partition to these characters--I found that out from Wikipedia. I liked this film, and it was certainly interesting throughout, but I was never involved enough emotionally for me to call it great.

5.5 DVD The first of Ritwik Ghatak’s films that I have seen (and as I understand it, his most well-known, certainly outside India), The Cloud-Capped Star is a film which has considerable aesthetic beauty, but sadly the simplistic, overwrought melodrama failed to hold my interest through its (excessive) two-hour running time. In terms of visuals, the opening scene in particular is an absolute stunner: our protagonist, Neeta (Supriya Choudhury) walks toward the camera, emerging from beneath the bows of a majestic tree (the camera placed far enough away that its entire massive frame is within shot).  As she draws level with a man singing by the adjacent riverbank (we subsequently learn that this is her brother, Shankar (Anil Chatterjee)), the camera angle changes to a sensational deep focus shot, showing Neeta in close up, Shankar in the middle-distance and finally a train whooshing past in the background.  Whilst nothing in the rest of the film can quite match the brilliance or flamboyance of this opening, Ghatak’s skill as a director (and presumably also Dinen Gupta as cinematographer) is clear throughout the film in terms of the blocking, lighting and framing of each scene, the intimacy and down-to-earth simplicity of which draw clear comparisons to the Italian neorealists, Satyajit Ray’s Apu trilogy and even the Japanese masters Mizoguchi, Naruse and Ozu. At a story level, unfortunately, I am less enthused.  The plot revolves around Neeta and her family, who live in poverty in the suburbs of Calcutta. Neeta is the only person in the family who makes a decent wage; she tries to balance being the breadwinner with persevering with her college studies, however finds it increasingly difficult to do so when her family and even her own fiancée refuse to get jobs themselves, preferring instead to leach off the good-natured Neeta so that they can prioritise their own selfish ambitions. However, after this set-up, The Cloud-Capped Star becomes increasingly and distractingly melodramatic, with misfortune after misfortune heaped upon the protagonist as the film devolves (slowly, agonisingly slowly) into an exercise in brow-beating moralism.  It doesn’t help that without exception the characters are absurdly simplistic: from Neeta, who is little more than a self-sacrificing martyr, to her intensely unlikeable, over-the-top mother to her fiancée, a weak and self-centered man who ends up having an affair with Neeta’s sister.  There is no nuance to any of these characters or the narrative in general (the family’s absurd level of cruelty towards Neeta seems designed simply to provide a contrast with Neeta’s uncomplicated wholesomeness), and as a result the film feels a million miles away from something like Pather Panchali . The other thing to mention is the rather avant-garde sound design, which at times felt like something from a surrealist film, in particular the use of non-diegetic sound effects to portray Neeta’s state of mind.  It’s a matter of taste, but personally I found the sound design rather distracting and distancing, especially within a setting which otherwise emphasises realism. So overall, I was disappointed and, by its end, more than a little bored with The Cloud-Capped Star .  I can see from other reviews on here that the film gets a lot of love and I wish I could share in that, but sadly it just did not work for me.
