The Swimming Pool turns a seemingly idyllic summer holiday into a tense study of desire, jealousy and guilt. Jean-Paul and Marianne appear to enjoy a carefree summer at their secluded villa until Marianne invites her former lover Harry and his daughter Penelope , whose arrival brings old feelings, insecurities, and unspoken resentments to the surface. What I liked most is how the film builds tension through small shifts in behavior rather than constant dramatic confrontation. Jean-Paul becomes increasingly jealous of Harry’s confidence and Marianne’s familiarity with him while Penelope’s presence adds another layer of attraction and uneasiness to the group. The beautiful Mediterranean setting and Alain Delon and Romy Schneider’s restrained performances create an atmosphere that feels both sensual and strangely suffocating. The slow pacing and emotionally distant characters kept me from fully investing but I liked how the film blurs desire, guilt and reality through Jean-Paul’s fears.

The first hour and a half were really great, but the last 30 mins felt longer than the entire film. I didn’t like how the detective was purely suggestive, never assertive — I would’ve loved to have seen a more explosive performance from either Romy or Alain in response to this, it ended up being quite mundane. I liked the confined setting, though characters leave the house often, we never see clips of these places (except the supermarket), building a sense of distrust for the audience as we can’t confirm the answer when another character asks what they were doing. I think the most interesting aspect of this film for me was the setting. The villa conveys a sense of noble and inexorable decay, as if it were a reflection of the protagonists’ age. The near-total absence of a soundtrack creates a sensation akin to a stillness—it doesn’t make the scene oppressive, but it does make it feel heavy, as if mirroring the sweltering heat. The murder is a natural consequence of the protagonists’ actions; they voluntarily decide to start teasing and annoying each other as if it were a game, but it eventually spirals out of control. The two protagonists are no longer so young and are already beginning to show their first wrinkles and imperfections. They aren’t the perfect embodiment of youth, but they don’t seem aged either. They’re in a middle ground, as if suspended in time. Both are beautiful but show the weariness that comes with more years under their belts. The most unrealistic element of the film? How could anyone decide to replace THE Romy Schneider; but above all, how could anyone prefer another man to THE FREAKING ALAIN DELON?

Estoy muy cachondo. Esta película es sensual, sutil, inquietante y perfecta para el verano. Desde la escena de apertura con Alain Delon al borde de la piscina, el erotismo está presente en pantalla en todo momento. De los tíos más guapos que he visto en mi vida. Es la primera película suya que veo y me dieron ganas de ver más, porque tiene una gran presencia en pantalla. Empieza como la fantasía de verano de cualquiera, y poco a poco va construyendo una tensión muy cargada, pero de forma muy natural. Hay que tener algo de paciencia, pero vale la pena porque el clima que crea es increíble, y lo más reseñable es precisamente esa tensión. Cada gesto y cada movimiento dice mucho y da pie a un sinfín de reacciones posibles del resto de personajes, todo presentado con una delicadeza y una estética impecable. La química sexual y esas micro reacciones son lo más importante a la hora de leer a los personajes, porque los principales acontecimientos ni siquiera aparecen en pantalla. No importa lo que haya ocurrido, solo lo que personajes (y tú) crean que ocurrió. Es cierto que cuando ocurre el asesinato y se descarga la tensión la película se hace un poco pesada, pero el final abierto es interesante.

La Piscine é um daqueles filmes que vivem quase exclusivamente daquilo que fica por dizer, senti tensão no silêncio. A narrativa é simples, mas a forma como Jacques Deray manipula o espaço, o tempo e as relações entre as personagens faz com que exista uma tensão constante, mesmo quando aparentemente nada está a acontecer, e foi algo que eu adorei. É um filme que percebe que o desconforto nasce muito antes do conflito e constrói essa sensação com uma subtileza rara. O mais interessante é a maneira como o calor, a piscina e aquela casa isolada deixam de ser apenas cenário e passam a refletir o estado emocional das personagens, tudo parece demasiado confortável, demasiado perfeito, e é precisamente essa aparência de tranquilidade que torna inevitável a implosão. A mise-en-scène é extremamente rigorosa, sem nunca chamar demasiado a atenção para si própria, e isso faz com que cada olhar ou pausa tenha um peso desproporcional. Maurice Ronet introduz uma presença que desestabiliza toda a dinâmica do grupo, eu gosto que não exista propriamente heróis nem vilões, há egos, inseguranças e um desejo constante de validação que acaba por contaminar todas as relações. O filme evita julgamentos morais fáceis e acredito que prefira explorar as ambiguidades que surgem quando o desejo, o ciúme e o orgulho coexistem. Visualmente continua impressionante, a fotografia luminosa nunca contradiz a crescente sensação de inquietação, pelo contrário, parece intensificá-la, e também existe uma elegância quase hedonista na forma como Deray enquadra os corpos e os espaços, mas essa beleza nunca é gratuita, funciona como um contraste permanente com a deterioração psicológica das personagens. O meu interesse, e acho que o interesse geral, nunca esteve em descobrir o que vai acontecer, mas em observar como pequenas fissuras emocionais se transformam em algo irreversível. É um filme sofisticado e psicologicamente muito mais complexo do que eu pensei, mas gostei imenso.

The Swimming Pool turns a seemingly idyllic summer holiday into a tense study of desire, jealousy and guilt. Jean-Paul and Marianne appear to enjoy a carefree summer at their secluded villa until Marianne invites her former lover Harry and his daughter Penelope , whose arrival brings old feelings, insecurities, and unspoken resentments to the surface. What I liked most is how the film builds tension through small shifts in behavior rather than constant dramatic confrontation. Jean-Paul becomes increasingly jealous of Harry’s confidence and Marianne’s familiarity with him while Penelope’s presence adds another layer of attraction and uneasiness to the group. The beautiful Mediterranean setting and Alain Delon and Romy Schneider’s restrained performances create an atmosphere that feels both sensual and strangely suffocating. The slow pacing and emotionally distant characters kept me from fully investing but I liked how the film blurs desire, guilt and reality through Jean-Paul’s fears.

The near-total absence of a soundtrack creates a sensation akin to a stillness—it doesn’t make the scene oppressive, but it does make it feel heavy, as if mirroring the sweltering heat. The murder is a natural consequence of the protagonists’ actions; they voluntarily decide to start teasing and annoying each other as if it were a game, but it eventually spirals out of control. The two protagonists are no longer so young and are already beginning to show their first wrinkles and imperfections. They aren’t the perfect embodiment of youth, but they don’t seem aged either. La Piscine é um daqueles filmes que vivem quase exclusivamente daquilo que fica por dizer, senti tensão no silêncio. A narrativa é simples, mas a forma como Jacques Deray manipula o espaço, o tempo e as relações entre as personagens faz com que exista uma tensão constante, mesmo quando aparentemente nada está a acontecer, e foi algo que eu adorei. É um filme que percebe que o desconforto nasce muito antes do conflito e constrói essa sensação com uma subtileza rara. O mais interessante é a maneira como o calor, a piscina e aquela casa isolada deixam de ser apenas cenário e passam a refletir o estado emocional das personagens, tudo parece demasiado confortável, demasiado perfeito, e é precisamente essa aparência de tranquilidade que torna inevitável a implosão. A mise-en-scène é extremamente rigorosa, sem nunca chamar demasiado a atenção para si própria, e isso faz com que cada olhar ou pausa tenha um peso desproporcional. Maurice Ronet introduz uma presença que desestabiliza toda a dinâmica do grupo, eu gosto que não exista propriamente heróis nem vilões, há egos, inseguranças e um desejo constante de validação que acaba por contaminar todas as relações. O filme evita julgamentos morais fáceis e acredito que prefira explorar as ambiguidades que surgem quando o desejo, o ciúme e o orgulho coexistem. Visualmente continua impressionante, a fotografia luminosa nunca contradiz a crescente sensação de inquietação, pelo contrário, parece intensificá-la, e também existe uma elegância quase hedonista na forma como Deray enquadra os corpos e os espaços, mas essa beleza nunca é gratuita, funciona como um contraste permanente com a deterioração psicológica das personagens. O meu interesse, e acho que o interesse geral, nunca esteve em descobrir o que vai acontecer, mas em observar como pequenas fissuras emocionais se transformam em algo irreversível. É um filme sofisticado e psicologicamente muito mais complexo do que eu pensei, mas gostei imenso.

Unfortunately, I believe this is one of those films where the concept and premise far surpasses how it is actually presented on screen. The whole plot feels like a rush to get Truman to discover the truth, rather than spending time with this pre-established world that could present a unique dynamic between characters. Culturally influencial but not the masterpiece it is often told to be. 6/10

Unfortunately, I believe this is one of those films where the concept and premise far surpasses how it is actually presented on screen. The whole plot feels like a rush to get Truman to discover the truth, rather than spending time with this pre-established world that could present a unique dynamic between characters. Culturally influencial but not the masterpiece it is often told to be. 6/10

The premise is too horrific and too impracticable for me to buy into. A corporation acquires a baby, imprisons him for 30 years, deliberately traumatizes him by staging his father’s death, manipulates every intimate relationship he has, prevents him from leaving through phobias and coercion, and broadcasts his entire existence for profit. I get that it's a satire. But there’s a realism problem. This isn’t merely exploitative reality television. It’s a human-rights atrocity happening in public. Where are the protesters? Lawyers? Governments? Religious groups? Journalists? People trying to break into the dome? Sylvia is essentially the only person behaving the way you’d expect millions of people to behave. The movie wants the audience to make the comparison to celebrity/Hollywood/reality TV -- but for me that was asking too much. I don't think celebs or reality tv stars are victims. Truman is. The logistics also become ridiculous if you think about them for 30 seconds. The number of people required to sustain this conspiracy, the legal structure permitting it, airspace, utilities, medical care, education, sex and reproduction, emergency situations, Truman’s legal identity, outsiders getting in, employees never exposing it, governments allowing it—the movie simply says, essentially, don’t think about that. I get that people love this movie for its message and the satire. It just wasn't for me.

The movie wants the audience to make the comparison to celebrity/Hollywood/reality TV -- but for me that was asking too much. I don't think celebs or reality tv stars are victims. Truman is. The logistics also become ridiculous if you think about them for 30 seconds. The number of people required to sustain this conspiracy, the legal structure permitting it, airspace, utilities, medical care, education, sex and reproduction, emergency situations, Truman’s legal identity, outsiders getting in, employees never exposing it, governments allowing it—the movie simply says, essentially, don’t think about that. The Truman show. Dirigida por Peter Weir. (1998) La película sigue a Truman Burbank, un hombre que descubre que su vida es un programa muy popular de televisión, pero debajo de esa premisa hay una película bastante inquietante sobre la libertad, la identidad, el control y nuestra necesidad de sentir que nuestra vida nos pertenece. Seahaven es prácticamente perfecto; es una pequeña isla con calles limpias, vecinos amables y casas bonitas. Todo eso está diseñado para que Truman no tenga motivos para querer irse de Seahaven. Prácticamente está encerrado por una rutina, y la manipulación constante. Su miedo al agua, por ejemplo, fue creado deliberadamente para impedirle abandonar la isla. No necesitan poner una pared delante de él si consiguen que él mismo crea que no puede atravesarla. •Al igual que Christof no se considera un villano. Él cree que le está dando a Truman una vida segura y auténtica dentro de un mundo diseñado exclusivamente para él. Y ahí está una de las partes más interesantes: Christof confunde conocer completamente a una persona con tener derecho y control sobre ella. Decide quiénes son sus amigos, quién será su esposa, dónde vivirá, qué verá y qué temerá. Incluso controla las circunstancias de sus relaciones. Es una forma extrema de paternalismo: "Yo sé qué es mejor para ti, aunque tú no lo sepas." •Sylvia es fundamental porque ella le dice, de alguna manera, que aquello que considera normal no es normal. Ella se convierte en la primera grieta de su realidad. La segunda fue sin duda la repentina aparición de su padre, el cual, en su historia, estaba muerto. En resumen. The Truman Show no trata solamente sobre un hombre que descubre que vive dentro de un programa de televisión. Trata sobre atreverse a cuestionar la realidad que nos entregaron. Y o sea fuera del tono serio, que miedo. Él realmente pensaba que se estaba volviendo loco. ¿Cómo podrías comprobarte a ti mismo que no estás alucinando cuando todos te dicen que es la realidad? Tipo, su mejor amigo desde los 7 años seguía un guión. Ay no, literalmente podría ser un episodio de black mirror. "In case I don't see ya. Good afternoon, good evening and good night" -Truman.

Jim Carrey's bombastic positivity matched with Ed Harris' flat-cap-wearing cruelty make this war over a world ...nearly enchanting. The Truman show is a rare thing, in that it gives itself away immediately, the wool is pulled back for the viewers so we, on our couches, are in step with all the characters and viewers slobbering on their couches within this world. The meta-handshake happens the moment we cue this one up. But don't be fooled, this is a film about cruelty, torture, and deception on a scale the likes of which too many of us might fail to notice hits too close to home. It is good art in the sense that this is a film that comments on something we were headed for... and now live within. Its relevance came to us, over time. So much of so much of this film is ubiquitous at this point. We watch it and shrug and fail to see that Carrey looking at himself in the mirror, ought to be us looking in the mirror. We watch him, watching himself... but the smoke and mirrors movie magic of it all is that it is us he is talking to, not himself - he is calling out for us to break out of the world we've been presented with, to question the nature of the system we live within. It doesn't hurt that he is willing to die to find the truth, a new reality, to push back against the status quo. But my lord, when you realize that he is walking into a world which has gleefully watched him be caged and lied to for a lifetime, that that is the choice he chooses... you begin to see that the overlord's offer is a better deal than its surface might suggest. This one ends where it should, before you see Carrey see people who love him vicariously, who want to meet him, who care for him as the celebrity of their own twisted obsessions to see people controlled. But maybe love is enough to blind him to reality? But once the gig is up, once the cruelty has transformed and lost its juice, us, just like those parking cops at the end, turn the channel to see what else is on.

“In case I don’t see ya, good afternoon, good evening, and good night!” What would you do if you found out that your entire life was fake? Every person in your life an actor dedicated to keeping you from discovering the truth. Every waking moment of your life broadcast to an audience that you don’t even know exists. Every aspect of your existence, from your job, to your marriage, even your birth; all meticulously scripted by an unseen hand with the intention of garnering ratings and views. It’s a profoundly existential concept, fit for an equally existential film. Jim Carrey’s best roles are ones where he can be emotional, yet still have moments that allow him to go off the rails when its appropriate, and his performance in this is a toss up with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind as a career best. Even though we the audience are privy to the fact that Truman’s life is an illusion from the very beginning, it still doesn’t make it any less devastating as Truman’s reality begins to unravel around him, thanks in no small part to Carrey’s fantastic performance. It’s no wonder he won over the hearts of so many viewers. Obviously everyone already knows about the brilliant commentary this film has on reality TV and celebrity culture, but this film is so rich with thematic depth that that’s only the tip of the iceberg. One could easily point out the film’s criticism of mass surveilance, which is more topical now than ever with Flock cameras popping up on every street corner. Coinciding with that, The Truman Show (the fictional show, not to be confused with the movie about said fictional show) is really an idealized vision of the long-outdated American Dream. As a child, Truman dreamt of exploring the world and taking in everything that life has to offer, but his dreams were shot down by the authority figures in his life. Now he lives in a copy-pasted suburban house, working a 9-5 cushy desk job day after day, returning home to a bland loveless marriage and a mortgage that will likely never be paid off; living in blissful ignorance of the world outside of his little pocket of suburbia. It’s a role that, as Americans, we’re expected to fill no matter what, and any deviation from that role is tantamount to heresy. Coupled with the constant bombardment of product placements and advertisements throughout his life, it’s clear that Truman’s false reality is a picture-perfect snapshot of life within a capitalist/consumerist system; a safe and comfortable existence, but one that is ultimately neither fulfilling nor sustainable. And yet, Truman still yearns to follow his heart and do what gives him joy and meaning, and so he must break free from the confines of the system, and in doing so find that meaning and fulfillment he’s been searching for his whole life. With Truman questioning his place in both society and the world at large, it’s no surprise that his breaking of the status quo incur wrath of both the systemic and divine variety. Christof, (whose name is emblematic of another certain religious figure) is not just the voice of the corporate backers of the show, but also the literal god of Truman’s reality. He’s also an enigmatic control freak with a god complex, and brought to life by a great performance from Ed Harris. Similarly to his presentation as a god-like figure, he also represents a concept not too dissimilar to 1984’s Big Brother; a controlling force dominating society with an all-seeing-eye (or in this case, moon) that eliminates any individual’s sense of privacy. Truman’s defiance against him is not only an act of rebellion against authority, but also metaphorically and literally standing in defiance of his god, Christof, whose divine edicts boom down from the heavens. Truman chooses not to follow the path chosen for him in Christof’s divine plan, but to carve out his own story and forge his own destiny, a concept that Christof, simply cannot fathom, and therein lies his folly. The scene in which these events take place has got to be one of my favorite endings to a film. I mean, you’ve all seen the shots by now, they’re just incredible. We may never know what happened to Truman. Maybe he reunited with Sylvia, and the two sailed off into the sunset, bound for Fiji. Maybe he lived a life constantly oppressed by paparazzi, as so many celebrities of his status are. Or maybe he just faded into obscurity after being cast out of the limelight. We’ll never know, but the point isn’t the story itself, it’s the concept of not following a story written for you, but to write one for yourself.

The Truman show. Dirigida por Peter Weir. (1998) La película sigue a Truman Burbank, un hombre que descubre que su vida es un programa muy popular de televisión, pero debajo de esa premisa hay una película bastante inquietante sobre la libertad, la identidad, el control y nuestra necesidad de sentir que nuestra vida nos pertenece. Seahaven es prácticamente perfecto; es una pequeña isla con calles limpias, vecinos amables y casas bonitas. Todo eso está diseñado para que Truman no tenga motivos para querer irse de Seahaven. Prácticamente está encerrado por una rutina, y la manipulación constante. Su miedo al agua, por ejemplo, fue creado deliberadamente para impedirle abandonar la isla. No necesitan poner una pared delante de él si consiguen que él mismo crea que no puede atravesarla. •Al igual que Christof no se considera un villano. Él cree que le está dando a Truman una vida segura y auténtica dentro de un mundo diseñado exclusivamente para él. Y ahí está una de las partes más interesantes: Christof confunde conocer completamente a una persona con tener derecho y control sobre ella. Decide quiénes son sus amigos, quién será su esposa, dónde vivirá, qué verá y qué temerá. Incluso controla las circunstancias de sus relaciones. Es una forma extrema de paternalismo: "Yo sé qué es mejor para ti, aunque tú no lo sepas." •Sylvia es fundamental porque ella le dice, de alguna manera, que aquello que considera normal no es normal. Ella se convierte en la primera grieta de su realidad. La segunda fue sin duda la repentina aparición de su padre, el cual, en su historia, estaba muerto. En resumen. The Truman Show no trata solamente sobre un hombre que descubre que vive dentro de un programa de televisión. Trata sobre atreverse a cuestionar la realidad que nos entregaron. Y o sea fuera del tono serio, que miedo. Él realmente pensaba que se estaba volviendo loco. ¿Cómo podrías comprobarte a ti mismo que no estás alucinando cuando todos te dicen que es la realidad? Tipo, su mejor amigo desde los 7 años seguía un guión. Ay no, literalmente podría ser un episodio de black mirror. "In case I don't see ya. Good afternoon, good evening and good night" -Truman.

Jim Carrey's bombastic positivity matched with Ed Harris' flat-cap-wearing cruelty make this war over a world ...nearly enchanting. The Truman show is a rare thing, in that it gives itself away immediately, the wool is pulled back for the viewers so we, on our couches, are in step with all the characters and viewers slobbering on their couches within this world. The meta-handshake happens the moment we cue this one up. But don't be fooled, this is a film about cruelty, torture, and deception on a scale the likes of which too many of us might fail to notice hits too close to home. It is good art in the sense that this is a film that comments on something we were headed for... and now live within. Its relevance came to us, over time. So much of so much of this film is ubiquitous at this point. We watch it and shrug and fail to see that Carrey looking at himself in the mirror, ought to be us looking in the mirror. We watch him, watching himself... but the smoke and mirrors movie magic of it all is that it is us he is talking to, not himself - he is calling out for us to break out of the world we've been presented with, to question the nature of the system we live within. It doesn't hurt that he is willing to die to find the truth, a new reality, to push back against the status quo. But my lord, when you realize that he is walking into a world which has gleefully watched him be caged and lied to for a lifetime, that that is the choice he chooses... you begin to see that the overlord's offer is a better deal than its surface might suggest. This one ends where it should, before you see Carrey see people who love him vicariously, who want to meet him, who care for him as the celebrity of their own twisted obsessions to see people controlled. But maybe love is enough to blind him to reality? But once the gig is up, once the cruelty has transformed and lost its juice, us, just like those parking cops at the end, turn the channel to see what else is on.

“In case I don’t see ya, good afternoon, good evening, and good night!” What would you do if you found out that your entire life was fake? Every person in your life an actor dedicated to keeping you from discovering the truth. Every waking moment of your life broadcast to an audience that you don’t even know exists. Every aspect of your existence, from your job, to your marriage, even your birth; all meticulously scripted by an unseen hand with the intention of garnering ratings and views. It’s a profoundly existential concept, fit for an equally existential film. Jim Carrey’s best roles are ones where he can be emotional, yet still have moments that allow him to go off the rails when its appropriate, and his performance in this is a toss up with Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind as a career best. Even though we the audience are privy to the fact that Truman’s life is an illusion from the very beginning, it still doesn’t make it any less devastating as Truman’s reality begins to unravel around him, thanks in no small part to Carrey’s fantastic performance. It’s no wonder he won over the hearts of so many viewers. Obviously everyone already knows about the brilliant commentary this film has on reality TV and celebrity culture, but this film is so rich with thematic depth that that’s only the tip of the iceberg. One could easily point out the film’s criticism of mass surveilance, which is more topical now than ever with Flock cameras popping up on every street corner. Coinciding with that, The Truman Show (the fictional show, not to be confused with the movie about said fictional show) is really an idealized vision of the long-outdated American Dream. As a child, Truman dreamt of exploring the world and taking in everything that life has to offer, but his dreams were shot down by the authority figures in his life. Now he lives in a copy-pasted suburban house, working a 9-5 cushy desk job day after day, returning home to a bland loveless marriage and a mortgage that will likely never be paid off; living in blissful ignorance of the world outside of his little pocket of suburbia. It’s a role that, as Americans, we’re expected to fill no matter what, and any deviation from that role is tantamount to heresy. Coupled with the constant bombardment of product placements and advertisements throughout his life, it’s clear that Truman’s false reality is a picture-perfect snapshot of life within a capitalist/consumerist system; a safe and comfortable existence, but one that is ultimately neither fulfilling nor sustainable. And yet, Truman still yearns to follow his heart and do what gives him joy and meaning, and so he must break free from the confines of the system, and in doing so find that meaning and fulfillment he’s been searching for his whole life. With Truman questioning his place in both society and the world at large, it’s no surprise that his breaking of the status quo incur wrath of both the systemic and divine variety. Christof, (whose name is emblematic of another certain religious figure) is not just the voice of the corporate backers of the show, but also the literal god of Truman’s reality. He’s also an enigmatic control freak with a god complex, and brought to life by a great performance from Ed Harris. Similarly to his presentation as a god-like figure, he also represents a concept not too dissimilar to 1984’s Big Brother; a controlling force dominating society with an all-seeing-eye (or in this case, moon) that eliminates any individual’s sense of privacy. Truman’s defiance against him is not only an act of rebellion against authority, but also metaphorically and literally standing in defiance of his god, Christof, whose divine edicts boom down from the heavens. Truman chooses not to follow the path chosen for him in Christof’s divine plan, but to carve out his own story and forge his own destiny, a concept that Christof, simply cannot fathom, and therein lies his folly. The scene in which these events take place has got to be one of my favorite endings to a film. I mean, you’ve all seen the shots by now, they’re just incredible. We may never know what happened to Truman. Maybe he reunited with Sylvia, and the two sailed off into the sunset, bound for Fiji. Maybe he lived a life constantly oppressed by paparazzi, as so many celebrities of his status are. Or maybe he just faded into obscurity after being cast out of the limelight. We’ll never know, but the point isn’t the story itself, it’s the concept of not following a story written for you, but to write one for yourself.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"
    }
  ],
  "observacao_geral": "<1-2 frases>"
}

[1] nota=2.5 estrelas:
I'm on vacation and I decided to sit down for a rewatch of this one, with company this time. The first watch was unbearable to me, like a fucking endurance test. So I wanted to see if my experience would be the same. My rating went up a point, but still, this movie is the most torturous thing I've ever watched. Cinematically, this is one of the best things I've ever witnessed. The thing is, the whole vibe and repetition of things just make me wanna peel off my skin and eat it. I think that might kinda be the point here. I also have to clarify that I'm a big Nietzsche fangirl, but I guess I'm kinda dumb too because I could only understand the movie after reading countless reviews or explanations to get it. And yeah, I like what it represents or has to say, but if I have to read about it to get it, uh I think that makes the experience worse. Anyway, I appreciate this movie a lot, especially the cinematography and its message. But it's still one of the most torturous things you can make me watch. And don't get me started on those potatoes..

''Werckmeister harmonies aura été d'une incroyable incroyable accessibilité en comparaison de ceci'' J'apprécie beaucoup le cinéma contemplatif, lent ou sans beaucoup de réels dialogues. Si ce n'est que l'expérience dans ces cas là passe souvent en priorité par la mise en scène. Si on place par exemple Terrence Malick à ce niveau sur une extrémité de ce spectre avec une mise en scène extrêmement dense et foisonnante, je pense que l'on peut placer Bela Tarr à son autre extrémité. C'est L'austérité pure. Une maisonnette isolée durant une tempête et de la répétition à tout les niveaux : Des plans fixes interminables, un thème musical unique rejoué en boucle une douzaine de fois, un vent qui souffle pendant deux heures trente, de la gestuelle répétée. Cela n'a même pas le sens que cela peut prendre chez Jeanne Dielmann. Bela ne nous donne rien et on doit faire avec. Qu'est ce qui fait que je ne ressens rien, que ça été une expérience extrêmement sensorielle agressive et éprouvante pour moi par rapport à tant de personnes qui ont aimé. Ça me semble plus intéressant comme réflexion que de trouver un sens au film en lui même.

I seem to remember Werckmeister Harmonies as one of the least enjoyable film experiences I’d had up to that time. I have, however, since then acquired a taste for slow films in which nothing happens. In other contexts at least - usually Asian. So I’m hanging out with Bela Tarr again to test my cineaste bonafides, and it’s slightly better this time, but still not for me. A father and daughter living in a small shack in the countryside is subject to unexplained misfortunes - they wake up one day and their well has dried up. The horse stops eating and working. Apocalypse surrounds them, as gales howl, and it appears that nature is abandoning them, humble as their life is. It’s all shot in this transcendent style, with long takes and slow moving cameras, and a beautifully deliberate use of zooms and framing. The black and white photography is lovely. The glacial pace is arguably appropriate in depicting this slow death of a family. Trust me, I get it. It’s just not particularly enjoyable, edifying, or enlightening. Only in small moments do the images suck you in to a point of flow. You’re never out of analysis mode. (When we observe the cart outside the house, we know in advance that Tarr is going to make us watch the entire thing be unloaded). If there’s a lack on my part, I guess that it’s not because I don’t understand it, or that I’m a Tik-Tok-addled millennial, but I’m simply not at a level of Zen not to let thought take over in the long scenes of people eating potatoes. There may come a time when I’m capable, but not yet. Still to come is all 400-so minutes of Satantango .

[8] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Olha… The Turin Horse é aquele tipo de filme que você respeita mais do que gosta. Dirigido por Béla Tarr, ele tem uma proposta claramente artística e até fascinante em teoria, mas na prática, pode ser extremamente cansativo. A rotina repetitiva do pai e da filha, comendo batata e encarando o vento infinito, até funciona como metáfora no começo. Você entende a ideia: o esgotamento da vida, o peso da existência, o mundo “apagando”. Só que chega um ponto em que o filme parece preso nessa mesma repetição e não evolui o suficiente pra sustentar o interesse. Visualmente, o filme é lindo. O preto e branco, os planos longos, a atmosfera pesada… tudo muito bem construído. Mas ao mesmo tempo, o ritmo é tão arrastado que acaba afastando mais do que envolvendo. Em vez de te puxar pra experiência, ele pode simplesmente te cansar. E aí fica aquela sensação: você entende o que o filme quer dizer, mas não necessariamente sente vontade de continuar ali. No fim, é um filme com intenção, estética e conceito fortes, mas que sacrifica demais o envolvimento em nome da proposta. Pra alguns vai ser uma obra-prima contemplativa; pra outros (como no meu caso), uma experiência interessante… só que arrastada demais pra realmente marcar. Bonito, simbólico e cheio de significado mas também excessivamente lento e pouco envolvente. Um daqueles que você admira mais do que gosta!!

The longer it runs, the more you notice all the small issues. Acting isn't great and all the repetition wears out even the aspects that I was initially really into. The music itself has a very nice tone, but it's repeated to such an extent, it's completely ruined after some point. I like a lot of what it's going for and there is a lot to analyze thematically. Béla Tarr is damn good at capturing the feeling of human suffering, but the experience of watching it is often frustrating in ways that don't seem intentional.

The Turin Horse stands as an unapologetic, uncompromising monument to apocalyptic nihilism. Opening with the famous anecdote of Friedrich Nietzsche’s mental collapse after witnessing a cabman whip a stubborn horse in Turin, the film shifts its gaze away from the philosopher to focus instead on the horse, its aging owner, and his daughter. Over six days, Béla Tarr meticulously tracks the slow, relentless unraveling of their basic existence. Shot in stark monochrome, the film is a mesmerizing work of pure atmosphere—its hypnotic rhythm and austere visuals immersing viewers in a vision of existential collapse. Unyielding in its artistic conviction, The Turin Horse offers a rare, uncompromising meditation on the futility of human struggle. It is a work that will resonate deeply with purists of extreme slow cinema, commanding respect for its bleak beauty and unwavering dedication to form.

Le Cheval de Turin est un film qui semble d’abord réduit à une sensation : le vent. Un vent incessant, presque agressif, qui empêche toute respiration et finit par envahir tout le film. Béla Tarr ne cherche pas à raconter une histoire mais à faire ressentir une fin, une extinction lente, silencieuse, sans explication. C’est un film difficile à commenter parce qu’il refuse le discours : on ne le comprend pas vraiment, on le subit.

Tak jak śmierć Davida Lyncha w zeszłym roku zmotywowała mnie do nadrobienia jego filmografii, tak odejście Béla Tarra sprawiło, że postanowiłem obejrzeć "Koń turyński". Niestety nie znalazłem wielu innych jego dzieł z polskimi napisami. Koń, którego niegdyś Nietzsche ocalił przed cierpieniem ze strony woźnicy, zaczyna niedomagać - odmawia jedzenia i pracy. Film opowiada też historię woźnicy i jego córki. Zdziwiłem się, że opowieść László Krasznahorkaia, którą obecnie czytam, stała się zaczątkiem dla ostatniego filmu węgierskiego mistrza kina. To było bardzo długie, 155 minut mojego życia. Nie jestem pewien, czy to nie był najmniej dynamiczny seans, jaki widziałem. Musiałem obejrzeć go w dwóch częściach, bo za pierwszym razem zasnąłem. Dlatego wydaje mi się, że próg wejścia jest bardzo wysoki dla przeciętnego widza. Ja ledwo przez niego przebrnąłem. To ponury, surowy i smutny obraz o wyraźnie apokaliptycznym klimacie. Jednocześnie urzekły mnie zdjęcia Freda Kelemena. Bohaterowie wykonują codziennie te same czynności, popadają w rutynę. Prawdopodobnie na długo zapamiętam odgłos wiatru, który towarzyszy nam niemal cały czas. Z jednej strony było to mocne, niezwykle pesymistyczne doświadczenie, w którym przez sześć dni świat powoli się kończy. Z drugiej, nie był to najciekawszy seans w moim życiu. Nie wiedziałem, że końcem świata będzie codzienne zajadanie się pulkami. "Koń turyński" to film, który imponuje artystycznie (atmosfera, zdjęcia), ale jest naprawdę ciężki w odbiorze, i to nie musi być wadą, lecz jego charakterem. Czy w Polsce mogę gdzieś obejrzeć inne dzieła tego reżysera, najlepiej z napisami polskimi?

''Werckmeister harmonies aura été d'une incroyable incroyable accessibilité en comparaison de ceci'' J'apprécie beaucoup le cinéma contemplatif, lent ou sans beaucoup de réels dialogues. Si ce n'est que l'expérience dans ces cas là passe souvent en priorité par la mise en scène. Si on place par exemple Terrence Malick à ce niveau sur une extrémité de ce spectre avec une mise en scène extrêmement dense et foisonnante, je pense que l'on peut placer Bela Tarr à son autre extrémité. C'est L'austérité pure. Une maisonnette isolée durant une tempête et de la répétition à tout les niveaux : Des plans fixes interminables, un thème musical unique rejoué en boucle une douzaine de fois, un vent qui souffle pendant deux heures trente, de la gestuelle répétée. Cela n'a même pas le sens que cela peut prendre chez Jeanne Dielmann. Bela ne nous donne rien et on doit faire avec. Qu'est ce qui fait que je ne ressens rien, que ça été une expérience extrêmement sensorielle agressive et éprouvante pour moi par rapport à tant de personnes qui ont aimé. I seem to remember Werckmeister Harmonies as one of the least enjoyable film experiences I’d had up to that time. I have, however, since then acquired a taste for slow films in which nothing happens. In other contexts at least - usually Asian. So I’m hanging out with Bela Tarr again to test my cineaste bonafides, and it’s slightly better this time, but still not for me. A father and daughter living in a small shack in the countryside is subject to unexplained misfortunes - they wake up one day and their well has dried up. The horse stops eating and working. Apocalypse surrounds them, as gales howl, and it appears that nature is abandoning them, humble as their life is. It’s all shot in this transcendent style, with long takes and slow moving cameras, and a beautifully deliberate use of zooms and framing. The black and white photography is lovely. The glacial pace is arguably appropriate in depicting this slow death of a family. Trust me, I get it. It’s just not particularly enjoyable, edifying, or enlightening. Olha… The Turin Horse é aquele tipo de filme que você respeita mais do que gosta. Dirigido por Béla Tarr, ele tem uma proposta claramente artística e até fascinante em teoria, mas na prática, pode ser extremamente cansativo. A rotina repetitiva do pai e da filha, comendo batata e encarando o vento infinito, até funciona como metáfora no começo. Você entende a ideia: o esgotamento da vida, o peso da existência, o mundo “apagando”. Só que chega um ponto em que o filme parece preso nessa mesma repetição e não evolui o suficiente pra sustentar o interesse. Visualmente, o filme é lindo. Em vez de te puxar pra experiência, ele pode simplesmente te cansar. E aí fica aquela sensação: você entende o que o filme quer dizer, mas não necessariamente sente vontade de continuar ali. No fim, é um filme com intenção, estética e conceito fortes, mas que sacrifica demais o envolvimento em nome da proposta. Pra alguns vai ser uma obra-prima contemplativa; pra outros (como no meu caso), uma experiência interessante… só que arrastada demais pra realmente marcar. Bonito, simbólico e cheio de significado mas também excessivamente lento e pouco envolvente. Um daqueles que você admira mais do que gosta!!

The Turin Horse stands as an unapologetic, uncompromising monument to apocalyptic nihilism. Opening with the famous anecdote of Friedrich Nietzsche’s mental collapse after witnessing a cabman whip a stubborn horse in Turin, the film shifts its gaze away from the philosopher to focus instead on the horse, its aging owner, and his daughter. Over six days, Béla Tarr meticulously tracks the slow, relentless unraveling of their basic existence. Shot in stark monochrome, the film is a mesmerizing work of pure atmosphere—its hypnotic rhythm and austere visuals immersing viewers in a vision of existential collapse. Unyielding in its artistic conviction, The Turin Horse offers a rare, uncompromising meditation on the futility of human struggle. It is a work that will resonate deeply with purists of extreme slow cinema, commanding respect for its bleak beauty and unwavering dedication to form.

À part cette force naturelle, il ne se passe presque rien, et c’est précisément ce “rien” qui déroute. Le quotidien se répète, les gestes s’épuisent, le monde paraît se vider de son sens. Béla Tarr ne cherche pas à raconter une histoire mais à faire ressentir une fin, une extinction lente, silencieuse, sans explication. C’est un film difficile à commenter parce qu’il refuse le discours : on ne le comprend pas vraiment, on le subit.

Niestety nie znalazłem wielu innych jego dzieł z polskimi napisami. Koń, którego niegdyś Nietzsche ocalił przed cierpieniem ze strony woźnicy, zaczyna niedomagać - odmawia jedzenia i pracy. Film opowiada też historię woźnicy i jego córki. Zdziwiłem się, że opowieść László Krasznahorkaia, którą obecnie czytam, stała się zaczątkiem dla ostatniego filmu węgierskiego mistrza kina. Prawdopodobnie na długo zapamiętam odgłos wiatru, który towarzyszy nam niemal cały czas. Z jednej strony było to mocne, niezwykle pesymistyczne doświadczenie, w którym przez sześć dni świat powoli się kończy. Z drugiej, nie był to najciekawszy seans w moim życiu. "Koń turyński" to film, który imponuje artystycznie (atmosfera, zdjęcia), ale jest naprawdę ciężki w odbiorze, i to nie musi być wadą, lecz jego charakterem. The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.

Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. I come away from this thinking there are two possible reasons for this decision by the filmmaker. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. The cart is before the horse; this man just wants to show us he has the capacity to make a long, slow movie. A massive waste of time.

La película empieza poderosa, en medio de la tempestad, un hombre con su caballo intentando que el viento no se los lleve, una música ensordecedora y te meten una cita de Nietzsche en una transición igual de magnífica que el comienzo. Esos son los primeros cinco minutos de película, parecía pometedor y luego ves al hombre entrando en su rutina, se mete a casa y... empiezan a comer papas. Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. No pasa nada, no pasa más nada. Bien, me quieres vender la cotidianidad, pero, ¿me tenías que hacerme tragar la rutina de varios días del mismo hombre comiéndose unas papas? Más o menos a mitad de película llega un sujeto a la casa y dije: finalmente se dignaron a que pasara algo. Pero no, el sujeto era una herramienta al espectador para darnos contexto de toda la situación, pero la actuación es pobre y es una inmediata verborrea con toques líricos y poco destellos narrativos. Perfectamente la película se pudo haber terminado con el hombre comiendo papas y hubiese sido la misma basura. Decepcionante, aburrida y muy pobremente escrita. I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

The Betrayal of the Horse: When a Horse Becomes a Verdict “This is my horse!” Mikolka cried, bringing the shaft down with a heavy blow. “Beat her to death! Why don’t you beat her?” someone shouted from the crowd. Mikolka raised the shaft again. The wretched horse collapsed on her haunches, then struggled up and tried once more to pull the cart. Six whips lashed her from every side. The shaft fell again, then again, with a terrible rhythm, as Mikolka, almost mad with rage, seemed determined to kill her in a single blow. The scene comes from Dostoevsky’s Crime and Punishment. Before Raskolnikov acts on his theory of the “extraordinary man,” he dreams of himself as a child watching a horse beaten to death. He runs to her, embraces her bloody head, kisses it, then clenches his small fists and throws himself at the man who has killed her. The dream is one of the novel’s great flashes of moral revelation. It exposes the compassion in Raskolnikov that theory has not yet destroyed. It also announces that his path will not end in the cold triumph of an idea, but in guilt, suffering, and redemption. History later produced a harsher joke. On 3 January 1889, Nietzsche is said to have seen a horse being whipped in Turin’s Piazza Carlo Alberto. According to the legend, he rushed forward in tears, threw his arms around the horse’s neck, and collapsed into madness. The story is probably apocryphal, a myth shaped after the fact, but it remains irresistible because it gives the philosopher of the Antichrist an almost Christ-like final gesture. Nietzsche, who called for the Übermensch and attacked pity as part of slave morality, is remembered as a broken man weeping over an animal. The irony is exact and cruel. The philosopher who distrusted pity is given an image of absolute pity. The voice that summoned the superman is turned into a figure of helplessness. Posterity betrayed Nietzsche by remembering him through the very kind of moral drama he would have despised. So where did the horse go? László Krasznahorkai once asked Béla Tarr that question, and the question became the origin of The Turin Horse. Tarr’s film imagines what happened after the famous Nietzsche anecdote. It takes the horse from the legend and places it in a wind-battered world of stone, mud, potatoes, silence, and extinguishing light. The problem with The Turin Horse is not its pessimism. Pessimism can still breathe. It can remain unstable, open to accident, alert to small changes in a body, a gesture, a glance, a delay. Tarr’s film is more severe than that. It turns pessimism into a verdict. Every object enters the frame already sentenced: the horse, the well, the potato, the lamp, the window, the wind. They do not move toward meaning. They have been assigned meaning in advance. Tarr begins with a horse and ends with a verdict. The animal never had a chance. That is the deepest violence of the film. The horse is introduced as body, labor, breath, muscle, resistance. In the opening carriage shot, we can still feel the animal pressing against the road, the weight of the cart, the force of the wind, the rhythm of hooves and wheels. For a moment, the horse appears as a creature caught in weather and work. It has mass. It has fatigue. It occupies the image. But almost immediately, the film begins to drain the animal of animality. The horse is no longer allowed to be hungry, stubborn, frightened, confused, irritated, exhausted in some opaque animal way. Its refusal to move cannot remain a refusal. Its silence cannot remain animal silence. Its body cannot remain a body. The horse becomes the visible form of a philosophical conclusion: the extinction of will. A horse in cinema should retain some remainder that does not translate into human meaning. It should resist us. In The Turin Horse, that remainder is crushed. The animal is not observed so much as converted. The film does not ask what a horse is. It decides what the horse must mean. Tarr’s defenders might say that this is exactly the point. The Turin Horse is not interested in the richness of ordinary life. It is interested in what remains after that richness has been stripped away. Its repetitions are not dramatic failures. They are the film’s method. The father dresses. The daughter fetches water. They eat. They look out. They sleep. The world does not develop. It diminishes. That defense is serious, but it only sharpens the problem. Even reduction can leave room for contingency. A stripped world can still surprise us. A repeated gesture can change in pressure, rhythm, tenderness, boredom, anger, fatigue. A daughter helping her father dress could disclose an entire history between them: dependence, resentment, care, old intimacy hardened into duty. Tarr gives us the action, but he seals off the variation. The repetition does not deepen life. It narrows it. The daughter dresses the father day after day, yet the ritual rarely gathers private history. It becomes another unit in the film’s machinery of depletion. Their silence is not the silence of two people who know too much to speak. It is the silence of a world emptied for metaphysical use. The potato scenes reveal the same problem. A hot potato should be one of cinema’s simplest material facts: skin, steam, fingers, hunger, salt, swallowing, disgust, impatience. Tarr films the potato with brutal attention, but the attention is strangely airless. The potato quickly ceases to be food. It becomes a survival rite, then a sign, then another confirmation that life has been reduced to endurance. The object is concrete, but its concreteness has been captured. It cannot wander away from the idea. The well runs dry in the same way. A dry well could be a practical disaster, a local mystery, an ecological fact, a social event. Here it feels like a symbolic program completing itself. The disappearance of water is not discovered. It is confirmed. The lamp that refuses to stay lit could have been a physical drama of oil, flame, wick, hand, air. Instead, the darkness arrives as an announcement the film has been preparing from the first frame. This is where the film’s images lose contingency. They look material, but they are not free. The wind is not weather. It is judgment. The window is not a window. It is a frame for waiting. The farmhouse is not quite a place. It is a metaphysical laboratory, built so that every object can be tested until it yields the same answer. Tarr’s long takes intensify this problem. They appear to grant time to things, but the time is not open. It is controlled with almost punitive precision. A long take can allow a body, a room, an animal, or a face to drift beyond interpretation. It can let duration produce accidents. In The Turin Horse, duration often does the opposite. It holds us inside a conclusion until we submit to it. We do not discover barrenness. We are instructed in it. This is why the film’s supposed return to “things themselves” feels so contradictory. If that phrase means a return to things before explanation, then The Turin Horse is in conflict with its own promise. Its objects appear with enormous physical force, yet they are never allowed to remain unstable. The horse, the well, the potato, the wind, the lamp: each arrives already bent toward the same verdict. The film does not trust things enough to let them exist without sentencing them. The contrast with Dostoevsky and Nietzsche matters because both also think through extremity. Crime and Punishment passes through murder, delirium, guilt, degradation, spiritual torment. Yet Raskolnikov is never identical with his theory. The horse in his dream tears open the system. It reveals the child who still suffers at the sight of suffering. It interrupts abstraction with pity. Nietzsche, too, is not simply a thinker of negation. Even after the death of God, his thought remains dangerous because it asks what new values might be created after collapse. The void is not only an ending. It is also a demand. However violent or unstable his answer may be, Nietzsche does not merely close the world. He hurls thought into the problem of what might come next. Tarr permits no such instability. His pessimism has no wound through which chance might enter. Every exit has been blocked before the film begins. The world is not dying in front of us. It has already been condemned, and the film spends nearly three hours making us watch the sentence carried out. That is why The Turin Horse is at once formidable and suffocating. Its craft is undeniable. Every shot is composed with terrifying discipline. Every sound seems carved into place. The wind, the footsteps, the breathing, the wooden surfaces, the silence: all of it has force. But the force serves a closed design. The film’s control is so total that life cannot surprise the image. Nothing arrives from the side. Nothing slips through the system. Nothing in the frame is permitted to escape its assigned fate. Kafka’s “A Country Doctor” offers another image of horses: irrational, sudden, terrifying, full of passage. They do not explain the world. They break it open. Tarr’s horse does the opposite. It closes the world. It does not carry us into the unknown. It stands as the completed emblem of a conclusion already reached. After nearly three hours of wind, repetition, darkness, and enforced exhaustion, the question is not whether The Turin Horse is a major work of cinematic craft. It plainly is. The question is what that craft has done to the living thing at its center. Tarr begins with a horse. A body. An animal. A creature that should have had hunger, fear, stubbornness, opacity, useless resistance. Then the film subjects it to a form so absolute that it can no longer remain alive in any unpredictable sense. The horse is not killed by Mikolka’s shaft. It is killed by meaning. The horse does not need to explain the world. It needs, at least once, to escape the meaning prepared for it.

I tried watching The Turin Horse , and I didn't get anything out of it. So I then listened to Jonathan Rosenbaum's audio commentary. hoping it might offer something I had missed. Rosenbaum talks about many things. He talks about his own relationship with Tarr, whom he calls a friend. About anecdotes from when they were in a jury together at a film festival, and they couldn't decide on a winner because Tarr hated all the films (he describes Tarr as an anti-cinephile). He describes Tarr’s shift from socio-political concerns toward something more "metaphysical" and "philosophical" from Sátántangó onward. He discusses Tarr’s collaboration with Ágnes Hranitzky, his wife and co-director, and with László Krasznahorkai, his closest collaborator, and the writer of The Turin Horse and several of Tarr's other films. Notably, what he doesn't talk about is the content of the film itself. Which is fitting, as the film offers nothing to talk about. That may be why I, too, am talking about Rosenbaum’s commentary instead of the film. --- One of the problems with films like these is that difficulty and tedium become their primary — and often only — defining characteristics. Questioning the work is then treated, by the cult of the initiated, as evidence of insufficient patience, seriousness, or artistic literacy. But art and cinema do not — and should not — earn significance merely by exhausting the viewer. Because the film itself offers remarkably little by way of internal articulation, even Rosenbaum has no choice but to turn outward: toward the director’s supposed philosophical inclinations, his biography, and Rosenbaum’s own authority as a friend of the director. If a work is so sparse that even its defenders cannot meaningfully discuss what happens within it, then the problem is not with the audience.
