Oh boy. There is perhaps an argument that Béla Tarr is one of the most predictable filmmakers in contemporary cinema. The film is going to be in black and white. It’s going to feature extremely long takes. Seconds will turn into hours. Characters’ speech will sometimes sound as if they’re reading straight from an intimidating philosophical treatise or hard-line manifesto. And it’s going to be one of the grimmest things you’ve ever seen in your sorry little life. With this movie, Tarr and Hranitzky amply follow through on all of these predictive suppositions, and just to add even more spice to proceedings, there is no dialogue for the first 30 minutes. There’s a short introductory voiceover, and then…no one speaks. At all. For half an hour. Meanwhile, a string refrain that sounds like Phillip Glass’s Koyaanisqatsi score under the influence of heavy sedatives repeats over and over and over and over and over and over and over and over again. The story? A father and daughter live in a dilapidated hovel in the middle of nowhere. That’s it. That’s the whole film. I just saved you 154 minutes. Oh yeah- and it’s the windiest place in the world. This is a film that is about wind as much as it is about anything else. The wind howls. The wind whistles. It howls. It whistles. It tugs at the windows and the doors. The hovel creaks. The string refrain scrapes its way through another tortuous, hopelessly despairing iteration. The daughter helps the father get dressed in an unbroken take- there’s 10 minutes. The daughter goes to the well- let’s follow her all the way there and all the way back again as she fights her way through the ridiculous wind. There’s another 10 minutes. Even by Béla Tarr’s standards, this was extreme. It was simply one of the most challenging films I have ever watched to completion. Imagine Robert Eggers’ The Lighthouse with 95% of the dialogue taken out and being played at 20% speed. Was it an allegory? Most certainly. Do I care? No. Will I be watching it again, ever? Only after death, if I find myself in hell. For more of my reviews, why not visit www.wilfullyobtuse.com.

Revendo 14 anos depois, com uma concepção formada sobre o que acredito ser a vocação do cinema, gostei bem menos deste trabalho final de Béla Tarr. Compreendo perfeitamente as intenções contra-hegemônicas do diretor. De modo geral, ele propunha o reverso do cinema de storytelling, em que tudo se resume a "contar uma boa história", conferindo-se ao enredo uma centralidade absoluta. E, de fato, o cinema de storytelling é a décima primeira praga do Egito. Mas Tarr, embora operando no regime do cinema narrativo, suprime consideravelmente o plot, com seu arco dramático, reviravoltas, surpresas etc. É quase um retorno aos Lumière. Em uma entrevista, o húngaro disse recusar-se ao esquema de montagem corriqueiro, baseado em "informação-corte-informação-corte". Às vezes não há informação alguma, e outras vezes a informação está algures na mise-en-scène. Mas até aqui tudo bem, já que há bons exemplos de mise-en-scène rica e naturalismo ajustado ao teor da narrativa. O problema de "O Cavalo de Turim" é que ele não é apenas anti-storytelling; é anti-cinematográfico. Para além do ascetismo à Bresson, com personagens cujos pensamentos e emoções são inescrutáveis, já que tudo que vemos são exterioridades distanciadas e economia expressiva, aplica-se a lógica documental ao material ficcional: longos planos-cena e raríssimos cortes, profundidade de campo e reprodução fotográfica do visível ao invés de sua transfiguração. Até existe uma narratividade mínima, onde pouco a pouco, em meio ao marasmo cotidiano, vemos algumas mudanças. Mas elas não são inseridas para catalisar a narrativa, voltá-la noutra direção, alterar objetivos de personagens, nada disso. Se assim fosse, poderíamos tentar examinar se a forma "documental" se justificaria em face delas. Entretanto, o que parece interessar ao diretor é simplesmente o contraste entre o vazio existencial da gente simples de Turim no fim do séc. XIX com a agudeza intelectual de Nietzsche, que passou naquele lugar seus últimos anos. Mas note o seguinte: não temos nenhum vislumbre deste na obra. É para o camponês, sua filha e o cavalo que Tarr direciona as câmeras, Ora, a encenação de um único incidente – aquele em que o filósofo alemão defende o cavalo do impiedoso açoite do camponês – até acentuaria tal contraste e justificaria o roteiro. Mas este não é um filme de "incidentes".

Nietzschean nihilism is a ground zero of nothingness. The lethargic decadence of once elite history makers allows for the virulent power grab of outside forces, that then deterritorialize the structures of society. This film hones in on the former (nothingness, zero, pure the dread of pure potentiality) while giving us only a glimpse of the latter (the takeover of the other), even though one cannot be without the other. Either: 1) he doesn’t fully grasp the dynamic nature of Nietzsche’s thought or 2) he focuses on nothingness because it gives him a reason to make a drab and slow movie. Maybe it’s a little bit of both, but either way, the idea here is secondary to the technique. And that for me is a disingenuous way to make a movie. You don’t make slow, motionless films because you want to make one, you make it because it’s a way to convey something. Esos son los primeros cinco minutos de película, parecía pometedor y luego ves al hombre entrando en su rutina, se mete a casa y... empiezan a comer papas. Toda la película es un hombre levantándose de la cama, comiendo papas y volviéndose a acostar. Hay un trecho enorme de la película donde el hombre solo se la pasa comiéndose unas malditas papas. I dip into slow cinema once every six months to challenge myself by going out of my comfort zone but this is my last detour in my journey to watch all of film canon. A father and daughter survive a storm which could be interesting if it was an hour shorter. There are only so many ways you could show a man peeling a potato before you send the audience running back to their phones. More than the slow pace I am bothered by the lack of narrative. I have mentioned in other reviews – The decision to let the visuals do the heavy lifting does not work for me in spite of some beautiful, painterly images. Cinema is not just a visual medium it is a visual storytelling medium. That is not a difference in semantics but in function. The slow pace is an invitation to think but the movie does not give me much food for thought. Arthouse films peaked in the 60s with the likes of Fellini, Bergman, Antonioni and Rohmer. All of them are on the slower side but they ask incisive questions about sex, religion and creativity. They reward thinking you have to ponder about the character motivation to get most out of them. On the other hand slow cinema from directors like Tarr, Claire Denis or Abbas Kiarostami has one-note characters who never give the impression of having rich inner lives so thinking about them adds nothing to the experience. They are just badly paced, thematically empty and unabashedly self-indulgent. I am not fond of either extremes – I hate both Fast and Furious and its ilk, and slow cinema. Neither has any semblance of story and to enjoy them one has to either stop thinking or give into overthinking.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

While the atmosphere is built well, everything else falls short. The plot is all over the place. The ending is unsatisfactory. The reveal is un-earned. Questions are left unresolved (not in an open to interpretation way - which I like). Protagonist is incompetent to a degree that makes him annoying to watch. It's a whodunnit with a ton of misdirection. Misdirection is cheap to generate, but good movies are able to resolve the plot in a way that makes the misdirection meaningful and clever. [2] nota=0.5 estrelas:
There are many reasons why I particularly avoid Korean films, yet I do not detest them entirely. One of the biggest factors is their tendency toward exaggerated theatricality at the expense of a tighter logical structure in the plots they follow. Park-Chan Wook is the most classic example of this phenomenon of Korean cinema with his films such as Oldboy where he tries to tie out a similar moral tragedy like the Danish film Jagten (2012) through a stylistically elaborate revenge spiral, but the plot eventually moves beyond the boundaries of grounded internal logic. Devices such as hypnosis can feel like one-time narrative bandages, introduced primarily to connect pieces that otherwise resist being connected. My problem isn't simply that Oldboy is unrealistic, it's that, for me, certain revelations and mechanisms feel retroactively installed to preserve a plot that has already stretched beyond its own credibility. The Handmaiden is also a victim of a massive twisted theatrical presentation with an underwhelming logical ground for plot. So are many many films such as I Saw The Devil, A Bittersweet Life, Forgotten etc... Decision To Leave is what I consider the most perfect Park-Chan Wook film and what I consider the film where he establishes a perfect route between a top-notch presentation, poetic moral complexity and an established ground of logic that complements the plot. The Wailing is no stranger to this victimisation but deliberately worse. Here we follow the story of a dad, who is a police in a remote town, where the guilty, the misdeeds, the victims and even the apparent solutions reveal themselves so early, yet the plot repeatedly demands that its characters descend further into its catacombs of uncertainty, not necessarily because the logic requires it, but because the theatrical experience does with its top-of-the-class cinematography, set design and the quote-unquote "thriller" ride of Korean cinema which is deemed to be so extraordinarily unique. Even the 2 hour 40 minutes runtime serves the furthest from being a momentum of an intrigued continuity. Instead, the film repeatedly pauses, expands, and obscures itself in pursuit of an exhilarating theatrical experience, backed by extraordinary cinematography and production design, but without enough narrative momentum to justify the journey. It could be a brilliant concept film, if only it was told with a better expression of plot in mind, better attachment of all the fragmentations of the elements since they were so obviously present. Yet none clicks except until the final reveal becomes the most emphasized point of the film. In short, my utmost frustration is specifically with the film's prolonged withholding of decisive movement. Underwhelming is an understatement for The Wailing. Bong Joon Ho is the only Korean director to ever do Korean cinema the justice of the trio- cinematic experience, established complementary logic and an unique narrative statement of being a Korean foreign cinema. Lee Chang Dong also comes to mind. Burning is my most favorite Korean cinema of all time. I just want to say this phenomenon is of course not exclusive to Korean cinema only. Any film can become a victim of its own grandiosity when cinematic spectacle begins demanding sacrifices from the internal logic that is supposed to sustain it. I'm looking right at you Amadeus .

[2] nota=0.5 estrelas:
There are many reasons why I particularly avoid Korean films, yet I do not detest them entirely. One of the biggest factors is their tendency toward exaggerated theatricality at the expense of a tighter logical structure in the plots they follow. Park-Chan Wook is the most classic example of this phenomenon of Korean cinema with his films such as Oldboy where he tries to tie out a similar moral tragedy like the Danish film Jagten (2012) through a stylistically elaborate revenge spiral, but the plot eventually moves beyond the boundaries of grounded internal logic. Devices such as hypnosis can feel like one-time narrative bandages, introduced primarily to connect pieces that otherwise resist being connected. My problem isn't simply that Oldboy is unrealistic, it's that, for me, certain revelations and mechanisms feel retroactively installed to preserve a plot that has already stretched beyond its own credibility. The Handmaiden is also a victim of a massive twisted theatrical presentation with an underwhelming logical ground for plot. So are many many films such as I Saw The Devil, A Bittersweet Life, Forgotten etc... Decision To Leave is what I consider the most perfect Park-Chan Wook film and what I consider the film where he establishes a perfect route between a top-notch presentation, poetic moral complexity and an established ground of logic that complements the plot. The Wailing is no stranger to this victimisation but deliberately worse. Here we follow the story of a dad, who is a police in a remote town, where the guilty, the misdeeds, the victims and even the apparent solutions reveal themselves so early, yet the plot repeatedly demands that its characters descend further into its catacombs of uncertainty, not necessarily because the logic requires it, but because the theatrical experience does with its top-of-the-class cinematography, set design and the quote-unquote "thriller" ride of Korean cinema which is deemed to be so extraordinarily unique. Even the 2 hour 40 minutes runtime serves the furthest from being a momentum of an intrigued continuity. Instead, the film repeatedly pauses, expands, and obscures itself in pursuit of an exhilarating theatrical experience, backed by extraordinary cinematography and production design, but without enough narrative momentum to justify the journey. It could be a brilliant concept film, if only it was told with a better expression of plot in mind, better attachment of all the fragmentations of the elements since they were so obviously present. Yet none clicks except until the final reveal becomes the most emphasized point of the film. In short, my utmost frustration is specifically with the film's prolonged withholding of decisive movement. Underwhelming is an understatement for The Wailing. Bong Joon Ho is the only Korean director to ever do Korean cinema the justice of the trio- cinematic experience, established complementary logic and an unique narrative statement of being a Korean foreign cinema. Lee Chang Dong also comes to mind. Burning is my most favorite Korean cinema of all time. I just want to say this phenomenon is of course not exclusive to Korean cinema only. Any film can become a victim of its own grandiosity when cinematic spectacle begins demanding sacrifices from the internal logic that is supposed to sustain it. I'm looking right at you Amadeus .

I know I’m probably in the minority with this one, but The Wolf of Wall Street just didn’t work for me. On paper, it has everything going for it: Martin Scorsese behind the camera, an incredible cast and a larger-than-life true story about greed, excess and corruption. Unfortunately, I never really connected with the film’s central character, and that made the whole experience feel like a very long slog. Leonardo DiCaprio is exceptional as Jordan Belfort, completely throwing himself into the outrageousness of the character. Jonah Hill is equally memorable, while Margot Robbie makes a huge impression in one of her breakthrough roles. The performances across the board are strong, and there’s no denying that everyone is giving it their all. My problem is that I simply didn’t care about Belfort or his journey. The constant partying, drugs, money and excess become repetitive rather than entertaining, and with a runtime of nearly three hours, that repetition really starts to drag. There are some genuinely funny and memorable moments, but they were never enough to keep me invested in the story. I can appreciate what Scorsese was trying to do, and I can absolutely see why this film has such a huge following. The performances are outstanding and the filmmaking is undeniably impressive. But for me, it’s a case of admiring the film more than actually enjoying it. Perhaps the biggest problem is simply that The Wolf of Wall Street never grabbed me. When a film is this long, you need to be invested in its characters or story, and unfortunately I was neither. A technically brilliant film with some fantastic performances, but one that just wasn’t for me.

The “wolf of wall street” is a film in which a criminal who managed to steal and send more than 1500+ working class/middle class people into financial hardship and debt can proudly boast and promote the film discussing his crimes as if it was a movie discussing the life of some scientist or humanitarian. The tone of the film mishandles the severity of the subject, which is probably the main reason why Jordan Belfort felt so comfortable endorsing this film and promoting it. This movie doesn’t depict Jordan for the flawed opportunistic greedy character he is , and even when it does attempt to show that, it is plainly “comedic” and it is not something to be criticized, it is something to be endorsed, it is just being “ambitious”, it is just being “smart”, it is just “wanting the best for yourself”. Being greedy, self-serving and opportunistic is alright and even good because then you get to have endless sex, do endless drugs, and afford everything from lavish parties to lavish trips . This film showed all “the good and the beautiful”, the beautiful women, the parties, the drugs, the trips, but when it came to the consequences of Belfort’s actions, we are shown practically nothing of use . In a way, watching this film you might even get the impression that even if you ended up doing everything that Jordan did you would manage to get away with a slap on the wrist, basically unscathed . We saw no real serious effects or consequences of his drug and sex addiction, no real or serious consequences of his crimes, we only see him playing tennis at jail . In this glorified romanticized piece of media, everything is lavish and extravagant, even jail time is portrayed as something that is not far away from pleasurable or hedonistic . This film intends to criticize hedonism while ironically taking a part of that same hedonistic lens that it is trying to argue against .

I know I’m probably in the minority with this one, but The Wolf of Wall Street just didn’t work for me. On paper, it has everything going for it: Martin Scorsese behind the camera, an incredible cast and a larger-than-life true story about greed, excess and corruption. Unfortunately, I never really connected with the film’s central character, and that made the whole experience feel like a very long slog. Leonardo DiCaprio is exceptional as Jordan Belfort, completely throwing himself into the outrageousness of the character. Jonah Hill is equally memorable, while Margot Robbie makes a huge impression in one of her breakthrough roles. The performances across the board are strong, and there’s no denying that everyone is giving it their all. My problem is that I simply didn’t care about Belfort or his journey. The constant partying, drugs, money and excess become repetitive rather than entertaining, and with a runtime of nearly three hours, that repetition really starts to drag. There are some genuinely funny and memorable moments, but they were never enough to keep me invested in the story. I can appreciate what Scorsese was trying to do, and I can absolutely see why this film has such a huge following. The performances are outstanding and the filmmaking is undeniably impressive. But for me, it’s a case of admiring the film more than actually enjoying it. Perhaps the biggest problem is simply that The Wolf of Wall Street never grabbed me. When a film is this long, you need to be invested in its characters or story, and unfortunately I was neither. A technically brilliant film with some fantastic performances, but one that just wasn’t for me.

“The wolf of wall street” is a movie that doesn’t take its subject matter seriously . It is rather insensitive, pretentious and empty . The fact that this movie is told from Jordan Belfort’s POV logically explains why some of the scenes are depicted the way they are, I wasn’t expecting this to be a moral awakening or a repentance type of movie, but I sure as hell did not expect this to glorify Jordan Belfort’s hedonistic lifestyle & crimes. I fail to see the so called “satire” in this film when the criminal & asshole himself makes a cameo in the film . The “wolf of wall street” is a film in which a criminal who managed to steal and send more than 1500+ working class/middle class people into financial hardship and debt can proudly boast and promote the film discussing his crimes as if it was a movie discussing the life of some scientist or humanitarian. The tone of the film mishandles the severity of the subject, which is probably the main reason why Jordan Belfort felt so comfortable endorsing this film and promoting it. This movie doesn’t depict Jordan for the flawed opportunistic greedy character he is , and even when it does attempt to show that, it is plainly “comedic” and it is not something to be criticized, it is something to be endorsed, it is just being “ambitious”, it is just being “smart”, it is just “wanting the best for yourself”. Being greedy, self-serving and opportunistic is alright and even good because then you get to have endless sex, do endless drugs, and afford everything from lavish parties to lavish trips . This film showed all “the good and the beautiful”, the beautiful women, the parties, the drugs, the trips, but when it came to the consequences of Belfort’s actions, we are shown practically nothing of use . In a way, watching this film you might even get the impression that even if you ended up doing everything that Jordan did you would manage to get away with a slap on the wrist, basically unscathed . We saw no real serious effects or consequences of his drug and sex addiction, no real or serious consequences of his crimes, we only see him playing tennis at jail . In this glorified romanticized piece of media, everything is lavish and extravagant, even jail time is portrayed as something that is not far away from pleasurable or hedonistic . This film intends to criticize hedonism while ironically taking a part of that same hedonistic lens that it is trying to argue against .

É um ótimo exercício de marketing, com cenas de caça que tiram o fôlego. E só! A sessão nostalgia tem agradado muito ao público nos últimos anos. Filmes que fizeram sucesso nos anos 80, 90 e até no início dos anos 2000 estão ganhando cada vez mais remakes, reboots ou, como neste caso, continuações. Há muitos críticos dizendo que Top Gun: Maverick é “maravilhoso”, uma “correção do passado”. No caso das cenas de voo, eu até concordo. São impressionantes e, sem dúvida, o grande destaque do filme. Mas todo o restante acaba sendo prejudicado pela repetição de trilha sonora — com exceção da música-tema, que continua linda —, de cenas e até de um contexto muito semelhante ao primeiro filme, tudo cuidadosamente pensado para manter os saudosistas encantados. Assim como no primeiro Top Gun , não temos um roteiro muito elaborado. Em alguns momentos, a história se mostra confusa, enquanto os personagens são explorados de maneira superficial. O próprio nome Maverick faz jus ao filme: tudo gira em torno dele. O maior destaque é, mais uma vez, Tom Cruise. Parece que o filme foi concebido também para mostrar que, mais de 30 anos depois, ele ainda consegue tirar o fôlego do público com suas performances — seja na moto, no caça ou simplesmente demonstrando um vigor e uma energia que continuam sendo sua marca registrada. Top Gun: Maverick entrega um espetáculo visual impressionante e cumpre muito bem a missão de despertar a nostalgia. Mas, quando retiramos todo esse aparato, sobra pouco além de uma continuação que se apoia demais no passado para funcionar no presente.

É um ótimo exercício de marketing, com cenas de caça que tiram o fôlego. E só! A sessão nostalgia tem agradado muito ao público nos últimos anos. Filmes que fizeram sucesso nos anos 80, 90 e até no início dos anos 2000 estão ganhando cada vez mais remakes, reboots ou, como neste caso, continuações. Há muitos críticos dizendo que Top Gun: Maverick é “maravilhoso”, uma “correção do passado”. No caso das cenas de voo, eu até concordo. São impressionantes e, sem dúvida, o grande destaque do filme. Mas todo o restante acaba sendo prejudicado pela repetição de trilha sonora — com exceção da música-tema, que continua linda —, de cenas e até de um contexto muito semelhante ao primeiro filme, tudo cuidadosamente pensado para manter os saudosistas encantados. Assim como no primeiro Top Gun , não temos um roteiro muito elaborado. Em alguns momentos, a história se mostra confusa, enquanto os personagens são explorados de maneira superficial. O próprio nome Maverick faz jus ao filme: tudo gira em torno dele. O maior destaque é, mais uma vez, Tom Cruise. Parece que o filme foi concebido também para mostrar que, mais de 30 anos depois, ele ainda consegue tirar o fôlego do público com suas performances — seja na moto, no caça ou simplesmente demonstrando um vigor e uma energia que continuam sendo sua marca registrada. Top Gun: Maverick entrega um espetáculo visual impressionante e cumpre muito bem a missão de despertar a nostalgia. Mas, quando retiramos todo esse aparato, sobra pouco além de uma continuação que se apoia demais no passado para funcionar no presente.

• I really enjoyed this one. It had a very independent-movie feel, with an edgy introduction and immersive (but disorienting) sound editing which tries to get you in the city and in the jewelry store. • Adam Sandler is excellent as an eccentric Jewish NY jeweller with patterns of erratic behaviour. Kevin Garnett was a surprising strong point in the movie too; he acted well. • I enjoyed living with Adam Sandler’s character in his hectic life and his bad decision-making. • The movie surprises you at times, and the ending is not gratuitous. • Initially I gave this 4/4 stars. Upon a rewatch in 2026, I’m downgrading it because I simply don’t appreciate this kind of movie as much anymore. I can see why it really appealed to me as a younger man. It has a frantic pace and a claustrophobic atmosphere that sets it apart from other Hollywood productions that you would see Sandler in. It’s funny, often at Sandler’s expense, because he puts himself in these catastrophic situations over and over. There is an element of fantasy to his affair with Julia Fox, the very attractive younger woman who is seemingly head-over-heels for our old, funny-looking, ambitious protagonist. And yes, the gag at the beginning is very good and the ending is punchy. But as a 30 year-old, I didn’t enjoy being in this world quite as much, with sleazy jewellers, bookies, groupies, and the like. Also, having seen a lot more independent cinema by now, it wasn’t as interesting or groundbreaking as before. However I can still appreciate that it’s well-crafted and does incredibly well at what it sets out to do.

• I really enjoyed this one. It had a very independent-movie feel, with an edgy introduction and immersive (but disorienting) sound editing which tries to get you in the city and in the jewelry store. • Adam Sandler is excellent as an eccentric Jewish NY jeweller with patterns of erratic behaviour. Kevin Garnett was a surprising strong point in the movie too; he acted well. • I enjoyed living with Adam Sandler’s character in his hectic life and his bad decision-making. • The movie surprises you at times, and the ending is not gratuitous. • Initially I gave this 4/4 stars. Upon a rewatch in 2026, I’m downgrading it because I simply don’t appreciate this kind of movie as much anymore. I can see why it really appealed to me as a younger man. It has a frantic pace and a claustrophobic atmosphere that sets it apart from other Hollywood productions that you would see Sandler in. It’s funny, often at Sandler’s expense, because he puts himself in these catastrophic situations over and over. There is an element of fantasy to his affair with Julia Fox, the very attractive younger woman who is seemingly head-over-heels for our old, funny-looking, ambitious protagonist. And yes, the gag at the beginning is very good and the ending is punchy. But as a 30 year-old, I didn’t enjoy being in this world quite as much, with sleazy jewellers, bookies, groupies, and the like. Also, having seen a lot more independent cinema by now, it wasn’t as interesting or groundbreaking as before. However I can still appreciate that it’s well-crafted and does incredibly well at what it sets out to do.

[1] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Whiplash has a strong premise centered around ambition, obsession, and the pursuit of perfection, but I found the execution quite uneven. The story follows a young drummer who becomes consumed by his desire to become one of the best, while facing constant pressure from an extremely demanding instructor. The strongest part of the film is its intensity. The rehearsal scenes create a lot of tension, and the editing makes the performances feel fast and energetic. The drumming itself is also presented in an exciting way, with the camera focusing closely on the physical effort and exhaustion involved. However, the characters and writing didn't work particularly well for me. The relationship between the student and teacher becomes repetitive, with the same cycle of pressure, humiliation, and confrontation happening again and again. The dialogue can also feel overly dramatic, and some of the character decisions seem designed primarily to push the story toward another intense scene. The film clearly has something to say about talent, sacrifice, and whether greatness can justify extreme behavior, but I felt these ideas were handled too simplistically. The final sequence is effective on a technical level, but it wasn't enough to completely change my overall impression.

Whiplash has a strong premise centered around ambition, obsession, and the pursuit of perfection, but I found the execution quite uneven. The story follows a young drummer who becomes consumed by his desire to become one of the best, while facing constant pressure from an extremely demanding instructor. The strongest part of the film is its intensity. The rehearsal scenes create a lot of tension, and the editing makes the performances feel fast and energetic. The drumming itself is also presented in an exciting way, with the camera focusing closely on the physical effort and exhaustion involved. However, the characters and writing didn't work particularly well for me. The relationship between the student and teacher becomes repetitive, with the same cycle of pressure, humiliation, and confrontation happening again and again. The dialogue can also feel overly dramatic, and some of the character decisions seem designed primarily to push the story toward another intense scene. The film clearly has something to say about talent, sacrifice, and whether greatness can justify extreme behavior, but I felt these ideas were handled too simplistically. The final sequence is effective on a technical level, but it wasn't enough to completely change my overall impression.

Good noir: Intellectually great, emotionally distant This was my first time watching Chinatown, and honestly, the thing that pulled me in the most wasn't the mystery, it was the vibe. The world-building is incredible: the clothes, the cars, the quiet jazz, the heat of 1930s Los Angeles, the backyard scenes, the hats, all of it. Jack Nicholson has this classy, effortless presence, and the film's whole aesthetic feels timeless. Great performance by Faye Dunaway too. But the movie itself is emotionally cold. It's a slow burn, and for most of the runtime, I felt like the film kept a distance from me. The message and themes are definitely strong, but for me, they don't fully hit until the final scene, and that's where I had a mixed reaction. It almost feels like the entire movie was built for that final moment, where everything becomes very obviously "noir" and you see the system's corruption laid out. But the thing is: even without that last scene, I already sensed the corruption throughout the film. It's implicit. It's in the world, the tone, the dialogue. So the movie didn't need to rely so heavily on that final punch for me to understand what it was doing. And maybe that's because we watch the film from a third-person perspective. We see signs of the system's rot throughout the story, long before the main character truly realizes it. If I were in the detective's shoes -if I were seeing things only through his head- it would probably feel more engaging and shocking step by step. But as viewers, we catch the overall darkness earlier, which made the ending feel powerful but also slightly predictable in feeling, even if not in plot. So overall, I loved the atmosphere and the classic detective tone, but emotionally it didn't grip me the same way other classics do. Chinatown doesn't grip emotionally at all. It's more observational. More philosophical. You're meant to watch the world and its corruption, not get pulled into the characters' inner lives.

Good noir: Intellectually great, emotionally distant This was my first time watching Chinatown, and honestly, the thing that pulled me in the most wasn't the mystery, it was the vibe. The world-building is incredible: the clothes, the cars, the quiet jazz, the heat of 1930s Los Angeles, the backyard scenes, the hats, all of it. Jack Nicholson has this classy, effortless presence, and the film's whole aesthetic feels timeless. Great performance by Faye Dunaway too. But the movie itself is emotionally cold. It's a slow burn, and for most of the runtime, I felt like the film kept a distance from me. The message and themes are definitely strong, but for me, they don't fully hit until the final scene, and that's where I had a mixed reaction. It almost feels like the entire movie was built for that final moment, where everything becomes very obviously "noir" and you see the system's corruption laid out. But the thing is: even without that last scene, I already sensed the corruption throughout the film. It's implicit. It's in the world, the tone, the dialogue. So the movie didn't need to rely so heavily on that final punch for me to understand what it was doing. And maybe that's because we watch the film from a third-person perspective. We see signs of the system's rot throughout the story, long before the main character truly realizes it. If I were in the detective's shoes -if I were seeing things only through his head- it would probably feel more engaging and shocking step by step. But as viewers, we catch the overall darkness earlier, which made the ending feel powerful but also slightly predictable in feeling, even if not in plot. So overall, I loved the atmosphere and the classic detective tone, but emotionally it didn't grip me the same way other classics do. Chinatown doesn't grip emotionally at all. It's more observational. More philosophical. You're meant to watch the world and its corruption, not get pulled into the characters' inner lives.

On my recent movie arc, a natural fulcrum point that you reach is whether the classics are worth visiting. Are you watching them because you'll think you'll like them or because movie buffs say you should like them so you HAVE to watch them? I've never been a huge fan of classical acting, a bane that plagues me with movies from the 40s all the way to the 80s. The style is very different and while understandable and appeals to some, I usually find it to date movies too much, it's dramatic in a more theatrical way. As ironic as it sounds I prefer movies that are a little less theatrical with their character portrayals. I prefer more realistic/grounded performances you find in modern acting or performances that are less like caricatures and more like the person they're supposed to be. But times were different, in bygone times of film-making people weren't looking for relatable they were looking for better versions of themselves. A detective that always has the perfect quip, a damsel in distress that is beautiful but sassy but also mysterious!? While I say all of that, I can't help but notice the bright spots in older movies that shine through every time I watch them. Old movies are time capsules of the past that allow you to see the origins of where the modern films you love came from; their humble beginnings. With little experience with Noir films of the 40s, 50s and 60s its easy for me to overlook just exactly HOW revolutionary this movie was for the genre at the time of its release. How purposefully theatrical the acting was and how much it used plot devices from these films and then subverted them or expanded upon them. Looking at it through that lens, everything started to click for me, and the biggest thing I noticed is that Jake Gittes isn't the typical noir detective he's actually a flawed man that fails to see the dark corners of the world and our "femme fatale" is actually a traumatized woman and a victim of those same dark corners. This movie is THE quintessential Noir film for me. It wears the influences of its predecessors on its sleeve while also influencing decades of films to follow. While carrying out the tropes you typically see in these movies, it, at least at the time, had an ending that made stomachs churn in defeat at the hopelessness that it leaves you with.  I can confirm that never having been spoiled, for me it had the same effect. It follows an intriguing mystery, that at parts is cliche but also provides nuance in strange places. The acting is great, despite my biases towards modern acting (it took me some getting used to). The shots were innovative for the time and its layered with thick metaphors to the corrupt vs life on the surface throughout. AND nearly every scene has a double-meaning or a callback for later. I was thoroughly engaged and it accomplished what I hope to see in any watching of a classic movie according to critics. It MADE SENSE why this movie was influential and considered a classic. Has the formula been improved upon since this film? Probably. Is it dated and completely different from a Noir film that would be made today? Yes.... I mean, noir as a genre itself is dated. BUT! Did I enjoy myself with this film? HELL YEAH! That's all I can ask for, and in my surprise of how much I enjoyed this movie I sometimes caught myself stopping to appreciate what it did at the time it came out. The fact that i'm a big Jack Nicholson fan also helped a tremendous amount.

El estreno de Chinatown en 1974 no sólo consagró a Roman Polanski, Jack Nicholson y Robert Towne, sino que transformó para siempre el cine policíaco. Es una de esas películas en las que todo parece ocupar exactamente el lugar que debe: el guion, los personajes, la fotografía, la música, la ambientación y, sobre todo, una concepción del mundo profundamente pesimista. No es casualidad que apareciera precisamente en 1974. Estados Unidos atravesaba una profunda crisis de confianza en sus instituciones. Watergate acababa de llevar a Nixon a la dimisión y Vietnam había dejado una enorme sensación de fracaso y desengaño. Chinatown recoge ese clima y lo convierte en ficción: aquí la corrupción no se encuentra en los bajos fondos, sino en las estructuras mismas del poder. Noah Cross no es simplemente un criminal; es un hombre integrado en el sistema, rico, respetado y prácticamente intocable. La película pertenece además, de lleno al Nuevo Hollywood, aquel cine de los setenta que empezó a desconfiar de los finales tranquilizadores y de la justicia poética. Y pocas películas llevaron esa desconfianza tan lejos. Jake Gittes investiga porque cree que, como detective, descubrir la verdad significa acercarse a una solución. Pero cada respuesta sólo abre una nueva puerta hacia algo peor. Su investigación no consigue restablecer el orden: consigue demostrar que el orden ya estaba podrido. El guión de Robert Towne es extraordinario precisamente por esa manera de hacer crecer el misterio. Lo que comienza como un caso aparentemente relacionado con la gestión del agua de Los Ángeles termina conectando corrupción política, intereses económicos y una tragedia familiar monstruosa. La investigación funciona simultáneamente como thriller y como descenso moral: cuanto más sabe Jake, menos capaz es de controlar las consecuencias de aquello que descubre. Y Polanski entiende perfectamente que ese mundo debe estar filmado bajo una luz completamente distinta a la del noir clásico. Chinatown utiliza el color, el Panavision y el sol abrasador de Los Ángeles para construir un auténtico noir a plena luz del día. No necesitamos callejones oscuros ni lluvia para encontrar la podredumbre. Está delante de nosotros, perfectamente iluminada, escondida detrás de mansiones, oficinas, piscinas y hombres respetables. Jack Nicholson está magnífico como Jake Gittes. Su detective conserva el cinismo, el ingenio y la arrogancia del protagonista clásico, pero Polanski le quita la seguridad de saber que al final podrá arreglar las cosas. Jake puede descubrir la verdad, pero no puede controlar el mundo en el que esa verdad existe. Y ahí está una de las grandes diferencias con el detective del cine negro tradicional: no fracasa porque no haya sido suficientemente inteligente, sino porque se enfrenta a un poder que está fuera de su alcance. Faye Dunaway convierte a Evelyn Mulwray en algo mucho más complejo que una femme fatale convencional. Parece inicialmente sospechosa, pero poco a poco comprendemos que ella también es una víctima. El verdadero poder no está en la mujer misteriosa que oculta secretos, sino en el hombre que posee los recursos para decidir qué secretos pueden salir a la luz y cuáles permanecerán enterrados. Y entonces llega ese final. Polanski decidió mantener un desenlace mucho más cruel que el que originalmente imaginaba Towne, y la decisión resulta fundamental para la película. Evelyn muere, Cross consigue lo que quiere y Jake sólo puede contemplar cómo todo aquello que había intentado evitar sucede delante de él. La investigación ha sido correcta; sus conclusiones también. Lo que resulta inútil es pensar que conocer la verdad basta para que exista justicia. “Olvídalo, Jake. Es Chinatown.” Pocas frases resumen con tanta precisión una película. Chinatown no es únicamente un lugar: es una forma de entender el mundo. Un territorio donde las buenas intenciones, la inteligencia y el esfuerzo individual pueden resultar completamente insuficientes frente a estructuras de poder mucho más grandes. Por eso considero que Chinatown no sólo es una obra maestra del cine negro, sino una de las grandes películas sobre la impotencia del individuo frente al poder. Toma todos los elementos del noir clásico —el detective privado, la mujer misteriosa, la corrupción, la investigación, la ciudad— y los conserva para después destruir las expectativas que llevaban asociadas. El detective no salva a nadie. La víctima no obtiene justicia. El culpable no recibe su castigo. Y descubrir la verdad no cambia absolutamente nada. Ese pesimismo, unido a una puesta en escena de una precisión extraordinaria, convierte Chinatown en una película prácticamente perfecta. Un misterio criminal que termina siendo algo mucho más oscuro: el descubrimiento de que, en determinados lugares, la verdad puede ser perfectamente conocida y seguir siendo completamente inútil.

On my recent movie arc, a natural fulcrum point that you reach is whether the classics are worth visiting. Are you watching them because you'll think you'll like them or because movie buffs say you should like them so you HAVE to watch them? I've never been a huge fan of classical acting, a bane that plagues me with movies from the 40s all the way to the 80s. The style is very different and while understandable and appeals to some, I usually find it to date movies too much, it's dramatic in a more theatrical way. As ironic as it sounds I prefer movies that are a little less theatrical with their character portrayals. I prefer more realistic/grounded performances you find in modern acting or performances that are less like caricatures and more like the person they're supposed to be. But times were different, in bygone times of film-making people weren't looking for relatable they were looking for better versions of themselves. A detective that always has the perfect quip, a damsel in distress that is beautiful but sassy but also mysterious!? While I say all of that, I can't help but notice the bright spots in older movies that shine through every time I watch them. Old movies are time capsules of the past that allow you to see the origins of where the modern films you love came from; their humble beginnings. With little experience with Noir films of the 40s, 50s and 60s its easy for me to overlook just exactly HOW revolutionary this movie was for the genre at the time of its release. How purposefully theatrical the acting was and how much it used plot devices from these films and then subverted them or expanded upon them. Looking at it through that lens, everything started to click for me, and the biggest thing I noticed is that Jake Gittes isn't the typical noir detective he's actually a flawed man that fails to see the dark corners of the world and our "femme fatale" is actually a traumatized woman and a victim of those same dark corners. This movie is THE quintessential Noir film for me. It wears the influences of its predecessors on its sleeve while also influencing decades of films to follow. While carrying out the tropes you typically see in these movies, it, at least at the time, had an ending that made stomachs churn in defeat at the hopelessness that it leaves you with.  I can confirm that never having been spoiled, for me it had the same effect. It follows an intriguing mystery, that at parts is cliche but also provides nuance in strange places. The acting is great, despite my biases towards modern acting (it took me some getting used to). The shots were innovative for the time and its layered with thick metaphors to the corrupt vs life on the surface throughout. AND nearly every scene has a double-meaning or a callback for later. I was thoroughly engaged and it accomplished what I hope to see in any watching of a classic movie according to critics. It MADE SENSE why this movie was influential and considered a classic. El estreno de Chinatown en 1974 no sólo consagró a Roman Polanski, Jack Nicholson y Robert Towne, sino que transformó para siempre el cine policíaco. Es una de esas películas en las que todo parece ocupar exactamente el lugar que debe: el guion, los personajes, la fotografía, la música, la ambientación y, sobre todo, una concepción del mundo profundamente pesimista. No es casualidad que apareciera precisamente en 1974. Estados Unidos atravesaba una profunda crisis de confianza en sus instituciones. Watergate acababa de llevar a Nixon a la dimisión y Vietnam había dejado una enorme sensación de fracaso y desengaño. Chinatown recoge ese clima y lo convierte en ficción: aquí la corrupción no se encuentra en los bajos fondos, sino en las estructuras mismas del poder. Noah Cross no es simplemente un criminal; es un hombre integrado en el sistema, rico, respetado y prácticamente intocable. La película pertenece además, de lleno al Nuevo Hollywood, aquel cine de los setenta que empezó a desconfiar de los finales tranquilizadores y de la justicia poética. Y pocas películas llevaron esa desconfianza tan lejos. Jake Gittes investiga porque cree que, como detective, descubrir la verdad significa acercarse a una solución. Pero cada respuesta sólo abre una nueva puerta hacia algo peor. Su investigación no consigue restablecer el orden: consigue demostrar que el orden ya estaba podrido. El guión de Robert Towne es extraordinario precisamente por esa manera de hacer crecer el misterio. Lo que comienza como un caso aparentemente relacionado con la gestión del agua de Los Ángeles termina conectando corrupción política, intereses económicos y una tragedia familiar monstruosa. La investigación funciona simultáneamente como thriller y como descenso moral: cuanto más sabe Jake, menos capaz es de controlar las consecuencias de aquello que descubre. Y Polanski entiende perfectamente que ese mundo debe estar filmado bajo una luz completamente distinta a la del noir clásico. Chinatown utiliza el color, el Panavision y el sol abrasador de Los Ángeles para construir un auténtico noir a plena luz del día. No necesitamos callejones oscuros ni lluvia para encontrar la podredumbre. Está delante de nosotros, perfectamente iluminada, escondida detrás de mansiones, oficinas, piscinas y hombres respetables. Jack Nicholson está magnífico como Jake Gittes. Su detective conserva el cinismo, el ingenio y la arrogancia del protagonista clásico, pero Polanski le quita la seguridad de saber que al final podrá arreglar las cosas. Jake puede descubrir la verdad, pero no puede controlar el mundo en el que esa verdad existe. Y ahí está una de las grandes diferencias con el detective del cine negro tradicional: no fracasa porque no haya sido suficientemente inteligente, sino porque se enfrenta a un poder que está fuera de su alcance. Faye Dunaway convierte a Evelyn Mulwray en algo mucho más complejo que una femme fatale convencional. Parece inicialmente sospechosa, pero poco a poco comprendemos que ella también es una víctima. El verdadero poder no está en la mujer misteriosa que oculta secretos, sino en el hombre que posee los recursos para decidir qué secretos pueden salir a la luz y cuáles permanecerán enterrados. Y entonces llega ese final. Polanski decidió mantener un desenlace mucho más cruel que el que originalmente imaginaba Towne, y la decisión resulta fundamental para la película. Evelyn muere, Cross consigue lo que quiere y Jake sólo puede contemplar cómo todo aquello que había intentado evitar sucede delante de él. La investigación ha sido correcta; sus conclusiones también. Lo que resulta inútil es pensar que conocer la verdad basta para que exista justicia. “Olvídalo, Jake. Es Chinatown.” Pocas frases resumen con tanta precisión una película. Chinatown no es únicamente un lugar: es una forma de entender el mundo. Un territorio donde las buenas intenciones, la inteligencia y el esfuerzo individual pueden resultar completamente insuficientes frente a estructuras de poder mucho más grandes. Por eso considero que Chinatown no sólo es una obra maestra del cine negro, sino una de las grandes películas sobre la impotencia del individuo frente al poder. Toma todos los elementos del noir clásico —el detective privado, la mujer misteriosa, la corrupción, la investigación, la ciudad— y los conserva para después destruir las expectativas que llevaban asociadas. El detective no salva a nadie. La víctima no obtiene justicia. El culpable no recibe su castigo. Y descubrir la verdad no cambia absolutamente nada. Ese pesimismo, unido a una puesta en escena de una precisión extraordinaria, convierte Chinatown en una película prácticamente perfecta. Un misterio criminal que termina siendo algo mucho más oscuro: el descubrimiento de que, en determinados lugares, la verdad puede ser perfectamente conocida y seguir siendo completamente inútil.

Iconic movies that I've put off watching because there is no way they could live up to the hype usually end up impressing me...unfortunately, Goodfellas was an exception to this. While it does a good job immersing you in the world of a mafia movie, and has some memorable characters, I found that it did a surprisingly poor job building consistent relationships between the characters and making the most of its runtime. While the relentless narration and freeze frames got old quick, where the movie lost me is the large time skips, where relationships or situations get better or worse arbitrarily, which lessens the time that we get to see with the characters. I get that the characters are supposed to be despicable, but they're not likable or unlikable enough to be properly invested in. They're consistently shown to be rolling in money, but take unnecessary risks to try to get more...I know the main character has a fifth grade education and isn't meant to be the best or brightest, but he's got nothing going for him. The way his life falls apart isn't in a "train wreck you can't look away from", but instead something I couldn't wait to get over with, given the day it all falls apart for him is the first time in ten years we've checked in with him, and he's making stupid decisions for no reason. The acting was pretty average in my opinion, Pesci and Deniro were the standouts but don't do anything they haven't done in other roles, and the plot beats were fairly predictable, and nothing too shocking. It was just a really long time to spend with characters that I didn't really have any interest or attachment to, due to the lack of depth, nuance, or originality in any of them. There was nothing particularly bad about this movie, and it wasn't actively unenjoyable. There are some really good long shots, and the setting and atmosphere are really solid, there is clearly care and thought put into the filming of this movie. There just wasn't a single moment I can think of that kept me glued to the screen, surprised me, or made me feel anything at all, other than indifference.

Iconic movies that I've put off watching because there is no way they could live up to the hype usually end up impressing me...unfortunately, Goodfellas was an exception to this. While it does a good job immersing you in the world of a mafia movie, and has some memorable characters, I found that it did a surprisingly poor job building consistent relationships between the characters and making the most of its runtime. While the relentless narration and freeze frames got old quick, where the movie lost me is the large time skips, where relationships or situations get better or worse arbitrarily, which lessens the time that we get to see with the characters. I get that the characters are supposed to be despicable, but they're not likable or unlikable enough to be properly invested in. They're consistently shown to be rolling in money, but take unnecessary risks to try to get more...I know the main character has a fifth grade education and isn't meant to be the best or brightest, but he's got nothing going for him. The way his life falls apart isn't in a "train wreck you can't look away from", but instead something I couldn't wait to get over with, given the day it all falls apart for him is the first time in ten years we've checked in with him, and he's making stupid decisions for no reason. The acting was pretty average in my opinion, Pesci and Deniro were the standouts but don't do anything they haven't done in other roles, and the plot beats were fairly predictable, and nothing too shocking. It was just a really long time to spend with characters that I didn't really have any interest or attachment to, due to the lack of depth, nuance, or originality in any of them. There was nothing particularly bad about this movie, and it wasn't actively unenjoyable. There are some really good long shots, and the setting and atmosphere are really solid, there is clearly care and thought put into the filming of this movie. There just wasn't a single moment I can think of that kept me glued to the screen, surprised me, or made me feel anything at all, other than indifference.

[وكل هذه الوسائل كانت متاحة لسكورسيزي] لكنه آثر في توسيع الدائرة الاجتماعية على حساب أي فعل نفساني، فقياس على ذلك ظل الجانب النفسي في العمل أدنى من اتساع العالم الذي يعيش فيه [حتى لا، يأتيني شخص سطحي في التعليقات ويتقوَّل علي بـ"لا تنتظر من العمل شيء هو لم يضيفه"] وبناء على الذي ذكرته [هنري] ظل شخص ثابت في نظرته إلى العالم، فبدأ وهو مذهول بالعصابات ورأى أنها مجال يعطي الاحترام والسلطة. وينتهي من ذلك تحت التهديد من ضغط العالم بالقتل بعد رحلة الصعود العظيمة الأبسلوت سينما [طبعًا هذا كان متوقع لكن لن ألتفت له الآن] بمعنى آخر، خروجه من عالم الجريمة جاء اضطرار وحفاظ منه على حياته، والقناعة الفيلم توب ون. أما كارين، ففتح السيناريو رؤية منظور سردي ثاني حين اعطاها مساحة روائية من خلال صوتها لكنه عاد ليجعل هنري هو الراوي والمتحكم في استمرار السرد مع إن منظور كارين في الكتاب كان أكثر قوة وحضور، والمعالجة السينمائية اختزلته. وهذا يعتبر مهم لأنه يتعلق بالبناء السردي الداخلي للعمل ففتح الفيلم أفق من منظور مختلف ثم أهملها، يتصنع توقع لدى المشاهد ثم يخيب ذلك التوقع وهذا شأنه أن يضعف تماسك بشكل مستقل عن العمق النفسي. طبعًا مقصدي من هذا الكلام ينأى على التشنيع على أعمال سكورسيزي فهو مخرج له مكانة عظيمة [حسب ما يزعم الأغلب] لكني شرحت شعوري له بعد الإعادة الرابعة للعمل [تقريبًا] وهذا موضع [18] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Martin Scorsese’s Goodfellas is the antithesis to Coppola’s romanticized mob opera—a hyper-kinetic, visceral descent into the intoxicating high and inevitable paranoia of organized crime. Driven by Thelma Schoonmaker’s relentless editing and Scorsese’s signature tracking shots, the film eschews tragic dignity in favor of an unvarnished, manic realism. Ray Liotta’s voiceover functions as a darkly intoxicating tour guide through a world where loyalty is a transactional facade and violence is merely an occupational hazard. It is a masterpiece of kinetic energy, soundtrack integration, and moral decay.

O kadar mübalağaya asla değen bir film değil, hepsi saçma sapan adamlar. Klasik vizyonsuzların bir araya toplanıp kendilerini bir şey sanması. Zaten aslında filmin tam olarak göstermek istediği gerçeğe parmak basan nokta da burası, filmdeki karakterlerin hepsi aslında bencil, fevri, vizyonsuz ve kendi sonlarını hazırlayan “saçma sapan” adamlar. Film bu insanların aslında ne kadar eğitimsiz, görgüsüz ve tetikte yaşayan canlı bombalar olduğunu gösteriyor fakat kitlenin çoğunun bunu anladığından şüpheliyim. Aslında film amacını başarıyor fakat benim böyle insanlara tahammülüm yok. Adamlar milyonlarca dolar çalıyor, parayı harcamayacağız diyorlar, neredeyse hepsi direkt harcıyor, bir de gidip birisi lüks çöp kamyonu falan alıyor. Sonra da polise yakalanmayacağız diye de birbirlerini öldürüyorlar, yani söyleyecek söz yok. Filmi izlerken zaten olmayan tahammül seviyem yok oldu. Henry, senden nefret ediyorum, çok sinir bozucusun.

Le casting est excellent et la mise en scène irréprochable. J'interprète ce film comme une réflexion sur l'immoralité. Contrairement à de nombreux films de gangsters, il ne cherche pas véritablement à glorifier ses personnages en leur attribuant des qualités chevaleresques, comme la solidarité ou l'honneur, qui viendraient en quelque sorte compenser leurs actes infâmes. Le film semble au contraire nous dire : regardez donc ce que vous, spectateurs, admirez tant. Pourtant, ce que je reproche à Martin Scorsese, c'est d'avoir choisi une approche extrêmement centrée sur les hommes. Comment peut-on représenter un tel univers en effaçant presque totalement une partie de la population ? Où est l'écosystème social qui entoure cette mafia ? Les femmes sont bien présentes, mais leurs personnages ne sont ni développés ni dotés d'une véritable personnalité, alors même qu'elles semblent constituer l'arrière-plan indispensable de cette structure. Certes, il n'était pas nécessaire de faire d'elles le sujet principal du film (ce n’est semble il pas l’objectif d’origine). Cependant, il aurait été intéressant de leur donner davantage de profondeur : quel regard portent-elles sur ce monde mafieux ? Comment vivent-elles cette proximité avec la violence, le pouvoir et la criminalité ? Ici, elles apparaissent essentiellement comme des objets de désir lorsqu'elles sont jeunes, comme des gardiennes du foyer lorsqu'elles deviennent épouses et mères, ou encore comme des mères âgées et aveugles aux agissements de leurs fils. Toutes, qu'elles soient jeunes femmes ou femmes mariées, semblent n'avoir qu'un seul désir : intégrer l'univers de l'homme mafieux, dangereux mais irrésistiblement fascinant. Nous sommes en plein dans les clichés. Je ne souhaite pas ici condamner de représenter le banditisme, l'immoralité et certaines formes de masculinité toxique (qui malgré cette intention critique, une forme de fascination ou de glorification peut transparaître aux yeux du spectateur dont l’ambiguïté fait la richesse du film, mais aussi sa limite) mais de déplorer avant tout l'absence d'un autre point de vue, qui aurait permis d'enrichir la réflexion. Au final, il appartient à chacun d'interpréter l'œuvre soit comme une représentation de la masculinité, soit comme une critique du masculinisme ; soit comme la mise en scène d'un idéal fantasmé, soit comme une satire destructrice.

Le casting est excellent et la mise en scène irréprochable. J'interprète ce film comme une réflexion sur l'immoralité. Contrairement à de nombreux films de gangsters, il ne cherche pas véritablement à glorifier ses personnages en leur attribuant des qualités chevaleresques, comme la solidarité ou l'honneur, qui viendraient en quelque sorte compenser leurs actes infâmes. Le film semble au contraire nous dire : regardez donc ce que vous, spectateurs, admirez tant. Pourtant, ce que je reproche à Martin Scorsese, c'est d'avoir choisi une approche extrêmement centrée sur les hommes. Comment peut-on représenter un tel univers en effaçant presque totalement une partie de la population ? Où est l'écosystème social qui entoure cette mafia ? Les femmes sont bien présentes, mais leurs personnages ne sont ni développés ni dotés d'une véritable personnalité, alors même qu'elles semblent constituer l'arrière-plan indispensable de cette structure. Certes, il n'était pas nécessaire de faire d'elles le sujet principal du film (ce n’est semble il pas l’objectif d’origine). Cependant, il aurait été intéressant de leur donner davantage de profondeur : quel regard portent-elles sur ce monde mafieux ? Comment vivent-elles cette proximité avec la violence, le pouvoir et la criminalité ? Ici, elles apparaissent essentiellement comme des objets de désir lorsqu'elles sont jeunes, comme des gardiennes du foyer lorsqu'elles deviennent épouses et mères, ou encore comme des mères âgées et aveugles aux agissements de leurs fils. Toutes, qu'elles soient jeunes femmes ou femmes mariées, semblent n'avoir qu'un seul désir : intégrer l'univers de l'homme mafieux, dangereux mais irrésistiblement fascinant. Nous sommes en plein dans les clichés. Je ne souhaite pas ici condamner de représenter le banditisme, l'immoralité et certaines formes de masculinité toxique (qui malgré cette intention critique, une forme de fascination ou de glorification peut transparaître aux yeux du spectateur dont l’ambiguïté fait la richesse du film, mais aussi sa limite) mais de déplorer avant tout l'absence d'un autre point de vue, qui aurait permis d'enrichir la réflexion. Au final, il appartient à chacun d'interpréter l'œuvre soit comme une représentation de la masculinité, soit comme une critique du masculinisme ; soit comme la mise en scène d'un idéal fantasmé, soit comme une satire destructrice.

messages.content:
Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"
    }
  ],
  "observacao_geral": "<1-2 frases>"
}

‘Your murderers come with smiles.’ Raucous humour and horrifying violence are not mutually exclusive in GoodFellas , the protagonists of Martin Scorsese’s gangster opus continually laughing through acts of incredible brutality. This tonal paradox that underscores the film provides unique insight into the strange culture of the American mafia, a world in which tales of death and destruction are reduced to bawdy anecdotes shared around the barroom. Murder is such a casual occurrence within this subculture that the characters are able to discuss chopping up a body as if they were talking about the weather, the likes of Tommy and Jimmy cracking jokes with Maury right up until the moment they drive a screwdriver through his skull. The main trio even share an inside joke about the body currently stewing in the trunk while eating dinner with Tommy’s mother, this kind of gallows humour arguably used as a defence mechanism to distract from the horror they have just inflicted upon another human being. It is a unique kind of sociopathy in which their responses to the injustices of the world are all the wrong way around, the characters reacting to the owner of a restaurant being hit over the head with a glass bottle not with outrage but amusement. Certain characters even go so far to use humour as an intimidation tactic, the character of Tommy blurring the lines between affection and hostility for his own pleasure during the infamous ‘funny how?’ scene. The ability to lie, cheat, and steal through a permanent grin is the calling card of a professional sociopath in Scorsese’s murderous masterpiece, the filmmaker walking the line between horror and hilarity with a skill few artists are able to achieve.

There’s not much that can be said about this film that hasn’t been said a million times already. It’s one of the few films out there that 100% deserves all the praise and hype it gets and is one that always gets a little bit better every time I see it. At this point, it’s more of a comfort movie for me than anything. Everyone here is at the top of their game, like I could gush on and on about how much I love Ray Liotta, Robert De Niro, Lorraine Bracco, and so on but we’d be here for hours. With that said, the clear standout from the cast is Joe Pesci, who is absolutely fucking electric in this. Every line spoken from this man’s mouth is pure comedy gold, yet he’s such a loose cannon that he can turn you from laughing to terrified in a matter of seconds. That Oscar was completely deserved. The structure of this film is also something that I can’t really get enough of, and to some extent, the same could be said for Scorsese (Wolf of Wall Street, The Irishman, etc.). I just love how much it builds up the mobster life in the first act, showing all the excesses that drew Henry into it in the first place. Then, the second act comes, you start seeing the cracks show, and you really get a bleak picture of how psychotic, deranged, and destructive these people are. As the third act arrives, everything falls apart in a chaotic way that puts you on edge until the very end. I think this structure is not only a great feat in writing but also editing, which can be attributed to Thelma Schoonmaker’s genius work. The entire sequence with the helicopter still gives me so much anxiety, and almost all of that is because of the frantic way it’s edited. From a director with such an iconic filmography, this film really stands out as a timeless classic that I think I could watch endlessly for the rest of my life.

‘Your murderers come with smiles.’ Raucous humour and horrifying violence are not mutually exclusive in GoodFellas , the protagonists of Martin Scorsese’s gangster opus continually laughing through acts of incredible brutality. This tonal paradox that underscores the film provides unique insight into the strange culture of the American mafia, a world in which tales of death and destruction are reduced to bawdy anecdotes shared around the barroom. Murder is such a casual occurrence within this subculture that the characters are able to discuss chopping up a body as if they were talking about the weather, the likes of Tommy and Jimmy cracking jokes with Maury right up until the moment they drive a screwdriver through his skull. The main trio even share an inside joke about the body currently stewing in the trunk while eating dinner with Tommy’s mother, this kind of gallows humour arguably used as a defence mechanism to distract from the horror they have just inflicted upon another human being. It is a unique kind of sociopathy in which their responses to the injustices of the world are all the wrong way around, the characters reacting to the owner of a restaurant being hit over the head with a glass bottle not with outrage but amusement. Certain characters even go so far to use humour as an intimidation tactic, the character of Tommy blurring the lines between affection and hostility for his own pleasure during the infamous ‘funny how?’ scene. The ability to lie, cheat, and steal through a permanent grin is the calling card of a professional sociopath in Scorsese’s murderous masterpiece, the filmmaker walking the line between horror and hilarity with a skill few artists are able to achieve.

The structure of this film is also something that I can’t really get enough of, and to some extent, the same could be said for Scorsese (Wolf of Wall Street, The Irishman, etc.). Then, the second act comes, you start seeing the cracks show, and you really get a bleak picture of how psychotic, deranged, and destructive these people are. As the third act arrives, everything falls apart in a chaotic way that puts you on edge until the very end. I think this structure is not only a great feat in writing but also editing, which can be attributed to Thelma Schoonmaker’s genius work. I always wanted to be a gangster. In this masterpiece, you get Scorsese’s absolute best direction—yes, even better than Raging Bull, alongside the single greatest performances of both Joe Pesci and Ray Liotta’s careers. Goodfellas translates the original story of a kid growing up in a neighborhood overrun by mobsters, captivated by the seductive pull of their lifestyle: the sharp suits, the endless cash, and the street justice that commanded everyone's respect. I’m a huge sucker for scripts that capture natural conversation between characters, and the specific scene where Scorsese’s own mother plays Tommy's mom is pure genius; I felt like I was right there in that era, sitting at that dinner table with that family. The dialogue between Tommy Devito and Henry Hill when Henry laughs at him "Funny how?" is one of the greatest displays of screen presence I have ever witnessed in my life. The whole context is spectacular a masterclass in camera angles, lighting, and contrast. Lorraine Bracco is flawless as well. While she shines even brighter in The Sopranos, she anchors crucial moments here, like that iconic tracking shot with Ray Liotta that provides an unreal level of immersion. You feel completely present every second of the runtime. After watching so many mob films, you realize that every interaction between these guys matters whether they're talking about food or planning a hit and Scorsese delivered that authenticity to the world better than anyone. I love you, Scorsese!

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

C’est un désastre politique on le sait, le riche dans la cinquantaine qui fui vers le bas en nettoyant les toilettes et qui le fait avec joie en contemplant les petits moments tout le monde en a assez parler. J’aime bien l’idée quand même, car d’une certaine manière, sans le faire exprès, wenders montre un truc auquel il a peut être pas pensé. C’est parce que le protagoniste est transfuge, parce qu’il a un certain capital culturel, une certaine sensibilité à la vie bonne qu’il fait autant d’effort pour être heureux (parce que c’est un effort de trouver entre les moment de travaux de beaux moment) c’est parce qu’il subit pas la précarité qu’il peut se permettre ce retrait. Mais. Ça reste désastreux et encore plus qu’on pourrait imaginer : le projet vient de Koji Yanai, dirigeant de Fast Retailing (Uniqlo), qui cherchait à faire connaître ces toilettes à l’international et voulait un documentaire signé par un grand réalisateur, c’est une commande de communication autour d’un projet d’architecture financé par une multinationale du textile, transformée en méditation sur la dignité. D’où le fait principal qui choque : Oui il est heureux et digne, les toilettes sont propres, peu fréquentée etc, parce que  ce sont des objets de design signés Ando, Ban, Kuma, qui sont l’objet « pub » du film. Le film ne peut pas montrer la réalité d’un métier ingrat et dégradant, et c’est pas son but car il faut d’abord montré une société de toilettes fonctionnelles belle et propre. Ça reste une petite méditation sur l’attention au détail et aux formes de vie donc oui c’est agréable à regarder, mais on peut pas fermer les yeux sur cette botte en cuir bourgeoise mise sur la tête de tout ceux qui peuvent pas se permettre de vivre car le travail leur prend toute l’énergie qu’il faut pour avoir ne serait-ce qu’un dixième de béatitude que ressent ce gentil monsieur agent d’entretien. Bob l’éponge est littéralement plus subtile sur la question et ça se défendra en long en large et en travers le jour où j’aurais un blog.

Demorei quase uma semana pra começar a escrever sobre esse filme, isso porque as sensações eram bem mistas e ele realmente me fez refletir sobre diversos temas. Eu gosto de como o filme começa, gosto de como a rotina ritualística de Hirayama é, apesar de repetitiva, diferente todos os dias por meio do que é ignorado, gosto da cadência com que ele nos é apresentado: aos poucos, enquanto nós só observamos sem compromisso, acompanhando a vida do protagonista sem de fato saber quem ele é. Entendo a posição contemplativa que Wenders tenta nos colocar, a de olhar através dos olhos do protagonista ou da lente de sua câmera. Creio que esse seja o principal ponto onde o longa pode ou não funcionar, a depender da capacidade individual de um espectador de enxergar beleza nessas pequenas coisas (o que não é nem um pouco fácil) e é também onde, pelo menos pra mim, Wenders fracassa em transmitir esse valor, chegando a soar artificial em certos momentos, pois o filme no fim das contas ainda é uma encomenda publicitária, e porque extrai sua beleza do que já é belo, não do que é banal e visto como tal. Não acho que o filme seja fetichista ou romantize um trabalho como o de limpador de banheiros, tampouco ingênuo em afirmar que tudo são flores e que problemas não existem, eles existem. Acredito que a escolha de não mostrar o impacto do preconceito ou do cansaço no protagonista pode ser interpretada como parte justamente da filosofia dele, e a forma como ele vive, mas até que ponto? A partir da segunda metade do filme, o usso e abuso da principal característica e filosofia de vida do personagem (resiliência estoica, contemplação, serenidade e deslocamento/distância) como justificativa para a falta de dramatização e proximidade expulsa a trama dos próprios trilhos. Parece que o filme frequentemente nos carrega pra uma situação dramática com grande peso para ele, mas sempre que algo precisa de tempo para ser sentido, até mesmo tempo para que haja a dúvida de por que um limpador de banheiros escolheria deliberadamente a vida que tem, o filme foge e inicia um novo dia, com a mesma desculpa. Tenho fé que deve existir alguém que nem o Hirayama por aí, mas que esse alguém É ou em algum momento foi/será maluco, eu tenho é certeza.
