MVFF 2023 #2 Maybe I haven't seen enough Wim Wenders yet but this was unexpectedly modest and wholesome. Yet, dare I say, not in a particularly earned manner? Hirayama could be an interesting character but the film does not probe him nearly enough, rather mainly showcases his content quotidian existence. I do generally like plotless slice-of-life films, and this is not quite an exception with its pleasant vibes and eschewing of narrative clichés. But I strongly prefer the genre to showcase some amount of complexity through their characters in lieu of much of a plot to lean on. Here, while there are a few small hitches via hints of Hirayama's past and being subjected to classist behavior, the film largely skates over them and feels too simple for my tastes. Hirayama appears to me as just a simple man with a simple job and simple hobbies. The film does ask ourselves why he is so content with his profession and quietude but without presenting even much of a hint, the answer(s) will not keep me up at night.

Magnifiques décors et cinématographie. Le film était tristement joyeux et paisible; on suis l’histoire d’un homme qui passe sa vie à nettoyer des toilettes et pourtant, elle n’est pas si ennuyeuse. Sa vie est répétitive , il fait toujours les mêmes activités en boucles ( laver les toilettes, aller au bain public et dormir ) et pourtant il réussi à l’apprécier. Et c’est justement ce que j’ai apprécié dans le film, le fait qu’il suffit juste de prêter attention à ce qui nous entoure pour réaliser la valeur de la vie. Car tout au long du film, le personnage principal fais des rencontres, des expériences, plus ou moins enrichissantes et longues, mais qui laissent toujours une marque dans sa vie. Et tout ce qu’il vis viens un petit temps et repars, en le laissant à sa vie routinière habituelle à la fin,  mais elles viennent, et le comblent de bonheur même pour quelques minutes. Et chaque mauvaise expérience qui va l’affaiblir amène toujours à quelque chose de plus beau. Le personnage ne se contente pas d’exister sans réellement vivre dans l’instant , il remarque chaque détails de son existence , et il est altruiste et humain. très peu de paroles sont dites , parce que ces moments là n’ont pas besoin d’être expliqués et je trouve ça cool. Cependant j’ai mis du temps à vraiment accrocher , et je suis pas trop film très lent, j’aurais quand même aimé qu’il sorte de sa routine et qu’il essaye de garder ou de relancer ce qui est venu dans sa vie, mais je conçois complètement qu’on puisse adorer le film pour les mêmes raisons qui m’ont fait un peu - l’aimer  ; j’aurais aussi aimé qu’il fasse des rencontres qui durent + longtemps et non uniquement des mots échangés de quelques minutes . J’aurais aimé voir des rebondissements, sa routine se déconstruire , mais je sais que ce n’était pas l’objectif du film et je trouve ça bien aussi. Je met seulement 3 ( j’aimerais mettre 3,25 si jpouvais) parce que perso la simplicité c’est pas mon truc, mais j’ai kiffé les messages du film Scène de fin superbe g kiffé J’ai passé un bon moment et le film m’a rendu triste autant qu’il m’a rendu heureuse.

[10] nota=3.0 estrelas:
C’est un désastre politique on le sait, le riche dans la cinquantaine qui fui vers le bas en nettoyant les toilettes et qui le fait avec joie en contemplant les petits moments tout le monde en a assez parler. J’aime bien l’idée quand même, car d’une certaine manière, sans le faire exprès, wenders montre un truc auquel il a peut être pas pensé. C’est parce que le protagoniste est transfuge, parce qu’il a un certain capital culturel, une certaine sensibilité à la vie bonne qu’il fait autant d’effort pour être heureux (parce que c’est un effort de trouver entre les moment de travaux de beaux moment) c’est parce qu’il subit pas la précarité qu’il peut se permettre ce retrait. Mais. Ça reste désastreux et encore plus qu’on pourrait imaginer : le projet vient de Koji Yanai, dirigeant de Fast Retailing (Uniqlo), qui cherchait à faire connaître ces toilettes à l’international et voulait un documentaire signé par un grand réalisateur, c’est une commande de communication autour d’un projet d’architecture financé par une multinationale du textile, transformée en méditation sur la dignité. D’où le fait principal qui choque : Oui il est heureux et digne, les toilettes sont propres, peu fréquentée etc, parce que  ce sont des objets de design signés Ando, Ban, Kuma, qui sont l’objet « pub » du film. Le film ne peut pas montrer la réalité d’un métier ingrat et dégradant, et c’est pas son but car il faut d’abord montré une société de toilettes fonctionnelles belle et propre. Ça reste une petite méditation sur l’attention au détail et aux formes de vie donc oui c’est agréable à regarder, mais on peut pas fermer les yeux sur cette botte en cuir bourgeoise mise sur la tête de tout ceux qui peuvent pas se permettre de vivre car le travail leur prend toute l’énergie qu’il faut pour avoir ne serait-ce qu’un dixième de béatitude que ressent ce gentil monsieur agent d’entretien. Bob l’éponge est littéralement plus subtile sur la question et ça se défendra en long en large et en travers le jour où j’aurais un blog.

[14] nota=3.0 estrelas:
Demorei quase uma semana pra começar a escrever sobre esse filme, isso porque as sensações eram bem mistas e ele realmente me fez refletir sobre diversos temas. Eu gosto de como o filme começa, gosto de como a rotina ritualística de Hirayama é, apesar de repetitiva, diferente todos os dias por meio do que é ignorado, gosto da cadência com que ele nos é apresentado: aos poucos, enquanto nós só observamos sem compromisso, acompanhando a vida do protagonista sem de fato saber quem ele é. Entendo a posição contemplativa que Wenders tenta nos colocar, a de olhar através dos olhos do protagonista ou da lente de sua câmera. Creio que esse seja o principal ponto onde o longa pode ou não funcionar, a depender da capacidade individual de um espectador de enxergar beleza nessas pequenas coisas (o que não é nem um pouco fácil) e é também onde, pelo menos pra mim, Wenders fracassa em transmitir esse valor, chegando a soar artificial em certos momentos, pois o filme no fim das contas ainda é uma encomenda publicitária, e porque extrai sua beleza do que já é belo, não do que é banal e visto como tal. Não acho que o filme seja fetichista ou romantize um trabalho como o de limpador de banheiros, tampouco ingênuo em afirmar que tudo são flores e que problemas não existem, eles existem. Acredito que a escolha de não mostrar o impacto do preconceito ou do cansaço no protagonista pode ser interpretada como parte justamente da filosofia dele, e a forma como ele vive, mas até que ponto? A partir da segunda metade do filme, o usso e abuso da principal característica e filosofia de vida do personagem (resiliência estoica, contemplação, serenidade e deslocamento/distância) como justificativa para a falta de dramatização e proximidade expulsa a trama dos próprios trilhos. Parece que o filme frequentemente nos carrega pra uma situação dramática com grande peso para ele, mas sempre que algo precisa de tempo para ser sentido, até mesmo tempo para que haja a dúvida de por que um limpador de banheiros escolheria deliberadamente a vida que tem, o filme foge e inicia um novo dia, com a mesma desculpa. Tenho fé que deve existir alguém que nem o Hirayama por aí, mas que esse alguém É ou em algum momento foi/será maluco, eu tenho é certeza.

MVFF 2023 #2 Maybe I haven't seen enough Wim Wenders yet but this was unexpectedly modest and wholesome. Yet, dare I say, not in a particularly earned manner? Hirayama could be an interesting character but the film does not probe him nearly enough, rather mainly showcases his content quotidian existence. I do generally like plotless slice-of-life films, and this is not quite an exception with its pleasant vibes and eschewing of narrative clichés. But I strongly prefer the genre to showcase some amount of complexity through their characters in lieu of much of a plot to lean on. Here, while there are a few small hitches via hints of Hirayama's past and being subjected to classist behavior, the film largely skates over them and feels too simple for my tastes. Hirayama appears to me as just a simple man with a simple job and simple hobbies. The film does ask ourselves why he is so content with his profession and quietude but without presenting even much of a hint, the answer(s) will not keep me up at night.

Sa vie est répétitive , il fait toujours les mêmes activités en boucles ( laver les toilettes, aller au bain public et dormir ) et pourtant il réussi à l’apprécier. Et c’est justement ce que j’ai apprécié dans le film, le fait qu’il suffit juste de prêter attention à ce qui nous entoure pour réaliser la valeur de la vie. Car tout au long du film, le personnage principal fais des rencontres, des expériences, plus ou moins enrichissantes et longues, mais qui laissent toujours une marque dans sa vie. Et tout ce qu’il vis viens un petit temps et repars, en le laissant à sa vie routinière habituelle à la fin,  mais elles viennent, et le comblent de bonheur même pour quelques minutes. Et chaque mauvaise expérience qui va l’affaiblir amène toujours à quelque chose de plus beau. Le personnage ne se contente pas d’exister sans réellement vivre dans l’instant , il remarque chaque détails de son existence , et il est altruiste et humain. très peu de paroles sont dites , parce que ces moments là n’ont pas besoin d’être expliqués et je trouve ça cool. www.fastretailing.com/eng/about/company/profile_yanai-koji.html so the film gives some nod to the fact that there's discontent within this worker despite his happy veneer throughout everything else that had transpired until that point. but does it explain what this could be or how it could come to happen? there is some interpersonal drama and we witness some cheating, but there is little if any attention paid to the structure these things exist in. when his coworker disappears and a new person shows up the next day, this just happens. the higher ups have taken care of it. and no further questions are asked. in [this one interview] yakusho says that his character sees the homeless man in the intersection and is moved by that he's the only one to really do so; but does he? this is a caricature too! and the film dupes us because we're grafted onto him. we have no choice in the operation, and it's made sure of that every step of the way. the whole thing is choreographed form the very beginning. take the tic-tac-to game, for example; there you have yakusho initially thinking it's just trash. the audience at this point is like, no! what are you doing, don't you see there's greater value there!! but then he realizes his mistake and even plays along. and this becomes a subplot of the film, of him filling out the tic-tac-to game, playing against some yet unseen opponent. and then when the game is over, he gets a thank you note for his role as such. and we get satisfaction in this because he did what we wanted him to. the film shines light on his face when his coworker's (ex?)girlfriend suddenly kisses him, but don't worry, it's just the light of the car door suddenly opening, no secondary function here. (by which i mean to say that this is specifically queuing us to receive this scene in a certain way). we get led along the whole time and then at the end there this pretense that it was all worth it but that life's tough and you just have to keep on. but what the real final shot is, it need be understood, gives the actual game away. that is, the grand city scape and the shining sun. while i'm not anti-city or anything like this, it's necessary to understand the relation to city that this film has from the point of its very inception. this is literally a propaganda piece for The Tokyo Toilet initiative -- an "urban revitalization" (we can just say gentrification, you don't have to be so coy) program masterminded by Yanai Koji, son of Uniqlo's CEO Yanai Tadashi. we can get another glimpse of this in a chance scene that happens when Yakusho comes across an older man standing in front of a developing plot. The old man asks Yakusho if he remembers what used to be here. Yakusho doesn't answer and the old man concludes, that's what it means to get old (you forget what used to be). But this is literally not true! Or, it doesn't have to be. It is not an inevitability of life that high end toilets financed by plastic industry and fast fashion will displace the perfectly functioning ones that existed before. It's not the fault of the people for forgetting, it's that there's a literal ongoing violence that makes people forget. And then part of this too can be the whole system of atomization that this is all tied up in, where people just exist as individual subjects, maybe tending to their own idiosyncratic archive, but there is no collective knowledge share -- there is no means of coming together and producing a history of what things have been like so that this knowledge can be passed down to future generations. Instead you get family heirlooms and hand-me-downs. Everything is purely familial, the film wants us to believe. Which has problems because generational wealth doesn't exist! This shit is stolen goods. And then so what, it's just too bad for people that never got a foothold to begin with? There has to be a better way. (More to come; this as to be the start of a research project; permitting everything goes alright tonight).

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

Formato de saída (JSON puro):
{
  "bucket": "<nome>",
  "temas": [
    {
      "tema": "<curto>",
      "mencoes_aproximadas": <int>,
      "n_reviews_analisadas": <int>,
      "exemplo_parafraseado": "<paráfrase>"
    }
  ],
  "observacao_geral": "<1-2 frases>"
}

Bucket: positivas
Total de reviews analisadas neste bucket: 40

Reviews (nota em estrelas + texto completo):
[1] nota=3.5 estrelas:
Beauty in the simplicity of life. Poetic repetition in an endless string of mundane days. The silent, dialogue-free stretches of action play well against the long music-driven drives. Very long and very uneventful, but also quite warm and lovely. Trim it down a bit, lean into more of that early rhythmic editing, and you’ve got a great film. Shame it’s an interesting concept stretched to the brink. But there’s enough here, especially towards the end, to make it worth watching.

I think the timing for me to enjoy this movie is not good enough. However, i still love the concept, a daily routine of a man who cleans toilets while discovering new things about his life.

Hayatta olmak, mutlu olmak için yeterli. Film bunu gerçekten çok güzel göstermiş. Bakış açısı o kadar önemli ki. Hayata nasıl baktığın, nasıl hissettiğini de etkiliyor.Karakterimizin hayatı gayet sıradan, hatta bazı insanlar için kötü bile sayılabilir ama o mutlu. Mutlu olmaması için aslında bir sebep yok çünkü etrafındaki en küçük şeylerin bile güzelliğini fark edebiliyor ve her saniyesinden keyif alıyor. Yaşamak çok güzel, dünya çok güzel. Önemli olan doğru şekilde bakabilmek. Verdiği mesajı çok beğendim ve beni rahatlattı açıkçası.Çünkü hayat muhteşem olmak zorunda değil.

Everything I appreciate from slow cinema A real look at the world Characters who are effortlessly charming even at their worst Appreciation for all the small beauty Just an absolute achievement of a film that makes me wonder how good life could be if we didn't live in a capitalist hell scape

Na początku bywa nużący, ale z czasem wraz z głównym bohaterem dajemy się porwać codzienności i tym malutkim momentom szczęścia w jego życiu. Chyba najbardiej comfort movie na tym festiwalu. Mam lekki problem z quasi dokumentalistyczną formą. Soundtrack absolutnie wybitny!

[9] nota=4.0 estrelas:
Is he growing old and lonely and watching the world as it moves past him or does he just have an immaculately curated vibe? Not for the faint of heart in terms of excitement. The first hour there's maybe 10 lines of dialog and the entire film has very little conflict. And yet it's a very captivating film, full of gorgeous views and well constructed dream sequences. Pretty much the perfect movie to have on at a party with (preferably 70s or 80s) music playing over top. EDIT: A few days after the festival and this and May December are the only movies I find myself reflecting on critically. I do think this movie is imperfect but 3 stars was too low of an initial review. 4 feels about right but it's all arbitrary anyway.

Te vas a morir sin saberlo todo pero, ¿ es esto un impedimento para saber un poco más cada día o un reto? Cada día es una nueva oportunidad para ser mejor que ayer

[11] nota=4.0 estrelas:
No es para todos y pienso que dentro de esta especie de subgénero de películas "no pasa nada" hay mejores, pero aún así Perfect Days es una película bellísima que cambia tu forma de ver la cotidianidad de la vida, es una historia realmente sencilla, sin grandes giros ni pretenciones solo la vida de un hombre que limpia baños. Una película muy necesaria, muy contraria a lo que lo acelerado de la vida actual nos tiene acostumbrados. Me gusto mucho lo relajante que es ver está película, si bien no es la película más estímulante en cuanto a trama de la historia pues es que eso no es lo que busca daré está obra, entre la excelente dirección, la fotografía que hace que cada momento del film sea bello e incluso el sonido ambiental te transmiten muchísimo esa paz de Hirayama, de apreciar los pequeños detalles. Eso mismo los detalles son un gran acierto de Perfect Days, ver está obra por encima es un gran error, por más que sea una película en la que no pase mucho el verla de fondo es no entender lo que te está tratando de decir, cosas pequeñas como la nota del gato (#) que Hirayama dejaba en el baño, sus fotos, en indígente que siempre veía son las cosas pequeñas y fugaces que hacen en conjunto a Perfect Days una película tan especial sobre ver el mundo sin toda la prisa con lo que lo solemos ver. Un tema que me gustó como fue plasmado fueron lo choque generaciónales entre Hirayama con su sobrina y el wey que lo ayudaba a limpiar, un contraste entre la forma calmada y serena de vivir de alguien que alguien con su experiencia formó contra la forma apresurada y caótica que la juventud y la sociedad actúal tenemos. También me gustaron estás escenas intermedias surrealistas y en blanco y negro entre cada día que la película tiene, como si fueran solo instante de los recuerdos que las rutinas largas nos dan. En fin, este tipo de películas que usan un ritmo lento para resaltar los momentos pequeños siempre son las que más terminan renonando conmigo con el pasar del tiempo y Perfect Days siento que va a ser una de las que más me voy a quedar.

Rutina diaria de un limpiador de baños públicos tokiota se convierte en meditación genuina sobre contentamiento y belleza cotidiana considerablemente presentada extensamente durante desarrollo narrativo pausado elaborado cuidadosamente. Nada sobre su simplicidad se presenta sin dignidad genuina considerable evidente presentado constantemente. Las actuaciones transmiten paz contenida con considerable sutileza emocional genuina presentada durante todo desarrollo narrativo extendido. El ritmo pausado refleja perfectamente filosofía de presencia y gratitud cotidiana considerada cuidadosamente. Esta película me conmovió profundamente, confiada en que simplicidad merece exploración cuidadosa sin necesidad de dramatismo excesivo forzado presentado. Es el tipo de película que mencionaré en conversación antes de que nadie pregunte siquiera.

This movie is so cute and mellow but bittersweet at the same time. It’s really both happy and sad all it one but in a purposeful way. And it had one of the greatest soundtracks I’ve ever heard. It was awesome sauce. It kind of helped bring this whole movie to life (as well as all the other components) and showcased his personality and character. The actor also did a really great job this entire movie. I was freezing my ass off during this which pulled some of my attention away at times so I would definitely love to watch this on a tv, inside, when I’m warm so I can feel the full affect and not be distracted from being chilly. But even besides all that I still liked it a lot. I just think I could appreciate and savor it more a second time around.

[21] nota=4.5 estrelas:
15-20 minutes into the film... what a heartwarming depiction of the joy found in the everyday moments of life. 20-40 minutes into the film... okay what the fuck is wrong with this guy? ~1 hour into the film... one of the most emotionally devastating scenes I can ever remember. Such is Perfect Days, which felt wholly unlike anything I've seen before. Watching this felt like dropping a pebble in a pond or holding a mirror up to a mirror, creating a nesting reflection that stretched to space. Can it be taken at face value? A one-sentence mission statement about the beauty all around us? Or Is there some kind of dark riptide that undermines that beauty? The unspeakable rift that separates a family or the confrontation with mortality; the black and white negatives of the otherwise sun-dappled trees? Or does the contrast of those fissures again underline all the light and goodness we wake up to every morning? Perfect Days is a meditation. Or, maybe It's a haiku - its simplicity and bareness allowing the audience to graft their own meaning upon it. If one test of a writer is to see how much they can communicate with few words, then what Koji Yakusho is doing as an actor in a near silent-film performance is unbelievable. While it must have been difficult to convince studios to greenlight a movie about a janitor in which nothing happens, it's not difficult to latch on to what made this film so moving. Watching it, I felt the same way I do whenever I travel. That when I step away from the interiority of my own life and consider it from a distance I feel as if I am swept up into a greater world around me where anything is possible.

[22] nota=4.5 estrelas:
elegant. minimalist without ever feeling empty. this movie reminds you that life doesn’t have to be extraordinary to be meaningful. It finds poetry in repetition, in routine, in the tiny moments most of us rush past. Hirayama’s life is quiet, but never small. His worth is not measured by his job, but by the way he moves through the world. His music, his books, his plants, his photographs, the way he notices light through the trees... all of it becomes a portrait of someone fully present, even if not someone free from loneliness or regret. as an exhausted corporate girlie, this one hit a little too close to home.

acho que “Dias Perfeitos” me pegou justamente por ser tão simples. não acontece nada absurdo, mas mesmo assim você fica pensando no filme depois. é sobre rotina, silêncio e encontrar felicidade em coisas pequenas. gostei muito, principalmente dessa sensação de paz e melancolia ao mesmo tempo.

[31] nota=5.0 estrelas:
Perfect Days is only my second Wim Wenders film after Paris, Texas , and somehow he’s already given me two incredible films. I honestly feel like I may have peaked way too early with his filmography, because I don’t know how he tops either of these for me. There’s just something so beautiful about the simplicity of this film. Hirayama’s life is incredibly routine and on the surface there isn’t a huge amount happening, but Wenders makes that routine feel meaningful without ever forcing it to be. The pacing is absolutely brilliant. The film is more than happy to sit with Hirayama as he goes about his day, and I never felt bored or impatient. If anything, I found myself becoming more immersed in the rhythm of his life. The sparse dialogue works perfectly with this too. So much of Hirayama’s character is communicated through his expressions, his routines, the people he interacts with, the books he reads and especially the music he listens to. There’s very little need for exposition because the film trusts you to simply observe him and gradually piece together who he is. I also loved the visual style. The colour palette is gorgeous, the editing is really neat, and the Tokyo cityscapes are beautiful throughout. There’s something about the contrast between the busy, overwhelming city and Hirayama’s incredibly simple existence within it that I really loved. Wenders somehow makes cleaning public toilets, eating lunch in a park and driving around Tokyo listening to music feel almost meditative. It’s also interesting comparing this to Paris, Texas. They’re very different films, but there’s definitely a similar fascination with loneliness, human connection and people who have seemingly withdrawn from a previous life. Paris, Texas is much more emotionally heavy and dramatic, whereas Perfect Days feels far more content with simply observing life. It almost feels like Wenders has arrived at a more peaceful understanding of some of the same ideas. And Koji Yakusho is incredible. He does so much with so little dialogue, and the final sequence in particular is such a beautiful example of that. His face says more than pages of dialogue ever could. I think what I loved most is that Perfect Days never feels like it’s trying to convince you that Hirayama’s life is perfect. It’s just showing you that there can be something beautiful in an ordinary life if you actually pay attention to it. The repetition, the routine, the little moments of connection, the music, the trees, the photographs - all of these tiny things gradually become meaningful. This is easily the best thing I’ve seen from Wenders so far, although I’ve only seen two films, so maybe I’ve just started with an unfairly strong pair. Either way, absolutely beautiful from start to finish. 10/10 Top100

[34] nota=5.0 estrelas:
“Next time is next time. Now is now.” Wow. This film is truly a hidden gem I’m surprised it isn’t talked about enough mainstream, but I think it’s better this way. Perfect days has very little monologue yet there’s so much meaning behind every frame. This film teaches us to look for the beauty within our every day routines. Every small action makes a huge impact within our day to day lives which can drastically change it, no two days are the same even if we feel like we’re living the same day over and over again. However there are some days which aren’t so “perfect” and it’s those ones where we have to push past it to make it to the next one and the one after that and so on. I really wish I watched this film sooner as I feel like I’ve learnt a lot that will now broaden my future and my every day life going forward. Highly recommend.

[35] nota=5.0 estrelas:
A rotina não é uma prisão. É uma prática. Todos os dias Hirayama acorda antes do sol, limpa banheiros públicos em Tóquio, ouve fitas cassete e fotografa árvores. Muitos veem nisso uma vida depressiva, sem ambição. Mas Dias Perfeitos não fala só de rotina. Fala de maneiras de encontrar o infinito no repetitivo. Ele não aspira ser outra coisa. Não há drama, não há "um dia eu vou ser...". Ele simplesmente é. E o filme trata isso como quem reverencia algo grandioso. Simplicidade não significa falta. Significa escolha. Cada gesto de Hirayama é intencional, cada movimento econômico. Não é minimalismo estético. É minimalismo existencial. Hirayama está sempre olhando para cima, capturando a luz filtrada pelas folhas. Isso tem um nome em japonês: komorebi. Não é luz, não é sombra. É o que existe entre elas. Quando ele levanta a câmera, não procura a árvore. Procura outra coisa. Algo que tem a ver com pausa, atenção e a coragem de parar enquanto o mundo corre. [Não por acaso, komorebi é a palavra que dá nome ao meu canal.] Wenders não fez um filme sobre um homem que limpa banheiros. Fez um filme sobre um homem que encontrou paz. E a paz não está em mudar de vida. Está em habitar a vida que a gente tem. Mas o que é, exatamente, um dia perfeito? O filme não responde. Ele mostra. E você? Quando foi a última vez que olhou para cima? 🎬 Eu crio vídeo-ensaios onde gosto de falar sobre filosofia, fotografia, direção de arte, roteiro, montagem, etc., de filmes que gosto ou que causaram uma 'mudança' em mim. Mas tudo isso de maneira bem 'informal' e 'despretenciosa'. Se você chegou até aqui e tiver interesse em conhecer, fique à vontade pra assistir: 👉 www.youtube.com/watch?v=_HNYE311-kw&t=2s

A couple years ago I lost my religion and there was so much dread and uncertainty that came with that. Even years later sometimes I get worried. What if I’m wrong? There is SO much on the line if I’m wrong. After this life I may never see my family again. Milly and I may never be together again. The family Milly and I long for may be eternally damned because I chose myself. What am I doing this all for? I’ve had to really accept a reality where this life is truly all there is. After this life, there could be nothing. While I hope for more after I die, I found so much peace and purpose in this life being all there is. Because if that’s true, then my only responsibility is to love so fully and deeply that when I die I’m satisfied. To love Milly with everything I have, because if this is it and I die and don’t get to see her again, I want to be confident that I couldn’t have loved her more. I didn’t have an ounce more of love to give. I gave it all in this lifetime. I think that’s a real privilege. I get to be with trees, I get to listen to music, I get to create, I get to love people and I get to try and deepen how I do that every single day. A beautiful film about solitude, routine, melancholy and enjoying the little things. Hirayama’s solitude is beautiful and meaningful, but it may also be a protective shell he has built around himself. Short, sometimes wordless human interactions can be deeply meaningful, yet he has effectively cut himself off from his family for reasons we never fully understand. There is joy in listening to music alone in your car, but also in sharing that music with someone else. He has built a tiny world for himself inside an enormous Tokyo: his apartment, small izakayas and bookshops, the park, the bath house. I loved the way such a vast and sometimes impersonal city becomes intimate through these small spaces, where you encounter the same regulars and gradually become part of one another’s lives. He follows almost exactly the same routine every day, yet every day is slightly different: the light hits the leaves differently and creates new patterns of shadow, the homeless man strikes another absurd pose, a salaryman or a group of children passes through one of the toilets he is cleaning. Routine becomes a way of noticing change rather than escaping from it. A good life can contain both happiness and sadness, tears and a smile at the same time, as in that beautiful final shot.

15-20 minutes into the film... what a heartwarming depiction of the joy found in the everyday moments of life. 20-40 minutes into the film... okay what the fuck is wrong with this guy? ~1 hour into the film... one of the most emotionally devastating scenes I can ever remember. Such is Perfect Days, which felt wholly unlike anything I've seen before. Watching this felt like dropping a pebble in a pond or holding a mirror up to a mirror, creating a nesting reflection that stretched to space. Can it be taken at face value? A one-sentence mission statement about the beauty all around us? Or Is there some kind of dark riptide that undermines that beauty? The unspeakable rift that separates a family or the confrontation with mortality; the black and white negatives of the otherwise sun-dappled trees? Or does the contrast of those fissures again underline all the light and goodness we wake up to every morning? Perfect Days is a meditation. Or, maybe It's a haiku - its simplicity and bareness allowing the audience to graft their own meaning upon it. If one test of a writer is to see how much they can communicate with few words, then what Koji Yakusho is doing as an actor in a near silent-film performance is unbelievable. While it must have been difficult to convince studios to greenlight a movie about a janitor in which nothing happens, it's not difficult to latch on to what made this film so moving. Watching it, I felt the same way I do whenever I travel. That when I step away from the interiority of my own life and consider it from a distance I feel as if I am swept up into a greater world around me where anything is possible.

Perfect Days is only my second Wim Wenders film after Paris, Texas , and somehow he’s already given me two incredible films. I honestly feel like I may have peaked way too early with his filmography, because I don’t know how he tops either of these for me. There’s just something so beautiful about the simplicity of this film. Hirayama’s life is incredibly routine and on the surface there isn’t a huge amount happening, but Wenders makes that routine feel meaningful without ever forcing it to be. The pacing is absolutely brilliant. The film is more than happy to sit with Hirayama as he goes about his day, and I never felt bored or impatient. If anything, I found myself becoming more immersed in the rhythm of his life. The sparse dialogue works perfectly with this too. So much of Hirayama’s character is communicated through his expressions, his routines, the people he interacts with, the books he reads and especially the music he listens to. There’s very little need for exposition because the film trusts you to simply observe him and gradually piece together who he is. I also loved the visual style. The colour palette is gorgeous, the editing is really neat, and the Tokyo cityscapes are beautiful throughout. There’s something about the contrast between the busy, overwhelming city and Hirayama’s incredibly simple existence within it that I really loved. Wenders somehow makes cleaning public toilets, eating lunch in a park and driving around Tokyo listening to music feel almost meditative. It’s also interesting comparing this to Paris, Texas. They’re very different films, but there’s definitely a similar fascination with loneliness, human connection and people who have seemingly withdrawn from a previous life. Paris, Texas is much more emotionally heavy and dramatic, whereas Perfect Days feels far more content with simply observing life. It almost feels like Wenders has arrived at a more peaceful understanding of some of the same ideas. And Koji Yakusho is incredible. He does so much with so little dialogue, and the final sequence in particular is such a beautiful example of that. His face says more than pages of dialogue ever could. I think what I loved most is that Perfect Days never feels like it’s trying to convince you that Hirayama’s life is perfect. It’s just showing you that there can be something beautiful in an ordinary life if you actually pay attention to it. The repetition, the routine, the little moments of connection, the music, the trees, the photographs - all of these tiny things gradually become meaningful. This is easily the best thing I’ve seen from Wenders so far, although I’ve only seen two films, so maybe I’ve just started with an unfairly strong pair. Either way, absolutely beautiful from start to finish. 10/10 Top100

Isso tem um nome em japonês: komorebi. Não é luz, não é sombra. É o que existe entre elas. Quando ele levanta a câmera, não procura a árvore. Procura outra coisa. Algo que tem a ver com pausa, atenção e a coragem de parar enquanto o mundo corre. [Não por acaso, komorebi é a palavra que dá nome ao meu canal.] Wenders não fez um filme sobre um homem que limpa banheiros. Fez um filme sobre um homem que encontrou paz. Mas tudo isso de maneira bem 'informal' e 'despretenciosa'. Se você chegou até aqui e tiver interesse em conhecer, fique à vontade pra assistir: 👉 www.youtube.com/watch?v=_HNYE311-kw&t=2s

A beautiful film about solitude, routine, melancholy and enjoying the little things. Hirayama’s solitude is beautiful and meaningful, but it may also be a protective shell he has built around himself. Short, sometimes wordless human interactions can be deeply meaningful, yet he has effectively cut himself off from his family for reasons we never fully understand. There is joy in listening to music alone in your car, but also in sharing that music with someone else. He has built a tiny world for himself inside an enormous Tokyo: his apartment, small izakayas and bookshops, the park, the bath house. I loved the way such a vast and sometimes impersonal city becomes intimate through these small spaces, where you encounter the same regulars and gradually become part of one another’s lives. He follows almost exactly the same routine every day, yet every day is slightly different: the light hits the leaves differently and creates new patterns of shadow, the homeless man strikes another absurd pose, a salaryman or a group of children passes through one of the toilets he is cleaning. Routine becomes a way of noticing change rather than escaping from it. A good life can contain both happiness and sadness, tears and a smile at the same time, as in that beautiful final shot.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

‘Sinners’ got a lot of hype and everybody was posting it to their Letterboxd Last Four, so I thought there must be something more to it. However, turns out it was a bit overhyped—certainly not worthy of 18 Oscar nominations. It’s basically a big-budget horror film with some not-so-subtle metaphors for cultural and human exploitation. I certainly appreciate the intent of the film to reach a mainstream audience with a political message delivered by way of an allegory. Unfortunately, it’s not a particularly clever plot or a smart script. There are moments of artistry—the blending of multiple anachronistic musical genres into one scene, for example—but all that smarts gets overtaken by the conventional horror story plot points. My first complaint is, everything feels phony. The period wardrobes feel too new and perfect. The art direction looks too theme park. There are backdrops that are obviously CG. Compare the look of this film to ‘Hamnet’ or ‘Days of Heaven’, and you’ll know what I mean. The past was dirty and messy. Then there’s the camerawork. I keep saying this, but beautiful photography and precise movement isn’t everything. The camera should tell the story without drawing attention to itself. I felt like I was always noticing the camera’s movements instead of following the characters. Most disappointing was the script, which not only spells out the metaphor—in case you didn’t get it—but it also reduces the characters to stereotype gangster tough guys and any true relationships to either sex or violence. That’s just not reality. There’s also the lack of logic. How would people in the ‘20’s before the 100 years of popular vampire films all inherently know all the methods of dispensing with vampires? They exist during the say but burn up when exposed to sunlight? It’s okay if you don’t think about it, I guess. I’m rating it a 6 because it’s decently produced and semi-entertaining, but man, the insight and the poignancy were lost in the traditional horror and gore.

‘Sinners’ got a lot of hype and everybody was posting it to their Letterboxd Last Four, so I thought there must be something more to it. However, turns out it was a bit overhyped—certainly not worthy of 18 Oscar nominations. It’s basically a big-budget horror film with some not-so-subtle metaphors for cultural and human exploitation. I certainly appreciate the intent of the film to reach a mainstream audience with a political message delivered by way of an allegory. Unfortunately, it’s not a particularly clever plot or a smart script. There are moments of artistry—the blending of multiple anachronistic musical genres into one scene, for example—but all that smarts gets overtaken by the conventional horror story plot points. My first complaint is, everything feels phony. The period wardrobes feel too new and perfect. The art direction looks too theme park. There are backdrops that are obviously CG. Compare the look of this film to ‘Hamnet’ or ‘Days of Heaven’, and you’ll know what I mean. The past was dirty and messy. Then there’s the camerawork. I keep saying this, but beautiful photography and precise movement isn’t everything. The camera should tell the story without drawing attention to itself. I felt like I was always noticing the camera’s movements instead of following the characters. Most disappointing was the script, which not only spells out the metaphor—in case you didn’t get it—but it also reduces the characters to stereotype gangster tough guys and any true relationships to either sex or violence. That’s just not reality. There’s also the lack of logic. How would people in the ‘20’s before the 100 years of popular vampire films all inherently know all the methods of dispensing with vampires? They exist during the say but burn up when exposed to sunlight? It’s okay if you don’t think about it, I guess. I’m rating it a 6 because it’s decently produced and semi-entertaining, but man, the insight and the poignancy were lost in the traditional horror and gore.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "negativas" (0.5–2 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews negativas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.

I mean, it is slow. The first half is littered with scenes that work the same way, recruiting a new party member, and we learn nothing new. 10mins in we know the two main characters are (1) brothers, (2) naughty, and (3) the brothers did naughty things in Chicago and now they're back home. And the film refuses to give us anything more. And the Chicago thing never gets paid off. Neither does the Native American stuff, or the KKK stuff, other than the shootout that feels so detached from the rest of the film it may as well have been a deleted scene. Is it meant to be a post-modern genre piece? The film plays with film form a bit (changes in aspect ratio, that one time travel music montage, the long post credits sequence) - but to what end? They may as well have made every third scene play out in black and white, it would be just as "interesting" and nonsensical as what they did do. Is it just a fun horror romp with a twist? If so, what was that first hour all about? Just watch From Dusk Til Dawn, or Shaun of the Dead, or Suspiria or something. And even the Oscar-winning best parts of the film fell flat for me. Michael B Jordon plays two versions of the same character, except one wears a blue hat and the other wears a red hat. The music is okay at times but laughably bad at others - with the ultra intense electric guitar licks sounding like something straight out of Lethal Weapon. And I get it - it's hard for a film to live up to the hype. But I saw Obsession way after the hype and I loved that film

Shallow Depth of Field, Soft Focus and Anomorphic Blur. The actual Hollywood cultural zietgeist. The biggest victim of this new ideology is the visual department, most films are entirley filmed in shallow depth of field, which to put it simply is enhancing a subject and basically leaving the entire background out of focus and blurry (anomorphic blur) this is also called soft focus, when only the subject is in focus. Before today where its now considered normal to shoot 80% of your film in soft focus, movies used alot more deep focus, where subjects are crisp but the backgrounds where enriched with detail, visible detail and not indescrible blurry backgrounds. Now there are positives to using soft focus, it's not like a new technique that suddenly has been founded, filmmakers have always used soft focus, but in moderation, restricting to key character moments when all that is important in a scene is the character. Nowdays soft focus is used to film every scene, it removes world building and the distinct personality of the film. And it's not always a filmmaker problem, this issue has stemmed from studios becoming too lazy to fund and budget set designs properly, and will encourage shallow focus to paste over the cracks of the image being built and spin it as a "cinematic" effect. "Raíces, blues y colmillos" Sinners es mucho más que una película de vampiros. Es un viaje al pasado para reivindicar la preservación de las culturas negras y minorías segregadas, su espiritualismo y esas raíces que la historia ha intentado arrancar. Y lo hace sin renunciar al entretenimiento: balazos, buena música y una acción que bebe de clásicos como Blade. La escenografía es un personaje más: el espacio se puede oler entre el sudor, la transpiración y la bebida. Ese filtro entre lo antiguo y lo nuevo funciona de maravilla. El final es satisfactorio y redentor, y te deja con el mensaje principal bien grabado: respetar siempre de dónde venimos. No todo es perfecto: los efectos cumplen (prostéticos y CGI), pero a veces flaquean, y los vampiros pierden poder en ciertos momentos, haciendo que la pelea contra la horda se sienta lenta e inverosímil. Ryan Coogler swinging for the fences and connecting almost every time. The first hour is pure hangout-movie pleasure — building this world, this juke joint, these characters — and then it just detonates once Remmick shows up and the vampire mythology kicks in. That music sequence where Sammie plays and the film bends time to show every era of Black music converging in one room is one of the most audacious, purely cinematic things I've seen in a theater in years. Ludwig Göransson's score is doing insane amounts of heavy lifting throughout. Michael B. Jordan pulling off two fully distinct performances as Smoke and Stack without it ever feeling like a gimmick, and the way the film uses vampirism as a metaphor for cultural theft never feels heavy-handed — it earns every beat. If anything holds it back from a full five it's that the back half's genre turn moves so fast some of the character work from the first hour doesn't fully pay off the way I wanted. Still, this is a filmmaker operating at the absolute top of his craft. Original, ambitious, and unlike anything else that came out last year.

"Raíces, blues y colmillos" Sinners es mucho más que una película de vampiros. Es un viaje al pasado para reivindicar la preservación de las culturas negras y minorías segregadas, su espiritualismo y esas raíces que la historia ha intentado arrancar. Y lo hace sin renunciar al entretenimiento: balazos, buena música y una acción que bebe de clásicos como Blade. La escenografía es un personaje más: el espacio se puede oler entre el sudor, la transpiración y la bebida. Ese filtro entre lo antiguo y lo nuevo funciona de maravilla. El final es satisfactorio y redentor, y te deja con el mensaje principal bien grabado: respetar siempre de dónde venimos. No todo es perfecto: los efectos cumplen (prostéticos y CGI), pero a veces flaquean, y los vampiros pierden poder en ciertos momentos, haciendo que la pelea contra la horda se sienta lenta e inverosímil. Aun así, la experiencia vale la pena.

Ryan Coogler swinging for the fences and connecting almost every time. The first hour is pure hangout-movie pleasure — building this world, this juke joint, these characters — and then it just detonates once Remmick shows up and the vampire mythology kicks in. That music sequence where Sammie plays and the film bends time to show every era of Black music converging in one room is one of the most audacious, purely cinematic things I've seen in a theater in years. Ludwig Göransson's score is doing insane amounts of heavy lifting throughout. Michael B. Jordan pulling off two fully distinct performances as Smoke and Stack without it ever feeling like a gimmick, and the way the film uses vampirism as a metaphor for cultural theft never feels heavy-handed — it earns every beat. If anything holds it back from a full five it's that the back half's genre turn moves so fast some of the character work from the first hour doesn't fully pay off the way I wanted. Still, this is a filmmaker operating at the absolute top of his craft. Original, ambitious, and unlike anything else that came out last year.

I wanted to like this film, I really really did, and while there are some very good attributes, this film suffers from building into something ambitious and not being able to neatly tie that ambition up by the end. Let me start off with the positives. This film has some really great cinematography that helps to build tension, and some very solid editing that makes sure this film doesn't ever drag. It's not the best I've seen, but it does it's job very well for the film. The costumes are 100% a standout of this film, telling you everything you need to know about a character's personality before they actually become fleshed out. The ensemble of this film, led by an excellent Matthew McConaughey, is also very solid, very comitted to the bit, and very good at really making the most of the material. Where this film struggles though is the writing and direction by Guy Ritchie. The screenplay is a big issue in my opinion, because it has good moments, namely the first act being a great setup and an excellent hook for a movie. The second act drops a little bit but is pretty solid overall. Where this film really ends up falling off a cliff is the third act. After setting up several characters, a very odd framing device, numerous character relationships, and very briefly mentioned ideas and other minor characters, the film seems to realize it only has about 30 minutes to tie all of it up, and I was dissapointed to find it done in a very messy manner. What happens is a very quick succession of strange plot twists, thrusting supporting characters that haven't been seen for upwards of 45 minutes into large, plot-essential roles, and even going as far as to introduce a new operation behind the scenes of characters we haven't met that are related to a character that was quickly killed off and used as a gag. Some of these suddenly important characters I really didn't have a strong connection to at all due to the fact that they were simply underwritten. There is so much exposition, that maybe cutting a few plotlines would've tightened the ending up a lot better. As for the direction, it struggles to decide whether this is supposed to be a campy serio-comedy, an intense crime thriller, or an all-or-nothing high stakes action film. There are so many jokes and odd inclusions that don't quite seem to line up with anything else in the film. Personally, the campy crime thriller seen in the first act of the film is where this really shines, and where it's performances feel the best. I really wanted to like The Gentlemen, but unfortunately, the film felt too ambitious to ever catch up to itself.

I wanted to like this film, I really really did, and while there are some very good attributes, this film suffers from building into something ambitious and not being able to neatly tie that ambition up by the end. Let me start off with the positives. This film has some really great cinematography that helps to build tension, and some very solid editing that makes sure this film doesn't ever drag. It's not the best I've seen, but it does it's job very well for the film. The costumes are 100% a standout of this film, telling you everything you need to know about a character's personality before they actually become fleshed out. The ensemble of this film, led by an excellent Matthew McConaughey, is also very solid, very comitted to the bit, and very good at really making the most of the material. Where this film struggles though is the writing and direction by Guy Ritchie. The screenplay is a big issue in my opinion, because it has good moments, namely the first act being a great setup and an excellent hook for a movie. The second act drops a little bit but is pretty solid overall. Where this film really ends up falling off a cliff is the third act. After setting up several characters, a very odd framing device, numerous character relationships, and very briefly mentioned ideas and other minor characters, the film seems to realize it only has about 30 minutes to tie all of it up, and I was dissapointed to find it done in a very messy manner. What happens is a very quick succession of strange plot twists, thrusting supporting characters that haven't been seen for upwards of 45 minutes into large, plot-essential roles, and even going as far as to introduce a new operation behind the scenes of characters we haven't met that are related to a character that was quickly killed off and used as a gag. Some of these suddenly important characters I really didn't have a strong connection to at all due to the fact that they were simply underwritten. There is so much exposition, that maybe cutting a few plotlines would've tightened the ending up a lot better. As for the direction, it struggles to decide whether this is supposed to be a campy serio-comedy, an intense crime thriller, or an all-or-nothing high stakes action film. There are so many jokes and odd inclusions that don't quite seem to line up with anything else in the film. Personally, the campy crime thriller seen in the first act of the film is where this really shines, and where it's performances feel the best. I really wanted to like The Gentlemen, but unfortunately, the film felt too ambitious to ever catch up to itself.

El Padrino no es una película: es un tratado audiovisual sobre la inevitabilidad del poder, la herencia y la corrupción moral disfrazado de cine de gánsteres. Coppola toma el sueño americano, lo estrangula con una corbata italiana y lo convierte en una tragedia shakespeariana donde la familia funciona simultáneamente como refugio y condena. Lo verdaderamente fascinante no es la violencia, sino la burocracia con la que se ejerce. Michael Corleone no desciende al crimen por ambición, sino por la lógica casi determinista de un sistema donde la ética termina subordinada a la sangre. Cada decisión parece una tesis sobre cómo el poder deja de ser una herramienta para convertirse en una identidad. La fotografía de Gordon Willis, conocida con toda justicia como "el Príncipe de las Tinieblas", no ilumina a los personajes: los juzga. Las sombras no son una elección estética, sino una declaración filosófica de que toda autoridad nace parcialmente oculta. Y Nino Rota compone una partitura que suena menos a música y más a un lamento histórico por una familia condenada desde el primer brindis. Decir que El Padrino es "una película de mafiosos" es como decir que La Odisea trata sobre un hombre que vuelve a casa. Es una reducción casi ofensiva. Lo que Coppola construye es un mito moderno donde el capitalismo, el honor y la violencia dialogan hasta volverse indistinguibles. Obra maestra. No porque sea perfecta, sino porque redefine el lenguaje con el que el cine habla sobre el poder.

Critiquing a movie with this much gravitas almost feels like internet suicide, but I’m gonna do it anyway. First of all, I’m happy this movie exists solely for the truckload of entertainment it has provided to me via all the media it has inspired. It is and always will be an absolute classic, and I’m honored to have finally seen it. But, judged on its own merits today, stacked up against a genre which it helped birth, I have to say, I didn’t like it. There are parts which I really liked, but they are too few and too far between. You know how some movies are three hours long yet they feel barely two? Well, The Godfather is a three-hour movie and feels like six. "Bloated" was the first thing that came to my mind when the credits rolled. Its insistence on showing you the mundane, dragging the hell out of it, and beating you over the head with it is truly something special. The plot points which should drive the story forward feel very unsatisfying. All the time that could have been spent on better character development is spent in the most inconsequential of all places, which hardly matters at the end of the day. And even though Al Pacino's presence and charisma is one of the few reasons why I stuck around until the end, his performance is still fairly plain—far removed from his best. Sadly, the biggest crime The Godfather has committed is that it must have been so good and influential when it came out that all the copycats have eventually caught up. All of the genre tropes have been done better a million times since, producing far more compelling stories than what the Corleone family has to offer today.

Man kann nachvollziehen, wieso er ein großes Publikum erreicht: Der Plot ist gefällig erzählt , die Figuren sind schlicht und die Bildsprache eingängig. Wir verstehen sofort, was Sache ist. Copolla lässt kaum Raum für Ambivalentes, auch Politisches hält er hier vollkommen raus. Dabei kann gerade das Mafia-Genre rasant über die Entstehung von Kapital erzählen, doch das geschieht hier nur randständig. Stattdessen verschafft man dem Publikum Zugang zum Film durch die nervende Betonung von Familienwerten – ja, The Godfather ist ein durch und durch konservativer Film. Die Schwermütigkeit und die Länge des Films ist dabei nicht mit einer anspruchsvollen Kost zu verwechseln. Im Gegenteil kann man es sich immer ganz warm und gemütlich machen, wenn Don Vito Corleone vor dem Bildschirm läuft: Hier wird zwar geschossen und gemordet, aber immerhin ist hier das patriarchale Familienmodell noch intakt. An einem Scoresese-Gangster-Film, geschweige denn an einem Coppola, kommt dieser nicht ran.

[30] nota=2.0 estrelas:
Critiquing a movie with this much gravitas almost feels like internet suicide, but I’m gonna do it anyway. First of all, I’m happy this movie exists solely for the truckload of entertainment it has provided to me via all the media it has inspired. It is and always will be an absolute classic, and I’m honored to have finally seen it. But, judged on its own merits today, stacked up against a genre which it helped birth, I have to say, I didn’t like it. There are parts which I really liked, but they are too few and too far between. You know how some movies are three hours long yet they feel barely two? Well, The Godfather is a three-hour movie and feels like six. "Bloated" was the first thing that came to my mind when the credits rolled. Its insistence on showing you the mundane, dragging the hell out of it, and beating you over the head with it is truly something special. The plot points which should drive the story forward feel very unsatisfying. All the time that could have been spent on better character development is spent in the most inconsequential of all places, which hardly matters at the end of the day. And even though Al Pacino's presence and charisma is one of the few reasons why I stuck around until the end, his performance is still fairly plain—far removed from his best. Sadly, the biggest crime The Godfather has committed is that it must have been so good and influential when it came out that all the copycats have eventually caught up. All of the genre tropes have been done better a million times since, producing far more compelling stories than what the Corleone family has to offer today.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "positivas" (3.5–5 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews positivas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

[1] nota=3.5 estrelas:
Turns out I do care for The Godfather.  The movie isn’t as bad as I thought now that I don’t have my film study teacher in my ear and pausing every five seconds to tell us when an important scene is coming up. This movie had a lot of dark scenes and a lot of violence, which was very well put together other than the part where Sonny beats up his sister‘s husband for abuse. You can clearly see his punch not hit the guy, yet he still reacts, but that was kind of funny so I enjoyed that. Seeing Michael evolve from the beginning of the movie to the end was very interesting to watch especially when you see the signs of his upcoming change. RIP Sonny he was very cool.

[2] nota=3.5 estrelas:
A product of its time. So many of the characters were so surface level for a fucking 3 hour long movie! I've unironically seen better character building over the course of 40 minute CW serials. I didn't find even Al Pacino that interesting/endearing, let alone any of the female characters. Don Corleone was the most interesting and complex to me, and I liked him - but unlike Tony Soprano, they didn't care to explore the moral implications and repercussions of his lifestyle. The people we see them kill are Bad and Evil and one-not and he Loves His Children and is Tough But Fair. The pacing was weird - I couldn't tell what the final act was leading up to, and then apparently it was the assassination of some randoms we've had 2 minutes of prior screentime of and who I couldn't feel the symbolic weight of anyways, by anonymous shooters we've never seen before. (That's not to say I didn't greatly enjoy mass-murder-baptism scene - in fact it was probably my favourite, in isolation - and I do appreciate that it represented a greater symbolic act of revenge for his brother's death, but it still didn't work for me.) And then we end with a brooding Al Pacino lying to his girlfriend who has no personality besides Pretty and I did not care about, and therefore fully adopting the new "don" role, becoming the new Godfather. And then a door slams. I guess. As the credits were rolling I was just left thinking... that's it? Where was the fallout, the consequences, for all that death and drama? Please, just one meaningful consequence? This pacing can only be justified if they were always intending on making a "Part II" to continue the story, because on its own it just feels incomplete to me. It was undeniably cinematically well-made and I recognise probably, to me, a victim of the "classic movie which was ground breaking and iconic for the time and was the first to do all these cool things that have now been done better a million times over and I take for granted" problem. Same as "Taxi Driver". But I'm not a film critic, I'm only going to review a movie taken on its own merit, and to me... I don't know. The themes were interesting...? I guess? The idea of Business getting conflated with the Personal was a throughline. Again, I've seen the revenge plot done better since. I recall enjoying the first part - the plot was well set up and the villains mysterious and threatening. But then they all just... die. With the fall-out captured in a five minute long montage of newspaper headlines. New villains appear, and then they die too. And this valiant "that's my familys work not mine" war hero just... flips, and becomes a mafioso the second he gets back from like a month max of exile in Italy where the most significant thing he did was watch his Italian wife get blown up in a car for no reason after having genuinely more dialogue with her father than her and then immediately forgetting about her. There's no consequences, no explicit moral reckoning, for what was supposed to be that climatic act of killing the men who shot his father earlier in the film. He doesn't even have one panic attack! The battered sister is used as a plot point and a pawn to advance the more important sophisticated business of mafia men. Even at the end when she's hysterically yelling at Pacino "you never even considered me [when you killed my abusive husband]" it's like... yeah, he didn't, in multiple ways. If he wasn't aware of his violence, he didn't care how she'd be affected by losing her loving husband, and if he was aware of his violence, that wasn't even the reason he killed him! He didn't care that she was being abused, he cared that he was part of some complex behind-the-scenes murder plot of him. That never went anywhere because everyone gets killed! Like, I get it. It was the 50s, who cares about women, but why include DV as a plot point - going so far as to have a too-long scene of a man chasing his pregnant wife around their house with a belt while she screams, and then beating her - and then just stomp on it? Maybe that was the point, that by the end of the film Pacino is just so far gone into the moral grey of the mob that he doesn't care and that's a bad thing. That would make it more interesting, but not necessarily better. He is explicitly positioned as the protagonist and yet shows so few positive qualities throughout the whole film. I just don't buy his character degradation, if that was the intention. These flat, tired depictions of women just cheapen any movie they're in. If you zoom out, you realise all you're watching is the product of a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking about a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking. Just jerk eachother off already. We want to believe the Author is this unbiased surveyor and imitator of the human condition, and that reckoning - it brings them down to earth for me. How brilliant can a man or his story be if they don't trascend or even attempt to transcend the cruelty and primitivism of their era? Oh well. It's fun to get all the Sopranos references now. Maybe watching that first was setting this film up for failure because there's so much more room over 6 seasons and 50+ hours for real, conscientious character development and moral complexity and getting attached to not just the people but the world being built, than a movie, even one as long as this. I should watch this again.

A product of its time. So many of the characters were so surface level for a fucking 3 hour long movie! I've unironically seen better character building over the course of 40 minute CW serials. I didn't find even Al Pacino that interesting/endearing, let alone any of the female characters. Don Corleone was the most interesting and complex to me, and I liked him - but unlike Tony Soprano, they didn't care to explore the moral implications and repercussions of his lifestyle. The people we see them kill are Bad and Evil and one-not and he Loves His Children and is Tough But Fair. The pacing was weird - I couldn't tell what the final act was leading up to, and then apparently it was the assassination of some randoms we've had 2 minutes of prior screentime of and who I couldn't feel the symbolic weight of anyways, by anonymous shooters we've never seen before. (That's not to say I didn't greatly enjoy mass-murder-baptism scene - in fact it was probably my favourite, in isolation - and I do appreciate that it represented a greater symbolic act of revenge for his brother's death, but it still didn't work for me.) And then we end with a brooding Al Pacino lying to his girlfriend who has no personality besides Pretty and I did not care about, and therefore fully adopting the new "don" role, becoming the new Godfather. And then a door slams. I guess. As the credits were rolling I was just left thinking... that's it? Where was the fallout, the consequences, for all that death and drama? Please, just one meaningful consequence? This pacing can only be justified if they were always intending on making a "Part II" to continue the story, because on its own it just feels incomplete to me. It was undeniably cinematically well-made and I recognise probably, to me, a victim of the "classic movie which was ground breaking and iconic for the time and was the first to do all these cool things that have now been done better a million times over and I take for granted" problem. Same as "Taxi Driver". But I'm not a film critic, I'm only going to review a movie taken on its own merit, and to me... I don't know. The themes were interesting...? I guess? The idea of Business getting conflated with the Personal was a throughline. Again, I've seen the revenge plot done better since. I recall enjoying the first part - the plot was well set up and the villains mysterious and threatening. But then they all just... die. With the fall-out captured in a five minute long montage of newspaper headlines. New villains appear, and then they die too. And this valiant "that's my familys work not mine" war hero just... flips, and becomes a mafioso the second he gets back from like a month max of exile in Italy where the most significant thing he did was watch his Italian wife get blown up in a car for no reason after having genuinely more dialogue with her father than her and then immediately forgetting about her. There's no consequences, no explicit moral reckoning, for what was supposed to be that climatic act of killing the men who shot his father earlier in the film. He doesn't even have one panic attack! The battered sister is used as a plot point and a pawn to advance the more important sophisticated business of mafia men. Even at the end when she's hysterically yelling at Pacino "you never even considered me [when you killed my abusive husband]" it's like... yeah, he didn't, in multiple ways. If he wasn't aware of his violence, he didn't care how she'd be affected by losing her loving husband, and if he was aware of his violence, that wasn't even the reason he killed him! He didn't care that she was being abused, he cared that he was part of some complex behind-the-scenes murder plot of him. That never went anywhere because everyone gets killed! Like, I get it. It was the 50s, who cares about women, but why include DV as a plot point - going so far as to have a too-long scene of a man chasing his pregnant wife around their house with a belt while she screams, and then beating her - and then just stomp on it? Maybe that was the point, that by the end of the film Pacino is just so far gone into the moral grey of the mob that he doesn't care and that's a bad thing. That would make it more interesting, but not necessarily better. He is explicitly positioned as the protagonist and yet shows so few positive qualities throughout the whole film. I just don't buy his character degradation, if that was the intention. These flat, tired depictions of women just cheapen any movie they're in. If you zoom out, you realise all you're watching is the product of a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking about a bunch of white men sitting around in a room talking. Just jerk eachother off already. We want to believe the Author is this unbiased surveyor and imitator of the human condition, and that reckoning - it brings them down to earth for me. How brilliant can a man or his story be if they don't trascend or even attempt to transcend the cruelty and primitivism of their era? Oh well. It's fun to get all the Sopranos references now. Maybe watching that first was setting this film up for failure because there's so much more room over 6 seasons and 50+ hours for real, conscientious character development and moral complexity and getting attached to not just the people but the world being built, than a movie, even one as long as this. I should watch this again.

Você é uma etapa de um pipeline que agrega reviews de usuários de um filme do Letterboxd. O pipeline separa as reviews em três faixas de nota ANTES desta etapa (negativas, medianas, positivas); você está recebendo EXCLUSIVAMENTE a faixa "medianas" (2.5–3 estrelas) — um recorte enviesado POR CONSTRUÇÃO, que NÃO representa a recepção geral do filme.

Sua função é descrever o que ESTE grupo específico de reviews diz. Outros módulos do pipeline cuidam das outras faixas de nota; o usuário final verá as três análises lado a lado, cada uma rotulada com sua faixa.

Consequência explícita: é PROIBIDO generalizar para "os críticos", "a maioria", "o consenso" ou "a recepção do filme". A `observacao_geral` deve se referir sempre a ESTE grupo (ex.: "as reviews medianas apontam...", "este grupo destaca..."), nunca ao filme em termos absolutos.

Instruções fixas (invariáveis):
1. Anti-spoiler: descreva as críticas em nível temático (ritmo, atuações, fotografia, roteiro em termos abstratos). É PROIBIDO mencionar eventos da trama, destinos de personagens, reviravoltas ou o final, mesmo que as reviews os mencionem.
2. `exemplo_parafraseado` é paráfrase, NUNCA citação literal de nenhuma review.
3. Temas ordenados por `mencoes_aproximadas` decrescente; no máximo 6 temas por bucket; não invente temas de menção única, salvo se o bucket tiver menos de 5 reviews.
4. As reviews podem estar em qualquer idioma; sua saída é SEMPRE em pt-BR.
5. Responda APENAS o JSON, sem preâmbulo, sem cercas de código.
6. É PROIBIDO usar aspas (simples, duplas ou angulares) dentro de `exemplo_parafraseado` — nunca cite nem reproduza um trecho entre aspas, mesmo traduzido; reescreva sempre em terceira pessoa, com suas próprias palavras.
7. Reforço de idioma: TODOS os campos de texto da saída devem estar em pt-BR, incluindo os NOMES DOS TEMAS — nunca deixe um tema em inglês ou outro idioma, mesmo que a review de origem esteja nesse idioma.

[1] nota=2.5 estrelas:
Cómo nos vendió humo en clase Giovanna Pollarolo. La entiendo igual, porque en esa época recién se había estrenado la peli de un libro que le gustó bastante. Cualquiera se hypea. Hablando del libro, me lo imagino perfectamente (es decir, qué es lo que seguramente la hace una gran obra) y la distancia que lo separa de la peli. Estoy seguro de que en la dirección decidieron "entonces hagamos sentir al espectador que está atrapado con el protagonista"... ¿POR QUÉ? ¿Me tienes que arrastrar a mí también, acaso, para demostrar tu punto? ¿Es la única manera creativa que se te ocurre? También, si vas a mostrar planos largos de personajes haciendo acciones pasivas, tienen que tener un sentido, o verse brutal o aportar o algo.
